items.content:
By Esther Onyegbula
For Eze Pauline Ijeoma, stepping onto Nigerian soil was more than a homecoming. It was a return to a place where she hoped she could finally live and work without fear.
After years in South Africa, where she said xenophobic attacks, police detentions and difficulties running her food business had made life increasingly difficult, Ijeoma was among 105 Nigerians who returned to the country in the second batch sponsored by the Redeemed Christian Church of God, RCCG.
“I would say that we are so grateful and we are so happy to be home because there is no place like home,” the Imo State indigene said.
“No more xenophobic, no more attack, no more police, no more problems. No more killings. So, we are so happy.”
Ijeoma’s relief, however, came against the backdrop of painful experiences she said she endured during her stay in South Africa.
‘I left in 2013’
“I left Nigeria in 2013, went home and came back again in 2023. It wasn’t like that before. But silently, they always do it. This period, it was so hard,” she said.
According to her, the situation affected her ability to earn a living as a food seller, as she became apprehensive about going out to conduct her business.
“I don’t go to business because every time you go to business, you come back with your food. I’m a food seller,” she said.
“So, it is very horrible for now. I don’t sell because anytime you go out, police will arrest you. And you sell it inside the cell.”
She also recounted the emotional burden of witnessing Nigerians lose their lives and the difficulties she said she faced during encounters with the police.
“Because seeing our brothers dying every time. Every time, police will arrest you for doing nothing. Even going to business is a problem,” she said.
Ijeoma, who disclosed that her husband died in South Africa, said she took to food vending as a means of survival but alleged that police harassment made it increasingly difficult to operate.
“My husband passed away in South Africa. It was not easy, that’s why I started selling food,” she said.
“Every time police will detain, asking for your papers or whatever. Even if your papers are complete, they will still fine you, fine one thing or the other to ask you, in order to extort money from you.”
For her, the return to Nigeria has therefore brought a renewed sense of hope.
“We are so happy that we are alive to come back. We are so grateful to God and the people who made it possible for us to be among the people,” she said.
‘Rescue’
Another returnee, Chukwuma Augustine Ayoka, also from Imo State, described the return as a rescue after what he said was a difficult period for Nigerians in South Africa.
“I’m so excited. I give all glory to God for them to come to our rescue,” Ayoka said.
He expressed appreciation to RCCG for sponsoring the return of Nigerians, including families, children and individuals.
“Lifting 500 people, including fathers, mothers, children and single ones from South Africa under xenophobic attack, afrophobic attack, it’s not easy. So it’s only by the grace of God,” he said.
According to Ayoka, the situation had affected businesses and the ability of some Nigerians to move freely.
“Although it was not a war zone, but with the case of xenophobia attack, afrophobic attack, with the killings, we have no other choice than to come back,” he said.
“They close our businesses, destroy our businesses, loot our businesses. Life became terrible. You can’t even get out of your house. So we have no other choice than to seek for rescue.”
RCCG
Ayoka, who said he returned alone, added: “Redeem came to our rescue and at the end of the day, we are here through the grace of God and through the help of RCCG.”
The Chairman, RCCG Task Force for the Reception of Nigerian Returnees from South Africa, Pastor Belemina Obunge, said the church’s intervention followed a “Save Our Soul” appeal from Nigerians in South Africa.
Obunge said the intervention was approved by the church’s General Overseer, Pastor E.A. Adeboye, after the plight of Nigerians stranded in South Africa came to the attention of the church.
He said the initiative was designed as a humanitarian contribution to the efforts of the Federal Government to bring Nigerians in distress back home.
“Basically, there was a Save Our Soul clarion cry by Nigerians in South Africa. It was echoed by the High Commission in South Africa. It got to the ears of our Heavenly Lord, the General Overseer, and he, being who he is with a heart of compassion, had determined that the church should intervene,” Obunge said.
He explained that the church resolved to sponsor the airlifting of 500 Nigerians from South Africa.
“By the grace of God, the first set of 100 had been brought in. This second set of 105 is now being brought in,” he said.
According to him, three more batches are expected to arrive as the process continues.
Obunge said the returnees should see their arrival in Nigeria as a new beginning rather than the end of their journey.
“What we are telling them, they are not forgotten. They should realise that this is a new beginning. God has a plan for them. They should connect with God,” he said.
He also encouraged the returnees to deploy the skills and experience they acquired abroad in rebuilding their lives in Nigeria.
“Once they begin to take advantage of the skills, the talents, and what they’ve learned over the years and put it in practice here in Nigeria, one thing is clear, the best is yet to come,” he said.
Obunge stressed that the humanitarian intervention was not restricted to members of RCCG.
He said the returnees were selected regardless of their religious or ethnic backgrounds.
“Our national anthem says, ‘no tribe and tongue may differ. In brotherhood we stand.’ We believe in that anthem,” he said.
“Those being brought are of different tribes, different tongues, different religions. Definitely, they are not all members of the Redeemed Christian Church of God. In fact, we don’t even know if any of them is a member of the Redeemed Christian Church of God.
“They are wonderful, glorious, spectacular Nigerians, and by the grace of God, they are part of those that we have an assignment towards.”
The returnees
Obunge said the latest batch comprised 55 adults, 45 children and five infants, bringing the number already brought back under the RCCG initiative to 205.
He said the church expected to receive about 295 to 300 more Nigerians, subject to the completion of the required processes by the Nigerian High Commission and South African authorities.
According to him, the returnees are profiled by the Nigerian High Commission before the relevant South African authorities complete their procedures for their return.
A representative of the Head of Operations, National Emergency Management Agency, Lagos Operations Office, said NEMA and other government stakeholders had been involved in receiving Nigerians returning from South Africa.
The official described the RCCG intervention as a complement to the Federal Government’s efforts.
“This is the second batch of returnees being sponsored by the Redeemed Christian Church of God,” the official said.
“As you are aware, NEMA and other stakeholders have been in the forefront representing the Federal Government, receiving Nigerian returnees from South Africa. And the RCCG has come to also complement the effort of the Federal Government.”
The official explained that the returnees’ details were being documented to facilitate possible government assistance and follow-up.
“If you observe from the arrival from South Africa, part of this process is to have their details, by registering them, getting their names and contacts and their other details. And this is for further assistance going to the extended later,” the official said.
The official added that the information would help the government contact the returnees when necessary and provide further assistance.
NEMA, according to the official, would also facilitate the transportation of the returnees to their respective states to enable them reunite with their families.
For Ijeoma, the journey home represents an opportunity to begin again after years of uncertainty.
“My expectation, by the grace of God, is that God will help us the way He has been with us, protecting us. If we can survive there, in our own homes, we will make more, by the special grace of God,” she said.
Vanguard News
The post ‘God has given us another chance’ – Nigerian returnees narrate South Africa ordeal appeared first on Vanguard News.

By Vincent Ujumadu
AWKA — Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, has recounted his experience with the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) following the end of his tenure as Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), saying the commission eventually cleared him of any wrongdoing in an investigation involving the Nigeria Security Printing and Minting Plc.
Soludo spoke on Friday during the commissioning of the EFCC Awka Zonal Directorate Complex, which will serve Anambra and Imo states.
The governor said he was invited for questioning after his name was mentioned in connection with an EFCC investigation into the activities of the Mint, where he had served as chairman of the board.
He said he appeared before the commission after receiving a month’s notice of the investigation but did not hear from the EFCC for about a year.
According to Soludo, he subsequently wrote to the commission seeking an update and was informed that the investigation had not established any corrupt conduct on his part.
“My personal testimonies about the professionalism of this Commission is that when I left office as CBN Governor, EFCC was investigating Nigeria Printing and Minting Company, the Mint, an agency within the bank.
“I was chairman of board of the Mint and was given one month notice of investigation and I showed up. After about a year, I didn’t hear from them, so I wrote them and they said that the investigation didn’t show any corrupt action about me,” he said.
Soludo further said the then EFCC chairman had clarified that he was not the subject of the investigation after his name was mentioned in connection with the matter.
He said the commission subsequently wrote to him confirming that its investigation had not established any wrongdoing on his part.
“When my name was mentioned in connection with the investigation, the former chairman of EFCC told them that I was not the subject of the investigation.
“Subsequently, the Commission wrote me a beautiful letter and said the investigation showed I didn’t have anything to do with the matter,” Soludo said.
The governor said his experience had reinforced his appreciation of the commission’s work, particularly the need for investigators to formally communicate the outcome of inquiries to persons who were invited but not found culpable.
“So I deeply appreciate the professionalism of the Commission. I want to urge that if you invite someone and later fail to find him complicit, you must write and say so, especially in this part of the world where, if you invite people, it finds its way into the pages of newspapers because they see invitation as an indictment,” he said.
On the establishment of the EFCC’s Awka Zonal Directorate, Soludo said the state was pleased to host the facility, saying its presence would facilitate faster investigation of financial crimes in the region.
“Some people might be asking why we are so excited about having the zonal office in our state. The reason for our excitement is that it will enhance quicker investigation,” he said.
The governor said the EFCC’s staffing constraints made it difficult for the commission to establish offices in all 774 local government areas, adding that the Awka directorate would, in the meantime, serve Anambra and Imo states.
“Ideally, EFCC should have offices in the 774 local government areas of the country, but with only about 6,000 staff, it is difficult to have offices in all LGAs. So this regional office will serve in the meantime and we will cooperate with you to serve the two states,” he said.
Soludo said the Anambra State Government would seek the commission’s assistance in areas relating to revenue and taxation, while also working to improve knowledge of financial crime prevention among civil servants and local government officials.
“We will not just be waiting for you to come from Abuja; we will be visiting you because it’s in our own interest that we should minimise financial crimes to the barest minimum. We assure EFCC of our fullest co-operation,” he said.
He said the fight against economic and financial crimes required collective responsibility, assuring the commission that Anambra would cooperate with it in every possible way.
According to him, the work of the EFCC was important to national development and required cooperation among government institutions and citizens.

items.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi
ABUJA: Minister of the Federal Capital Territory FCT, Nyesom Wike, has said his predecessor, Chibuike Rotimi Amaechi, has nothing to show for 24 years as Speaker, Governor and Minister.
He challenged the people of Evo Kingdom in Obio-Akpor Local Government Area of Rivers State to point to any tangible development or political empowerment Amaechi attracted to their land.
According to a statement on Friday night by Lere Olayinka, his Senior Special Assistant on Public Communications and Social Media, the minister spoke at an interactive session with leaders and stakeholders of Evo Kingdom.
“Someone was Speaker of the House of Assembly for eight years, Governor for eight years, and Minister for eight years, that is 24 years in top leadership positions! What can anybody point to that he attracted to Evo Kingdom or Rivers State in all those 24 years? Nothing! Not one single thing!” Wike said.
He drew a contrast with his own record. “I was a Minister of State for Education, and as I sit here, I can count the projects I brought to Rivers State and my people. But somebody was Speaker, Governor, and headed a very lucrative ministry as a full Minister for eight years, yet brought nothing back home! How can someone who spent 24 years in power without empowering his people or raising new leaders now turn around to tell you he loves you?” he asked.
Wike also reiterated his decision to resign as Minister should President Bola Ahmed Tinubu lose in Rivers State and the FCT.
He made the declaration at a strategic consultative meeting with stakeholders of Akpor Kingdom in Obio-Akpor on Friday, where he rallied the political structure of Rivers State behind the President.
“My interest in Rivers State is for God to use me as a vessel to help our people. I am back here not for what I will get, but for what I will be to raise my people,” he said.
He said politics was driven by the collective interest of the people and not by perpetual animosity. “There is no permanent enemy in politics; what we have is permanent collective interest. It is all about the interest of our people. The more you are in number, the happier you become. Leadership is like a waste dustbin. If you cannot absorb things, both the good and the bad, then you cannot be a true leader,” he said.
Wike told political actors in the state not to be distracted by social media criticism of his open-door policy towards former detractors, saying true political strength lies in numbers.
He demanded an all-inclusive campaign structure across Obio-Akpor. “Whether you are a politician, whether you are a traditional ruler, whether you are a pastor, or whether you are a native doctor, I need everybody now,” he said, adding: “For the purpose of voting and elections, we must bring everyone together.”

items.content:
By Esther Onyegbula
The human cost of the prolonged demolition dispute involving residents of Okokomaiko, Church Estate 1, Church Estate 2, Igbenyadu Community and Jubilee Estate came into sharp focus when an elderly retiree collapsed in the courtroom during proceedings before a Federal High Court in Lagos.
The retiree, identified as one of the affected homeowners, reportedly slumped in the full view of the presiding judge on September 24, 2026, leaving lawyers, litigants and others in the courtroom scrambling to save his life.
The incident occurred amid a legal battle over alleged demolition and acquisition of properties in the affected communities, with homeowners insisting that their properties should not be demolished without due process and adequate compensation.
Some persons in the courtroom who had basic first-aid knowledge reportedly administered cardiopulmonary resuscitation, CPR, in a frantic effort to revive the elderly man.
He was eventually moved to a nearby hospital for further medical attention.
The incident, according to affected property owners, was a grim reminder of the enormous emotional and psychological burden the demolition dispute has imposed on residents who say they invested their lifetime savings in their homes.
The affected landlords alleged that demolition activities linked to the Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority, LAMATA, and other agencies had continued despite court proceedings and an injunction they said was issued in April.
They also alleged that structures continued to be demolished in the affected communities while the matter was still pending before the court.
Adding to the controversy, the property owners alleged that the house of Mrs. Blessing Okere was demolished on September 26, 2026, despite what they described as existing court orders and instructions from the Federal High Court.
The allegation could not be independently verified from the materials available for this report, while no response from LAMATA or the Lagos State Government was provided by the affected homeowners.
For the residents, however, the alleged demolition has intensified fears that more homeowners could lose properties they spent decades acquiring.
‘People are dead, people are in despair’
Speaking to Journalists immediately after the court hearing on Friday October 2nd at the Federal High Court, Lagos, legal practitioner and human rights activist, Femi Dodo, who is counsel to the affected communities, said the dispute had already taken a heavy toll on residents.
According to him, five people had died in connection with the situation, while another applicant was suffering from a debilitating stroke.
“People are dead. People are in despair,” Dodo said.
He confirmed that the second applicant, whom he identified as the person who collapsed in court, was still alive.
“Yes. The second applicant is still alive, by the grace of God,” he said.
odo said the plight of the affected homeowners was particularly painful because many had spent their productive years acquiring properties they expected would provide shelter and financial security in old age.
“How can somebody labour? We all know that in this part of the world, people labour for their whole lives to acquire one or two properties so that by the time they are old, they will have somewhere to rest,” he said.
“They may also have tenants paying rent so they can survive on those benefits because the government itself has failed to provide adequate retirement benefits.”
He added that many workers retire only to face prolonged battles over their retirement benefits, making property ownership an important form of security for many families.
“In that situation, some people have decided to labour to acquire property for themselves. All of a sudden, the government comes and says that because it wants to carry out a project, their property is gone overnight,” he said.
The lawyer said the collapse of the retiree occurred as parties were before the court, with lawyers on both sides making submissions on the matter.
He said the incident heightened the urgency of the case and led the judge to express concern about the alleged consequences of the demolition dispute on human lives.
According to the affected landlords, the judge questioned how demolition activities could continue while the matter was before the court and an injunction was said to be subsisting.
The property owners said the court consequently directed the parties to return for an early and comprehensive hearing, rather than allowing further prolonged adjournments.
Dodo said the residents were not opposed to development or the government’s power to acquire land for public purposes.
“We are not saying that we are against development. We are for development. We are not saying the government does not have the right to acquire people’s property. But my property should not be taken for public interest without compensation,” he said.
“That is why we are saying that there must be compensation. Evidence of compensation must be before the court.”
Compensation controversy
A major point of contention, according to Dodo, is the adequacy and proof of compensation allegedly paid to some affected property owners.
He questioned what he described as reliance on photographs of individuals allegedly receiving documents as evidence that compensation had been paid.
“In this digital age, where you can go to a bank and obtain bank records from three or four years ago, you cannot simply photograph people holding a sheet of paper presented as a cheque and claim that as evidence of compensation. It is ridiculous,” he said.
Dodo maintained that compensation must reflect the value of what property owners were losing.
“Compensation is compensation. Compensation must be adequate. If compensation is not adequate, that is not compensation,” he said.
“You cannot come and take a piece of land and tell me you want to pay me $10,000 when the property is worth far more.”
‘Which acquisition notice will the court rely on?’
Dodo also said the legal battle involved questions surrounding the government’s acquisition of the affected properties and whether the necessary notices had been properly served on the property owners.
He said documents presented before the court included different acquisition notices and gazettes dating from 1979, 1982, February 2025 and May 2025, as well as a notice allegedly issued by the governor.
“They attached notices of acquisition. They first attached a Gazette of 1979, another Gazette of 1982, another notice of acquisition by the government in May 2025, another one in February 2025, and then one by the governor himself,” he said.
“So, we want to know, which we don’t know yet, which of the notices of acquisition or which of the Gazettes will the court rely on to agree that the property was actually acquired?”
According to him, the residents’ position is that affected property owners must be properly served with notices of acquisition.
“If you claim that you have revoked an interest in a property and acquired it, you must serve that notice of acquisition on the affected individual. That is the law. That is what the court will determine,” he said.
Dodo alleged that documents available to his legal team did not show evidence that the relevant notice of acquisition signed by the Lagos State Governor had been served on the affected individuals.
Jurisdiction dispute
Another major issue in the case, according to Dodo, is jurisdiction.
He said the defendants had argued that the Federal High Court lacked jurisdiction to entertain the case and that the matter should instead be heard by the Lagos State High Court.
“Their argument, as usual, has always been that we cannot come by way of fundamental rights. They say the matter should go to the State High Court,” he said.
Dodo, however, said the residents’ case was based on compulsory acquisition of land and fundamental rights.
“I would like to be careful about commenting on something the court is about to rule on. But the issue of jurisdiction is important,” he said.
“Our case is based on the compulsory acquisition of land and fundamental rights, or human rights as people generally call them.”
He said the residents also had the right to challenge compensation they considered inadequate.
“Even though the government claims that it wants to pay compensation, I have the right to challenge the amount of that compensation if I believe it is not commensurate with what I am about to lose,” he said.
“That is the right to fair hearing.”
Homes built for old age
For the affected homeowners, the dispute goes beyond the physical structures facing demolition.
Many say their homes represent decades of labour, sacrifice and planning for old age.
Dodo said the emotional pressure was particularly severe for elderly homeowners who had expected to spend their retirement years in properties they had worked for throughout their lives.
He said the residents were therefore seeking judicial protection while the dispute over acquisition and compensation was being determined.
“We are hopeful that the court will do justice in this matter,” he said.
As the legal battle continues, the alleged demolition of Mrs. Blessing Okere’s house on September 26 has added another layer to the controversy, with affected residents questioning how demolition could allegedly continue while the dispute remains before the court.
For the homeowners, every demolished wall represents more than a lost structure. It represents years of savings, family memories and the security they believed they had finally secured for their old age.
The post ‘People are dying’: Retiree collapses in court amid Lagos demolition dispute appeared first on Vanguard News.

By Ike Uchechukwu, Calabar
CALABAR — Three persons were reportedly injured on Friday after gunmen disrupted two consultative meetings organised by the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Calabar South Local Government Area of Cross River State.
The incident also resulted in damage to several vehicles belonging to members and supporters of the party, according to the PDP governorship candidate in the state, Sir Arthur Javis Archibong.
Archibong, who spoke with journalists after the incidents, said the first attack occurred at the palace of the Paramount Ruler of Calabar South, Etubom Nyong Edet Okon I, where the party was holding a consultative meeting.
He said three persons were injured and taken to hospital for treatment.
According to him, the situation later escalated at the African Club along Calabar Road, venue of a second consultation, where vehicles belonging to members of the party’s consultative team were damaged.
Archibong also alleged that gunmen opened fire on the party’s convoy and vandalised vehicles belonging to some supporters.
He said about 3,000 supporters attended the consultation, adding that the police had been notified of the meetings and that the party expected adequate security arrangements.
The candidate said the party restrained its supporters from retaliating and instead moved its convoy to the office of the Commissioner of Police for protection.
He added that the PDP would petition the Inspector-General of Police, the Department of State Services (DSS) and other relevant security agencies over the incidents.
Archibong warned that continued disruption of political activities could undermine peaceful political participation ahead of the 2027 elections.
“Let the party not be held accountable when such disruptions lead to a total breakdown of law and order,” he said.
In a separate statement, the PDP State Publicity Secretary, Mike Ojisi, described the incidents as attacks on the party’s consultative engagements.
Ojisi said the matter had been reported to the Commissioner of Police, Cross River State Command, CP Ajo Geoffrey Ordue, and urged security agencies to identify and prosecute those responsible in accordance with the law.
The PDP also appealed to its members and supporters to remain calm and shun reprisals, stressing that political consultations should not become an avenue for violence.
APC denies involvement
Reacting, the state chapter of the All Progressives Congress (APC) denied involvement in the incidents.
The APC Publicity Secretary, Emmanuel Inyang, said the party was focused on its own political activities and advised the PDP to look elsewhere for those responsible.
Police commence verification
Confirming the incident, the Cross River State Police Command said it had deployed personnel to the affected areas and that the situation was under control.
The command’s spokesman, ASP Sunday Eitokpah, said police were verifying reports of gunfire, injuries and damage to property.
“The Cross River State Police Command is aware of reported incidents during political activities in Calabar South today, 2nd October 2026.
“Police personnel have been deployed to the affected locations, and the situation is presently under control.
“The Command is verifying the circumstances surrounding the incidents, including reports of gunfire, injuries, and damage to property,” he said.
Eitokpah urged residents to remain calm, avoid affected areas where necessary and refrain from circulating unverified information.
He added that police presence and monitoring had been strengthened to maintain peace and public order.
As of the time of filing this report, the police had not attributed responsibility for the incidents to any political party or group.
The post Three injured as gunmen disrupt PDP meetings in Calabar appeared first on Vanguard News.

By Esther Onyegbula
The Federal Government has been urged to declare a state of emergency in Nigeria’s health sector amid the mass exodus of medical professionals from the country.
Convener and host of The Convergence 2026, Mr. Fakuyi Adewale Banjo, made the call during the annual Independence Day medical outreach organised by The Convergence 2026 in partnership with Emzor, Inside Out with Agatha Foundation, IOWA, Rave Television, Royal Home Foundation, International Foundation, Saba Realtor, Mental Health Relationships Alliances, Pottersnest and other organisations.
The outreach, held at the Rave Television Complex, featured free medical examinations, vital signs checks, blood sugar tests, health counselling and distribution of drugs to beneficiaries as part of activities marking Nigeria’s 66th Independence Anniversary.
Banjo, while speaking at the event, expressed concern over the continued migration of medical professionals from the country, popularly known as the “Japa syndrome”, warning that the trend was contributing to the weakening of the nation’s healthcare system.
He called on the government to urgently take decisive steps to address the challenges confronting the sector and improve the welfare and working conditions of health professionals.
The convener also urged Nigerians to take personal responsibility for their health by embracing preventive healthcare and regular medical checks.
According to him, a healthier population is critical to the development and prosperity of the country.
The sixth edition of The Convergence, which has evolved from earlier editions focused on youth and labour, brought together partners, health professionals, volunteers and members of the public to commemorate Nigeria’s independence with a focus on health and national wellbeing.
The programme opened with a prayer by Empress Ene and a one-minute silence in honour of fallen heroes whose sacrifices contributed to Nigeria’s journey as an independent nation.
Speaking during the health session, Dr. Oluwasanmi Akinyera stressed the importance of prioritising healthcare, declaring that “a healthy nation is a wise nation.”
He encouraged participants to pay greater attention to their health and seek medical attention when necessary rather than waiting until health conditions deteriorate.
The outreach also featured a mental health session anchored by Mrs. Maryam Owolabi Silas, while Counselor Mrs. Tomilola Akintunde provided counselling support to participants.
Over 40 beneficiaries reportedly received medical attention during the programme, with professional nurses and counsellors attending to participants after the various health checks and examinations.
Among the beneficiaries was Clementina Ojishunite Onyekachi.
Goodwill messages were also received from Mr. Sabastine Onyewe, CEO of Saba Realtor, and Mr. Abimbola Akambi, who emphasised the importance of the family in building a strong and stable nation.
Akambi described the home as the foundation of a strong nation, stressing the need to strengthen family values as part of efforts to build a better society.
The Convener said the 2026 edition recorded significant partnerships with organisations and individuals who contributed to the success of the programme.
Participants, who were dressed predominantly in the national colours of green and white, expressed satisfaction with the medical examinations, health consultations and other activities organised as part of the Independence Day celebration.
Banjo said the initiative was designed not only to commemorate Nigeria’s independence but also to demonstrate the importance of collective responsibility in building a healthier nation.
He expressed appreciation to the partners, volunteers, medical personnel, counsellors and psychologists who supported the programme, including the Docas, Madam Funmilola Ayinla and My Harry.
The event was also attended by representatives of the media, with both television and print media organisations covering the activities.
The Convergence 2026, now in its sixth year, has previously organised editions centred on youth and labour before consolidating the initiatives under the current platform.
Banjo said the continued evolution of the programme reflected the organisers’ commitment to addressing issues affecting Nigerians and promoting national development through partnerships and community-focused interventions.
The post FG urged to declare emergency in health sector as Nigeria marks 66 appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
By Matthew Johnson
Apify, a global software development platform, has partnered with She Code Africa to increase the participation of Nigerian women in the developer economy, after identifying low female representation among developers using its platform.
Senior Developer Community Manager at Apify, Mr. Sauray Jain, disclosed this during a two-day hybrid hackathon organised in partnership with She Code Africa in Lagos, where women developers showcased technology solutions to real-life challenges.
Jain said the partnership was conceived to create more opportunities for women developers in Nigeria and other African countries to build software, participate actively in the developer economy and monetise their technical skills.
He said the need for the intervention became apparent after Apify recorded strong participation from Nigeria and other African countries in its previous global software-building challenge but noticed that female participation remained low.
According to him, the company was particularly concerned about the gender imbalance among Nigerian developers using its platform and decided to work with women-focused technology communities to address the gap.
He said: “We saw that there are not enough female or women community members who are joining our community and making these software. So this year we made a pledge that we will participate with many women communities all over the world, and especially in Africa. This DEMO is just the first phase.”
Jain explained that the initiative was not only aimed at increasing the number of women participating in software development but also at addressing the gap between the technical capabilities of African developers and their ability to earn income from their skills.
He said the hackathon offered participants an opportunity to develop practical solutions while gaining exposure to tools that could enable them to commercialise their products.
Jain said the competition had three cash prizes of $700, $500 and $300 for the first, second and third winners respectively, while the top 10 participants would receive $100 worth of Apify prepaid platform usage.
He added that entries would be assessed based on technical quality, effective use of the Apify platform, potential impact on local communities, relevance of the solutions and quality of demonstrations.
According to him, Apify would also monitor its developer community in Nigeria and across Africa over the next six months to assess whether the initiative translates into increased female participation.
Also speaking, She Code Africa Community Manager, Mfonobong Umondia, said the hackathon brought together women and girls from different technology tracks to collaborate and develop solutions to real-world challenges.
Umondia said the programme covered areas including fintech and cybersecurity, stressing that the impact of the initiative would extend beyond the competition through mentorship, technical workshops and continued access to resources.
She said the top three teams would receive direct mentorship from the Apify team, while all participants would remain connected through a community where they could continue to receive technical support.
Umondia said the participants demonstrated several locally focused innovations during the hackathon.
Among the solutions was AgriLens Africa, a platform designed to provide real-time agricultural commodity prices and market trends from markets across Nigeria.
Another team developed Lumio, an AI-powered educational application designed to study students’ learning patterns and adapt lessons to their pace, while another team showcased FIX, an AI troubleshooting platform for equipment including generators, inverters, refrigerators, freezers and thermal printers.
She added that participants also demonstrated a job-matching application designed to search official job boards and match available vacancies with users based on their skills, location and preferred work arrangements.
Meanwhile, She Code Africa Community Associate, Oluwaseun Oladeji, said the programme was designed to equip participants with the skills to build, design and monetise Apify Actors.
Oladeji said participants would continue to receive technical support after the hackathon, while winners would have access to additional mentorship sessions aimed at strengthening and improving their products.
“This is not the stoppage for both the winners and other participants. Both Apify and sheCodeAfrica have decided to put them all on a mentorship programs so they won’t lag behind in their career,” Oladeji said.
The organisers said the partnership was designed to move women beyond acquiring technology skills by creating practical pathways for them to develop, deploy and monetise digital products capable of addressing challenges within their communities.
The initiative also underscores the growing emphasis on connecting technical training with opportunities for women to participate meaningfully in Africa’s expanding digital and developer economy.
The post Gender gap: Apify, She Code Africa back women developers with mentorship, funding appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
By Ozioruva Aliu
BENIN CITY – A cleric, Engineer Osaze Egbenusi has criticized the increasing appointment of clinicians to head hospitals across Nigeria while professional health administrators exist.
Speaking at a public lecture organised by the Institute of Health Service Administrators of Nigeria (IHSAN), University of Benin Teaching Hospital (UBTH) Chapter, with the title “Still Diligent: The mindset of the public servant in a healthcare system in flux” Egbenusi also criticised the government for inadequate funding for government health institutions which he said is responsible Nigerian political leaders to always run abroad for every slight health challenge that they have.
In his lecture, Eng. Egbenusi spelt out the roles of Administrators which has been shifted to Clinicians.
He maintained that “Clinicians are not administrators and cannot be” lamenting that administrators in health facilities are largely relegated to file recorders to even the cleaners yet “there can be no smooth clinical activities in their absence”.
He said that if this misappropriation of duties continues, it would lead to dearth of resources and advised that doctors should be made to face their primary assignments because they presently are in short supply in the country.
The speaker who is also a lawyer defined the distinct line between working by motivation and working by diligence and postulated that understanding these conditions is key to advancing the health sector in Nigeria.
He therefore encouraged administrators to have a mindset of resilience without bitterness and do their works with dedication despite the lacuna in the system.
He appealed to the Federal government to properly fund the health sector to build trust in the country’s services and bid farewell to the constant “health pilgrimage.”
Earlier in his remarks, Chairman of the IHSAN UBTH, Joshua Uwaila Esq, said the lecture was the first organised by the association.
“It is the visionary prospect of the union that has ensured the inclusion of various unions and public servants in today’s public lecture to educate all on responsive roles and commitments towards the smooth running of health institutions on particular” he said.
The post Cleric critises appointing clinicians as administrators in health institutions appeared first on Vanguard News.

He said many Nigerians have lost confidence in the current judiciary because of those of them who have been exposed politically.
According to him, “When there is a perception that a public officer seems to have control over the judiciary, and cases are assigned in a particular judicial division in Abuja to a certain number of judges, when we have about 12 judges, and when you assign such sensitive cases to just about 3 or 4 such judges, it engenders suspicion.
“For example, why should one particular judge be assigned with 4 major cases by DSS? It doesn’t make any sense. It couldn’t have been by happenstance. So even when the judge rules by fact and by law in favour of the government, people will say, what do we expect? So it’s a matter of perception, which has to change.
He said: “I tried to make some comparison between the judiciary under the military and the judiciary under the current dispensation, unfortunately, I came to the painful conclusion that the judiciary under the military seems to be much more independent and fearless than what we have currently, which is most unfortunate. “Justice is rooted in public confidence. Professionals and business leaders have been urged to move beyond mere activities and translate their ideas and efforts into measurable results through accountability, continuous learning and effective systems.
The convener of the High Impact Professionals Seminar, HIPS, and founder of the TALK Office, Njuara Njama, gave the charge at the fourth edition of the seminar, stressing the need for professionals to become more intentional, adaptable and results-oriented in the workplace.
Njama, a legal practitioner, human capital and organisational development strategist, said the 2026 edition of the seminar, themed “Impact That Scales,” was designed to address the growing gap in strategic conversations around the workplace and help professionals navigate challenges confronting employees and employers.
She said: “The reality is that less and lesser strategic conversation is happening within the workspace. And I say this because it looks like entrepreneurship is the main thing. Wherever you go people are doing business this, business that, business this. And nobody’s focusing on the workplace. People who are actually moving those businesses forward.”
According to her, the seminar was conceived to provide a platform where employers and employees could discuss workplace challenges without resorting to the blame game.
“There’s always this contradiction between who is to be blamed for the problems that we have at work. Is it the employer? Is it the employee? Or is it the country at large?
“And so I thought, instead of us continuing to play this blame game, why don’t we come to a forum where we can understand each other? And that’s how the conversation started.
“From the first year to this year, our goal is simple. There are challenges that we have in the workplace. Why don’t we pick a topic and discuss those challenges within that topic by giving us perspective, clarity, direction, connection, and hopefully a system that we can move from one place to another.”
Njama said the impact of the seminar could be measured by the testimonies of participants who had translated lessons from previous editions into concrete actions.
She recalled the testimony of a participant who attended the first edition in Lagos and said some of the activities at the event encouraged her to take steps towards achieving goals she had documented.
“If you were in the session when I just finished speaking on execution intelligence, there was somebody who gave a testimonial that she was at our first edition in Lagos. And some of the activities that we did encouraged her, motivated her to begin to take steps. And the things she wrote down are the things that she has already succeeded at,” she said.
Explaining how professionals could turn ideas into results, Njama said many people were engaged in numerous activities without producing tangible evidence of progress.
“The truth is that a lot of people are doing a lot of activity, but those activities are not producing any kind of evidence,” she said.
“So the goal is for us to move from activity to motion and from motion to result. And how do we do it? We’re doing this by creating a system that empowers us to take action.”
She identified accountability as one of the critical tools required to transform ideas into action, warning that individuals who failed to establish systems to hold themselves accountable could struggle to turn their ambitions into reality.
“You cannot just wake up and say you want to change the world and you’re not holding yourself accountable. Nobody’s holding you accountable. You don’t have any tools or systems that support your accountability. You don’t write things down. You don’t have the right conversation.
“You just want to change the world in your mind. I’m sorry to announce to you, it’s just going to end in your mind.”
Njama also urged professionals to overcome the fear of imperfection and begin from where they were, using the resources available to them.
“As somebody wise once said that, the graveyard is the richest place because it dies with people who never took action. So the next thing is action. And for many of us, action is a problem because we think that we have to be perfect, but that’s not what it is.
“Action is starting from where you are, starting with what you have. Just start.”
She said the growth of HIPS itself demonstrated the value of taking action despite uncertainty, noting that the organisers initially planned to hold the event only in Abuja.
“When I started HIPS, I never thought that it’s going to be like this. We just started, or we just wanted to have one Hibbs in Abuja. And four years later, we’re having Abuja and Lagos consecutively every year. And I can tell you that I am still learning as I grow.”
On overcoming fear, she said: “There’s always going to be fear. As long as you’re building something that is bigger than you, the fear is there.”
She, however, encouraged professionals to see results not only as conventional success but also as lessons gained from actions taken.
“Results might not always be success in the traditional way that we define success. But results means you have now learned something that maybe works or maybe does not work.”
On the need for professionals to combine expertise with versatility, Njama urged workers to develop both vertical and horizontal competencies.
She said the traditional perception that being a “Jack of all trades” was necessarily negative no longer reflected the demands of many modern workplaces.
“Before now, they used to make us feel like Jack of all trade, master of none was the problem. But if you see the kind of people that organizations are looking for, they are looking for people who are probably a seven, seven, seven, seven in different places.
“They’re not looking for somebody who is a 10 in one thing and just one thing alone. But in this other place, you can be a seven, seven, seven. What that means is that you are vertical and horizontal at the same time.”
She added that professionals needed technical competence as well as social and emotional intelligence because workplace challenges were not limited to technical issues.
“There are people’s challenges. So if you do not have social skill or emotional intelligence, you will lose out on the people side. So that’s my advocacy.
“Be balanced. Don’t focus on just one thing and you’re doing it though and every other thing is no. Have multiple things that are complementary that make you function well in the workplace.”
Njama also spoke about the challenges she encountered while building the seminar, saying one of the biggest was translating her personal vision to other people.
“One of the interesting things, challenges that I faced was how to get people to see a vision that was just my vision. It’s easy for me to tell myself that, oh, this is going to work and it’s going to work well.
“But how do I translate my vision exactly as I’m seeing it to the people that I’m interacting with? So that was a real issue for me.”
She said continuous learning and understanding the behaviour of people involved in the initiative helped her address the challenge.
“I started learning the behavior of employees, employers, people, speakers, panelists, and all of that. And with that, I started incorporating it into the development of what we’re doing. We’re not there yet, but I assure you, we’re going to soon know where we start.”
Speaking on “Systems Thinking,” the guest speaker, Dr Oludare Akinlaja, called for greater reliance on data, systems and processes in business and professional practice.
Akinlaja said businesses and professionals should move away from approaches driven largely by sensationalism and adopt more structured and scientific methods.
“I was trying to bring people back to saying that, let’s be big on science, let’s be big on data, let’s be big on system, let’s be big on processes.
“Let’s not just be sensational, and design the process of anything goes. Whatever it is, whatever we be, we be, right? We can’t have that kind of thinking. We have to be more process-oriented, more data-driven, and a bit more scientific.”
He said stronger systems and data-driven approaches could improve the ability of small businesses to survive, grow, employ workers and contribute to economic activity.
“Small businesses are literally the backbone of any economy, and if we are more data-driven, more intentional, more systems-thinking, these small businesses can employ people, right? It can make people more, we earn daily.”
Also speaking, development consultant at Lustrefeel Economic Empowerment Foundation, David Lawal, urged young professionals to begin preparing for leadership and the changing demands of the future workplace.
Lawal, who spoke on building future professionals and leaders, said leadership should not be regarded as something reserved for people already occupying prominent positions.
“There are a lot of young leaders today, young professionals today, who don’t see leadership as a thing to aspire to be, right? They think leadership is far-fetched.
“Leadership is something that is far away from them. You know, from the spaces that we all occupy, everyone can be a leader, right? But there’s a level of information, there’s a level of skill that’s required, there’s a level of preparedness, there’s a level of professionalism that is required for you to emerge as a leader.”
He urged young people to anticipate changes in the labour market and acquire skills that would keep them relevant.
“What’s the future of work like? How can you stay relevant as a leader in the future of work that we’re looking at? Shifts are happening, right? We have a lot of jobs now that we didn’t have a couple of years back, many years back.
“We didn’t have robotic engineers like 10 years ago. We didn’t have drone pilots like 10 years ago. We didn’t have social media managers like 10 years ago, right, but most of those jobs are coming on now.”
Lawal said young professionals should prepare ahead of emerging opportunities rather than wait until the opportunities became available.
“The opportunities of those times will be available to those that are prepared now. So it’s best that young people begin to prepare now, rather than spending time on social media. Even social media can be used productively.”
He said social media could also serve as a platform for leadership, creativity and positive social impact.
Similarly, the Lead Consultant and Managing Director, Cordless Consulting Limited, Tosin Gbadebo, urged professionals to maintain professionalism and separate emotions from their responsibilities at work.
Gbadebo, who spoke on “The Execution Gap: Taking Life from Effort to Professionalism,” said the focus should be on developing structures that would make individuals more effective in their daily activities, businesses and professional engagements.
“Professionalism is the hallmark of success,” he said, adding that his participation in the seminar over three editions had exposed him to useful insights and experiences.
“I have been on the three occasions and I have been at the ends of planning and also execution. And I’ve come to realize that it’s a very, very important event, that people who are looking to scale their impacts professionally should attend because words will come out, insights will be shared, experiences would also be shared that would pave the way for you to become that person you want to be from the person who you are right now.”
Gbadebo, who identified himself as an HR expert and manager, advised workers to remain professional irrespective of workplace pressures.
“One of the things I would always say is stay professional, stay professional, just stay professional. Always know how to devise sentiments and emotions from work. Do your work as you’re supposed to do it and you will get the reward as you’re supposed to get it.”
On workplace politics, he said its prevalence could be influenced by leadership structures and organisational culture.
“Workplace politics comes with leadership. How you structure your organization would depict how the politics would either exist or be minimized or subsidized. It’s everywhere, everywhere, everywhere.
“But again, it’s back to human resources because these people who play politics are human beings, right? So it’s back to human resources, knowing the problem, solving the problem.”
He advocated healthy workplace cultures supported by sound policies, saying, “Having a healthy culture starts with healthy policies where you can build healthy policies in workplaces.”
The post Scaling impact requires action, systems, accountability — Njama appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
By Esther Onyegbula
The Federal Government has stepped up efforts to increase local production of essential medicines and position Nigeria as a major pharmaceutical manufacturing hub in Africa, with a target of producing 70 per cent of the country’s essential medicines domestically.
The government also disclosed plans to deepen incentives for local pharmaceutical manufacturers and strengthen regulatory systems to enable Nigerian drug manufacturers expand into West Africa and the wider African market.
The Minister of State for Industry, Trade and Investment, Senator John Owan Enoh, represented by the Director of Chemical and Non-Pharmaceutical Industry, Mr John Okpe Oluwa, disclosed this at the 8th Nigeria Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Expo, NPME 2026, held at Harbour Point, Victoria Island, Lagos.
Enoh said the Federal Government was committed to moving Nigeria from an import-dependent market towards greater self-sufficiency under the Renewed Hope Agenda.
According to him, increasing domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity would not only strengthen Nigeria’s medicine security but also provide the foundation for the country to become a major exporter of pharmaceutical products across Africa through the African Continental Free Trade Area, AfCFTA.
He said: “The government is targeting 70 per cent domestic production of essential medicines while developing a resilient ecosystem capable of meeting the country’s medical needs.”
To achieve the target, the minister listed proposed interventions, including expanded tax exemptions, tariff waivers on raw materials and machinery, incentives for backward integration in the production of active pharmaceutical ingredients and excipients, as well as dedicated pharmaceutical intervention funds.
He added that the government was working with regulatory agencies, including the Standards Organisation of Nigeria and the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, NAFDAC, to ensure that locally manufactured pharmaceutical products meet international standards and become more competitive in export markets.
The move comes as pharmaceutical manufacturers seek policy consistency and stronger investment support to enable them expand production, reduce dependence on imported medicines and compete in the African market.
The Chairman of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Group of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria, PMGMAN, Oluwatosin Jolayemi, said the Nigerian pharmaceutical manufacturing sector was undergoing significant transformation, noting that the group now represents more than 200 local pharmaceutical manufacturing companies.
Jolayemi, however, said the gains recorded by the industry must be protected through policy consistency and a predictable investment environment.
He identified high energy and production costs, supply-chain challenges, port inefficiencies, limited access to long-term capital and market-access constraints as some of the challenges limiting the industry’s growth.
He therefore appealed to the Federal Government to extend the Presidential Executive Order supporting local pharmaceutical manufacturing, whose current policy window is expected to expire in March 2027, by another two years.
According to him, the extension would enable manufacturers deepen investments, expand production capacity and consolidate gains made in medicine security.
Jolayemi said Nigeria’s ambition to become a regional pharmaceutical manufacturing hub must be anchored on a competitive, scalable and resilient domestic manufacturing ecosystem.
He called for coordinated action among government, regulators, manufacturers, financiers and development partners to address structural barriers and move the industry beyond domestic production towards a globally competitive and regionally integrated manufacturing ecosystem.
Earlier, the Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Dr Iziaq Adekunle Salako, reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to expanding domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing as a pathway to medicine security, healthcare resilience and economic development.
Salako stressed the need to strengthen capacity across the pharmaceutical value chain, covering research and development, innovation, sourcing of active pharmaceutical ingredients and excipients, formulation, manufacturing and quality assurance.
He also called for increased investment in sophisticated areas of pharmaceutical production, including biologics, vaccines and other critical health technologies.
The minister urged stronger regional cooperation to address regulatory barriers limiting access to African markets.
The Director-General of NAFDAC, Prof. Mojisola Christianah Adeyeye, disclosed that 37 local manufacturing facilities were undergoing retrofitting and construction upgrades to meet international standards.
Adeyeye said NAFDAC had made significant progress towards WHO global benchmarking and strengthened regulatory enforcement against non-compliant facilities.
She said reforms under the 5+5 policy had contributed to reducing drug importation and encouraging local manufacturers to improve their standards.
She stressed that Nigeria could not afford to reverse the gains recorded in local pharmaceutical manufacturing and urged the country to intensify efforts towards the production of vaccines and other critical health commodities.
Also speaking, the Director-General of the African Medicines Agency, Dr Delese Mimi Darko, called for stronger regulatory cooperation among African countries to accelerate access to quality-assured medicines and create a more integrated pharmaceutical market.
Darko said the African Medicines Agency was established to strengthen and coordinate national regulatory systems rather than replace them.
She said regulatory harmonisation would enable manufacturers to navigate African markets more efficiently.
Darko also stressed the need for African manufacturers to invest in research and development, technology transfer, skilled manpower, intellectual property and quality systems, arguing that localisation must go beyond simply producing medicines locally.
In his welcome address, the Chairman of NPME 2026, Pharm. Dr Patrick Ajah, said no nation could achieve sustainable greatness without manufacturing what its citizens consume, describing the pharmaceutical sector as fundamental to national development.
Ajah recalled that Nigeria’s drug consumption had historically been skewed towards imports, with about 70 per cent of medicines imported and 30 per cent produced locally.
He, however, said public-private collaboration over the past two years had begun to shift the balance.
He called on stakeholders to partner with PMGMAN to drive sustainable growth, stressing that the expo had created opportunities for businesses to expand across Nigeria, Africa and the global market.
The Lagos State Government, represented by the Special Adviser on Health, Dr Kemi Ogunyemi, pledged continued support for the pharmaceutical manufacturing sector, particularly in addressing energy costs, infrastructure, long-term financing, skilled manpower and regulatory predictability.
The expo attracted representatives of the European Union, UNICEF, European Investment Bank, Bank of Industry, IFC/World Bank, NAFDAC, Pharmacy Council of Nigeria, Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Federal Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment, as well as other industry and academic institutions.
One of the highlights of the expo was the Founders and Industry Leaders Session, which brought together leading figures in Nigeria’s pharmaceutical manufacturing industry, including Dr Stella Okoli of Emzor Pharmaceuticals, Dr Fidelis Ayebae of Fidson Plc, Dr Olakunle Ekundayo of Drugfield Pharmaceuticals and Elder Varkey Verghese of Jawal International Limited.
The session provided emerging pharmaceutical entrepreneurs with insights into leadership, investment, innovation, succession, manufacturing and the challenges of building sustainable pharmaceutical businesses in Africa.
PMGMAN also unveiled its Industry Self-Regulation Quality Plus, ISRQ+, Project, which includes a five-year Medicine Security Industry Advocacy Strategy for 2027–2031, an ISRQ+ laboratory and a Data Repository and Learning Centre.
The group said the initiative was designed to strengthen industry intelligence, quality capacity, evidence-based advocacy and continuous learning, with its various components expected to be commissioned progressively within the next six to 10 months.
As the 2026 edition came to a close, PMGMAN said its focus would shift towards translating progress recorded in domestic manufacturing into a stronger, more integrated and competitive regional pharmaceutical ecosystem.
The closing remarks, delivered by Pharm. Frank Muonemeh, emphasised the need for stakeholders to remain committed to closing Nigeria’s medicine access gap and advancing greater medicine security across Africa.
PMGMAN also announced plans for the 9th Nigeria Pharma Manufacturers Expo in 2028, while preparations continue towards the commissioning of the ISRQ+ project.

It was adjudged the winner owing to its credible news, current affairs, public affairs and entertainment radio platform with a strong focus on issues that matter to Nigerians.

items.author: Daily Trust
items.content:
Governor Dauda Lawal declared that his administration’s rescue mission is transforming Zamfara State across critical sectors.
On Thursday, the governor began a series of events and project commissioning to mark Zamfara State’s 30th Anniversary.
The 30th Anniversary and commissioning were attended by the Pioneer Military Administrator of Zamfara State, Col. Jibril Bala Yakubu (Rtd.), former governors Ahmed Sani Yarima and Mahmud Aliyu Shinkafi, and other dignitaries.
During his speech at the National Independence Day parade and Zamfara’s 30th Anniversary at the Trade Fair Complex in Gusau, Governor Lawal said Zamfara has moved from despair to an era of clear execution, transparency, and sustainable development.
He said, “Today, we join Nigerians in celebrating Independence Day and mark three decades since Zamfara State was created on October 1, 1996. Alhamdulillah for Allah’s grace, mercy, and protection that have guided us through trials and triumphs, uniting us in a shared destiny.
“As we watched our gallant security forces, paramilitary agencies, vibrant students and youth march in unity on this parade ground, we were reminded of the resilience that defines the Nigerian spirit and, most specifically, the strength of character of our people.
“We must reflect intentionally on the profound sacrifices of our founding fathers, who fought tirelessly to break the chains of colonial rule and give birth to a free, sovereign nation. We owe them an eternal debt of gratitude for protecting this country’s unity, peace, and territorial integrity.
“As we look forward to the next decade, we must understand that true independence demands collective responsibility. Government alone can’t do this. I call on traditional rulers, religious scholars, civil servants, traders, and our resilient youth to unite. We must set aside divisions—ethnic, political, sectarian—and protect the peace we fought for.”
On Friday, Governor Lawal commissioned phase III of the renovated and modernised J.B. Yakubu Secretariat in Gusau as part of his effort to rebuild government institutions and create a modern, efficient, technology-enabled, results-oriented Public Service for Zamfara State.
The J.B. Yakubu Secretariat houses critical Ministries, Departments, and Agencies whose responsibilities span virtually every aspect of governance and service delivery.
Governor Lawal said modernising the Secretariat will deepen coordination among MDAs, strengthen communication, promote institutional synergy, and support faster, more effective implementation of government decisions.
“Today’s occasion is significant as we welcome His Excellency, Col. Jibril Bala Yakubu (Rtd.), Zamfara’s pioneer Military Administrator, after whom this Secretariat is named. As Zamfara marks thirty years since its creation, it’s fitting that a leader from our foundation is here to witness this milestone.”
Earlier, the pioneer Military Administrator of Zamfara State, Col. Jibril Bala Yakubu (Rtd.), lauded Governor Lawal’s giant strides, particularly in infrastructure, education, and health.
On the same Friday, His Eminence, the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammadu Sa’ad Abubakar III, CFR, mni, commissioned the reconstructed and remodelled Jumu’at Mosque (Yardole) and its attached shopping complex.
The mosque, named after Malam Sambo Dan Ashafa, a renowned Islamic scholar and companion of the great (MUJADDADI) and leader of the 1st Sokoto Jihad, Sheikh Uthman Ibn Fodiyo, will also serve as an Islamic and research learning centre.

items.author: Daily Trust
items.content:
Governor Uba Sani has granted clemency to 27 inmates in correctional facilities across Kaduna state, to mark Nigeria’s 66th Independence anniversary, in an effort to give deserving innates opportunity to rebuild their lives.
A statement issued by the Commissioner for Information and Culture, Malam Ahmed Maiyaki on Friday, stated that the latest clemency brings the number of beneficiaries to more than 500, since the Governor assumed office.
The Commissioner added the intervention included the release of eligible inmates as well as the payment of fines and compensation of over N300 million for victims since 2023.
The statement quoted state Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Sir James Kanyip, as saying that the latest exercise is part of the Governor’s practice of extending mercy to deserving inmates on national occasions.
According to the Chief Law Officer of Kaduna State, previous exercises were carried out on New Year day, during Democracy Day and Independence Day celebrations.
He said the prerogative of mercy was exercised through established processes, taking into consideration accountability, rehabilitation and the responsibilities that come with freedom.
Kanyip said the beneficiaries were expected to return to society with a renewed sense of responsibility and appreciation of their obligations to others.
The statement said the payment of fines and compensation is also intended to give the clemency a restorative justice dimension by addressing barriers to the release of deserving inmates while recognising the interests of victims.
It said the interventions were based on the belief that public safety, human dignity, rehabilitation and the possibility of redemption should form part of the administration of justice.
The statement added that clemency goes beyond freeing inmates from custody, as it also provides an opportunity for beneficiaries to reconnect with their families and communities.
The statement further said the administration would continue to support rehabilitation, reconciliation and the reintegration of deserving inmates into society.
According to the statement, the government remains committed to a justice system that protects society, respects victims’ interests and gives deserving individuals an opportunity to become responsible and productive members of their communities.

By Vincent Ujumadu
AWKA — One person was feared dead and several others injured following a fresh communal clash between Amaeze Aguleri and Umuoba Anam communities in Anambra East Local Government Area of Anambra State.
Several buildings, including a microfinance bank in Aguleri, were reportedly set ablaze during the violence.
The latest incident is believed to be linked to a longstanding land dispute between the two communities, which dates back to 1999 and had previously attracted the intervention of the administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo.
Accounts surrounding the dispute indicate that Amaeze Aguleri had decades ago given a portion of its land to Umuoba Anam on trust. The ownership of the disputed area later became a source of disagreement between the communities.
The Anambra State Police Command confirmed the death of one person and said it had deployed personnel to the affected communities to restore peace and maintain law and order.
The Commissioner of Police, CP Nnanna Oji Ama, led the state Deputy Governor, Dr Onyekachukwu Ibezim, other government officials, security agencies and community stakeholders on an on-the-spot assessment of the affected areas.
The visit was aimed at assessing the security situation, safeguarding lives and property and preventing further escalation of the conflict.
The delegation assessed the extent of the reported destruction and the impact of the violence on residents and the affected communities.
The stakeholders also reviewed immediate measures to restore peace and strengthen security, while exploring longer-term steps to prevent a recurrence.
During the assessment, Oji Ama reiterated the commitment of the Police Command to protecting lives and property and ensuring that residents could carry out their legitimate activities without fear.
He urged residents of Aguleri and Umuoba Anam to remain calm and refrain from actions capable of escalating the situation.
The police commissioner also appealed to residents to cooperate with security agencies by providing credible and timely information that could assist ongoing investigations and peace-building efforts.
Speaking during the visit, Deputy Governor Ibezim urged traditional rulers, community leaders, youth organisations, town unions and other stakeholders to work with the government and security agencies towards finding a lasting solution to the dispute.
He said security was a shared responsibility requiring the cooperation and commitment of all stakeholders.
The Police Command assured residents of Aguleri and Umuoba Anam that security measures were being strengthened in the affected areas to prevent further breaches of peace.
It added that efforts were ongoing to address the underlying issues through dialogue and other lawful channels.

By Vincent Ujumadu
AWKA — The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) secured 1,370 convictions from 1,889 cases filed in court during the first half of 2026, the commission’s Executive Chairman, Ola Olukoyede, has said.
Olukoyede disclosed this on Thursday while speaking at the commissioning of the EFCC Awka Zonal Directorate Complex, which will serve Anambra and Imo states.
He said the commission also recovered ₦1,233,612,040,411.11, $684,478,457.32, £373,905.78 and €9,343,803.66 during the period, in addition to recoveries in other currencies.
Giving a broader account of the commission’s activities, Olukoyede said that between October 2023 and July 2026, the EFCC received 49,673 petitions, investigated 39,615 cases, filed 14,476 cases in court and secured 10,872 convictions.
He said the figures represented a conviction-to-filing ratio of 75.1 per cent.
According to him, the commission had introduced reforms aimed at improving its operations, including changes to its processes and procedures, which he said had contributed to its performance across various law-enforcement indicators.
On the new Awka directorate, Olukoyede said its establishment was part of the EFCC’s expansion programme, supported by appropriations from the National Assembly and interventions by the Federal Government.
He said Anambra and Imo required effective institutional presence because of their economic activities, describing the states as centres of enterprise, commerce and industry.
Olukoyede said the EFCC’s mandate went beyond arrests and prosecution to include prevention and coordination in the fight against economic and financial crimes.
“The EFCC exists not merely to arrest and prosecute. Our official mission encompasses prevention, enforcement and coordination in the effort to eradicate economic and financial crimes,” he said.
He said preventing financial crimes before they occurred could help reduce the economic and social costs associated with fraud and diversion of public resources.
“If we can identify vulnerabilities before billions of naira are lost, prevent fraudulent transactions before citizens lose their savings, strengthen procurement systems before public resources are diverted and interrupt criminal financial flows before they mature, then we would have saved the nation enormous economic and social costs,” he said.
The EFCC chairman said the Awka directorate would place emphasis on corruption prevention and engagement with government institutions, businesses, financial institutions, professional bodies, schools, markets, civil society organisations, traditional institutions, religious bodies and communities.
He urged members of the public to provide credible information about suspected economic and financial crimes, while cautioning against using whistleblowing to settle personal scores.
“Whistleblowing must become an act of responsible citizenship,” Olukoyede said.
“However, whistleblowing must be responsible and based on fact. It must not become an instrument for settling scores.”
He called on traditional rulers, religious leaders, town unions, market associations, professional bodies, youth and women’s groups, civil society organisations and the media to support efforts to prevent corruption.
Olukoyede also urged the new directorate to build sustained relationships with state and local governments, tertiary institutions, the organised private sector and community structures in Anambra and Imo.
Speaking on behalf of President Bola Tinubu, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Tajudeen Abbas, said the commissioning reflected the Federal Government’s efforts to strengthen the capacity of anti-corruption agencies.
The President said his administration had, since assuming office, worked to improve the institutional capacity of anti-corruption agencies to carry out their mandates.
He said the Awka directorate would strengthen the EFCC’s presence in Anambra and Imo, particularly in major commercial and industrial centres.
“From the industrial towns of Onitsha and Nnewi, to the oil and gas town of Egbema and the rapidly growing economic city of Owerri, Imo State, the presence of EFCC will improve the ease of doing business,” Tinubu said.
He said the government would continue to provide an enabling environment for anti-corruption agencies to carry out their responsibilities.
Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, assured the commission of the state government’s cooperation in carrying out its duties.
Soludo said reducing financial crimes was in the interest of the state and expressed satisfaction that Anambra would host the regional directorate.
“Some people might be asking why we’re so excited about having the zonal office in our state. The reason for our excitement is that it will enhance quicker investigation,” he said.
The governor, however, observed that the EFCC’s staffing capacity made it difficult for the commission to establish offices in every local government area.
“Ideally, EFCC should have offices in the 774 local government areas of the country, but with only about 6,000 staff, it is difficult to have offices in all LGAs,” he said.
Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodinma, commended the EFCC for bringing its services closer to residents of the two states.
Uzodinma also appealed to the commission to establish a dedicated state office in Imo to enhance its coverage and operations in the state.
