By Onyeka Ezike
Tourists Club International (TCI) has announced the establishment of two new tourism destinations in Badagry, Lagos State—the Tourists Club International Art Gallery and the Tourists Club International Forest Reserve.
The announcement was made on Sunday to commemorate the 2026 World Tourism Day, whose theme is “Digital Agenda and Artificial Intelligence to Redesign Tourism.”
The theme highlights the growing influence of digital platforms and artificial intelligence on how travellers discover destinations, plan journeys and experience tourism. The official global celebration is being hosted by El Salvador.
President of TCI, Dr. Osa Mbonu-Amadi, said the initiative represented the organisation’s practical response to the global theme.
“The establishment of the Tourists Club International Art Gallery and the Tourists Club International Forest Reserve is our practical response to the 2026 World Tourism Day theme. We are using documentation, digital visibility and responsible tourism development to ensure that Badagry’s artistic, historical and natural assets are not overlooked in the rapidly changing tourism landscape,” Mbonu-Amadi said.
He added that the destinations belonged not only to TCI but also to the people of Badagry and future generations who deserved to experience, understand and protect them.
According to the organisation, the initiative is aimed at documenting, preserving and promoting destinations that might otherwise remain invisible in the digital tourism ecosystem.
Art gallery for Badagry
The Tourists Club International Art Gallery is expected to become the first purpose-built art gallery in Badagry, an ancient town renowned for its historical, cultural and tourism significance.
TCI said the gallery was being established primarily to provide a secure and appropriate home for important artworks acquired by the organisation in recent years.
It added that the facility would serve as a platform for cultural preservation, artistic appreciation, tourism education and digital storytelling.
The organisation noted that although many art galleries in Lagos were concentrated on Lagos Island and Victoria Island, the growth of virtual tourism and AI-assisted travel planning had changed the traditional idea of where tourism destinations could be located.
According to TCI, a destination can attract local and international attention from anywhere, provided it is properly documented, digitally accessible and connected to the wider tourism ecosystem.
The organisation said it would document the gallery, its collections and the stories behind the artworks to make Badagry’s artistic heritage more discoverable to visitors, researchers and AI-powered travel platforms.
Forest reserve for conservation
The Tourists Club International Forest Reserve is described as a small but important natural area in Badagry and the only surviving forested space in the host community.
TCI said the forest provides a habitat for a colony of monkeys whose natural environment is increasingly threatened by unsustainable development.
The reserve, according to the organisation, reflects its commitment to developing tourism in a manner that protects nature and respects host communities.
It said the site offered opportunities for environmental education, nature-based tourism, biodiversity conservation and public awareness of the need to preserve Nigeria’s remaining urban and peri-urban forests.
“Through appropriate documentation, responsible visitor management and digital promotion, the forest reserve can become part of a broader conversation about sustainable tourism and the protection of threatened natural habitats,” the organisation said.
Making Badagry visible
TCI said travellers increasingly relied on digital platforms and AI tools to determine where to go, what to see and where to stay.
It therefore stressed the importance of documenting destinations if they were to appear in answers generated by digital platforms and AI-powered travel tools.
The organisation said it was working to place Badagry’s cultural and natural assets within the digital information landscape through verified descriptions, visual documentation, location data and stories reflecting the experience and voice of the host community.
TCI said its approach was consistent with the central concern of World Tourism Day 2026: who benefits from the digital transformation of tourism and who determines which destinations travellers see.
It added that the beneficiaries should include Nigerian communities, artists, conservationists, guides, small tourism businesses and culture-bearers.
The organisation also said the initiative would promote more inclusive tourism narratives by giving visibility to emerging attractions and community-based tourism projects, rather than focusing exclusively on established commercial destinations.
Public unveiling
TCI said it would unveil the art gallery and forest reserve to the public at a date to be announced.
The unveiling, it said, would form part of its continuing efforts to promote international tourism, peace and universal friendship; develop and preserve tourism sites; disseminate reliable tourism information; and encourage respect for the heritage and traditions of host communities. Mbonu-Amadi said the initiative would help place Badagry more firmly on Nigeria’s tourism map.
“Artificial intelligence can only recommend destinations that have been properly documented and made visible. By establishing these two sites, TCI is helping to place Badagry more firmly on Nigeria’s tourism map while promoting cultural preservation, environmental responsibility and community participation,” he said.
The post 2026 WTD: TCI introduces two tourism destinations in Badagry appeared first on Vanguard News.

DAMATURU — The Yobe State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA) has alerted motorists to a major road hazard along the Bauchi-Maiduguri highway following the cutting off of a significant portion of the road near the Darazo exit in Bauchi State.
SEMA issued the warning in a public alert posted on its official Facebook page on Sunday, September 27, 2026, urging motorists using the affected routes to exercise extreme caution.
According to the agency, “as of Sunday, 27th September 2026, a significant portion of the Bauchi–Maiduguri road has been cut off near the Darazo exit.”
It advised motorists travelling along the Bauchi-Yobe-Maiduguri route, as well as those travelling from Kano to Gombe, to “exercise extreme caution and take all necessary safety precautions.”
The warning comes amid the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) forecast of rain and thunderstorms across several parts of the country.
In its latest weather bulletin covering September 26 to 28, NiMet forecast thunderstorms and rainfall in several locations, including Bauchi, Gombe, Abuja, Kaduna, Jos, Makurdi, Lagos, Port Harcourt, Uyo, Owerri, Enugu, Akure and Abeokuta, among others.
For Bauchi, NiMet forecast thunderstorms during parts of Sunday, while Gombe was also expected to experience thunderstorm conditions.
However, partly cloudy conditions were forecast for Maiduguri and Potiskum.
NiMet has also identified areas with potential flash-flood risks in its September 21–30 outlook and urged stakeholders to use weather information for preparedness and early action.
The road disruption could pose additional risks to motorists, particularly amid wet-weather conditions that may affect visibility, road surfaces and travelling time.
SEMA urged motorists to remain vigilant and take necessary precautions while using the affected routes.
The agency concluded its alert with a warning to travellers: “Stay safe.”

By Maryam Abdul-Aziz Usman, Damaturu
The All Progressives Congress (APC) has won all 17 chairmanship seats in Saturday’s Yobe State local government elections, with 10 political parties participating in the exercise.
The Yobe State Independent Electoral Commission (YOSIEC) declared the results on Sunday in Damaturu, the state capital, with the ruling party also winning 176 of the 178 councillorship seats contested across the state.
The Chairman of YOSIEC, Dr Ibrahim Mohammed Yabani, said the election was conducted across the 17 Local Government Areas and 178 electoral wards.
He said 10 political parties participated in the election, fielding candidates for the chairmanship and councillorship positions.
While the APC secured all 17 chairmanship seats, the Action Peoples Party (APP) won one councillorship seat in Fune Local Government Area, while the Action Democratic Party (ADP) secured one in Karasuwa.
“Out of the 178 councillorship seats, the APC won 176 seats, while APP won in Fune and ADP won in Karasuwa,” Yabani declared.
According to the commission, councillorship results were declared at the respective ward collation centres, while chairmanship results were declared at the local government collation centres before the final collation at the YOSIEC headquarters in Damaturu.
Yabani said the electoral process, which commenced on April 23, 2025, under the leadership of the late former chairman of the commission, Dr Mamman Mohammed, had now been concluded.
Meanwhile, the Yobe State chapter of the Inter-Party Advisory Council (IPAC) accepted the outcome of the election.
Speaking at the NUJ Secretariat in Damaturu, IPAC Chairman, Comrade Umar Adamu Jajere, described the exercise as free, fair, credible and successful.
Jajere commended YOSIEC for conducting the election and urged the newly elected chairmen and councillors to regard their mandates as a responsibility to serve the people at the grassroots.
He also urged candidates who lost the election to remain resilient and continue participating in the democratic process.

By Udeme Akpan
Kenyan President William Samoei Ruto has described the Dangote Petroleum Refinery as “a masterpiece of science, engineering and art” following a tour of the world-class facility in Lagos, while reaffirming Kenya’s commitment to partnering with Dangote Group on the proposed $17 billion East African Oil Refinery and Petrochemical Complex in Lamu.
President Ruto, who visited the refinery after attending the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), said witnessing firsthand the scale, sophistication and operational excellence of the 700,000 barrels-per-day Dangote Petroleum Refinery had strengthened his confidence in the East African refinery project.
“Coming here and seeing it for myself, I can confirm that I have seen a masterpiece of science, engineering, with art. To my brother Aliko, congratulations. I always knew Nigerians to be very brave people and go-getters, but I did not anticipate that it was at this scale,” President Ruto said.
The Kenyan leader disclosed that preparations had been concluded for the groundbreaking ceremony of the East African refinery project in Lamu, which is expected to become a strategic regional asset for East Africa.
According to him, the refinery will drive industrialisation, create jobs, strengthen engineering and technical capacity, enhance energy security and promote regional economic integration.
“This is not a Kenyan refinery; it is going to be a regional refinery. We are positioning our continent as an emerging growth centre, and this project will help accelerate industrialisation, create jobs, enhance engineering capabilities and strengthen Africa’s economic competitiveness,” he stated bureaucratic bottlenecks to ensure efficient project execution.
“The Government of Kenya is 100 per cent behind this project. We have secured the required land and are working to ensure that we spend our time building rather than navigating administrative delays,” he said.
The President further commended the leadership and commitment of Dangote Group President and Chief Executive, Aliko Dangote, highlighting his deep understanding of the refinery’s technical and operational processes.
“The detail with which Aliko Dangote understands this plant is remarkable. Unless you understand the details, you are unable to make the right decisions. That commitment to excellence is one of the reasons behind the success of this project,” he added.
Dangote Group’s Chief Strategy Officer, Aliyu Suleiman, disclosed, during the visist that the conglomerate generated approximately $17 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026 and is on course to achieve a record $36 billion in revenue for the full year, representing a 100 per cent increase over the $18 billion recorded in 2025.
“The revenues of the Group have grown significantly over the last five years. From $18 billion last year, we are on track to get to $36 billion this year. Our half-year revenue is already about $17 billion,” Suleiman said.
He attributed the strong performance to sustained investments across key sectors, including cement, sugar, fertiliser, petroleum refining, upstream oil and gas, and other strategic businesses.
Suleiman noted that Dangote Group’s growth ambitions are anchored on its Vision 2030 Strategy, aimed at expanding the company’s industrial footprint across Africa and creating globally competitive businesses on the continent.
“Between 2020 and 2025, the Group executed a capital expenditure programme of approximately $50 billion. Over the next five years, we intend to invest twice that amount as we accelerate our expansion across Africa,” he stated.
Suleiman emphasised that the proposed 700,000 barrels-per-day greenfield refinery and petrochemical complex in Lamu, estimated at approximately $17 billion, will be a cornerstone of the Group’s ambition to build a $100 billion African industrial enterprise.
“The East African refinery in Kenya is going to be a key component of our journey and our dream to get to $100 billion. It is going to be a major contributor,” he said.
He added that Dangote Group’s expansion plans span a broad range of sectors, including port infrastructure, gas infrastructure, LNG, upstream oil and gas, power generation, mining and other strategic industrial investments across Africa.
As part of preparations for the project, Dangote Group has signed a contract worth more than $450 million with Engineers India Limited (EIL) to provide project management consultancy and engineering, procurement and construction management services for the Lamu refinery and petrochemical complex.
The partnership builds on EIL’s experience and involvement in the successful development of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery in Lagos.
Once completed, the East African refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day, strengthening regional energy security and supporting industrial development across East Africa.
Dangote Group is also progressing plans to expand the processing capacity of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery in Nigeria from 700,000 barrels per day to approximately 1.4 million barrels per day through the addition of a new 750,000 barrels-per-day crude distillation unit.
The expansion is expected to further solidify Nigeria’s position as a leading exporter of refined petroleum products and enhance Africa’s energy self-sufficiency.
President Ruto’s visit and Dangote Group’s ambitious growth plans highlight the increasing impact of African-led investments in driving the continent’s industrial renaissance.
With record revenue growth, a robust investment pipeline, expansion of refining capacity in Nigeria and the planned development of the East African Oil Refinery in Kenya, Dangote Group is reinforcing its role as a key driver of Africa’s economic transformation, energy security, industrial development and regional integration.

By Udeme Akpan
The Federal Government has commissioned a 581kWp interconnected solar mini-grid with a 1.4MW battery energy storage system at Oke-Oyi, Ilorin East Local Government Area of Kwara State.
The project, designed to supply power during the day and night, is expected to serve about 1,800 households and businesses in the community.
Commissioning the facility, Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, said the battery storage system would enable the mini-grid to continue supplying electricity after sunset, strengthening the government’s drive to expand reliable power to underserved communities.
The project was delivered under the Interconnected Mini-Grid Acceleration Scheme (IMAS) and supported by the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP), with funding and technical support from the European Union, the Federal Republic of Germany through GIZ and other development partners, including UNICEF.
Tegbe described IMAS as a model for public-private collaboration in the power sector, saying the scheme uses public funding to attract private developers, establishes clear market rules and promotes commercially viable projects.
“As we energize this community, we are also energizing businesses, creating opportunities, empowering young people, improving livelihoods, and building a more resilient future for Nigeria,” he said.
He urged residents to protect the facility from vandalism and criminal interference, stressing that the infrastructure was built for the benefit of the community and future generations.
The Managing Director of the Rural Electrification Agency (REA) said the Oke-Oyi project demonstrated the potential of interconnected mini-grids to combine renewable energy with existing distribution networks.
He said the agency would continue to scale the model through stronger financing, regulatory and institutional frameworks, while ensuring proper maintenance and community ownership.
He acknowledged the contributions of the Federal Ministry of Power, Kwara State Government, development partners, Ibadan Electricity Distribution Company and Nayo Tropical Technologies Limited to the project.
Representing Kwara State Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, Speaker of the State House of Assembly, Yakubu Danladi-Salihu, said the project would help strengthen economic activity in rural communities and reduce rural-urban migration.
He commended the Federal Government’s power-sector initiatives and the project’s focus on extending infrastructure beyond major urban centres.
The Oke-Oyi facility adds to the Federal Government’s portfolio of rural and off-grid projects under the Renewed Hope Agenda.

items.content:
By Christopher Ameh, Bauchi
Six governorship candidates of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in the North-East have rejected the appointment of former Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Engr. Babachir Lawal, as the party’s leader in the region.
The candidates, in a joint statement addressed to the national leadership of the party and signed by Senator Henry Seriake Dickson, said they would not recognise Lawal in the position.
They described their position as “collective, firm and final,” arguing that the appointment was made without consultation with them or other key stakeholders involved in building the party’s structures and mobilising support across the six states of the North-East.
The governorship candidates said on Sunday that, after due consideration, they had unanimously resolved not to recognise Lawal as the NDC leader in the region.
“After due consideration, we have unanimously resolved not to recognise Engr. Babachir Lawal as the Leader of the NDC in the North-East, and we will not recognise him as such,” they stated.
They argued that political decisions should take into account local realities and urged the national leadership to consider the views of stakeholders directly involved in the party’s activities and electoral mobilisation across the region.
The candidates also expressed concern that Lawal’s appointment could affect the party’s electoral prospects in the North-East, maintaining that the decision, in their view, would not add electoral value to the party in the region.
According to them, consulting the governorship candidates before making the appointment would have allowed the national leadership to better understand the political realities and concerns in the six states.
They therefore appealed to the party’s national leadership to review the appointment and engage with the affected governorship candidates in the interest of unity, cohesion and the strengthening of the NDC ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The statement was signed by Aishatu Dahiru Ahamed of Adamawa State, Barr. Ibrahim Muhammad Kashim of Bauchi State, Rear Admiral S. Kashim Ibrahim (Rtd.) of Borno State, Dr. Babayo Ardo of Gombe State, Prof. Mohammed Sani of Taraba State and Ibrahim M. Shitu of Yobe State.
While acknowledging the efforts of the NDC national leadership in providing a platform for political participation ahead of the 2027 elections, the candidates maintained that their opposition to Lawal’s appointment remained unchanged.
“For the avoidance of doubt, our position is collective, firm and final: we do not recognise Engr. Babachir Lawal as the Leader of the NDC in the North-East, and we will not recognise him as such,” they stated.

items.content:
—Meets Amina Mohammed as Nigeria rallies behind UN reform
By Johnbosco Agbakwuru
ABUJA —THE Vice President, Senator Kashim Shettima has said Africa’s continued exclusion from permanent membership of the United Nations (UN) Security Council undermines the fairness and legitimacy of the global governance system.
He reaffirmed Nigeria’s support for urgent reform of the United Nations, noting that the nation would remain a dependable partner in efforts to rebuild trust among nations, defend international law and address hunger, violence and exclusion.
The Vice President stated this during a meeting with United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, Hajiya Amina Mohammed, on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Shettima commended the UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, for his consistent support for a more representative Security Council, particularly his declaration that a 21st-century Council without permanent African representation is “unjust and indefensible.
“A continent cannot be summoned to bear the burdens of the international order and then denied an equal hand in directing it,” the VP said.
He maintained that Nigeria would continue to support reforms that make international institutions more representative, responsive and credible, stressing that global decisions must better reflect contemporary geopolitical and demographic realities.
The Vice President also praised Guterres for defending international law and human dignity amid widening global conflicts and rising geopolitical tensions.
“You have remained a voice of reason as individual states drift from the obligations they assumed under the United Nations Charter and the rules of international law. You have insisted that sovereignty carries duties, that might confers no licence to injure, and that the worth of a human life cannot vary with the flag above it,” he said.
He warned that diplomacy must not lose sight of the human consequences of war and instability.
“The mother searching for her child, the family driven from home and the hungry child awaiting food must never become abstractions in the language of states,” he added.
VP Shettima also commended UN Deputy Secretary-General, Amina J. Mohammed, for her contributions to multilateral diplomacy and sustainable development, describing her service as a source of pride to Nigeria.
“Nigeria will remain a willing ally in the work of restoring trust among nations and dignity to lives diminished by hunger, violence and exclusion. We owe our children a world in which conscience has authority and the law has meaning,” he said.
The Vice President added that the credibility of the international system would eventually depend on its ability to respond fairly to human suffering and provide all regions with a meaningful voice in global decision-making.
“Civilisation endures only when the suffering of a stranger becomes a claim on our conscience,” he said.
Earlier, the United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, Hajiya Amina Mohammed, expressed profound gratitude to Nigeria and the administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for the support to the UN as an institution and to her office as the deputy scribe of the global body.
Her words: “It’s deep honour to have your esteemed delegation here to come and surprise me. I am truly honoured and grateful.
“I want to thank through you, the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, and you for embracing me wholeheartedly not just as the DSG but as a daughter of the soil. He has been an incredible support to me, and he has also supported this institution.”
The Vice President was accompanied on the visit by Governors Abdulrahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara State, Hyacinth Alia of Benue, Siminalayi Fubara of Rivers, and Dauda Lawal of Zamfara; Minister of Foreign Affairs, Amb Bianca Odumegwu-Ojukwu, and Nigeria’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Amb. Jimoh Ibrahim, among other top officials.
The post Security council exclusion of Africa subverts global governance legitimacy – Shettima appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
‘People do not have the assurance that they will get justice.’
Originally published on Global Voices
August 4, 2024, Dhaka. People celebrated in jubilation after Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina resigned and left the country. Photo by: Rafi Al Ahnaf (used with permissin.
This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Mob violence is on the rise in Bangladesh. According to the United Nations (UN) Special Rapporteur on freedom of expression Irene Khan, unchecked impunity is contributing to the trend. Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK), a Dhaka-based legal aid and human rights organization, reported in its monthly Statistics of Human Rights Violations that at least 154 people were beaten to death in mob violence across Bangladesh between January and August 2026. ASK compiled the figure from national newspapers, online news outlets and its own documentation.
In Pabna, Bangladesh, 10-year-old Kamrunnahar Koli went missing from her village on September 9, 2026. Her body was recovered from a pond near her home seven days later. Police identified two suspects, arrested them on September 17, and sent them to jail.
But the following day, hundreds of people gathered outside the home of one of the accused and vandalized the property while police were present.
Md Torikul Islam, officer-in-charge of Pabna Sadar Police Station, told The Daily Star that officers tried to control the crowd, but “the small force could not stop such a large mob.” Police removed the suspect’s family members and secured valuables, but, he said, “we could not prevent the structural destruction.”
A broader pattern
The attack came amid a broader pattern documented by rights groups. In its review of the interim government that took office after Bangladesh’s 2024 uprising, Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) reported an increasing tendency to take the law into one’s own hands and a growing trend of forming mobs to press demands. In some cases, it said, those demands were met. TIB also pointed to police apathy, reluctance to perform duties and questions over law-enforcement capacity.
The pattern continued after the BNP-majority government took office following the February 2026 parliamentary elections. In its assessment of the government’s first 100 days, TIB reported 69 to 80 incidents of mob violence nationwide during March and April, resulting in between 31 and 42 deaths.
For Bangladeshi broadcast journalist Rifat Alam Risan, the speed at which a crowd can turn against an individual became a personal experience.
In December 2025, Risan went to Dhaka Medical College Hospital to collect footage after political activist and then-independent parliamentary candidate Sharif Osman Bin Hadi had been shot in Dhaka. News reports also documented an attack on Risan while he was gathering news there.
Speaking to Global Voices in person in Dhaka on September 20, 2026, Risan said that the situation changed after someone in the crowd accused him of being involved in Hadi’s shooting.
“Someone said, ‘He shot Hadi, and now he has come back to attack us.’ The accusation spread through the crowd, and people who gathered around began attacking me without any judgment or consideration,” Risan recalled.
“They beat me and forced me out of the hospital. At one point, I collapsed on the road, and they also tried to take my phone. I was eventually rescued by a fellow television reporter and other media workers who were there.”
Speaking to Global Voices by phone on September 20, 2026, Jamal Ruhany, another Bangladeshi broadcast journalist, described a pattern he said he had observed in how a crowd can turn on an individual.
“First, one or two people target a specific person. Once one or two people attack that person, many others nearby join in,” Ruhany said. “The people doing the beating often do not even know whether the person is actually guilty, and the person being attacked may not even know what they are accused of. Someone simply says, ‘Beat him,’ and it happens.”
August 2, 2024. Manik Mia Avenue, Dhaka. Earlier, police had attacked protesters. In response, enraged protesters set fires on the streets. Photo by Rafi Al Ahnaf. Used with permission.
Instigations on social media
Social media can add another layer to the violence.
On April 11, 2026, an old video containing remarks alleged to be offensive to Islam circulated on Facebook before an attack on a Sufi shrine in Kushtia, Bangladesh. The Bangla Daily Prothom Alo reported that the 36-second video was circulated from three Facebook pages and four personal accounts. Police became aware of the possibility of unrest at about 9 a.m. and contacted local leaders. Later that day, more than 100 people attacked the shrine.
Its spiritual leader, Abdur Rahman, also known as Shamim al-Jahangir, was beaten and hacked to death. The shrine was vandalized and set on fire.
Ruhany said mobs do not depend on social media alone.
“It also happens on the ground. When there is a movement, people come into the streets and mobs form there,” he said. “Social media still plays a role, particularly when a religiously offensive post circulates on Facebook and creates anger among people, pushing the situation toward violence.”
The subsequent murder case also raised questions about political affiliations. The victim’s brother filed a case naming four people and another 180 to 200 unidentified suspects. According to the Daily Star, the named accused included a former Kushtia district president of Islami Chhatra Shibir who was also a Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami member, a local Jamaat activist and the local president of Bangladesh Khelafat Majlis. Jamaat representatives denied that their members were involved.
Four days after the killing, police had yet to arrest any of the four named accused. By May 1, however, four suspects had been arrested in connection with the attack.
The Pabna and Kushtia cases unfolded differently. In Pabna, police were already at the scene but said they were outnumbered. In Kushtia, police knew several hours before the attack that unrest was possible. Together, the cases raise questions about both prevention and accountability.
Lack of enforcement of justice
Ruhany linked crowd action partly to perceptions of the justice system.
“People do not have the assurance that they will get justice,” he said. “Judgments are delivered, but they are not always enforced. And the lengthy judicial process also contributes to this.”
His observation is one explanation rather than evidence that everyone involved in mob violence acts for the same reason. Such incidents in Bangladesh have emerged from different circumstances, including criminal accusations, claims of religious offense and attempts to press particular demands.
Ruhany also questioned police preparedness.
“The police no longer have the same morale they had before August 5,” he said. “And in areas where mob violence occurs, the police are often not prepared. We do not see the police maintaining a constant state of preparedness.”
Bangladesh’s reliance on street mobilization did not begin with the 2024 uprising. Rallies, strikes, blockades, and marches have shaped the country’s political life for decades, while ASK’s human rights statistics archive contains records of mob beatings going back more than a decade.
The July 2024 uprising again demonstrated the power of mass street mobilization. After weeks of student-led protests that expanded into a broader movement, then-prime minister Sheikh Hasina resigned and left Bangladesh on August 5.
July 11, 2024, Quota Movement, Shahbagh, Dhaka. Photo by Sabbirul Islam. Used with permission.
But street protest and mob punishment are not the same. The distinction has also appeared in the government’s response. The Home Minister of the current government, Salahuddin Ahmed, said on his first working day in February 2026 that mob action would not be tolerated, while lawful meetings, rallies and other democratic activities could continue.
The issue has also reached the courts. On February 2, 2026, following a public-interest petition filed by ASK, Bangladesh’s High Court asked the government to explain why its failure to prevent and control mob killings and mass beatings should not be declared unlawful. The court also asked why authorities should not be directed to take effective legal measures to prevent such violence.
Six months later, the government was still publicly addressing the problem. In parliament on August 27, Ahmed said the government was following a “zero tolerance” policy toward mob violence. He said punishing or physically assaulting someone without due legal process was illegal and cited measures including increased patrols, intelligence surveillance, CCTV installation and social-media monitoring in areas considered at risk.
In Bangladesh, rights groups continue to record deaths, the High Court has questioned the state’s response, and the government has promised tougher action. Whether those commitments translate into preventing attacks and moving cases from arrest to prosecution remains an open question.
Written by Maksuda Akter

By Kingsley Omonobi
The FCT Police Command said on Sunday night that it’s operatives, working in conjunction with personnel of the federal fire service have contained the fire which occured in Byazhin at a cooking gas sales plant.
The Police also noted that a manhunt for the erring driver that caused the fire as a result of driving against traffic is ongoing.

Cooking gas sale plant nearby.
“Following receipt of the report, a Police team from the Kubwa Police Division was promptly deployed to the scene, where they were met with a raging inferno at the gas plant, which had engulfed nearby shops and other properties.
“The Police team promptly contacted the Federal Fire Service, which responded and aided in containing the fire.
“Preliminary investigations by the Police team revealed that the fire outbreak was caused by the driver of an unregistered Toyota
4Runner Jeep, who was driving against traffic (one-way).
“The driver reportedly lost control of the vehicle and crashed into the nearby cooking gas plant, causing an explosion which engulfed nearby shops and other properties.
“The driver and occupants of the vehicle fled the scene immediately.
“While the Command is currently on the trail of the erring driver, having established his identity, the fire has been contained and no casualties have been recorded.
“However, a detailed assessment of the value of properties lost in the inferno is yet to be determined.
“The Command assures residents that normalcy has been restored and residents can return to their lawful businesses.
“Members of the public are enjoined to remain security conscious and vigilant of their surroundings.
“Suspicious persons or activities should be promptly reported to the nearest police station or through the Command’s emergency
numbers: 08032003913, 08028940883.”

items.content:
Goncalo Ramos started in place of Cristiano Ronaldo and scored the winner as Portugal made it back-to-back victories to start their UEFA Nations League title defence by beating Norway 2-1 in Oslo on Sunday.
Jorge Jesus’s men have responded well to their tame World Cup last-16 loss to Spain, having also beaten Wales 1-0 in Group A4 on Thursday.
The 41-year-old Ronaldo was named among the substitutes for the first time for Portugal since a Nations League game against Scotland in September 2024, and did not get onto the pitch as Jesus looks to manage his minutes across an expanded international break.
His replacement Ramos showed what he could do with his 12th international goal and an industrious performance.
“Every moment is important. The most important thing is to show what I can do whenever I’m called upon and to contribute to the team,” Ramos told Sport TV.
“It was a demonstration of my work, of what I can offer the team -– not just goals, but everything I do on the pitch.”
World Cup quarter-finalists Norway were left to rue some wasteful finishing in front of goal as they failed to build on their opening 3-2 win over Denmark.
The first big chance fell to Erling Haaland, but the Manchester City striker mishit his attempted volley after being picked out by Martin Odegaard, and Portugal goalkeeper Diogo Costa was able to make the save.
The away team quickly made Haaland pay as Joao Felix stroked a fine finish into the bottom corner from the edge of the box in the 17th minute.
Haaland looked certain to equalise shortly afterwards when Costa spilled the ball into his path, but he was denied by a superb block from his City teammate Ruben Dias.
The Norway talisman was foiled by Costa again 10 minutes before half-time as the ‘keeper made an excellent stop from his downward header.
Haaland finally converted six minutes into the second half, tapping in from Patrick Berg’s header across goal.
But Norway gave back the lead immediately to their opponents, as goalkeeper Orjan Nyland passed the ball straight to Ramos, who coolly chipped it into the net.
Rafael Leao had a shot deflected onto the crossbar as Portugal pushed to make the game safe.
Nyland had his blushes spared when a VAR review ruled out another opportunistic Ramos effort for the tightest of offsides.
The ‘keeper waited for a long pass over the top to reach him, then took a swipe at thin air as Ramos got to the ball before him and rolled it into an empty net.
Norway threw everyone forward, including Nyland, in the closing stages, but could not find another leveller.

items.content:
Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in a Nations League clash on Sunday amid an eerie and sombre atmosphere that saw the Irish players wear black armbands over the war in Gaza.
Ireland’s players also bowed their heads as the Israeli national anthem was played at the near-empty Debrecen stadium in Hungary.
The teams skipped the traditional pre-match handshakes and did not exchange pennants either.
Troy Parrott made a heart sign with his hands after opening the scoring on 14 minutes, while Jack Moylan kissed the Irish badge on his jersey and his black armband after netting the third goal 25 minutes in.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accused Ireland of being “on the wrong side of history” over the players’ actions.
In a lengthy post on X, Saar referenced the Irish team of 1939 giving the Nazi salute ahead of a match against Germany in Bremen.
He also referred to Irish neutrality during the Second World War and the condolences offered by then-prime minister Eaemon de Valera to the German representative in Dublin following Adolf Hitler’s death.
“Almost 90 years have passed. Ireland’s unique talent for finding itself on the wrong side of history remains intact,” he added.
The game, in which Israel were the nominal hosts, had been in doubt earlier in the week until Ireland’s players voted overwhelmingly to fulfil the fixture, despite pressure from back home to boycott the match.
Only one player, goalkeeper Gavin Buzunu, pulled out, saying “it would be wrong to participate” in either this match or the return fixture in Serbia on October 4 due to the “killing of innocent people”.
The Irish federation did not reserve any tickets for fans to attend the match and public broadcaster RTE was due to show it without commentary.
“Sports, soccer, basketball, everything is for the public, the people, and not for politics,” 31-year-old software development teacher Mol Michael, draped in an Israeli scarf, told AFP.
“Once you decide, because of politics, to cancel the Irish audience, this is a really stupid move from Ireland, in my opinion.”
Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy often linked to the country’s own history of British rule.
Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway, and has repeatedly criticised Israel over the Gaza conflict.
Israel strongly rejects allegations its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide.

items.content:
Everyone who starts planning a trip to the Everest region eventually hits the same wall: there isn’t one obvious way to do this. You can fly over the Khumbu in a helicopter and be back in Kathmandu in time for dinner. You can walk the whole way up and take a chopper back down instead of retracing your steps on foot. Or you can treat the trek as just the warm-up and go climb something. Three very different trips, all sold under the umbrella of “Everest,” and most first-time researchers don’t realize how different they actually are until they’re knee-deep in tour operator websites at 1am.
So let’s sort it out properly. The three main options are the Everest base camp helicopter tour, the Everest base camp trek helicopter return, and Island Peak climbing. They’re not three flavors of the same trip — they ask completely different things of your body, your schedule, and your tolerance for discomfort. Short on time? The helicopter route probably makes more sense. Want the actual walking experience, the tea houses, the yak trains on the trail? Go with the trek-and-fly-back option. Already trekked before and craving something with real technical stakes? That’s when Island Peak enters the conversation.
This isn’t a listicle dressed up as advice. It’s meant to help you figure out what each of these trips actually feels like day to day, what your body has to deal with at altitude, and what you should honestly expect before you hand over a deposit.
Understanding the Everest Region Before You Choose
Almost every route into this part of the Himalayas starts the same way: a flight from Kathmandu into Lukla, followed by a walk up the Khumbu Valley through Namche Bazaar, Tengboche, Dingboche, and Lobuche before reaching Gorakshep and, finally, Everest Base Camp itself. On a map it doesn’t look far. In practice, altitude does more to shape the experience than distance ever does.
Namche Bazaar sits at around 3,440 meters and already feels like a different world — thinner air, sharper light, colder nights. Keep climbing past Tengboche’s monastery and into Dingboche, and the landscape strips down to rock, prayer flags, and glacier moraine. This is Sagarmatha National Park, home turf of the Sherpa communities who’ve lived and worked in these valleys for generations, and the backdrop against which Mount Everest and Kala Patthar eventually come into view.
Here’s the thing people underestimate: reaching Everest Base Camp by helicopter and reaching it after four or five days of walking are, in a strange way, two completely different destinations, even though the GPS coordinates match exactly.
Altitude Is Part of the Adventure
Above roughly 3,000 meters, your body needs time to adjust to less available oxygen — that’s acclimatization, and it’s not optional just because you’re fit. Headaches, unusual tiredness, dizziness, or nausea aren’t signs of weakness; they’re signs you went up too fast. Marathon runners get altitude sickness. So do mountain guides, occasionally. A sensibly built itinerary bakes in acclimatization days and gradual elevation gain for exactly this reason, and it’s one of the few things worth not cutting corners on.
Everest Base Camp Helicopter Tour: Seeing the Himalayas With Less Trekking
The Everest base camp helicopter tour suits a specific kind of traveler: someone with a week of vacation rather than three, someone older or simply not drawn to multi-day walking, or someone stacking Everest onto a broader Nepal itinerary that already includes Chitwan or Pokhara. Families traveling with a mix of ages often lean this way too.
The experience is genuinely different from trekking, not just a faster version of it. From a helicopter, the terrain changes in seconds — green terraced hills give way to rock and ice almost before you’ve adjusted your camera settings. A trek reveals the same landscape gradually: villages, monasteries, mule trains, and the slow shift in vegetation as you climb. Neither is wrong, they’re just different lenses on the same mountains.
A typical itinerary leaves Kathmandu early, flies toward the Khumbu, passes over or near several high-altitude landmarks, and — depending on the specific package, the weather, and operational clearance that day — may include a brief landing before heading back. It’s worth being precise here: “seeing Everest” and “landing at Everest Base Camp” aren’t always the same product, so read the itinerary closely rather than assuming.
Helicopter operations in the high Himalayas are genuinely weather-dependent. Visibility, wind, and landing conditions all factor into whether a flight goes ahead as planned, gets rerouted, or gets postponed. Bring sun protection, sunglasses, warm layers even for a short flight, and follow whatever the flight crew tells you — mountain aviation isn’t a place for improvisation.
What You Miss When You Fly Instead of Trek
Honestly? Quite a lot. You skip the gradual physical adjustment to altitude, the conversations with lodge owners, the changing forest-to-alpine vegetation, and the daily rhythm that makes a trek feel earned. What you gain instead is time — days, not hours, saved — which for some travelers is simply the more important currency.
Everest Base Camp Trek Return by Helicopter: A Middle Ground
This is the option for people who want to actually walk the trail but aren’t attached to walking back down it too. You still get the full ascent — Namche’s switchbacks, the monastery at Tengboche, the increasingly bare landscape past Dingboche — and you still arrive at Base Camp on foot, which for a lot of trekkers is the whole point. The difference comes after you’ve reached the high point: instead of retracing four or five days downhill on tired legs, you fly back to Kathmandu (or Lukla, depending on arrangements) when weather and aircraft availability line up.
There’s a real physical logic to this. The descent on a standard EBC trek isn’t dangerous exactly, but it’s repetitive and hard on the knees, and by that point in the trip most people are running on fumes anyway. Cutting that out doesn’t cheapen the achievement — you still did the climb — it just changes how your body feels afterward.
One caveat worth repeating: a helicopter return is not guaranteed the way a scheduled bus ticket is. Weather, aircraft availability, and landing conditions in the mountains can shift plans at short notice. If you’re booking this kind of itinerary, don’t schedule an international flight home for the same evening you’re expecting to land back in Kathmandu — give yourself a buffer day.
Trekking to Everest Base Camp vs Flying Both Ways
Walking both directions gives you the deepest version of the trail experience and the most time actually spent in the Khumbu. The trek-plus-helicopter-return option keeps that trail experience but trims the return journey down to under an hour in the air. The pure helicopter tour, by contrast, maximizes time efficiency at the cost of almost all the walking. None of these is objectively “best” — it depends entirely on what you’re actually after.
Island Peak Climbing: When Trekking Turns Into Mountaineering
Island Peak climbing — also known locally as Imja Tse — sits in a different category altogether. It’s approached through the same Everest region trails, but somewhere past Base Camp the trip stops being a trek and starts being a climb. You’re now dealing with glacier travel, snow and ice conditions, fixed ropes, crampons, and a level of physical and technical demand that a standard EBC trek simply doesn’t ask of you.
This matters because a lot of trekkers assume that finishing the Base Camp trek qualifies them for Island Peak. It doesn’t, automatically. What actually matters is prior mountain experience, genuine physical conditioning, how your body handles sustained altitude, and — just as important — climbing under the guidance of properly qualified professionals who know the current route and snow conditions, which can shift meaningfully from one season to the next.
How Island Peak Changes the Everest Experience
The mental shift is as big as the physical one. Instead of a long walk with stunning views, you’re now dealing with pre-dawn starts in freezing temperatures, deliberate and careful movement on rope, and a level of concentration that doesn’t let up until you’re back down. It’s not a sightseeing trip with extra steps — it’s a genuine climb, and it should be chosen by people looking for exactly that, not as a default upgrade from trekking.
Three Ways to Experience the Everest Himalayas
For Limited Time: Helicopter Experience
Ideal if your priority is seeing Everest and its neighboring giants without committing days of walking to get there.
For the Trail Experience: Trek + Helicopter Return
Ideal if you want the villages, the culture, and the walking rhythm of the Khumbu, with a shorter return journey at the end.
For a Bigger Challenge: Island Peak
Ideal for properly prepared trekkers ready to move from walking into actual mountaineering, under professional guidance.
Practical Planning: What Travelers Should Think About Before Going
Acclimatization — take altitude seriously, especially above Namche.
Weather — mountain weather can disrupt flights and helicopter schedules, so build in flexibility.
Fitness — sustained walking fitness for trekking; additional conditioning and skills for climbing.
Equipment — warm layers, solid trekking footwear, sun protection, gloves, and appropriate headwear.
Insurance — confirm your policy explicitly covers high-altitude trekking or climbing at the elevations involved.
Guides and operators — choose properly registered providers with experienced guides and clear emergency procedures.
Permits — check exactly what’s required for your specific route and activity before you leave home.
Responsible travel — respect Sherpa communities, monasteries, and the fragile mountain environment.
The Human Side of the Himalayas
It’s easy to talk about altitude charts and flight logistics and forget that this region is, first and foremost, someone’s home. The Sherpa communities who run the lodges, guide the climbs, and carry the loads have been doing this work for generations, and walking through Namche or the upper Khumbu makes that far more obvious than any helicopter window ever could. Prayer flags snapping in the wind, mani walls you pass on the correct side, monasteries tucked into the hillside — these aren’t just scenery, they’re part of daily life here.
Responsible tourism in this context is fairly simple in practice: hire local guides and porters, ask before photographing people or ceremonies, pack out what you pack in, and treat religious sites with the same respect you’d want shown at home.
Which Everest Adventure Fits You?
Traveler priority
Most suitable experience
Very limited time
Everest Base Camp helicopter tour
Wants to experience the trail
Everest Base Camp trek
Wants the trail but a shorter return
Trek with helicopter return

Island Peak climbing

Helicopter experience
Wants deeper cultural and walking experience

Your own health, altitude tolerance, weather luck, budget, and available time should shape the final call more than any table can.
Frequently Asked Questions
Is an Everest Base Camp helicopter tour suitable for beginners?
It can be, since it doesn’t demand the multi-day walking commitment a trek does. That said, “beginner-friendly” doesn’t mean risk-free — high-altitude exposure and mountain weather still need to be taken seriously, even on a short flight.
Can I do the Everest Base Camp trek and return by helicopter?
Yes, this kind of itinerary is offered by a number of operators, though the specifics depend on weather, flight conditions, and aircraft availability on the day. Confirm the exact pickup location and backup plan before you leave.
Is Island Peak harder than the Everest Base Camp trek?
Yes, clearly so in technical terms. EBC is a high-altitude trek; Island Peak adds glacier travel, ropes, and mountaineering skills on top of everything a trek already demands.
How much time should I allow for an Everest Base Camp adventure?
It depends heavily on which version you choose — flying, trekking, trekking with a helicopter return, or adding Island Peak on top. Whatever you pick, build in buffer days, since mountain weather can shuffle schedules with little warning.
What should I consider before choosing a high-altitude adventure in Nepal?
Acclimatization, fitness, weather flexibility, insurance coverage, equipment, guide quality, permits, and your own comfort with risk. The practical bottom line: pick the experience that matches your actual ability and available time, not just the most famous itinerary.
Closing — The Himalayas Are Experienced at Different Speeds
There isn’t a single correct way to experience Everest, and honestly, that’s part of what makes this region so compelling. A helicopter gives you perspective and speed. Trekking gives you immersion and the slow accumulation of small moments — a cup of tea in Dingboche, a monastery bell in Tengboche, the first glimpse of Everest’s summit pyramid from the trail. Island Peak adds something else again: a genuine climb, with all the discipline and reward that comes with it.
The right adventure is simply the one that matches your time, your preparation, your physical ability, and — maybe most importantly — the reason you wanted to come here in the first place.

items.content:
Jurgen Klopp tasted defeat for the first time as Germany manager as his side lost 1-0 to Greece in Augsburg on Sunday, with Dimitrios Kourbelis scoring the only goal.
In his first game on home soil, Klopp’s side offered little in attack and lacked the energy they had displayed on the former Liverpool coach’s debut in a 1-1 away draw with the Netherlands on Thursday.
The Germans had struggled to find a way through the Greek defence for the opening hour before the visitors broke through on the counter, with Kourbelis scoring in the 74th minute.
It was Greece’s first ever win against Germany.
Several regulars missed out with Klopp trying to get a better idea of the talent at his disposal, but the defeat illustrated the scale of his task in reviving the flagging giants.
“I think the important thing is that we stand together and that won’t change,” Germany defender Jonathan Tah told ARD.
“Of course, with the enthusiasm surrounding the new coach, things can get very hyped up from the outside, but ultimately, it comes down to what we do on the pitch and how we perform.”
The 59-year-old took over Germany in July after the four-time World Cup winners were eliminated at the last-32 stage of the global showpiece in North America, their third consecutive early exit from the tournament.
Klopp had included 16 uncapped players in his 44-man squad as he warned that he would be using the competition to have a look at the players at his disposal.
Among the five alterations to his starting XI was Hoffenheim forward Bambase Conte, a shock call-up after playing just four top-flight matches.
Conte looked sharp and shot just wide with two minutes gone.
Barcelona forward Karim Adeyemi had the best chance of the opening half when he stormed past the Greek defence on the counter, but sprayed his shot just over the crossbar.
Conte was again dangerous after the break, forcing a low fingertip save from Greek goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis.
With Germany dominating possession but offering little in attack, the visitors grew bolder and more incisive on the counter and should have taken the lead when Fotis Ioannidis blasted wide of the goal with just Alexander Nuebel to beat.
Greece broke through moments later, however, when Kourbelis’s low shot took a wicked deflection off Joshua Kimmich and rolled into the bottom left corner.
Greece then held firm for a breakthrough win over Germany, after seven defeats and three draws dating back to 1960.

The Presidency has said President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is hale and hearty and has continued to discharge his responsibilities while on a working vacation outside Nigeria.
The Special Adviser to the President on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, disclosed this in a post on his X platform on Sunday.
Onanuga said Tinubu was not required to be physically present in Abuja to perform his duties, particularly with the availability of digital communication tools.
“Nigeria’s President is hale and hearty. He has been on a working vacation, which he is perfectly entitled to. In this digital age, he does not need to be physically present in Abuja to do the work for which he was elected in 2023,” he said.
According to him, the President had continued to work during his vacation, including meetings with investors in France.
Onanuga said Tinubu had most recently facilitated a $7 billion deep-sea port project in Ogun Waterside, an initiative of the Ogun State Government.
He also compared Tinubu’s absence from the ongoing United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York with that of other African leaders.
“Two other important African leaders were not in New York for the UNGA: South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa and Egypt’s Abdel Fattah el-Sisi,” he said.
Onanuga said Ramaphosa had booked himself off public engagements, while Egypt had not faced public uproar over President el-Sisi’s absence from the UNGA.
He said Tinubu had announced his annual vacation and delegated Nigeria’s representation at the UNGA to Vice President Kashim Shettima.
The presidential aide also criticised former Anambra State governor and 2023 presidential candidate of the Labour Party, Peter Obi, over comments concerning Tinubu’s whereabouts.
“Yet Peter Obi pretends to be unaware of President Tinubu’s whereabouts and asks the puerile question his followers are asking on X,” Onanuga said.
He added that Tinubu was expected to return to Nigeria during the week to participate in activities marking the country’s 66th Independence Anniversary.
According to Onanuga, the President would also honour the late Chief MKO Abiola, whom he described as a martyr of Nigeria’s democratic struggle, by attending the premiere of a movie produced in his memory in Lagos.

items.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) has reaffirmed its commitment to neutrality, fairness and transparency in the conduct of the 2027 general elections.
The Commission disclosed this on its official X platform on Sunday, following a visit by its Chairman, Prof. Joash Amupitan, SAN, to the Emir of Zazzau, Amb. Ahmed Nuhu Bamalli, CFR.
The visit was part of activities ahead of the Commission’s planned interactive meeting with staff and readiness assessment for the 2027 general election at the zonal level.
Amupitan was accompanied by National Commissioners, the Acting Director-General of the Electoral Institute, his Chief Press Secretary, Chief Technical Assistant, Chief of Staff, other special aides and directors of the Commission.
At the palace of the 19th Emir of Zazzau, the INEC chairman described the visit as an important stakeholder engagement ahead of the 2027 electoral activities.
He said traditional institutions remained important stakeholders in the electoral process because of their influence and grassroots reach.
According to him, elections are fundamentally about the social contract between citizens and those entrusted with public office, making public trust critical to the success of democracy.
Amupitan said INEC had commenced preparations early because of the size and complexity of conducting elections in Nigeria.
He said the Commission had moved away from last-minute preparations and was testing, auditing and strengthening its operational systems well ahead of the 2027 polls.
The INEC chairman assured the Emir that the Commission remained committed to neutrality, fairness and transparency.
“We have no candidates, we have no political party, we have no interest other than the sovereign will of the people of Nigeria,” he said.

items.author: Akinbayo Wahab
items.content:
Gov. Abba Kabir Yusuf of Kano State has thrown his weight behind the continued rotation of presidential power between the Northern and Southern parts of Nigeria.
Yusuf made this known on Sunday at the Government House, Kano, while unveiling 50 vehicles donated by Chief Government Oweizide Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Tompolo.
The governor commended Tompolo for donating the vehicles to support APC campaign mobilisation in Kano ahead of the 2027 general elections.
He said his position was based on the principle that presidential power should rotate between the North and South, with each region given the opportunity to produce a president for two consecutive terms.
According to the governor, allowing each region to complete two terms will provide sufficient time for an administration to implement major policies, programmes and development projects.
He, therefore, called for support for President Bola Tinubu to complete a second term, arguing that this would allow the South to complete its two-term cycle before power returns to the North.
Yusuf urged political stakeholders, particularly in the North, to exercise patience and allow the current political arrangement to run its course.
“Power will return to the North after the completion of the Southern region’s two-term cycle in 2031,” he said.
He said the rotational presidency should be viewed as a means of promoting fairness, national cohesion, mutual trust and a sense of belonging among Nigerians from different parts of the country.
The governor also urged politicians and political parties to run peaceful, issue-based campaigns ahead of the 2027 general elections.
He called on political actors to focus on policies, programmes and development plans rather than personal attacks, inflammatory rhetoric or actions capable of undermining peace.
The governor reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to peaceful democratic engagement.
He urged all stakeholders to place the unity, peace and development of Kano State and Nigeria above partisan differences.

items.author: Hamisu Kabir Matazu
items.content:
Governor Babagana Umara Zulum of Borno State has called on political aspirants who lost out during party primaries to put their grievances aside, forgive past shortcomings, and rally behind the All Progressives Congress (APC) ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Governor Zulum made the appeal on Sunday upon returning to Maiduguri from Canada and the United States, where he was honored with Pan-African top leadership award.
He was received at the airport by party executives, federal and state lawmakers, top government officials and a mammoth crowd of supporters.
Addressing the gathering, the governor urged political contenders to view electoral defeat as an act of divine will.
“For those who contested the party primaries, from governorship down to the House of Assembly, if we offended anyone, he should forgive us,” Zulum said.
“Take it as a will of God, because it’s only God that gives power to whom He wishes. The choice is from God, and no one has the might to fight God’s choice. We love every party member equally.”
Reflecting on his administration’s performance over the past seven years, Zulum maintained that his government had operated with integrity and fairness.
“Throughout the over seven years we spent in administration, we have not cheated anyone. Whatever we had not achieved was not of our making, but we tried our best,” he stated.
Acknowledging that his administration might have fallen short of some expectations, Zulum sued for reconciliation. “I’m appealing to you, whoever holds a grudge that we fell short in meeting his expectations should forgive us. We are human, and where we erred, I assure you that the incoming governor, Mustapha Gubio, will execute [the remaining tasks].”
Positioning the APC as the sole dominant political force in Borno, Zulum asserted that no other party possessed the strength to rival the ruling party in the state.
He charged party loyalists to vote massively across the board, from the presidency down to the 27 state assembly seats, urging them to leverage the current political standing of the state.
He highlighted that with the Vice Presidential position currently occupied by a son of the state, Borno is uniquely positioned to secure more federal projects and interventions, provided the electorate remains united under the APC banner.
While stressing the importance of total party loyalty, the governor issued a firm note to dissenters, stating that anyone who refuses to support the party would not benefit from the incoming administration, though he expressed confidence in total victory regardless.
Governor Zulum also expressed appreciation to party stakeholders, current officeholders, and executives for their steadfast support, assuring women and youth groups that more empowerment programs would be rolled out within the week.
Reiterating his commitment to governance, the governor admitted that while it is humanly impossible to satisfy everyone, his administration remains dedicated to fulfilling its remaining promises, with the incoming leadership poised to complete any unfinished business across all 27 local government areas.

Y Mobile, an Apple Authorized Reseller, today announced the grand opening of its newest flagship store at Ocean Mall, Karachi, alongside the launch of its Bahadurabad location. The dual launch drew an overwhelming turnout, with customers lining up from the early hours to experience the brand’s expanded presence in the city.
The new stores mark a significant milestone in Y Mobile’s growth in Karachi, offering customers a premium, authentic Apple retail experience backed by expert guidance and dedicated customer service. Visitors on launch day had the opportunity to explore Apple’s full product lineup, with the recently launched iPhone 18 Pro Series drawing particular attention as the centerpiece of the event.
Throughout the day, both locations saw a steady stream of visitors, including technology enthusiasts, families, content creators, and long-standing Y Mobile customers. The response reflected strong demand for authorized Apple retail in Karachi and reinforced the brand’s growing footprint in the market.
“We are humbled by the trust and enthusiasm shown by the people of Karachi,” a Y Mobile spokesperson said. “This launch is more than an opening: it is a reflection of the relationship we have built with our customers over the years, and we are committed to bringing them closer to the best of Apple.”
Y Mobile plans to continue expanding its retail presence across Pakistan, with further store launches, exclusive offers, and customer initiatives expected in the coming months.
The Ocean Mall and Bahadurabad locations are now open to the public.

items.author: Qaisar Kamran
items.content:
The colours, cultural identity and changing character of Karachi were brought to the runway at 'Kaleidoscopic Karachi', a showcase held as part of LAAM Fashion Week 2026.
The one-day event, held at the Indus Valley School of Art and Architecture, brought together several leading fashion houses on a single runway, while also paying tribute to the history of fashion photography in Pakistan.
Collections by Deepak Perwani, Wardha Saleem, Khaadi, The Pink Tree Company and Sana Safinaz were presented during the show. The collections featured a mix of eastern and western silhouettes, with designers offering their own interpretations of Karachi's colours, contrasts and evolving fashion trends.
The event also brought together personalities from the fashion and entertainment industries, including Sharmila Farooqi, Aly Khan , Sarwat Gillani, Fahad Mirza, Maheen Khan, Preshay Adnan and Zainab Qayyum.
The appearance of two of Pakistan's well-known 1990s models, Fariha Altaf and Simi Pasha, was among the highlights of the evening. Their runway appearance brought back memories of an era that played an important role in shaping Pakistan's fashion industry.
Fashion designer Hassan Sheheryar Yasin, widely known as HSY, told Express Tribune that he was pleased to see designers from across Pakistan coming together and appreciating each other's work.
"We just finished watching a show, where I felt so good that all the designers from Pakistan came together and saw the collections. We cheered each other up," he said.
HSY also highlighted Karachi's creative potential, saying the event offered a glimpse of a side of the city that he felt had not been seen for a long time.
"Along with that, we saw the potential of Karachi, which I felt we haven't seen in a long time," he said.
Starting as a fashion choreographer in 1994, Yasin worked both as a choreographer and designer to various shows within Pakistan and international shows including Dubai, London, New York City and Toronto. 2000 marked the introduction of Yasin's own fashion label, HSY. Starting as a bridal and formal wear couture house, it became one of Pakistan's most recognized fashion labels. In 2007, Yasin introduced a jewellery line under the HSY brand.
Speaking about LAAM Fashion Week, HSY described it as an important platform for the growth of the country's fashion industry.
"It's a great platform. It's a platform where fashion will continue to grow, and that's the most important," he said.
Co-created by LAAM and Design 651, LFW is a long-term platform built to activate the entire fashion ecosystem. Anchored by LAAM's e-commerce prowess and driven by Design 651's strategic and creative leadership, LFW serves as a business development engine for the wider fashion community, a cultural and creative showcase for the region, and a retail channel for growth and visibility.
A major part of the event was a retrospective celebrating renowned fashion photographer Tapu Javeri's four decades of work.
The exhibition featured a selection of Javeri's memorable photographs, offering a visual journey through different periods of Pakistani fashion and documenting how the industry and its aesthetics have changed over the years.
Reflecting on the transformation of photography, Javeri recalled a time when taking photographs required considerable care and patience.
"There was a time when photography was done with a lot of effort. There were only a few photographs on one roll, so you had to be very careful while taking a picture that it did not go wrong," he said.
According to Javeri, the arrival of Photoshop changed photography by making image editing much easier and more accessible.
He said the industry had now entered another major phase with the arrival of artificial intelligence, which allows people to create millions of images and alter almost anything in a photograph.
Javeri said he felt traditional photography was now facing a significant transformation, with the nature of the photograph itself changing in the age of AI.
The event ultimately presented Karachi through its many visual identities, its colours, cultural influences, fashion trends and changing relationship with photography bringing its past and present together on a single runway.

items.title: Shohei Ohtani’s $700 million Dodgers contract and what it means for MLB
items.summary: Shohei Ohtani’s $700 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers sounds like a blockbuster headline figure, but the deal is far more unusual than that. The deal shifted the Dodgers' payroll strategy with $680 million deferred until 2034-43, and Ohtani's commercial appeal drew major attention in Japan and around the world. The deal also helped to change how massive player contracts can be structured by MLB teams.

The Punjab government has decided to shut down marriage halls across the province that continue to operate without suction hoods
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has directed its field teams to take action against marriage halls that failed to comply with the government’s instructions.
EPA Director General Abdullah Nayyer Sheikh issued orders to field officers to begin enforcement against non-compliant venues.
The move comes after the January 31 deadline for installing suction hoods in marriage halls expired.
