Gates mendukung keterlibatan pembuat kebijakan, penegak hukum, dan regulator dalam menentukan standar pengamanan serta mekanisme pengawasan AI.
“Tidak ada yang menganggap peraturan mandiri itu cukup,” kata Bill Gates, sebagaimana dikutip dari NBC, Sabtu (26/9/2026). Ia menjawab “tentu saja”
items.author: Yus Lianson
items.content:
Bill Gates kembali menyuarakan kekhawatirannya terkait kecerdasan buatan (AI) yang berkembang pesat hingga saat ini. Pendiri Microsoft itu menilai, pengawasan terhadap AI tidak bisa hanya mengandalkan perusahaan yang kembangkan teknologi tersebut.
Mantan bos Microsoft tersebut menyebutkan, pemerintah dan regulator juga harus ikut terlibat aktif untuk mengawasi perkembangan AI secara global.
Dalam wawancara dengan NBC News untuk program Meet the Press, Gates mengatakan, pendekatan self-regulation atau pengawasan mandiri oleh industri tidak cukup untuk menghadapi risiko muncul dari perkembangan AI.
Baca Juga: Apple Akui Bug Face ID iPhone 18 Pro, Siap Hadirkan Perbaikan Segera Lewat Pembaruan Software
Gates mendukung keterlibatan pembuat kebijakan, penegak hukum, dan regulator dalam menentukan standar pengamanan serta mekanisme pengawasan AI.
“Tidak ada yang menganggap peraturan mandiri itu cukup,” kata Bill Gates, sebagaimana dikutip dari NBC, Sabtu (26/9/2026). Ia menjawab “tentu saja”, saat ditanya apakah diperlukan legislasi terkait AI di Washington.
Menurutnya, pemerintah perlu terlibat dalam menentukan seperti apa safeguards atau pagar pengaman yang harus diterapkan industri AI. Ia mengakui, langkah tersebut dapat menambah beban bagi perusahaan, tetapi tidak harus menghambat inovasi secara signifikan.
Bill Gates Soroti Risiko Penyalahgunaan AI
Dalam wawancara yang sama, Bill Gates juga menyinggung potensi risiko apabila teknologi AI digunakan oleh pihak yang memiliki niat buruk.
Ia mengatakan, AI memiliki kemampuan yang cukup besar untuk memicu peristiwa yang dapat menyebabkan korban dalam skala sangat besar. Gates menyebut belum pernah ada senjata yang sekuat kombinasi antara aktor jahat dan teknologi AI generasi terbaru.
Meski demikian, pernyataan tersebut disampaikan dalam konteks diskusi mengenai potensi penyalahgunaan AI dan bukan prediksi bahwa skenario tersebut pasti akan terjadi. Fokus utama Gates tetap berada pada pentingnya membangun mekanisme pengawasan sebelum teknologi berkembang lebih jauh.
Perdebatan AI Safety Kembali Menguat
Komentar Bill Gates muncul ketika perdebatan mengenai AI safety kembali menjadi sorotan di industri teknologi.
Ilustrasi AI (Sumber: Freepik)
Beberapa pekan terakhir, sejumlah tokoh AI termasuk CEO Anthropic Dario Amodei dan CEO OpenAI Sam Altman dilaporkan mendukung perlambatan laju pengembangan model AI tertentu agar aspek keamanan dapat mengejar perkembangan kemampuan teknologi.
Di sisi lain, perdebatan mengenai bentuk regulasi yang ideal masih berlangsung. Sebagian pihak menilai pengawasan pemerintah diperlukan karena dampak AI berpotensi menyentuh keamanan siber, ekonomi, pendidikan, hingga keamanan nasional.
Namun ada juga yang khawatir regulasi yang terlalu ketat dapat menghambat inovasi dan memperkuat dominasi perusahaan besar yang sudah memiliki sumber daya lebih besar untuk memenuhi persyaratan regulasi.
Bagi Gates, persoalan utamanya bukan apakah perusahaan AI peduli terhadap risiko teknologi yang mereka kembangkan. Menurutnya, dampak AI terhadap masyarakat jauh lebih luas daripada ruang lingkup perusahaan teknologi, sehingga pemerintah dan institusi publik perlu ikut menentukan aturan mainnya
OpenAI Akui Agen AI Retas Situs Pemerintah Australia Saat Cari Data
OpenAI memperkenalkan framework baru untuk melacak dan melaporkan perilaku model AI yang tidak sesuai dengan instruksi.
Di sisi lain, OpenAI kembali menjadi sorotan. Kali ini, sebuah agen AI milik perusahaan kecerdasan tersebut dilaporkan sukses mengakses file non-publik di portal statistik Medicare Australia.
Disebutkan, agen AI milik OpenAI tersebut berhasil menembus sistem keamanan portal tersebut ketika sedang dipakai untuk menjalankan tugas riset internal.
Insiden peretasan oleh AI tersebut diungkap langsung oleh Perdana Menteri Australia, Anthony Albanese. Menurut pemerintah Australia, kejadian tersebut berlangsung pada 18 Juni ketika model AI milik OpenAI sedang melakukan penelitian tentang pengeluaran obat-obatan publik di Australia.
Dilansir The Hacker News, Kamis (24/9/2026), agen AI yang mencoba memperoleh data dari Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal tersebut beberapa kali ditolak oleh sistem.
Alih-alih berhenti, model tersebut menemukan cara lain untuk mendapatkan informasi yang dicari dan akhirnya memperoleh akses tidak sah ke sebagian area portal.
“Agen AI menemukan jalan untuk melewati pembatasan tersebut,” kata Albanese dalam konferensi pers di New York. Pemerintah Australia menyebut model tersebut mengakses file publik maupun non-publik yang berada di dalam portal statistik tersebut.
Portal yang Diretas Agen AI Tidak Berisi Data Pasien
Sam Altman beri clue kehadiran Orion lewat ketikan di X.
Meski terdengar mengkhawatirkan, pemerintah Australia menegaskan bahwa portal yang diakses bukan sistem yang menyimpan data pribadi pasien atau memproses klaim Medicare.
Portal tersebut digunakan untuk menyediakan statistik agregat terkait layanan kesehatan dan pengeluaran pemerintah. Hingga saat ini, pemerintah maupun OpenAI menyatakan belum menemukan bukti bahwa data pribadi warga Australia ikut diakses.
OpenAI mengatakan informasi yang diperoleh model mencakup statistik kesehatan agregat dan nama file internal. Perusahaan juga menyebut tidak menemukan indikasi bahwa rekam medis pasien berhasil diakses.

Source: Inc42
Key Startup Funding Highlights Of The Week
AI emerged as the most funded sector this week. Five AI startups bagged a cumulative $89.3 Mn, with Ema’s $77 Mn round alone contributing 86% to the sector’s total haul. Following suit was cleantech, which bagged $85 Mn across just one deal.
Ecommerce led in deal activity, with six startups collectively raising $3.8 Mn.
Early stage funding activity remained strong this week as seed-stage startups raised $20.3 Mn across five deals. Rivet’s $10.5 Mn round accounting for more than half of the total.
Peercheque and Sauce.VC were the most active investors of the week, backing two startups each.
Startup Fund Updates Of The Week
The Centre is considering an anchor investment of ₹15,000 Cr to ₹20,000 Cr in the proposed National Frontier AI & Compute Fund (NFAICF) to build compute infrastructure and support frontier AI startups.
Nykaa and L’Oréal’s corporate venture fund BOLD have banded together to invest in Indian beauty and personal care brands. The partnership will offer capital and industry expertise while allowing founders to retain operational and creative control.
Startup IPO Updates Of The Week
Moneyview’s IPO was subscribed 6.01X at the end of the second day of bidding, receiving bids for 139.8 Cr shares against 23.25 Cr shares on offer. The IPO will now close on September 28, with a tentative listing scheduled for October 1.
Snapdeal parent AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO was subscribed 23% at the end of the first day of bidding, with investors placing bids for 1.72 Cr shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer.
Furniture and appliance rental startup Furlenco is gearing up for an FY28 IPO, with an eye on a potential ₹1,000 Cr to ₹1,200 Cr public issue. The startup is targeting a valuation of around ₹7,000 Cr.
Used-car marketplace Spinny has confidentially filed its DRHP with SEBI. The Gurugram-based startup is looking to raise ₹2,500 Cr to ₹3,000 Cr via a mix of fresh shares and an offer for sale (OFS), with a potential listing targeted for 2027.
Other Developments Of The Week
Enterprise tech startup CodeKarma is in talks to raise $5 Mn to $6 Mn in a fresh funding round expected to be led by existing investors Prosus and Accel.

items.summary:
Microsoft angkat bicara tentang laporan yang menyebutkan mayoritas pre-order Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) datang dari PlayStation 5 (PS5), dengan menegaskan pre-order GTA 6 di platform Xbox berada di atas ekspektasi perusahaan.
Pernyataan ini disampaikan langsung oleh Xbox Chief Strategy Officer, Matthew Ball. Lewat akun media sosial X (dulu bernama Twitter). Sabtu (26/9/2026), Ball menyebut GTA 6 turut memecahkan rekor pre-order di ekosistem Xbox.

Menurut Ball, distribusi pre-order GTA 6 mencerminkan kondisi pangsa pasar konsol saat ini, bukan indikasi Xbox tertinggal. Ia menyebut porsi pre-order yang diterima Xbox kurang lebih sejalan dengan pangsa pasar konsol Xbox dibanding PlayStation, sehingga Microsoft tidak melihat angka tersebut sebagai masalah.
“Klaim bahwa Xbox tertinggal jauh menjadi kurang relevan jika dibandingkan dengan ukuran basis pengguna masing-masing platform,” kata Matthew Ball.

Microsoft angkat bicara tentang laporan yang menyebutkan mayoritas pre-order Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) datang dari PlayStation 5 (PS5), dengan menegaskan pre-order GTA 6 di platform Xbox berada di atas ekspektasi perusahaan.
Pernyataan ini disampaikan langsung oleh Xbox Chief Strategy Officer, Matthew Ball. Lewat akun media sosial X (dulu bernama Twitter). Sabtu (26/9/2026), Ball menyebut GTA 6 turut memecahkan rekor pre-order di ekosistem Xbox.
Baca Juga: Indonesia Kembali Jadi Tuan Rumah WEC26, Pertandingkan 5 Game Esports
Menurut Ball, distribusi pre-order GTA 6 mencerminkan kondisi pangsa pasar konsol saat ini, bukan indikasi Xbox tertinggal. Ia menyebut porsi pre-order yang diterima Xbox kurang lebih sejalan dengan pangsa pasar konsol Xbox dibanding PlayStation, sehingga Microsoft tidak melihat angka tersebut sebagai masalah.
“Klaim bahwa Xbox tertinggal jauh menjadi kurang relevan jika dibandingkan dengan ukuran basis pengguna masing-masing platform,” kata Matthew Ball.
Sejauh ini, Microsoft tidak mengungkap angka pasti pre-order GTA 6 di Xbox, termasuk rekor yang diklaim Ball.
Pre-order GTA 6 Didominasi PS5
Sebelumnya, laporan yang beredar menyebut pre-order GTA 6 jauh lebih banyak berasal dari PS5 dibanding Xbox. Namun angka tersebut berasal dari estimasi pihak ketiga dan bukan data resmi yang dirilis Rockstar Games maupun Take-Two Interactive.
Karena itu, hingga saat ini belum ada gambaran resmi mengenai distribusi penjualan GTA 6 di masing-masing platform.
GTA 6 Jadi Ujian Penting bagi Platform Konsol
GTA 6 diperkirakan menjadi salah satu peluncuran game terbesar dalam sejarah industri video game. Tingginya antusiasme pemain membuat performa pre-order game ini ikut menjadi indikator yang diperhatikan pelaku industri.
Bagi PlayStation, dominasi pre-order dapat memperkuat posisi platform tersebut sebagai rumah bagi sebagian besar pemain konsol.
Sementara bagi Xbox, fokusnya tampaknya bukan mengejar angka absolut, melainkan memastikan performa penjualan tetap sejalan dengan ukuran ekosistem yang dimiliki saat ini.
Karena itu, Microsoft menilai hasil pre-order GTA 6 masih berada dalam jalur yang sesuai ekspektasi perusahaan, meski berbagai laporan menunjukkan PS5 memiliki porsi yang lebih besar.
Sejauh ini Rockstar Games maupun Take-Two Interactive belum mengungkap data resmi terkait distribusi pre-order GTA 6 di masing-masing platform.
PS5 Pro Mulai Langka di AS Setelah GTA 6 Tampilkan Gameplay Terbaru
Bocoran GTA 6 belum berhenti, Take-Two mulai buru CyberLeek
Lebih lanjut, Sony PlayStation 5 Pro dilaporkan mulai sulit ditemukan di sejumlah retailer besar Amerika Serikat setelah Rockstar Games menampilkan Extended Look untuk Grand Theft Auto VI. Kondisi ini menarik perhatian karena GTA 6 telah dikonfirmasi mendapatkan optimasi untuk PS5 Pro, meskipun Rockstar belum menjelaskan secara detail peningkatan yang akan diberikan.
Harga resmi PS5 Pro di AS berada di angka US$899. Namun, kelangkaan stok membuat sejumlah penjual pihak ketiga menaikkan harga secara signifikan. Di Amazon dan Walmart, beberapa unit bahkan ditawarkan hingga US$1.300, sementara listing baru di eBay disebut mencapai sekitar US$1.200. Angka tersebut tentu belum bisa dianggap sebagai harga transaksi sebenarnya karena belum diketahui berapa banyak konsumen yang benar-benar membeli di harga tersebut.
Di sisi lain, kondisi ini belum tentu berarti PS5 Pro akan benar-benar langka hingga peluncuran GTA 6. PlayStation Direct masih menyediakan konsol dengan harga normal, sementara Sony diperkirakan akan kembali mengisi stok retailer menjelang peluncuran game pada 19 November 2026.
GTA 6 Memang Mendapat Optimasi PS5 Pro
Rockstar telah mengonfirmasi bahwa GTA 6 akan mendapatkan peningkatan khusus untuk PS5 Pro. Sayangnya, detail mengenai resolusi, kualitas visual, maupun frame rate masih belum diumumkan. Hal ini membuat cukup sulit untuk menilai seberapa besar perbedaan pengalaman antara PS5 standar dan PS5 Pro.
Ada pula keterbatasan dari sisi CPU yang perlu diperhatikan. PS5 Pro memang menawarkan GPU yang jauh lebih kuat, tetapi peningkatan performa CPU tidak sebesar peningkatan GPU. Karena GTA 6 diperkirakan menjadi game yang cukup berat di sisi CPU, PS5 Pro belum tentu mampu menjalankan game tersebut secara konsisten pada 60 FPS.
Beli Sekarang atau Tunggu Restock?
Bagi gamer yang memang mengincar pengalaman terbaik untuk GTA 6, PS5 Pro tetap menjadi pilihan yang menarik. Namun, membayar hingga US$1.200–US$1.300 kepada reseller berarti memberikan tambahan ratusan dolar untuk konsol yang peningkatannya pada GTA 6 masih belum diketahui secara jelas.
Dengan Sony yang diperkirakan menyiapkan stok tambahan menjelang November, menunggu menjadi pilihan yang lebih masuk akal bagi calon pembeli yang tidak terburu-buru. Terlebih lagi, jika PS5 Pro ternyata tetap dibatasi oleh CPU untuk mencapai 60 FPS di GTA 6, selisih harga tersebut mungkin tidak sebanding dengan peningkatan yang didapat.

items.content:
By Anayo Okoli, Dennis Agbo, Chinedu Adonu & Juliet Umeh
Presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress, NDC, and former Anambra State governor, Mr Peter Obi, has charged editors and the Nigerian media to guide politicians towards issue-based campaigns ahead of the 2027 general elections.
Read Also: Atiku: Produce conviction evidence or… – ADC challenges APC
Obi, who spoke while addressing editors at the 22nd All Nigeria Editors Conference in Enugu State, however, began by making it clear that he was not invited to the conference but had come because, as a politician, he believed that wherever people gathered to discuss issues concerning the country, politicians would naturally want to be there.
He was also quick to acknowledge that the editors’ conference was not a campaign platform, stressing that he had not come to campaign for the 2027 election but to pass on some messages about the state of the country and the responsibility of the media as Nigeria approaches another election.
Obi said he was mindful of the purpose of the gathering and would, therefore, restrict himself to issues he believed were important to Nigeria’s democracy, governance and development.
The theme of the conference is “The Ballot, the Media and the Task of Keeping Democracy Alive.”
He said editors should challenge politicians whenever they resort to name-calling, personal attacks or other distractions rather than addressing issues affecting Nigerians.
“As we approach the election, I have only one thing I will plead that you include in your discussion. We made a choice to be a democratic country, and that choice is a choice that can help our country to grow,” Obi said.
“It is important that you help us, the politicians, to ensure that as we approach elections, our discussions, our campaigns, everything we do, is strictly based on issues that will bring good governance, unity, security and prosperity for the country, strictly.”
The NDC presidential candidate also urged the media to insist on free, fair and credible elections, particularly by speaking out whenever candidates are prevented from campaigning in any part of the country.
He recalled that as Anambra governor, he allowed political opponents to campaign freely in the state, citing instances involving former Lagos State governor, Babatunde Fashola; former President Olusegun Obasanjo; and former Abia State governor, Orji Uzor Kalu.
According to him, Fashola once visited Anambra to campaign for Chris Ngige, then a candidate of the Action Congress of Nigeria, ACN, and he provided his official convoy for Fashola while remaining in his office.
He said Obasanjo also campaigned for Andy Uba in Anambra in his presence, while Kalu campaigned for Uche Ekwunife. He hosted them to a launch. He stressed that political differences should not result in personal quarrels.
“It is the people that we are talking to. So we need that conducive environment to campaign as a country, to make it work,” he stated.
On his relationship with Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, Obi dismissed reports of any conflict between them, describing Soludo as a respected elder brother.
“There is no issue between me and Soludo. Me and Soludo are close,” he explained, adding that he respects Soludo’s office as governor.
Obi also defended his record as governor of Anambra State, particularly concerning the state’s debt profile and savings, saying he left $150 million in savings when he left office.
He urged journalists to question politicians directly about their records and claims rather than relying on proxies.
“Question us based on our backgrounds. Question us based on what we say. Question us on our qualifications and everything,” he said.
The former governor said politicians should be prepared to personally respond to allegations against them, adding that where an allegation was true, the individual should acknowledge wrongdoing rather than deploy supporters to deny it.
He further charged the media to scrutinise Nigeria’s governance and development indicators, particularly in healthcare.
Obi lamented the decline of major teaching hospitals in the country, saying Nigerians should not be forced to rely on religious centres for treatment because of inadequate healthcare facilities.
He also criticised what he described as disparities in healthcare funding, urging journalists to investigate government budgets and question spending priorities.
“We must, you people must help us. It’s your country. Help us to stop the abuse, or it will take its revenge on your children,” Obi said.
Reacting to questions from the audience, Obi said Nigeria had enough resources to address its major developmental challenges, insisting that the country’s problem was how its resources were deployed.
He said, contrary to claims that the country lacked resources to fund critical sectors, billions of naira could be redirected to healthcare, education and other essential services if corruption and waste were reduced.
On healthcare, Obi said no teaching hospital was listed as a capital project in the Federal Government’s budget, alleging that none received up to N200 million for capital expenditure.
Obi also clarified his position on fuel subsidy, following a question on his alleged disagreement with former Kano State governor, Rabiu Kwankwaso, over the issue.
According to him, Kwankwaso had not advocated the outright removal of subsidy but had proposed introducing a different subsidy regime.
“What Kwankwaso said is that we will introduce our own style of subsidy. In fact, he didn’t say he would return the subsidy,” Obi said.
He, however, maintained that corruption in the subsidy regime had made the system unsustainable.
“If you remove the corruption in subsidy, there might not be any subsidy,” he noted, alleging that the subsidy regime had become a major avenue for corruption.
Obi argued that savings from the removal of fuel subsidy could be channelled into healthcare infrastructure.
On health, he said Nigeria needed about 1,000 kidney centres but currently had fewer than 300, while the country also required about 5,000 dialysis machines but had fewer than 1,000.
Using his own estimates, he said establishing 1,000 kidney centres, equipped with five machines each, would cost about N250 billion.
He also said Nigeria’s cancer burden required urgent investment, claiming that the country had fewer than 10 functional cancer centres.
According to him, establishing 20 cancer centres at an estimated cost of N5 billion each would require about N100 billion.
Obi further advocated increased investment in primary healthcare, saying only about 10 per cent of primary healthcare facilities were functional.
He noted that Nigeria had 8,809 wards and argued that establishing 10,000 functional primary healthcare centres at an estimated N100 million each would cost about N1 trillion.
“Why wouldn’t we take it from our N15.8 trillion — N1 trillion to put healthcare in every ward in Nigeria? We have the money. It is a question of how we use our resources,” he said.
Obi also rejected the idea that he was positioning himself against other politicians, saying Nigeria’s leadership challenge affected all political actors.
“I am not excluding any politician. I am not excluding myself. We have a problem,” he said.
He added: “Nigeria has no problem with our weather, with anything. God blessed us with everything, but our leadership is wrong. And we must correct it.”
On food security, Obi cited Bangladesh as an example of a country that had transformed its rice production from dependence on imports to becoming a major producer.
He said Nigeria, despite having significantly more land, was still unable to produce enough rice to meet domestic consumption.
On the possibility of political cooperation ahead of the 2027 elections, Obi said his focus was on structural reforms rather than personalities or past disagreements.
He said Nigeria had about 94 million registered voters, while total votes cast in the last presidential election were about 25 million, representing roughly a quarter of registered voters.
According to him, low voter participation was partly linked to citizens’ perception that their votes would not count.
“That’s where you come in; that’s where you get to do something. Let’s get those who are not voting to vote.
“The day our votes count, that will change,” he told the editors.
Obi said having several candidates contesting elections was not necessarily a problem, provided the electoral process was free, fair and credible.
“What we are asking is, in 2027, let’s have free, fair, credible elections,” he said.
He also said electoral malpractice should attract criminal sanctions.
“I can state here today, I know I’m not going to have the opportunity, but if I have the opportunity, anybody who rigs the election will go to jail,” Obi said.
He stressed that his political activities were driven by his desire to see Nigeria function better. “I am not desperate to be President. I am desperate to see Nigeria work. Our commitment is to Nigeria, to work for a better Nigeria, where things work for everybody,” he said.
Tunde Rahman warns against fake news
Also speaking, the Special Adviser to President Bola Tinubu on Media and Publicity, Tunde Rahman, said the media had a critical role to play in ensuring that Nigerians were adequately informed ahead of the 2027 general elections.
He said the emergence of artificial intelligence, fake news and deepfakes had made the work of journalists more difficult, warning that misinformation could outpace official information during elections.
According to him, “Everybody can sit on WhatsApp and announce fake election results. Only you can debunk it. Police lies with facts and propaganda with professionalism,” stressing that the media must protect its credibility ahead of the 2027 elections.
“Let us not allow cliques to kill credibility. The media should not be pro-APC, pro-Labour Party or pro-PDP. It should be pro-Nigeria, pro-truth and pro-people. If the balance is clean and the media is straight, democracy will not just survive in Nigeria, it will thrive,” he said.
The presidential spokesman said the Tinubu administration inherited an economy that was “on life support” but had embarked on bold reforms which, he said, were beginning to yield results.
Speaking earlier, a foremost legal scholar, Prof. Auwal Yadudu, spoke on issues that could engender voter apathy.
He listed them to include lack of or failure of good governance; violence, thuggery and intimidation during elections; as well as incompetence of the electoral management body.
Also, in his paper, former Managing Director and Editor-in-Chief of The Guardian Newspapers, Martins Oloja, cautioned against reporting terrorism without adequate verification of the real situation.
According to him, reporting terrorism without adequate verification and accuracy could turn such reports into tools for terrorism itself.
Vanguard News
The post 2027: Election riggers should go to jail — Obi appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
By Dayo Johnson, Regional Editor, South West
The polity is already awash with threats of violence and intimidation against those who do not support the ruling All Progress Congress. Few days ago, Chairman of Esan West Local Govt Area of Edo state threatened a hotel hosting Nigeria Democratic Congress meeting that any building hosting any other party apart from APC would be bought down.
Read Also: From Obasanjo and Tinubu camps to Atiku’s war room, by Emmanuel Aziken
He also went to Ekpoma motor park where he ordered that any commercial driver wearing any other cap other than APC cap would be barred from entering the park. In Abuja, a council chairman told the residents who would not support the APC to relocate from the Federal Capital territory while in Borno, a commissioner threatened that any resident who dared to oppose the ruling party would be flogged. Across the states, thugs have disrupted political gatherings, attacked the people and destroyed property.
Concerned lawyers in the country have therefore raised the alarm over the threats and attacks ahead of the January general elections. They warned that such violence can plunge the nation into a state of chaos and this portends a great danger for our democracy.
Threatening citizens’ freedoms erode confidence in election result before ballot — Ahia
A Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), Mr Kenneth C. Ahia, said: “Demolishing a hotel for hosting an opposition meeting, forcing drivers into party caps, banishing residents from the FCT, threatening floggings, or vowing to remove elected council chairmen who fail to ‘deliver,’ all violate Sections 34, 40, 41 and 42 of the Constitution, which protect the dignity of the person, the rights of assembly, association and movement, and freedom from discrimination on account of political opinion.
“The Supreme Court has also settled that no governor can remove democratically elected local government councils. An election remains meaningful only when citizens can campaign, speak and vote without fear.
“When officials threaten those freedoms, they discourage participation and erode confidence in the result before a single ballot is cast. Every reported threat should be investigated fairly, and any official found to have abused public power should face appropriate consequences. Leaders of all parties should make clear that votes must be won by persuasion and performance, never by coercion.
“Those in power must also remember that power is transient. Years ago, the PDP held sway across the country and acted with impunity; today it is the APC. No party holds power forever, and there is always a time for reckoning.”
It’s a reflection of our democracy is degenerating — Akinlaja
Another SAN, Mr. Dayo Akinlaja, insisted that Nigeria should have grown beyond politics of bitterness and intolerance. He said: “It is clear beyond any measure of doubt that all these threats are highly unconstitutional, illegal, unfortunate and disturbing. They have no legitimate space in a proper democratic culture. It is a pointer to the fact that our democracy is not improving but degenerating. Over these years, we should have gone beyond this level of intolerance and incivility. Issues, not threats, should define electioneering campaigns.
“Sadly, issues are relegated to the background. Fear Mongering is elevated in their place. The situation is tragic, and that is even an understatement.”
Infringing on people’s rights to choose unconstitutional, actionable —Akpan
For an Abuja-based senior lawyer, Mr. Nkereuwem Akpan, threats emanating mostly from states controlled by the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) constitute an electoral offence. He said: “This ugly trend by supporters of the ruling APC is a cause for concern. I say so because a multi-party democracy such as ours thrives where there is a constitutional guarantee of freedom of choice and the right to self-determination.
“Even under military rule, we had options to choose from. Recall that Gen. Ibrahim Babangida gave us the choice between the National Republican Convention (NRC) and the Social Democratic Party (SDP). That was the basis on which we had Chief Moshood Abiola going up against Alhaji Tofa. Again, during the General Sani Abacha years, we had a slew of political parties to choose from. I think the APC must learn from the history of our recent past, from the tragedy that befell the PDP. I remember a time, about 15 years ago, when the PDP was the biggest political party in the whole of Africa.
“In fact, members of the PDP became so boisterous, unruly and careless that one Ogbulafor came out on national TV boasting that the PDP would rule Nigeria for sixty years. In those days, you were either PDP or you were wasting your time. It took Nyesom Wike, working from within the ranks of the PDP, to destroy it. Democracy thrives on the choice that the electorate is able to make at the polls every four years.
“The APC was an outsider until 2015 and cannot be greater than the masses. It goes without saying that ours is a constitutional democracy founded on the principle of one man, one vote, where the right to cast a vote for a candidate of one’s choice is a fundamental right. Any attempt, before, during, or after the elections, to infringe on this right to choose is clearly unconstitutional and actionable in the law courts. Secondly, it will also constitute an electoral offence to attempt to stifle freedom of choice or to discriminate against a person on the basis of party membership or political affiliation.
“These are the very foundations of our democracy. In other jurisdictions, the police would have arrested, prosecuted and jailed anyone engaged in this conduct, but they won’t, because orders will come from Abuja to truncate the case”.
Doomsday beckons if political actors don’t comply with the laws — Chief Nwachukwu
For his part, another senior legal practitioner, Chief Chukwuma Nwachukwu, said: “All I can see in the above scenarios is the impunity and arrogance of our politicians, especially those of the ruling party. It is important to state that no one is above the law, and by virtue of Section 1(1) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended), all authorities and persons are subject to the grundnorm and all laws of the land, without exception.
“Chapter Four of the Constitution preserves the fundamental rights of citizens, and such rights cannot be tampered with, except in accordance with the provisions of the law. No party member or government official has any right whatsoever to infringe on the guaranteed rights to freedom of association, freedom of movement, etc and, more especially, the right to life of a fellow citizen, under the guise of politics.
“The various criminal laws make provision for offences and the punishments therefore, and it is the duty of the relevant law enforcement agencies to carry out their statutory functions in preserving public order. Furthermore, the Independent National Electoral Commission should, as a matter of urgency, read the riot act to political office holders, regardless of their party leanings and affiliations, on the importance of desisting from inflammatory rhetoric as we approach the general elections, so as not to overheat the polity and destabilise the upcoming elections.
“As for the issue of imposing huge sums of money as fees for the erection of campaign billboards, I do not see the necessity of imposing a prohibitive sum different from what is generally applicable to other advertisements. This is a deeply tense period in our national life, and if political actors don’t
comply with the laws of the land, doomsday beckons”.
Political intimidation transforms elections into marketplace of fear — Evans Ufeli
Another lawyer, Evans Ufeli said, “Threats by public officials against citizens, workers, traders, civil servants, or businesses because they support opposition parties strike at the foundation of constitutional democracy. Under the 1999 Constitution, Nigerians enjoy rights to freedom of expression, peaceful association, political choice, and protection from discriminatory treatment.
“These rights are not gifts bestowed by office holders; they are guarantees that restrain the power of the state and its agents. From an electoral law perspective, intimidation is especially grave where it is intended to compel a person to vote, abstain from voting, abandon a political party, or support a preferred candidate. The Electoral Act 2026 criminalises undue influence and conduct involving threats, coercion, violence, or the threat of injury, loss, and harm designed to distort a voter’s free choice. A threat to terminate employment, withdraw government services, close a business, deny contracts, or unleash security agencies against perceived opposition supporters may therefore amount to more than reckless political speech.
“Where evidence establishes intent and action, it may trigger electoral offences, abuse of office allegations, civil claims for fundamental-rights enforcement, disciplinary sanctions, and in appropriate cases criminal liability. Political intimidation transforms elections from a contest of ideas into a marketplace of fear. A voter who fears losing a job, a licence, personal safety, or access to public services cannot be said to be exercising an entirely free franchise.
“Such a climate suppresses turnout, entrenches incumbency, weakens opposition mobilisation, and erodes public confidence in election outcomes. A public office is a trust, not a weapon. The survival of credible elections depends on ensuring that no Nigerian must choose between political conscience and personal survival.
Credibility of the electoral process at risk — Femi Aborisade
Mr Femi Aborisade argued that; “These developments are a very dangerous sign for our democracy. They amount to an unacceptable attempt to constrict the democratic space and intimidate citizens into political conformity. Democracy is founded on the freedom of citizens to make political choices without fear, coercion or intimidation.
“Nobody should be threatened or punished simply because he or she chooses to support a political party different from the party in government. What we are witnessing is particularly disturbing because some of these threats are reportedly coming from public officials who ought to be protecting the rights of citizens, irrespective of their political affiliations. A public office must never be used as an instrument of political coercion.
“Government officials have a constitutional duty to protect citizens, not to dictate their political choices or threaten them with reprisals for exercising their democratic rights. Political competition should be about ideas, policies, programmes and the records of those seeking public office. Where intimidation replaces persuasion, democracy is inevitably weakened.
“If this pattern continues unchecked, it could create an atmosphere of fear in which citizens become reluctant to participate openly in political activities or express their genuine preferences. That would have serious consequences for the credibility of the electoral process.”
Threats against opposition anti-democratic — Dr Omare
Dr Eric Omare, former President, Ijaw Youth Council (IYC) worldwide contended that: “The verbal threats by members of the ruling APC against opposition party members pose a threat to peace and security going into the 2027 general elections. There is no legal basis for those threats.
“In a multi-party democracy, people have the right to support the political party and candidates of their choice; hence, the threats are anti-democratic. I would advise the security agencies to take proactive steps to nip such threats in the bud and address their potential effect on the peaceful conduct of the 2027 general elections.”
APC’s strong-arm posture, recipe for anarchy ahead 2027 elections — Clarkson
On his part, Amaebi Clarkson, argued that: “It is disheartening when public officials and supposedly elected representatives speak in such an unbridled manner. It reveals how far we have descended into lawlessness. Their unguarded utterances give the impression that the country is governed by the rule of men rather than the Constitution.
“Chapter 4 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, is clear on the unfettered rights of the people. Section 40 specifically echoes the freedom of association and the right to peaceful assembly. This is an inalienable right that cannot be circumvented by anybody, including the President.
“Our democracy is anchored on a multi-party system which gives the people a wide spectrum to choose their political party and who to vote for. The ruling APC, which came to power in 2015, benefited from these democratic tenets when the people voted out the then ruling PDP government. The APC’s strong-arm posture is a recipe for anarchy in the forthcoming elections. But this government should be reminded that Nigeria is not a banana republic but a country steeped in the rule of law.”
It portends a great danger for our democracy — Oviawe
A Port Harcourt based lawyer, Amarachi Owhoeli also said: “This portends a great danger for our democracy. Sadly, this is a recurrent phenomenon during electioneering periods. We have seen similar threats like this in Lagos State and other states in Nigeria during the 2023 general elections. It is sad that these politicians and their thugs will still go ahead to carry out their threats and the security agencies will not do anything about it.
“Every Nigerian citizen is free to campaign and vote for a candidate of their choice; if anybody threatens or coerces them from freely doing so, then that person ought to be arrested and prosecuted accordingly, no matter his position or qualifications.
“Threats of violence like this and actual violence can plunge the country into a state of chaos, because nobody has a monopoly on violence. I will advise the security agencies to swiftly move in and invite the culprits responsible for these threats, make them sign an undertaking not to carry out those threats, so that if these threats later materialize, they will be held responsible for their unguarded utterances.”
INEC must create a level playing field — Akiki
George Akiki, Ex Chairman of the NBA Young Lawyers Forum, Calabar Branch, stated that “one of the features of democracy is a free, fair and violence-free election, devoid of duress, vote buying, threats, and ballot snatching. Nigeria has been a democracy for over 27 years and should by now have moved past situations where voters are threatened by political thugs.
“During the 2023 elections a woman was harassed, molested, and beaten by thugs at her polling unit, as reported in the media. The country’s constitution guarantees freedom of choice of political affiliation and membership under Sections 39 and 40, while Section 77 guarantees the freedom to vote and choose representatives. Furthermore, such actions amount to electoral offences punishable by law.
“Therefore, INEC, as the election umpire, has a duty to put up modalities that will encourage a level playing ground for all political parties to participate in elections, while security agencies have a role to ensure that voters and election participants do not suffer any elements of coercion, threat, or duress.”
On his part, John Ola Mafo said: “The combined reading of all the threats, barking, howling and vituperations from Edo to Ebonyi, Abuja to Bornu, gives a picture of APC as a political family at the breaking point, weighed down by desperation, frustration and the fear of the unknown.
“Nigeria is not a Banana Republic and certain inalienable rights are granted by the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria (as amended), which includes Section 34 on Dignity of Human Person, 35 on Right to Personal Liberty, 38 on Freedom of Thoughts, Conscience and Religion, 39 on Right to Freedom of Expression and the Press, 40 on Right to Peaceful Assembly and Association, and 41 on Freedom of Movement”.
Mr Tajudeen Olutop, former Chairman, Nigeria Bar Association, Owo Branch
“No citizen should be intimidated, assaulted, denied access to public facilities or forced to relocate merely because of his or her political preference. Nevertheless, such inflammatory statements are not entirely new in Nigerian politics. At different times, politicians belonging to various parties have employed similar language when their parties controlled the machinery of government.
“They are often part of political manoeuvring, propaganda and attempts to create an exaggerated impression of dominance rather than policies capable of lawful implementation. However, these statements should not be treated lightly. Even when the speakers have no genuine intention or legal capacity to carry them out, such rhetoric can embolden overzealous supporters, heighten political tension and undermine public confidence in the electoral process.
“Public office holders must therefore exercise restraint and remember that government institutions and public spaces belong to all Nigerians, irrespective of political affiliation. Ultimately, elections are determined by the freely expressed will of the electorate not by threats, intimidation or coercion”.
Similarly, Chief Ola Amure said: “The reported threats from some government officials reveal a dangerous attempt to turn political competition into an exercise of power, intimidation and coercion. A government has a responsibility to protect the rights of its citizens, not to threaten them for belonging to, supporting, or voting for another political party.
“The right to vote, freedom of association, freedom of expression and the right to participate in political activities are not privileges granted by the ruling party. They are fundamental democratic rights. What happens when a commercial driver is denied access to his livelihood because of the political cap he wears? What happens when a hotel owner is threatened because he provides a venue for a lawful political meeting? What happens when an elected council chairman is pressured to deliver votes for a particular party under threat of removal? These are not merely political disagreements. They raise questions about the use of public authority, the protection of livelihoods, electoral fairness and the rule of law. The 2027 elections must not become a contest of intimidation, coercion and the abuse of state power. They must be an opportunity for Nigerians to freely choose their leaders based on policies, performance, character and their vision for the future.
“The opposition must not be denied the right to campaign. Citizens must not be forced to support a political party. Public resources and government institutions must not be used as instruments of political punishment. A democracy is measured not only by the ability of the ruling party to win elections, but also by its willingness to respect the rights of those who disagree with it.
Moruff Balogun, Former Vice Chairman, Nigerian Bar Association, Ijebu Ode Branch
“The more important question is what happens to an election when those who control public institutions begin to communicate to citizens that their political choices may have consequences.
Politicians have always used strong language during election campaigns. The more serious concern is that some of these statements are coming from people who occupy public offices and therefore have access to governmental authority and resources. One may dismiss some of these statements as political rhetoric. But when similar statements begin to emerge from different jurisdictions, the issue becomes more fundamental. It creates the possibility of a political environment in which citizens do not merely ask, “Who do I want to vote for?” but also, “What will happen to me if I vote differently?
“That is where the concern for democratic freedom arises. A democracy is not defined merely by holding an election on a particular day. It requires citizens to be able to make political choices freely. If a trader fears that his business may be affected because he supports the opposition, if a transport worker believes that displaying the wrong political symbol could cost him access to his livelihood, if a public servant thinks that his position depends on delivering votes for a particular party, or if an ordinary resident feels that supporting the opposition could make him unwelcome in his own community, then the ballot may remain secret while the political environment itself becomes coercive.
“The 2027 election should not only answer the question of who will govern Nigeria. It should also test whether our political institutions are mature enough to permit citizens to disagree with those in power without being treated as enemies of the State.
In his own submission, Mr Bukola Onifade said: “The problem with our democracy is the lack of respect for the rule of law. Public office holders and politicians generally are not giving enough regard to the constitution which is very dangerous for the development of our democracy and allowing such to continue without check can truncate democracy in the country.
“It is unlawful for anyone to resort to threat as a means of campaigning or canvassing votes or to even threaten others from canvassing for votes in any part of the country. The moment we allow the threat to become part of our democracy, we are heading for anarchy and we must use legal means to stop the country from falling into that ditch.
We need to preach political tolerance – Bewaji
Dr Wunmi Bewaji, a Solicitor of the Supreme Court of Nigeria and former Minority Leader of the House of Representatives, described the threat as excessive enthusiasm, stressing the need for tolerance in the country. He said, “I rather see this as an isolated manifestation of excessive enthusiasm and that is not to be confused for illegality.
“Every now and then you find over-zealous officials making statements, which when you look at it, is not really more than an over-zealous pursuit of a legitimate political objective, which is not a crime. I think the focus should be on how to promote political tolerance by all sides, because we will be missing the point if the focus is only on the ruling party, because every government official within their terrain would want to implement one policy or the other that will not be favourable to the other party. So, even within the same party, you can have evidence of intolerance.
“For instance, you find a situation where after people have pasted their posters all over the place, exuberant party supporters would go about to pull down billboards to tear posters belonging to the opposition. So, I think we need to preach political tolerance.”
Mr Chika Eze, said “The Electoral Act 2026 is quite explicit. Section 97 prohibits a political party, candidate, aspirant or any person or group from directly or indirectly threatening another person with force or violence during a political campaign in order to compel support or prevent support for a candidate. Section 130 also addresses conduct around polling units, including possession of offensive weapons or conduct calculated to intimidate voters.
“More importantly, Section 132 criminalises the use or threat of force, violence or restraint, as well as threats of injury, damage or harm intended to influence how a person votes or whether that person votes at all. It also covers conduct that prevents a political aspirant from freely campaigning or mobilising support. Therefore, incidents involving alleged threats or intimidation should not simply be viewed as political rhetoric. Where the facts establish the elements of an offence under the Act, the appropriate authorities have a legal basis to investigate and prosecute.
“The real issue is enforcement. The law must be applied consistently, evidence must be properly preserved, and investigators must establish who made the threat, what was threatened, the electoral context and whether the conduct was intended to influence voting or political participation. Where there is evidence of sponsorship or direction by others, investigators should also examine that chain of responsibility rather than stopping with the person who physically carried out the act.”
Election law expert, Mr Emeka Nwosu said, “The problem is not necessarily the absence of laws; it is the failure to consistently move cases from allegation to investigation, investigation to prosecution and prosecution to conviction. In many instances, evidence is not properly preserved, investigations are delayed and cases lose momentum before they reach a decisive stage.
“A functioning enforcement chain requires specialised investigators who understand electoral offences, proper documentation and preservation of evidence, timely legal advice, dedicated prosecutors and courts or tribunals capable of handling electoral cases expeditiously. There must also be clear institutional responsibility for tracking each case from the point of complaint to its final determination. Most importantly, prosecution must not be selective. Whether the offender is a political heavyweight, a party operative or an ordinary voter, the law should apply equally. Without credible enforcement and consequences, electoral offences will continue to be viewed by some actors as risks worth taking.”
According to Mr Chinedu Okafor, “The 2027 election must not become another contest where violence, intimidation and misinformation determine the outcome. Security agencies must be professional, neutral and firm in dealing with anyone who attempts to disrupt the process, irrespective of political affiliation. Political parties and their candidates must also understand that elections are not a do-or-die affair. They must campaign on issues, respect the rules and accept the outcome where due process has been followed.
“Citizens, too, have a critical role to play by refusing to participate in violence, vote buying, hate speech or the spread of unverified information. A credible and peaceful election is a collective responsibility. If the security agencies do their job, political actors play by the rules and citizens protect the integrity of their votes, Nigeria can have an election that strengthens rather than weakens public confidence in democracy.”
Dapo Akinrefon; Samuel Oyadongha; Rotimi Ojomoyela; Ikechukwu Nnochiri; Shina Abubakar; Ozioruva Aliu; Ike Uchechukwu; Davies Iheamnachor; James Ogunnnaike; Adeola Badru; Juliet Umeh & Gift Chapi-Odekina also contributed to this report.
Vanguard News

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
By Juliet Umeh
For 27 uninterrupted years, Nigerians have lived under elected governments. They have queued under scorching sun and rain to vote, watched presidents and governors come and go, and seen disputed elections move from polling units to courtrooms.
Read Also: All Nigeria Editors Confab, 2026: Before ballot box, Africans already knew democracy — Achebe
Yet, for the ordinary Nigerian, John Cardinal Onaiyekan believes a fundamental question remains: Has democracy really put the people at the centre of governance?
At 82, the Archbishop Emeritus of Abuja has witnessed Nigeria’s journey through colonial rule, independence, military governments and civilian administrations. His conclusion is sobering: having democracy is one thing; making it work for ordinary people is another.
“I speak as an 82-year-old Nigerian who has seen this nation going up and down with hopes of greatness that have continued to elude us,” Onaiyekan told editors at the All Nigeria Editors Conference, ANEC 2026, in Enugu.
For him, the true test of democracy is not merely how many elections have been conducted or how long civilians have remained in power. It is whether the government serves the people.
When citizens become pawns
Nigeria has achieved something that once seemed difficult: more than a quarter-century of uninterrupted civilian government.
But elections alone, Onaiyekan argued, do not make democracy meaningful.
He said: “Democracy must be governance for the good of the people. The leaders must be serving the interests of the governed, and people must be at the centre of governance – what we call the common good.”
It is, he said, “the kind of democracy that Nigerians have been dreaming about.”
Yet, that ideal is tested whenever elections become primarily struggles among politicians for control of power
Onaiyekan accused some politicians of adopting a “do-or-die” attitude because political office brings wealth and influence.
“In all this, the people hardly count at all,” he said. “Rather, they are just pawns on the political game.”
That is perhaps one of the contradictions of Nigeria’s democracy: the citizen who is supposed to be its most powerful participant can become its least influential actor.
Who owns the vote?
Since Nigeria returned to civilian rule in 1999, successive elections were expected to strengthen democratic institutions.
“We have had several elections since 1999. It is difficult to believe that we have been making progress. In fact, it seems that the quality of the elections has been reducing from one election to the other, and this is not good news at all,”  he said.
His concerns range from the conduct of politicians to the independence of INEC, deployment of security agencies and role of the judiciary.
But he reserved one of his sharpest questions for politicians who boast that they will “deliver” entire states to preferred candidates.
“Where is the freedom of the people of the state to vote according to their individual consciences?” he asked.
“Or does the governor intend to vote for everybody in his state?”
Behind that question lies another: Who owns the vote – the citizen who casts it or the political structure claiming to control it?
Ballot box or courtroom?
Onaiyekan also questioned the growing prominence of courts in electoral outcomes.
“The judiciary is not to determine elections about who wins, but rather to adjudicate disputes when they arise.
“If elections were well conducted, there ought not to be any need for judicial cases.”
But Nigeria, he observed, has increasingly witnessed electoral battles moving from polling units to tribunals.
“Our experience in the recent past has almost become that we have been witnessing a situation where our elections are being determined not at the polls, but in the courts by the tribunals.”
For voters who queued to exercise their franchise, such prolonged disputes can raise questions about where electoral power ultimately resides.
‘Power belongs to the people’
For Onaiyekan, Nigeria’s democratic journey must eventually return to its simplest promise: government exists for citizens.
He said: “In political terms, we say that power belongs to the people. By that, we mean that it does not belong to the political leaders and office holders.”
He also rejected arguments that Nigerians should simply wait for democracy to mature over generations.
“We must never give up our efforts to keep pushing for a government of the people, by the people, for the people.
“We cannot accept the specious argument that democracy has taken centuries to build in some nations, and that so we should wait for hundreds of years to achieve our own.
“We have the experience of history, and we cannot be re-inventing the wheel.”
After 27 years, therefore, Nigeria’s democratic challenge is no longer merely keeping soldiers out of government or conducting another election.
It is ensuring that the ordinary Nigerian who stands in a polling queue truly has a stake in determining how the country is governed.
“The ultimate objective,” Onaiyekan said, “is to install a government that is freely chosen by the people and that works for the common good of the people.”
Until that promise reaches the ordinary citizen, Nigeria’s democracy, in Onaiyekan’s reckoning, remains unfinished.

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
By Juliet Umeh
Long before ballot papers, polling booths and electoral commissions became features of Nigeria’s political life, communities gathered to deliberate, question those who exercised authority and arrive at decisions affecting their collective existence.
Read Also: 2027: You must play according to rules, Jonathan warns politicians
There were no voter cards or electronic accreditation machines. Yet, according to the Obi of Onitsha, His Royal Majesty, Igwe Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, beneath those traditional systems lay an important democratic principle: power required the consent and participation of the people.
For Achebe, therefore, democracy should not simply be regarded as a foreign political idea handed down to Africans. Its fundamental values, he argued, have deep roots in indigenous African society.
Speaking as chairman of the All Nigeria Editors Conference, ANEC, in Enugu, Achebe reached into Igbo traditional governance to make his point.
“In our Igbo tradition, the Obi does not rule by decree. He rules in council, in dialogue, in the constant testing of truth against the wisdom of elders and the voice of the people.
“Igbo democratic instinct is ancient. Even kingship here has always been checked by the community, by consultation, by honest speech,” he said.
It was a striking intervention at a conference devoted to the ballot, media and survival of democracy.
Democracy beyond election day
Modern democracy is commonly associated with periodic elections, political parties, legislatures and constitutions. But Achebe’s argument goes deeper: these institutions may be modern, but the underlying idea that leaders should listen to the people is not necessarily new to African societies.
He declared: “The ballot box, in this sense, is not an import grafted onto our soil. It is a modern vessel for an old African value, which states that legitimate power flows from the consent, the voice, and the informed judgment of the people.”
That distinction is significant.
It suggests that the real test of democracy is not merely whether citizens queue every four years to cast ballots, but whether their voices continue to matter after the votes have been counted.
Achebe, who reflected on Nigeria’s journey from independence through military rule to democratic government, described the country’s democracy as a continuing project rather than a finished achievement.
“I have watched Nigeria’s journey from the optimism of independence, through the turbulence of military rule, into the fragile and still-unfinished project of democratic self-governance,” he said.
His message was that democracy requires constant protection.
“Democracy is not a monument we erect and then walk away from,” Achebe warned.
“It is more like a fire lit to keep the house warm. It must be tended, fed, protected from wind and rain, or it dies quietly in the night while everyone believes it still burns.”
Consent must be informed
But Achebe also identified a complication in the principle of popular consent.
For the people’s choices to confer meaningful legitimacy, he argued, those choices must be informed.
“Consent is only meaningful if it is informed,” he said.
That is where he placed journalism at the heart of the democratic process.
“The ballot is the citizen’s voice. The media is the mirror by which that citizen sees the world clearly enough to know what to say with that voice.
“When the mirror is cracked, or worse, deliberately distorted, the citizen no longer votes from truth but votes from illusion.And a democracy built on illusion is not genuine democracy but drama. It becomes a theatre,” he said.
For editors gathered in Enugu, the traditional ruler’s argument effectively connected two institutions separated by centuries: the village council where voices were heard and the modern newsroom through which citizens receive information.
In both, he suggested, honest speech matters.
When the people stop mattering
Achebe’s reflection also raises a larger question for Nigeria: if consultation, consent and accountability are deeply rooted values, why should democratic participation begin and end at the polling booth?
His description of traditional leadership offers an interesting contrast to any system in which obtaining political office is treated as sufficient authority to govern without listening.
Even an Obi, he stressed, is subject to restraints.
“Even kingship here has always been checked by the community, by consultation, by honest speech.”
It is perhaps one of the most important messages from his address.
Democracy may have acquired modern institutions and technologies, but its survival still rests on an old and remarkably simple principle: those who govern must remain connected to those they govern.
And citizens, in turn, must have truthful information with which to judge them.
That explains why Achebe charged journalists not merely to report democracy, but to help preserve it.
“In the face of challenges, politicking, electioneering and partisanship, you must stand upright for democracy and the nation.
“Even if politicians, electoral body, institutions, and other things fail, you must be the ultimate last man standing in the task of defending democracy,” he told the editors.
From the traditional council to the modern ballot box, Achebe’s argument is ultimately about the same thing: power derives its legitimacy not simply from those who wield it, but from the people whose consent gives it meaning.

items.title: From Obasanjo and Tinubu camps to Atiku’s war room, by Emmanuel Aziken
items.summary:

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
Atiku Abubakar’s choice of leaders for his 2027 presidential campaign tells a larger story than the announcement of a campaign council. Its chairman, Kashim Ibrahim-Imam, was once firmly identified with Olusegun Obasanjo. Its deputy chairman, Nasir El-Rufai, served on a panel that examined allegations against Atiku during his bitter struggle with Obasanjo. Both later moved through the political camp that brought Bola Tinubu to power. Now they are to help Atiku defeat him.
Read Also: 2027: You must play according to rules, Jonathan warns politicians
The appointment of Ibrahim-Imam is an illustration of how far Nigeria’s political relationships can travel. At the start of the Fourth Republic, Obasanjo made him presidential liaison officer to the Senate. It was a delicate assignment: relations between the presidency and the legislature were already fraught. Ibrahim-Imam was accused of involvement in moves against Senate President Chuba Okadigbo and declared unwelcome at the National Assembly. The accusation did not establish his guilt, but it reinforced his reputation as an unwavering Obasanjo man.
That association carries particular irony for Atiku. His partnership with Obasanjo ended in one of the Fourth Republic’s most enduring political feuds. Only this year, the former president again described choosing Atiku as his vice-president as a mistake. One of the politicians who built his early career close to Obasanjo is now entrusted with directing Atiku’s bid for the office they once occupied together.
Ibrahim-Imam’s own ambition was to govern Borno State. He won the Peoples Democratic Party ticket in 2003, but Ali Modu Sheriff—“SAS” to his political followers—defeated him on the opposition All Nigeria Peoples Party platform. Ibrahim-Imam tried again in 2007. Sheriff beat him again and completed two terms as governor. For an Obasanjo loyalist flying the president’s party flag, the double defeat was a bruising lesson in the limits of presidential proximity.
There have long been suggestions that Sheriff enjoyed a separate relationship with Obasanjo through his father, who was said to have carried out contracts during Obasanjo’s military administration. Such accounts help explain the intrigue that surrounded the Borno contests. They do not prove that Obasanjo secretly worked against Ibrahim-Imam. The electoral record is clear enough: twice the president’s party candidate confronted Sheriff; twice he lost.
Thereafter, Kashim remained in the political background from 2007 for more than a decade. It is alleged that in that period he quietly formed an alliance with Asiwaju Bola Tinubu, and that it was on that basis he received one of the few appointments President Muhammadu Buhari gifted to Tinubu. It was no small job. The chairmanship of the Tertiary Education Trust Fund, TETFund, was one of the juiciest positions on offer during the Buhari years.
Kashim was among those considered for running mate to Tinubu in the run-up to the 2023 election, but he lost out to his fellow Borno man and namesake, Senator Kashim Shettima. There were insinuations that he was not happy with it. Tinubu tried to mollify him by nominating his 25-year-old son as chairman of FERMA, but that nomination drew a national outcry and was withdrawn. For whatever reason, Kashim then withdrew from the Tinubu space and subsequently emerged in the ranks of the opposition, and then in Atiku’s ADC. El-Rufai’s history with Atiku is more personal. In the early Obasanjo years, he headed the Bureau of Public Enterprises under a privatisation programme supervised by Atiku as vice-president. They had worked together before becoming adversaries.
The break became consequential during the Petroleum Technology Development Fund affair. In 2006, Obasanjo established an administrative panel to review allegations involving Atiku.
When the Obasanjo government exited and he fell out with the successor, he quickly pitched camp with Muhammadu Buhari and reinvented himself as a son of the former military head of state.
He won the governorship of Kaduna State on the coattails of the Buhari phenomenon in 2015 and served out two terms of what many still call one of the most divisive administrations in the history of the state. At the peak of Buhari’s power, and with Tinubu in seeming decline, El-Rufai took up tirades against Tinubu and at one point came to Lagos to lecture political actors on how to overthrow political godfathers.
Shockingly, by 2022, El-Rufai was among the northern APC governors backing a southern successor to Buhari. He then supported Tinubu’s candidacy against Atiku in 2023.
A place in Tinubu’s government appeared to follow. Tinubu nominated El-Rufai as a minister, and El-Rufai spoke of plans for the power sector. The Senate withheld his confirmation, citing security clearance. El-Rufai later said Tinubu had changed his mind about appointing him. The contents of the cited security concerns were not publicly settled, and the competing accounts offer no firm basis for claiming who engineered his exclusion. The partnership ended; El-Rufai moved into opposition politics.
There is a further complication for Atiku’s campaign. El-Rufai remains in custody while facing trial over alleged money laundering and conversion of public property. Those allegations are unproven. His circumstances nevertheless raise a practical question about how a deputy chairman can help coordinate a national campaign while unable to move freely.
Atiku’s team calls its structure lean: Senator Austin Akobundu will manage campaign operations through six directorates and 30 directors. Its two political leaders bring formidable experience, along with the baggage of the governments and rivalries that shaped them. The appointments show Atiku’s willingness to reconcile with old opponents. The test will be whether Ibrahim-Imam and El-Rufai can offer voters a convincing reason for their new alliance—and a governing purpose that reaches beyond removing Tinubu.

In a statement by its Director of Strategic Communications, Phrank Shaibu, the Council said Morka could raise questions about Atiku’s record but could not present allegations as established convictions.
“Morka has become an untutored spin doctor for a party caught in the conundrum of a sinking regime,” Shaibu said.
He challenged the APC spokesman to identify the court and produce the judgment if he claimed Atiku had been convicted of corruption.
“Morka may raise each matter. He may not strip away the report’s distinctions and present the resulting fiction as a judgment against Atiku,” Shaibu said.
The Council then turned the APC’s attack on Atiku’s suitability to manage public funds against President Bola Tinubu, citing the United States forfeiture proceedings involving $460,000 from an account in Tinubu’s name.
Shaibu said the proceedings and associated financial records raised questions about transactions involving Tinubu and individuals named in the case.
“A bank introduction. A transfer. A cheque. A company. Tinubu should explain those transactions and why the same names kept appearing around his finances,” he said.
The Council also cited the US litigation over access to FBI and other investigative records concerning Tinubu, arguing that Nigerians should be allowed to see the relevant documents, subject to lawful protections.
“Morka’s colleagues will rush to tell Nigerians that a search result is not a conviction. Nobody has said it is,” Shaibu said.
He said the distinction did not erase the questions surrounding the records.
“Yes, the case before the court concerns access to records. The records concern an investigation. Both facts can be true at once,” Shaibu said.

By Ikechukwu Nnochiri
As campaigns for the 2027 general elections heat up, former President Goodluck Jonathan has warned politicians to play according to the rules, saying it would be wrong for candidates to maneuver the system just to win an election.
Read Also: 2027: I’ll lead Tinubu’s campaign team in FCT, Rivers — Wike
Jonathan’s admonition appears to counter President Bola Tinubu’s earlier remark that “all is fair in politics.”
Delivering a goodwill message at a public lecture held to mark the 80th birthday of a former Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Mr. Kanu Agabi, SAN, ex-President Jonathan, who voluntarily conceded defeat to the opposition party in 2015, maintained that politicians cannot justify every action taken to win an election by simply describing it as politics.
According to him, electoral contests must be governed by established rules, and politicians should not treat the quest for victory as justification for misconduct.
He said: “In politics, it is a disaster. People do stupid things, also even criminal things, and they will tell you it is politics. It is not politics. Politics has rules.
“Politics is like a soccer match. You play according to the rules, and that is why the courts step in to mediate if you go against the rules. Otherwise, you can do anything and win an election and walk away.”
The erstwhile president also stressed that the anti-corruption fight in the country requires more than laws and enforcement agencies, emphasising that enduring change would depend on building a society where ethical conduct is valued above wrongdoing.
“The challenge before Nigeria is not simply to make laws against corruption. It is to build a culture in which ethical conduct becomes the norm, where public office is treated as a trust, and where institutions are strong enough to uphold accountability.
“We cannot continue to claim that private corruption will just keep going around in circles. It cannot go anywhere until we develop that culture, and nobody does wrong willingly,” he added.
Recalling an experience in Rwanda, Jonathan said the country’s social values discourage public officials from accepting gifts that could be considered inappropriate. He said the experience demonstrated how deeply rooted social norms can influence public conduct beyond what formal laws prescribe.
“I gave this to my aides to give to the people who take care of me. If you give me a hotel room where nobody can see anybody, where it is free, they say it is not the culture of Rwanda to accept the little gift — just a gift,” he said.
Meanwhile, he stressed that key institutions in the country, especially the judiciary, have an important role to play in ensuring accountability when rules are violated.
“All of us Nigerians have a major role to play if we want to suppress corruption, not just the bodies established by law to discipline and punish those who do it,” he stated, even as he urged politicians to exhibit higher moral standards.

Minister of the Federal Capital Territory FCT, Nyesom Wike, has announced plans to inaugurate and personally lead the campaign machinery for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in Abuja and Rivers State.

Wike disclosed this on Friday in Chikuku, a community along the Kuje-Gwagwalada artery, Abuja, after inspecting the ongoing construction of Phase Two of the Kuje-Gwagwalada road dualisation project, noting that political parties across the spectrum were organising their ranks, while supporters of the President were fully prepared to kick off an aggressive campaign.
“The ruling All Progressives Congress APC, I believe, is putting itself together for an aggressive campaign. For us who are supporting Mr President from different political platforms, we have put our machinery ready to fully kickstart. Very soon, I will inaugurate the campaign team for Tinubu in the FCT and Rivers State, which I will lead. All elements of the APC are ready, Mr President is ready, we are ready, and you can see the enthusiasm,” he said.
Addressing critics and political opponents, Wike argued that visible development projects would drive electoral support in the FCT, dismissing allegations of electoral malpractice ahead of time.
He said; “People are happy, and I don’t know who will contest against Mr President as far as this election is concerned. This is governance, and this is what people expect. It will translate directly into actual votes”.
The minister expressed confidence that the administration’s infrastructure record would secure victory across the board in the FCT, including for Sen. Philip Aduda and the territory’s two House of Representatives seats. “It is very obvious. Nobody will be able to claim rigging in the FCT. The ‘rigging’ is the projects we are delivering, making the people happy,” he added.
On the Kuje-Gwagwalada project itself, Wike assured stakeholders that adequate funding would be disbursed to guarantee completion by December.
“This is my first time getting to this side of the road, and I can see how highly populated this area is,” he said, stressing that delivering functional infrastructure remains the cornerstone of good governance and public satisfaction.
“You can imagine the enthusiasm and happiness on the faces of the people. That is why we say the essence of governance is to make people happy. When the people are happy, those in authority are happy,” he said, expressing gratitude to Tinubu for his sustained support for capital projects in the territory.
