items.author: Oboh
items.content:
Gboko, 24 September 2026
Mr. President,
I am writing to you from Gboko, where government is not experienced through communiqués or presidential briefings. People meet government when they go to the market, when they travel to the farm, when they pay school fees, when transport fares rise and when they have to decide which household expense can wait until next month.
But that is not the whole story of what it means to live here.
I am also writing from a place where fear is not an abstract word. In Benue, news of another attack is no longer something people encounter only in newspaper reports. Communities have been attacked, families have lost relatives and farmers have been forced to think carefully about whether it is safe to return to their fields. On September 10 and 11, an attack on Ayilamo in Logo Local Government Area left four police officers and seven civilians dead. Four days later, two more police officers were killed in an ambush while returning to the same community.
So when I write to you from Gboko, I cannot write only about the price of food, the cost of transport or the hardship created by economic reforms. There is another question that sits underneath all of them: whether people are safe enough to live, work and farm in their own communities.
That is the country I am thinking about as I look at your latest stay in Paris.
There is nothing wrong with a Nigerian president travelling to France. Nigeria needs France, just as France needs Nigeria. We need diplomatic relationships, investment, technology, trade and cooperation with countries whose decisions can affect our interests. A president should be able to sit across the table from another head of state and negotiate for Nigeria.
But there is a question that ought to follow every presidential journey: what comes home with the President?
On September 18, French President Emmanuel Macron received you for a private dinner at the Élysée Palace. The Presidency described the meeting as reflecting the enduring relationship between Nigeria and France and a shared commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation. You also met Vincent Bolloré in Paris, where his group announced plans to deepen its investment and localisation in Nigeria’s creative and digital economy, including film, entertainment and fibre-optic infrastructure.
Those are legitimate areas of engagement. But Nigerians should be allowed to ask what these meetings mean beyond the photographs and official descriptions. What commitments were made? What does Nigeria stand to gain? What obligations, if any, has Nigeria assumed? What should Nigerians expect to see from these conversations, and when?
What do you bring back for us after these meetings?
Those questions are not hostility to France. They are the ordinary questions citizens should ask of their government.
They are even more reasonable because Paris has become one of the most frequent destinations of your presidency. The PUNCH reported this month that you had spent more than 270 days abroad since assuming office, on 51 trips covering at least 30 countries, with more than 50 days spent in Paris across official, working and private visits.
The number alone does not prove that every journey was unnecessary. Your administration has maintained that you continue to receive briefings, issue directives and oversee government while abroad. The Presidency has described the current European stay as a working vacation and has pointed to official engagements conducted during it.
But governing is not only the ability to issue instructions from another country.
There is a difference between being informed about Nigeria and being physically present in the country whose problems you are being briefed about.
That difference matters.
From Gboko, the question is not whether the President is permitted to travel. Of course he is. The question is whether the frequency and length of those absences are proportionate to the condition of the country he leads and the sacrifices Nigerians are being asked to make.
And this is where the picture from Paris becomes difficult to separate from the picture at home.
At the Élysée Palace, there was a table laid for a presidential dinner, polished glasses, fine surroundings and two heads of state seated together in one of France’s most important rooms. In Nigeria, displaced families are still struggling with food, shelter and the basic necessities of life after losing their homes.
The contrast does not mean that the President should not sit down to dinner with the French President. It means that a country should be able to look at both pictures at the same time. One shows Nigeria represented at the highest level of international diplomacy. The other shows Nigerians who need their own government to remember what life looks like when a person has lost the security of home.
A presidential dinner can last a few hours. Hunger does not keep diplomatic time. For a displaced family, an empty plate is not a metaphor, and there is no communiqué that can make it less empty.
The table in Paris is important. So is the Nigerian who has no table at all.
And while Nigeria is being represented abroad, Nigerians at home are asking a more immediate question: will we be safe tomorrow?
That question deserves the attention of the presidency as much as any foreign investment deal does.
Nigeria was never a French colony. That history matters, not because Nigeria should keep France at arm’s length, but because it should remind us of the basis on which the two countries meet: sovereignty.
We should trade with France. We should welcome French investment where it serves Nigerian interests. We should cooperate with France on security, culture, technology and diplomacy. We should also disagree with France whenever Nigeria’s interests require disagreement.
A sovereign country should be able to do all of that without the psychology of dependence.
Our relationship with France should therefore be a relationship between countries with interests to negotiate, not between a former colony and a former colonial power. Nigeria does not need to approach Paris with reverence. It needs to approach Paris with clarity about what Nigeria wants.
And whatever is negotiated in Paris in Nigeria’s name should eventually be understandable to Nigerians at home.
That is where transparency becomes important.
The Presidency has told Nigerians what happened at the Macron dinner. It has told us about the meeting with Bolloré and the investment interests discussed there. But an official account is not the same thing as public accountability. Where important national interests are involved, Nigerians deserve to know enough to understand what their government has agreed to pursue on their behalf.
This becomes particularly important in a presidency that has asked Nigerians to accept painful economic changes
The petrol subsidy was removed. The naira was allowed to adjust sharply. Transportation costs rose. Food prices became harder for ordinary households to absorb. Businesses were forced to confront higher operating costs. Your administration has argued that these reforms were necessary to correct structural weaknesses and put the economy on a more sustainable footing.
That argument can be made.
But the people making the sacrifice are entitled to ask what the sacrifice is producing.
A family in Gboko does not experience economic reform as a policy paper. It experiences it when the same amount of money buys less food, when transport consumes a larger part of household income and when a young person with qualifications still cannot find work.
If Nigerians are being asked to endure the immediate pain of reform in anticipation of a better future, government must be prepared to show them the road from one to the other.
Otherwise, what exactly was the sacrifice for?
The same principle applies to the continuing dispute in the United States over access to investigative records involving you. Your legal team has challenged the release of records sought through a Freedom of Information Act case, while the Presidency has stressed that the proceedings are a civil records-disclosure dispute and that no US court has found you guilty of criminal wrongdoing.
That distinction matters and should not be erased.
An allegation is not a conviction. A record is not automatically proof of wrongdoing. A court dispute over access to documents should not be presented as though it were itself a criminal judgment.
But transparency has another side.
When questions about a public official persist, citizens are entitled to ask whether as much information as the law permits should be available to them. Public confidence is not strengthened merely by telling people that a matter is complicated. It is strengthened when the facts that can lawfully be disclosed are placed beyond unnecessary doubt.
The same standard should apply to public contracts, government honours and access to state opportunities.
Whenever the government gives an individual or corporation a significant public benefit, Nigerians should be able to ask what due diligence was conducted, what qualifications justified the decision and what the country received in return. That is not an attack on business or investment. It is what accountability looks like when public resources and public institutions are involved.
Mr. President, this is why I am writing from Gboko.
The concern is larger than Paris.
It is about the relationship between the places where presidential decisions are made and the places where Nigerians have to live with their consequences.
Here, insecurity is not a line in a briefing. It is the community wondering whether another attack will come. It is the farmer calculating whether returning to his field is worth the risk. It is the family that hears the news of another killing and wonders how long before its own community is mentioned.
Here, economic reform is not a policy argument on television. It is the household trying to make the same income stretch further.
Here, unemployment is not merely a statistic. It is the young graduate who has spent years looking for a job and is beginning to wonder whether there is any place for his education in the country.
These are realities that official reports can describe but cannot fully convey.
You may conduct government from abroad. You may meet presidents, investors and international business leaders there. Some of those meetings may produce agreements that eventually benefit Nigeria. That is precisely why Nigerians should insist on knowing what those agreements contain and how their benefits will reach the country.
The world will continue to invite the Nigerian President. Paris will continue to receive you. Investors will continue to request meetings. Foreign governments will continue to seek Nigeria’s attention because Nigeria matters.
But none of those audiences is the final audience of your presidency.
That audience is here.
It is in Gboko and Makurdi, Kano and Maiduguri, Lagos and Enugu, Port Harcourt and Kaduna. It is the Nigerian who wakes up every morning and has no choice but to live with the consequences of what government decides.
Mr. President, you do not need to stop travelling.
You need to make every journey answerable to the people whose country you are travelling on behalf of.
Engage France. Engage Europe. Engage America. Bring investment home. Negotiate firmly. Build partnerships. Open markets. Pursue opportunities
But do not allow the foreign capitals where Nigeria’s President is received to become more familiar to the presidency than the Nigerian communities where the consequences of presidential decisions are endured.
The people of Gboko do not have the luxury of stepping away from Nigeria when things become difficult. They stay. They work. They struggle. They adjust. They wait.
They are entitled to expect the government that asks them for patience to remain close enough to understand what that patience is costing them.
Nigeria is a sovereign country. Its resources belong to its people, and its institutions are supposed to work for the public. Those principles should not become less important because the President is dealing with foreign governments, investors or powerful individuals.
The presidency, too, exists because of the Nigerian people. It should never become so removed from their daily reality that the country being governed begins to look different from the country being represented abroad.
Whatever is discussed in Paris, whatever is negotiated abroad and whatever is committed in the name of Nigeria must eventually be capable of being explained to Nigerians.
That is not too much to ask.
It is the minimum owed to the people whose country you lead.
From Gboko, that is the question I leave with you:
After all the journeys, all the meetings and all the conversations abroad, can Nigerians still see themselves clearly in the government being conducted in their name?
Nigeria belongs to Nigerians.
Please govern accordingly
The post An open letter to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, by Stephanie Shaakaa appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.content:
Zinedine Zidane’s debut as France coach was overshadowed by an injury to captain Kylian Mbappe in a 1-0 win away to Turkey on Friday, while Roberto Mancini’s first game back in charge of Italy ended in a 2-0 defeat to Belgium.
Read Also:AFCON: Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers results
Zidane, the France legend and member of the team that won the World Cup in 1998, was taking charge of Les Bleus for the first time since being appointed in late July as the successor to Didier Deschamps.
Mbappe gave his side the lead nine minutes into the second half in the UEFA Nations League Group A1 clash at the Kocaeli Stadium in Izmit, just over 100 kilometres outside Istanbul.
But the Real Madrid superstar injured himself in the process of shooting, and looked to be in clear pain when he came off a few minutes later after initially attempting to carry on.
“It’s not great. Unfortunately I think he’s going to have to go home. We don’t want to take any risks,” Zidane told broadcaster TF1, suggesting that France’s all-time record goal-scorer will play no part in the three Nations League matches still to come over the next 10 days.
“He overextended his knee while shooting. It’s not very encouraging.”
France held on for the win without their captain, while Turkey finished the game with 10 men after goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir was sent off late on for handling the ball outside his box as he raced out to deny Bradley Barcola.
So it looks set to be without Mbappe that France will head to Brussels for their next game against Belgium on Monday.
Belgium, playing their first match since losing to eventual winners Spain in the World Cup quarter-finals, spoiled Mancini’s return to the Italian national team by beating their hosts at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome.
Mika Godts of Paris Saint-Germain ran through to give Belgium a 20th-minute lead, and substitute Dodi Lukebakio fired in from outside the box to double their advantage after the break.
Isak, Gyokeres strike for Sweden
“We need to think positively and not keep banging on all the time about what has happened in the past,” Mancini said later when asked if Italy’s failure to qualify for the World Cup was still hanging over the nation.
“In any case we can’t change what happened now,” added Mancini, who also said that boos by the home fans in the crowd of almost 50,000 were “normal” and “part of the game”.
Mancini was previously Italy coach between 2018 and 2023 and led them to victory at Euro 2020.
Elsewhere on Friday, Shea Charles of Fulham scored the winner deep in stoppage time as Northern Ireland won 1-0 away to Georgia in Group B2.
That was after PSG star Khvicha Kvaratskhelia had a penalty saved for the home side.
Danylo Sikan’s goal gave Ukraine a 1-0 victory in Hungary in the same group, with the visitors holding on after having Oleksandr Nazarenko sent off late on.
Robert Lewandowski captained Poland in their 0-0 draw with Bosnia and Herzegovina in Group B4, while Alexander Isak and Viktor Gyokeres both scored as Sweden beat Romania 2-1 in Stockholm in the same section.
There were also wins for Armenia and Montenegro in League C.
The Nations League action continues on Saturday with England hosting Spain, who are playing their first game since winning the World Cup in July.

items.content:
By Juliet Umeh
Senior Special Assistant to President Bola Tinubu on Media and Special Duties, Chief Tunde Rahman, has warned politicians hoping to contest the 2027 general election that social media popularity cannot substitute for serious political organisation and nationwide mobilisation.
Rahman, who spoke at the All Nigeria Editors Conference, ANEC, said winning a national election required more than maintaining a strong presence on social media, arguing that politicians must demonstrate the capacity to organise and field candidates across the country.
Rahman said: “We now have politicians who only prepare to contest elections on social media, not by campaigning to the people.
“Elections call for serious preparation. You cannot want to win a national election when you cannot even produce candidates across the country.”
Speaking on the theme, “The Ballot, the Media and the Task of Keeping Democracy Alive,” Rahman said the media had a critical responsibility to ensure balanced coverage as political activities intensify ahead of 2027.
“These times are critical. We are preparing for a most consequential election. So, we must ensure a balance of media space.
If you allow the opposition to speak, as you have done with Mr Peter Obi, the government too must speak,” Rahman said.
Rahman described the ballot and the newsroom as critical institutions in sustaining democratic rule.
“Democracy lives in three places: the ballot, the barracks and the newsroom. The soldiers have returned to the barracks. What is left is the ballot and the newsroom. If either fails, democracy fails.”
According to him, “The ballot is the only thing that makes a market woman equal to a billionaire. For four hours on election day, they have the same power.
“Our job, as political actors and as government, is to protect that power – to ensure that votes count, that BVAS works and that INEC remains independent.”
Rahman also warned editors about the growing danger posed by Artificial Intelligence, AI, fake news and deepfakes to electoral credibility.
“In this age of AI, fake news and deepfakes, your task has become harder. Anyone can sit on WhatsApp and announce a fake election result. Only you can debunk it with credibility.”
He urged journalists not to allow the competition for online engagement to undermine professional standards.
“Let us punish lies with facts. Let us punish propaganda with professionalism. Let us not let clicks kill credibility,” he said.
Rahman added: “The media should not be pro-APC or pro-LP or pro-PDP. It should be pro-Nigeria, pro-ballot, pro-people.
“If the ballot is free and the media is fair, democracy will not just survive in Nigeria, it will thrive.”

items.author: Ayobami
items.content:
Former Kaduna Central Senator, Shehu Sani, has warned that the informal arrangement of rotating the presidency between Nigeria’s northern and southern regions could come to an end if African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate Atiku Abubakar wins the 2027 election.
Sani made the comment on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday while arguing that political parties should field southern candidates in the 2027 presidential election.
“If Atiku wins, it means that is the end of rotational presidency in Nigeria, and there is going to be hard and bitter feelings from the southern part of Nigeria. I don’t think anyone will like to preside over a country full of hate, animosity, and conflict. Right now, the political system is managing a lot of crises,” he said.
“I don’t think a northerner taking over power here will come in with ease and conveniently to the people in the southern part of Nigeria. But if we allow the South to have their eight years, by 2031, a northerner takes over, there will be no challenge from southern Nigeria. That is my own view.”
Sani, however, acknowledged that the Constitution does not prevent Atiku or any other northerner from contesting the presidency.
“I never said Atiku should not run. Constitutionally, he has a right to run for any election, but what I said was that a southern part of Nigeria should be allowed to have its eight-year tenure in office, just like the way the North has from 2015 to 2023,” he said.
He called on opposition parties to field southern candidates and allow the region to compete for the presidency in 2027.
“The NDC should field Peter Obi, the APM should field Makinde, let the South struggle it out and see who wins for four years. And when the tenure is done by 2031, the North should have its unchallengeable opportunity to produce the leadership of the country,” Sani said.
He also rejected the argument that a region’s larger population or electorate should automatically translate into prolonged control of the presidency.
“You cannot say that because you have the largest electorate and population, so you should continue dominating politics,” he said.

items.author: Ayobami
items.content:
Kylian Mbappe scored the only goal of the game before having to come off grimacing with a knee injury as France won 1-0 in Turkey in the UEFA Nations League in new coach Zinedine Zidane’s first game in charge on Friday.
The Real Madrid superstar was moved out to the left wing by his new coach after being used through the middle of the France attack under former coach Didier Deschamps at the recent World Cup, which he ended as the top scorer with 10 goals.
It was from the left that Mbappe, France’s all-time top scorer, notched his 67th international goal, controlling and firing in low at the near post after being set up by Michael Olise.
He winced in pain as his teammates came across to celebrate the goal at the Kocaeli Stadium in Izmit, just over 100 kilometres outside Istanbul.
Mbappe tried to carry on after receiving treatment, but eventually slumped to the ground and looked concerned as he prodded the outside of his left knee, before walking off to be replaced by Desire Doue.
France and Real will now nervously wait to discover the extent of the injury, with Les Bleus playing three more games over the next 10 days before the club season resumes.
The sight of his star player and skipper coming off overshadowed Zidane’s first match since being appointed coach in late July on a deal to 2030.
The France legend and 1998 World Cup winner is making his return to elite coaching for the first time since his second stint in charge of Madrid ended in 2021.
France, beaten in the semi-finals at the World Cup by eventual winners Spain, are in Group A1 of this edition of the Nations League and will now go to Brussels to face Belgium on Monday. Belgium won 2-0 away to Italy on Friday.
– Cherki plays –
Zidane, whose last match as a player came for France against Italy in the 2006 World Cup final, will then make his home debut as coach against the Italians at the Stade de France next Friday.
His first team selection was not dramatically different to the side that regularly played at the World Cup, although Bournemouth’s Adrien Truffert was in at left-back while Manchester City’s Rayan Cherki came into the starting XI.
Olise, the Bayern Munich star who lit up the World Cup, was unlucky not to open the scoring late in the first half when his superb strike was tipped over by home goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir.
France goalkeeper Mike Maignan responded at the start of the second half as he tipped over an attempt by Abdulkerim Bardakci for Turkey, who finished bottom of their group at the World Cup despite a 3-2 win over co-hosts the United States.
Mbappe’s goal came shortly after, and the visitors later saw Jules Kounde hit the post before Turkey were reduced to 10 men late on.
Cakir came flying out of his area to halt Bradley Barcola as the France substitute raced through on goal. German referee Felix Zwayer initially waved play on before undertaking a VAR review after which he decided the goalkeeper had handled the ball, which meant a red card.
Turkey, coached by former Italian international Vincenzo Montella, host Italy next on Monday.

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Friday that Tehran had offered Washington a plan that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened to maritime navigation within seven days once agreed.
Read Also: Iran president says Tehran wants return to memorandum with US
Araghchi met for talks on Tuesday with US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel.
“Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN Friday.
“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure.
“I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared.”
Earlier media reports suggest the new plan calls for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East for seven days, including in Lebanon.
It also reportedly calls for the release of frozen Iranian assets estimated to be worth at least $12 billion, as well as the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade of Iran.
On the seventh day of the truce, Iran would reopen Hormuz.
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for the Revolutionary Guards, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran’s demands.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June that aimed to end the war, reopen the strait and launch talks on Iran’s nuclear program.
But the deal broke down shortly afterward when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorization before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Bahrain’s PROCODE is an AI-native e-sports platform built to become the operating system for competitive gaming.
When Shahd AlZaki and co-founder Rami Jamal began exploring the competitive gaming sector, they found an industry growing quickly but still relying on disconnected tools and manual processes.
Tournament organisers were managing competitions through spreadsheets and multiple platforms. Coaches were handling bookings and player development separately, while payments and players’ competitive histories were often spread across different systems.
This fragmentation inspired them to establish PROCODE in 2024. The Bahrain-based startup is developing an AI-native operating system through which organisations can manage esports competitions, training, payments and other operational functions.
“Competitive gaming has grown enormously, particularly in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region, but much of the industry still operates through fragmented and manual systems. Tournament organisers use multiple tools and spreadsheets, communities operate through platforms like Discord, coaches manage sessions separately, payments happen outside the ecosystem, and a player’s competitive and development history can be scattered across different platforms,” founder and CEO Shahd AlZaki told Disrupt Africa.
“Ultimately, our vision is to connect the entire esports journey in one place.”
PROCODE’s platform is organised around four areas: Compete, Train, Pay and Deploy.
“Organisers can run tournaments, leagues and multi-season circuits; players can access verified coaches and AI-powered VOD analysis; payments and prize distributions can be managed through the platform; and organisations can deploy PROCODE through white-label solutions, APIs, SSO and analytics. Underneath these layers, we’re building AI agents to automate much of the manual administration involved,” explained AlZaki.
According to the startup’s research, 49% of tournaments globally are managed manually, while coaches can spend about a quarter of their time on administrative work. PROCODE estimates that MENA accounts for more than US$ 100 million in competitive players within a global market of approximately US$ 540 million.
While global platforms solve individual parts of this journey, PROCODE has seen an opportunity to connect these fragmented functions into one AI-native esports operating system, built with MENA in mind from day one.
“That includes being Arabic-native rather than simply translating an English platform, as well as developing payment infrastructure and experiences suited to the region,” AlZaki said. “So in many ways, our biggest competition isn’t one specific company — it’s the fragmented and manual way the industry still operates today.”
Uptake has been encouraging, particularly as PROCODE is seeing engagement from different sides of the e-sports ecosystem, rather than from players alone.
“We’ve attracted till today a total of 4,000 users, seven coaches, and managed 10 tournaments.
We have a total of three brand ambassadors, and our ambassador network currently includes three creators across MENA with a combined following of more than 550,000, helping us build communities around competitive gaming and bring their audiences into the PROCODE ecosystem,” said AlZaki.
By bringing tournaments, coaching and payments into one platform, PROCODE is helping make competitive gaming easier to access and manage across the MENA region. Players can find coaching and track their development, while organisers can run competitions without relying on disconnected tools and manual processes.
Support from Women in Tech
PROCODE has raised a pre-seed round of funding, as well as grant capital from the Standard Chartered Foundation’s Women in Tech Accelerator. The programme, implemented locally by Innovate for Bahrain with support from Village Capital, is part of a multi-region initiative that supports impact-creating, tech-enabled, women-led startups in building thriving businesses across Africa, the Middle East, and Pakistan.
“The grant prize supported us in further platform development and hiring to grow our team. We would recommend the programme as the one-on-one mentoring was very beneficial, being part of a community that can support you is very important, and the prize money can support a startup that has just started on its journey,” said AlZaki.
Building in MENA, with global ambitions
Headquartered in Bahrain, PROCODE is nonetheless built for the wider MENA market.
“Our immediate focus is establishing a strong presence across the GCC and wider MENA, where e-sports is growing rapidly but much of the supporting infrastructure remains fragmented,” AlZaki said.
“The product reflects that regional strategy. For example, PROCODE is being built as a genuinely Arabic-native product with full right-to-left functionality rather than Arabic being added as a translation layer. We’re also developing payment infrastructure designed around MENA-native payment rails.”
PROCODE, which has both B2B and B2C business models, is not limiting its ambition to MENA.
“The problems we’re solving — tournament administration, fragmented player data, coaching operations and payments — exist globally. Our approach is therefore simple: prove it in MENA, build it for the world,” she said.
The post Meet Bahrain’s PROCODE, an AI-native e-sports platform appeared first on Disrupt Africa.

By Davies Iheamnachor, PORT HARCOURT
The Rivers State House of Assembly has issued warrant of arrest on the Vice Chancellor of PAMO University of Medical Sciences.
The Assembly took the decision deliberating on the report of its Ad hoc Committee on the investigation of scholarship funds to PAMO University.
The report was presented to the house by the Chairman of the Committee and Deputy Speaker of the house, Hon. Dumle Maol, on Friday, at the 53rd Legislative sitting of the house.
The committee had in their report recommended that warrant of arrest be issued on the Vice Chancellor, and for the State Government to set up a committee to recover all unaccounted funds in possession of the PAMO University and deposit them in the Consolidated Revenue Account of the State.
The assembly had opened an investigation into the state government’s funding of programmes in the university since 2017 and had invited the Vice Chancellor of the University for questioning.
House, however, took the resolution amidst the alleged refusal of the PAMO University Vice Chancellor to appear before the Ad hoc Committee after several invitations, to explain how money given to the university under the scholarship scheme was expended.
The report recounted how the university received over N29 billion from the state government with allegedly no corresponding students enrolment, giving credence to the reason behind the Vice Chancellor’s refusal to honour the invitations.
Speaking, Rt. Hon. Martin Chike Amaewhule said though the intentions of the government in entering into the scholarship scheme agreement was good, but the implementation failed.
Amaewhule frowned at the situation where documents presented by the Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Education, and the Office of the Accountant-General were at variance; adding that by simple deduction, out of the over N29 billion released by the State Government to PAMO University, it merely utilized only N5 billion.
The speaker according to the statement by his Special Assistant On Media Martins Wachukwu harped on the determination of the Assembly under his leadership to do the right thing irrespective of whose is involved.

items.author: Oboh
items.content:
The US Supreme Court on Friday granted a Trump administration request to allow the use of a federal database to weed out potential non-citizens from the voter rolls.
A majority of the nine justices on the top court joined the unsigned opinion, providing a victory to President Donald Trump ahead of the November mid-term elections.
The three liberal justices on the conservative-dominated court dissented.
Trump has baselessly claimed for years that many non-citizens vote in US elections and that mail-in ballots are vulnerable to fraud.
Friday’s Supreme Court decision lifted a lower court order that had blocked the use of a Department of Homeland Security program known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) to verify the citizenship of individuals on the voter rolls.
SAVE is used to identify citizenship status to determine whether someone is eligible for benefits.
Ruling against the Trump administration in June, the lower court said, “States have partnered with the federal government to access the database and are actively removing United States citizens from voter rolls based on inaccurate information.
“All in all, the federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote,” the court said.
In its ruling, the Supreme Court said the federal government “has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters.”
The lower court order blocking the use of SAVE “prevents the Federal Government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task.”
Attorney General Todd Blanche welcomed the Supreme Court ruling as a “huge victory for election integrity,” saying it will “allow states to clear the voter rolls of illegal voters.”
Election experts, however, said the ruling is unlikely to have a major impact on the November elections because most US states ban purges of voters 90 days ahead of an election.
“Both the majority and dissent agree that this case is likely to have limited impact on the midterms,” Rick Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said in a blog post. “Compared to the recent mail-in voting case, this one is not very important substantively.”
Hasen was referring to a Supreme Court decision earlier this month that blocked a Trump plan that would have restricted the use of mail-in ballots.
Trump reacted furiously to that ruling calling it “horrible” and “highly political” in a Truth Social post.

items.author: Juliana Harsianti
items.content:
Online vs offline protest, how effective it is?
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Gerd Altmann from Pixabay. Used under a Pixabay license.
This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.
The growing popularity and expanding use of social media have influenced the ways people express themselves. While protests once involved taking to the streets with banners and chants, such activities can now be carried out in the virtual realm. Messages and slogans are now conveyed through hashtags, digital posters, or videos posted across various social media channels. Events such as the Arab Spring and the Occupy Movement have further reinforced the phenomenon of online protest.
Both of them are effective, no?
What is the difference between online and offline protests? According to anthropologist Yatun Sastramidjaja, writing for the University of Amsterdam, there is no significant difference between offline and online protest, other than the setting — the real world versus the virtual world. Despite this difference in location, both forms can mobilize crowds, voice opinions, and support one another. A protest that begins online can spill over into the streets, as seen with the Arab Spring and the Occupy Movement. Such online-initiated protests can also raise awareness of specific issues, subsequently leading to offline protests.
These online movements are compelling because they tap into modern cultural trends, such as memes, hashtags, posters, and online petitions. Well-executed campaigns often employ dedicated graphic designers to select specific colors and typefaces that convey underlying meaning, carefully tailored to the nature of the protest. These chosen visual elements are then applied consistently across all online platforms, including websites, social media channels, posters, and other communication media. In essence, the protest is treated much like a product brand, requiring a clear and powerful identity.
This approach is indeed effective for embedding a social movement in people's minds, reaching both those accustomed to participating in protests and those drawn to the specific issues raised or the branding created by the organizers. It also proves effective across diverse demographics with varying modes of self-expression. These online protests have successfully mobilized a wide range of groups, including K-Pop fans from all over the world.
K-Pop, especially its fandom, is cited here as a prime example of youth culture that exerts influence across various spheres. In Korea, it played a role in the ousting of President Yoon, while in other countries — including Indonesia — K-Pop fandoms have actively participated in protests addressing social and political issues. Interactions among K-Pop fans typically take place online (on platforms like X, Facebook, and TikTok); consequently, movements often begin as online protests, with some individuals subsequently taking to the streets alongside other demonstrators.
But then, there are some disadvantages.
Although online protest is gaining popularity — especially among young people — it also has several drawbacks. One of them is uneven internet connectivity.
In her book “Social Media and Politics in Southeast Asia,” Merlyna Lim notes that early studies of digital networks hailed them as a new space for democratic processes, as they could transcend country borders and ultimately spur participation and social movements. But nowadays, the current distribution of digital technology is uneven; consequently, even though it can transcend national borders, the individuals involved are still primarily those who already possess good access to digital technology. Lim stated:
I contend that, setting aside the issue of unequal access, digital networks are not egalitarian networks where citizens have equal opportunities to participate in public discourse. First and foremost, the internet is never inherently egalitarian. Instead, the structure of the internet exhibits the characteristics of a scale-free network—a network in which the degree distribution follows a power law.
This uneven distribution of connectivity will hinder civil society organizations seeking to recruit new members from demographics different from their existing base. Furthermore, existing echo chambers are made worse by internet algorithms that suggest topics based on a user's interests, creating a limiting environment. For instance, if you are interested in environmental activism, your inbox will be flooded with suggestions on similar topics, and you will likely not see other appeals for activism that might also interest you, since the algorithm has latched on to your response to environmental activism.
Another concern is the assumption that people who participate in online protests are not necessarily willing to take to the streets or remain consistently engaged with the issues raised. Many people participate in online activism because, aside from the ease of doing so (such as posting memes or online posters), they can also take shelter behind anonymity. This differs from actually taking to the streets, which carries a higher risk of clashes with security forces. In response to this, the Open Society Foundation (OSF) has the view that online protests attract young people who are engaging with social issues for the first time, and it is the first step on the ladder to offline activism.
It is undeniable that there are various shortcomings, but in this short article, OSF suggests that civil society organizations (CSOs) can develop long-term strategies by incorporating online movements to champion specific issues. This involves planning for both online and offline engagement, as well as facilitating a seamless transition between the two. In essence, CSOs must devise ways to sustain public interest so that those initially engaged online remain committed to the cause over the long term and are willing to participate in offline activities.
To address the disparity in internet access, CSOs must continue to conduct face-to-face educational sessions and discussions that reach individuals with poor internet connectivity. Ultimately, even if access remains unequal, both online and offline activism can contribute meaningfully to a movement and complement each other.
Written by Juliana Harsianti

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Friday called for renewed diplomacy to end escalating conflicts in the Middle East while warning India that any attempt to stop, impede or divert Pakistan's share of river waters would be treated as an act of war.
Addressing the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, the prime minister urged a world fractured by war, occupation and mistrust to rediscover the courage of diplomacy, declaring that Pakistan had chosen dialogue over confrontation, cooperation over coercion and peace over war.
"We live at a dangerous moment. But our future is certainly not predetermined," he told leaders of the 193-member body.
"War is a choice. Peace is also a choice. And sometimes, the greater courage lies not in starting a war, but in preventing one," he said. "Pakistan has made its choice. We have chosen dialogue over confrontation. We have chosen cooperation over coercion. We have chosen peace over war."
Speaking under the session's theme, "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All," Shehbaz Sharif presented Pakistan's position on conflicts in the Middle East, Palestine and Jammu and Kashmir, tensions with India, terrorism emanating from Afghanistan, climate change, economic inequality, debt distress and reform of the United Nations.
He opened his address with traditional salutations and a verse from the Holy Quran on peace, followed by Quaid-e-Azam MuhammadAli Jinnah's declaration of Pakistan's steadfast support for the UN Charter.
Turning to the escalating conflicts in the Middle East, Shehbaz Sharif said diplomacy must not be drowned out by the sounds of war.
"Amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voices for diplomacy must echo even louder," he said.
The prime minister said Pakistan had moved swiftly after the outbreak of the regional conflict to help bring Washington and Tehran to the negotiating table in Islamabad, ultimately leading to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.
Calling the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb vital arteries of the global economy, he said they must remain open as passages connecting nations rather than becoming flashpoints of confrontation.
"These waters must carry the promise of prosperity, not the perils of war," he said.
Sharif strongly condemned recent Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, particularly what he described as an attempted strike on the holy city of Makkah.
"Any threat to the safety and sanctity of the Haramain Sharifain is a red line that must never be crossed," he said, reaffirming Pakistan's solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
Referring to the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, the prime minister said the alliance was not directed against any country but represented a collective commitment to regional defence, stability and peace.
On South Asia, Shehbaz Sharif recalled last year's conflict between Pakistan and India, saying Pakistan had exercised its inherent right to self-defense and that its armed forces, led by Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, had responded with precision and professionalism.
"They silenced the enemy, repulsed its attacks and taught it a lesson it shall never, ever forget," he said.
The prime minister praised US President Donald Trump, saying his "resolute and visionary" intervention at a critical moment had helped prevent a potentially catastrophic confrontation between the two nuclear-armed neighbors and saved hundreds of millions of lives.
Shehbaz told the General Assembly that lasting peace in South Asia remained inseparable from a just settlement of the Jammu and Kashmir dispute.
He said the Kashmiri people had waited for decades for the United Nations to fulfil its commitment to a free and impartial plebiscite. He accused India of arbitrary detentions, extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, sexual violence, and collective punishment in Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir.
He also accused New Delhi of attempting to alter the disputed territory's legal status and demographic character through unilateral measures.
"Helpless Kashmiri mothers and fathers yearn for their sons and daughters who never return," Shehbaz Sharif said. "Their homes lie silent, under curfew and in deep grief. For many, there is no closure - only a lifetime spent searching for graves that bear no names."
He reaffirmed Pakistan's diplomatic, political and moral support for the Kashmiri people until they attained their inalienable right to self-determination.
Turning to water security, the prime minister strongly opposed the weaponization of water and described the Indus River system as the "lifeblood" of Pakistan and the wider region.
He said India's unilateral decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance had no legal basis, adding that the position taken by UN experts and the Court of Arbitration had vindicated Pakistan's stance on the treaty's continuing validity.
"Water must never be weaponized. Rivers should nourish nations, not divide them," Shehbaz Sharif said.
He warned that Pakistan would regard any attempt by India to stop, impede or divert its rightful share of the waters as an act of war.
"India must make no mistake about it," he declared.
The prime minister devoted a significant portion of his address to the suffering of Palestinians, invoking the deaths of children, including Hind Rajab and eight-year-old Wafaa Akila, as symbols of what he called the international community's silence and failure.
"Does not a child born in Gaza deserve the same life, the same future and the same dream as a child anywhere else in the world?" he asked.
"The tragedies of Hind Rajab, Wafaa Akila and countless others will echo through history as an indictment of our collective silence and inaction."
Condemning the widening violence in the West Bank, Lebanon and Syria, Shehbaz Sharif reiterated Pakistan's position that an independent and viable Palestinian state based on the pre-1967 borders, with Al-Quds Al-Sharif as its capital, offered the only just and lasting solution.
On terrorism, the prime minister said Pakistan had lost nearly 100,000 civilians and members of its armed forces and suffered economic losses exceeding $150 billion in the fight against militancy.
He said the world was safer because of Pakistan's sacrifices and warned that Afghan territory continued to be used by the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan and the Balochistan Liberation Army - groups Islamabad officially refers to as Fitna al-Khawarij and Fitna al-Hindustan - to destabilize the country.
"This must come to a grinding halt," he said.
Sharif urged Afghanistan's Taliban authorities to meet their international obligations and take verifiable and decisive action to prevent Afghan territory from being used against Pakistan or any other country.
He also called on Kabul to respect the fundamental rights of the Afghan people, particularly women and girls, under all circumstances.
The prime minister highlighted Pakistan's long-standing contribution to UN peacekeeping missions and expressed concern over the global rise of Islamophobia, including hate speech, attacks on mosques and the desecration of the Holy Quran.
He warned of what he described as cross-border threats arising from RSS-driven Hindutva ideology and cited the recent demolition of a 150-year-old mosque in Saharanpur, India. Religious hatred, he said, must have no place in the world.
On climate change, the prime minister said Pakistan contributed less than one per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions but continued to endure some of the crisis's most devastating consequences.
He called on developed countries to fulfil their climate finance commitments, accelerate funding for loss and damage, and provide adequate support for adaptation and resilience.
"The theme of this session calls upon us to restore trust. But trust cannot be restored by simple words alone. It must be earned through actions and behavior," Shehbaz Sharif said.
Calling for a stronger and more effective United Nations, Shehbaz Sharif said the Security Council must become more representative, democratic, and accountable. Reform, he stressed, should reflect the aspirations of the majority of nations rather than protect the privileges of a select few.
He reaffirmed Pakistan's guiding principle: "Reform for All, Privilege for None."
Concluding his address, the prime minister returned to the defining choice confronting the international community.
"Let this 81st General Assembly make the same choice - for us, for our children and for generations yet unborn," he said.
"Let us restore trust. Let us preserve peace. And let us prove that, even in a divided world, humanity can still choose to stand together."

items.author: Kamran Yousaf
items.content:
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on Friday held an urgent meeting of their top military commanders in Riyadh under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), marking the first exclusive high-level military coordination between the three countries since the trilateral defence pact was signed last month.
Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, Turkish Chief of General Staff Gen Selcuk Bayraktaroglu and Saudi Chief of General Staff Gen Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili attended the meeting in the Saudi capital, according to a statement issued by the military's media wing.
The chiefs of defense forces and chiefs of general staff reviewed the security situation and the threats facing the kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
They strongly resented the attacks targeting the holy city of Makkah and civilian and economic infrastructure, the Inter-Services Public Relations said.
They appreciated the vigilance and professionalism of the Saudi armed forces for ensuring safety of the people and security of the kingdom, it added.
The participants also discussed ways to further advance cooperation among the armed forces of the three countries and to enhance intelligence sharing, military coordination, and capability integration, thereby strengthening deterrence and collective defense.
The participants commended the longstanding relations and mutual trust that bind the people and the armed forces of the three countries. They noted that their meeting in Riyadh reflects the strength of their defense partnership and their shared determination to immediately translate the commitments of the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement into effective military cooperation.
The participants strongly affirmed their commitment to collective defense thereby demonstrating the resolve of the three countries in defending the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
The meeting came hours after the foreign ministers of the three countries agreed in New York to convene their military chiefs amid intensified attacks targeting Saudi Arabia. The development effectively takes the Makkah agreement from the political and institutionalisation phase into military-level consultations.
The military commanders' meeting assumes particular significance because the MJDA contains a collective-defence provision under which an attack against any one of the three parties would be considered an attack against all.
The immediate backdrop is the escalation of attacks from Houthis targeting Saudi territory and critical infrastructure. Türkiye had already publicly expressed readiness to help meet Saudi Arabia's military requirements under the defence agreement, while Pakistan has reiterated its commitment to Saudi Arabia's defence.
The exact outcome of Friday's meeting, including whether the three sides agreed on any specific military assistance, deployments or operational arrangements, was not immediately disclosed.
The meeting follows a decision by the foreign ministers in New York to prepare for urgent military consultations. Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan had reviewed progress on institutionalising the agreement and condemned attacks targeting Makkah as well as Saudi civilian and economic facilities.
The ministers also reaffirmed Saudi Arabia's right to take measures it considers necessary for its defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence in the event of an armed attack.
The Riyadh meeting therefore provides the first opportunity for the military leadership of the three countries to discuss how the collective-defence commitment could be translated into practical cooperation.
The three countries have been steadily building the institutional architecture of the alliance since the agreement was signed in Makkah on August 7 by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman.
At the first meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee in Istanbul on August 31, the three sides agreed to establish a permanent secretariat in Riyadh and discussed military interoperability, defence capabilities, defence-industry cooperation, joint production and research, as well as counterterrorism coordination.
Pakistan subsequently appointed retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood as the first secretary general of the Makkah Defence Alliance, formally setting the process of establishing the Riyadh-based secretariat in motion.
The three countries have also stressed that the alliance is defensive in nature and is not directed against any particular state. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said the alliance was founded on respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and non-interference and remained open to other countries that shared those principles.
For Pakistan and Turkiye, however, the current crisis presents a more immediate test of the agreement's collective-defence clause. Both countries have simultaneously sought to support Saudi Arabia's security while advocating de-escalation and diplomatic efforts to resolve the wider regional conflicts.
The Riyadh meeting is consequently the first concrete military-level test of how the Makkah pact will operate when one of its members faces sustained attacks.

items.author: Ahtesham Bashir
items.content:
Acknowledging the difficulties and potential consequences of holding a long march amid extensive security and traffic restrictions imposed by the PML-N-led federal and Punjab governments, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) on Friday announced postponing its much-touted long march on Islamabad, originally scheduled for September 27, until October 4.
The decision appeared to render the federal government in a bind as it with the coordination of the Punjab government made an extensive security operation, which included blocking access points to Islamabad for traffic from Punjab with nail-studded metal barriers, erecting walls of shipping containers across the city, and deploying Rangers and large contingents of police.
Addressing a news conference in Peshawar, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, after securing formal approval from the party's political committee, announced that a "sea of people" would leave Peshawar on the new date as part of the party's political strategy.
He said the decision had been taken purely as a political strategy and that the march would now depart from Peshawar on October 4.
The decision had not, however, been endorsed by PTI's allies in TTAP as of the filing of this report, according to sources, who attributed the disagreement to a lack of coordination. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said TTAP leaders would join him on stage during the march, while acknowledging differences between PTI and the alliance.
Speculation over a possible postponement had circulated for about 40 hours, with the proposal first discussed at the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa level during a Zoom meeting, according to party sources. A political committee meeting was subsequently convened to formally approve the decision, which sources said was endorsed without significant debate.
One party leader suggested not announcing a new date for the march, arguing that this would keep the government uncertain about PTI's plans. Asad Qaiser disagreed, saying that postponing the march without announcing a new date could be interpreted as a withdrawal, according to the sources.
The party also informed opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai about the decision. The postponement to October 4 was also reported by multiple outlets following the political committee's decision.
Interestingly, Afridi held two news conferences on Friday. At the first, during the day, he vowed to proceed with the march at all costs but remained vague about its date. At a second news conference after the party meeting, he announced that the march had been postponed to Oct 4.
Based on Afridi's remarks, the move appeared aimed at allowing the party to mark PTI founder Imran Khan's birthday, which falls on Oct 5, in Islamabad.
Afridi said October 5, the birthday of PTI founder Imran Khan, would be observed by party workers, who would cut cakes and celebrate a "Victory Day".
The decision to postpone the September 27 march was taken by the PTI political committee. Afridi said a proposal had been placed before the committee two days earlier to defer the march until the first week of October. Following lengthy consultations, the committee agreed to postpone it until October 4.
He said the decision was unanimous and reiterated that the postponement was part of a political strategy.
Afridi claimed that the federal government had become unnerved by the planned march and alleged that all routes leading into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had been blocked.
He likened the government's actions to the "same conspiracy" that had preceded the events surrounding East Pakistan and alleged that the measures were aimed at breaking up Pakistan. He questioned what the government hoped to prove by closing the routes.
"We are political people and will pursue a political struggle," Afridi said, adding that those expecting a repeat of the May 9-style operation against PTI were mistaken and that his party would foil "a conspiracy" against it.
He said that if the authorities wanted to arrest people or stop the march, they should come in uniform.
Afridi said PTI respected uniformed personnel, but those arriving in plain clothes would be dealt with differently.
He claimed that Imran Khan could be released within a minute if the courts began functioning properly, adding that the Supreme Court had ordered the PTI founder's transfer to hospital but the order had not been implemented.
Afridi said all relevant issues had been discussed by the political committee and that the committee had agreed that the march would depart from Peshawar on October 4.
He also referred to a statement made some time ago by Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz that she feared other provinces rather than India, and questioned the message such remarks sent to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Afridi criticised Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah for calling PTI members terrorists and asked what message the federal government was giving to the province.
He alleged that PTI members of the provincial assembly were being picked up and that roads had been blocked along the K-P border.
Afridi insisted that PTI was a political and peaceful movement and alleged that the government wanted to build cases against the party again in a manner similar to those following May 9.
"Our fight is for the supremacy of the Constitution and the law," he said.
 
'Conspiracy against K-P'
The K-P chief minister alleged that efforts were being made to keep PTI and the establishment locked in confrontation, while planes and vehicles were being purchased.
He further accused the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) of effectively becoming the Punjab police and alleged that PML-N leaders were creating a "terrorist" narrative against PTI.
Afridi alleged that some people were being brought into PTI ranks and said he was warning in advance that anyone planning any action against the party should come in uniform.
He said PTI would not raise sticks against uniformed personnel.
Afridi appealed to the chief justice of the Supreme Court to take action over "efforts to cut Khyber Pakhtunkhwa off from Pakistan".
He said the political struggle was a "Test match" and added that PTI had already won the toss.
Afridi said negotiations would continue after the long march and criticised the extensive use of containers in Islamabad, saying the federal capital had effectively been turned into a "container city".
He warned that those who came out on October 4 would not be under anyone's control.
The decision to postpone the march and the new date were also conveyed to Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas by PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan, Afridi said.
He reiterated that postponing the long march was part of PTI's political strategy.
The postponement followed days of uncertainty over the September 27 schedule. PTI had previously been preparing for a nationwide protest and long march towards Islamabad, while opposition leaders had been consulting over the timing and political strategy surrounding the mobilisation.
It is pertinent to note that the decision came amid an internal debate over the feasibility and timing of the march, as party sources said there had been a proposal to "exhaust" the federal government and law-enforcement agencies because the federal capital and several routes had already been closed or restricted.
The sources claimed that the PTI had already achieved what it wanted through the march, with roads shut and hundreds of millions of rupees being spent on law enforcement.
The announcement was welcomed by PTI and some members of TTAP, who said the decision recognized the cost to the government of either maintaining the security arrangements until Oct. 4 or redeploying them closer to the new date.
A TTAP leader described the move as a significant setback for the government, saying the chief minister had gained an advantage simply by postponing the march. The leader said measures introduced to restrict PTI's planned mobilisation could ultimately impose a greater burden on the government if they had to be maintained or reinstated.
According to PTI leaders, the march will now leave Peshawar on October 4. Earlier discussions within the party had also considered October 5 to 10 as a possible new window.
The party sources said the decision had nothing to do with the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI), whose own protest march against the petroleum levy had been postponed at the request of the prime minister.
A senior PTI leader said the postponement offered the party two main advantages: it would increase pressure on a government that had taken extensive measures to prevent the march, while also creating an opportunity for negotiations to resume. PTI leaders have, however, said no meaningful negotiations were currently under way.
The decision was rejected by TTAP, whose leader said Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Nasir Abbas had been repeatedly sidelined by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister during consultations on major decisions. The leader said TTAP had also not been consulted before the Sept. 27 date was announced and was again left out of consultations over the latest postponement, describing it as adding "insult to injury."
Asked about the criticism, Afridi said PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan had communicated the party's decision to both leaders.
According to sources, PTI leadership had contacted Achakzai and requested that he announce a new date for the long march. At the time, however, Achakzai had refused to announce its postponement and maintained that the countrywide movement would begin on September 27.
Sources said Achakzai's position was that the movement would begin in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and other provinces on September 27 and would gradually move towards Islamabad.
The disagreement over postponing the long march between PTI leadership and Achakzai remained unresolved for a time, while efforts to persuade the opposition leader continued.
PTI leadership also continued consultations with opposition leaders over the date of the long march.
Against this backdrop, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan arrived in Islamabad from Mianwali to meet Achakzai and other opposition leaders.
Gohar subsequently met Achakzai and briefed him on the PTI's position regarding the long march, according to sources.
The sources said PTI leadership wanted the long march postponed and wanted Achakzai, as opposition leader, to announce the decision.

It rejected the Afghan Ministry of Defence's account as an attempt to dismiss Pakistan's account as propaganda, saying the claim that the Pakistani post had been destroyed and that Afghan forces suffered no casualties was fabricated.
The ministry further said the Afghan Ministry's attempt to present a contrary account was no surprise, stating that the Taliban were habitual liars with no moral or reputational standing.
"Truth prevails over falsehood," the ministry said.

items.content:
AAMIR ILYAS RANA
Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif has said that aggression against either Pakistan or Saudi Arabia would be treated as aggression against both under their defence agreement, while revealing that Islamabad has also discussed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia with Iran.
In an exclusive interview with The Express Tribune in New York, Asif said that responding to attacks by the Houthi militia on Saudi Arabia was the responsibility of all three countries covered by the Makkah Defence Alliance.
"The Makkah defence agreement binds Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in such a way that in the event of any aggression against Saudi Arabia, standing by it becomes an important responsibility for Pakistan," the minister said.
He added that the defence agreement would further strengthen the longstanding relationship between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which extended beyond defence cooperation to encompass religious, historical and fraternal ties.
Asif revealed that Pakistan had raised the issue of non-state actors operating in the region during a meeting with the Iranian president, stressing that such groups needed to be rendered ineffective because their activities were undermining regional peace efforts. "The Iranian leadership has been told that non-state actors should not carry out operations in any country," he added.
He said the Iranian president had responded positively and agreed that tensions and instability in the region would ultimately harm the people of all sides. He added that Iranian leaders had indicated that they would engage with the Houthis, although practical progress would depend on subsequent steps.
Asked about the need to activate the Makkah agreement in practical terms, Asif said the pact represented a strong bond between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. "Besides the religious ties, the two countries now have a defence agreement under which Pakistan will stand by Saudi Arabia in the event of aggression," he said.
On the country's domestic political situation, Khawaja Asif said the government had tried to pursue negotiations with the PTI and had also offered talks, but the opposition party had chosen the path of protest and confrontation.
"Even a PTI leader spoke about turning Islamabad into 'Somnath'," he said. "The government does not want political tensions at a time when the country is going through a phase of economic recovery," the minister stated, warning that political tensions and protest activities could affect the recovery process.
Speaking about the law and order situation in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), the minister criticised the provincial government, saying federal institutions were playing their role in the fight against terrorism, but the basic responsibility for maintaining law and order rested with the provincial government.
"If the provincial government effectively fulfilled its constitutional responsibilities, it could help control terrorism in the province," Asif said.
However, he alleged that the K-P government wanted to take powers away from the police. Asif said that through amendments to laws, the provincial government wanted the police force to remain under its control, which would make the maintenance of law and order difficult.

items.author: Shahbaz Rana
items.content:
The government on Friday asked trade leaders to play their part in creating awareness of the fixed tax scheme, as so far only three new shopkeepers had submitted returns amid high hopes that over 9,800 newly registered persons would soon become filers.
Against the annual tax collection target of Rs50 billion under the new scheme, the government received Rs32.5 million by Friday.
The poor response to the 1% fixed tax scheme could be gauged from the fact that one of the two leading trade leaders, Ajmal Baloch, who negotiated and finalised the scheme with the government, did not submit his tax return. "I have to do it now. I haven't got time," he said.
Minister of State for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani on Friday reviewed the implementation of the scheme. In a meeting, he was informed that so far 428 shopkeepers had filed returns, according to a press statement. However, out of the 428, the new traders who joined the scheme were only three.
The finance ministry said that so far 1,929 new traders had registered themselves for joining the tax system. However, out of these, only 57 have drafted returns but have not yet submitted, according to government officials. They said so far 9,806 shopkeepers had drafted their return statements but did not file with the FBR. But only 57 of them were new.
Kayani urged the trade leaders to play their role in getting the scheme successful. However, the representatives of traders put the responsibility on the FBR and also complained about hurdles to the online filing of returns. Kayani directed the FBR to immediately address the technical objections raised by shopkeepers and lawyers. He also directed the authorities to provide FBR plates at the earliest to the shopkeepers who had filed returns.
Kayani remarked that the fixed tax scheme "is a unique facility designed specifically for shopkeepers and is not available to any other business". Traders have been given exemption from audit, installation of digital devices for transactions and are required to pay only 1% tax on turnover, compared to 35% for a salaried person.
The salaried class has raised concerns over the preferential treatment meted out to the traders, who contributed very little to the exchequer compared to Rs630 billion in taxes paid by the salaried class in the last fiscal year. To a question, Kayani said it was irrelevant at this stage to say how many new traders had filed returns, hoping that 9,800, including the 1,929 newly registered, would submit their statements by September 30.
He expected that more shopkeepers would join the scheme, saying there was no reason to remain non-filers after the launch of the Asaan Tax scheme. The meeting decided to make daily contacts between the traders and FBR officials to facilitate implementation of the scheme. It was also agreed to further enhance engagement with the tax bars.
The meeting was informed that an Urdu language information booklet had been issued to explain the new scheme, the previous procedure for filing returns and details of penalties applicable after the deadline. A penalty of Rs10,000 would be imposed in the first month after the deadline, Rs25,000 in the second month and Rs50,000 in the third month, the finance ministry said.
Traders' representatives assured the meeting of their full cooperation, stating that the scheme was a good initiative and it might take some time to create awareness among shopkeepers. It is the second such initiative by the government aimed at bringing traders into the tax net after the earlier Tajir Dost scheme failed to deliver desired results. Kayani was hopeful about the success of the scheme due to the involvement of traders in its design and execution.
Although the state minister did not officially give any target for the first year, he voiced hope that a majority of 3.5 million traders would opt for the scheme.
New faceless system
Meanwhile, the FBR has established the National Faceless Centre (NFC) in Islamabad. The decision was taken by the Board in Council in its meeting held on Friday. The centre is a major reform that changes how tax audits and assessments are carried out in Pakistan.
Until now, a taxpayer whose return was picked for audit had to deal with a particular officer in a particular office, often in person. Under the new system, contacts between the taxpayer and the taxman come to an end. Cases will be selected by a computerised, risk-based system rather than by any officer.
Each case will then be assigned automatically to an officer, who may be sitting anywhere in the country. The taxpayer will not know who the officer is and the officer will have no say which case comes to him. Every case will pass through three separate hands. One officer will conduct the audit, the second will make assessment and the third will review the work for quality before any order is issued. No officer will control a taxpayer's case from start to finish.
All notices, replies and hearings will take place electronically through the FBR's IRIS system. Where the law requires a physical verification or recovery, this will be carried out by a separate field team.
The faceless centre draws its legal authority from the Finance Act 2026. It will be headed by a chief commissioner Inland Revenue, with dedicated wings for faceless audit, faceless assessment, quality control and field operations. A Programme Management Unit has already been set up to oversee its rollout.
