items.content:
Punjab Governor Sardar Saleem Haider Khan has called for establishing a policy framework to promote the domestic manufacturing of solar systems, saying Pakistan can create millions of jobs, generate clean and affordable energy and earn foreign exchange by developing a local solar industry.
"It is unfortunate that solar system manufacturing is not being done due to the lack of a government policy," the governor said while addressing the 3rd International Solar Power Conclave & Solar Technology Excellence Awards 2026, organised by the Energy Update in collaboration with the Pakistan Solar Association (PSA), the Renewable Energy Association of Pakistan and the Pakistan Alternative Energy Association on Friday.
He said the high cost of electricity had made solar energy increasingly important for ordinary Pakistanis, describing sunlight as "Allah's gift" that should be utilised to reduce the burden of electricity bills while also protecting the environment.
"If we are able to set up a solar manufacturing industry, it will create millions of jobs and also produce clean, green energy, which is cheaper for consumers' pockets and better for the environment," he said.
The governor urged the solar business community to take the initiative and begin manufacturing solar systems locally instead of waiting indefinitely for a government policy. He pointed out that the industry had already brought solar technology to Pakistan without substantial state support and said a similar initiative could now help establish a domestic manufacturing base.
With local production, he said, Pakistan would not only meet its own growing demand but could also export solar systems and earn much-needed foreign exchange. He stressed that it was encouraging to see the rapid spread of solar panels across the country, observing that "almost 90% of roofs" in cities appeared to be covered with solar panels.
Highlighting the government's efforts to expand access to solar energy, the governor said the Sindh government had distributed hundreds of thousands of solar panels free of cost among livestock farmers and flood-stricken communities. "We have been bestowed with abundance of sunlight, which must be used to serve the interests of the masses," he remarked.
Referring to recent disruptions to the energy supply chain caused by the war in the region, the governor said electricity load-shedding had increased when LNG containers could not arrive. However, the growing availability of solar energy could eventually make expensive grid electricity less relevant for domestic consumers.
Speaking on the occasion, Punjab Minister for Energy Faisal Ayub said Pakistan had experienced its worst electricity load-shedding crisis beginning in 2009-10, which was overcome during the PML-N government's 2013-18 tenure. He recalled that in Punjab, the then chief minister Shehbaz Sharif had installed power plants to address electricity shortage, but said the country was now facing a different challenge - the high cost of electricity.
"Although it is a federal subject, we will provide support to the solar energy sector to overcome this challenge of expensive electricity," Ayub said. He observed that whether or not governments promoted solar energy, consumers and the industry would eventually move towards it because of the economics of solar power. "The government, therefore, needs to align its policies with this transition."
The minister assured the solar sector of the Punjab government's full support, saying the provincial government would engage the federal energy minister and bring PSA representatives on board to devise a policy to facilitate the expansion of solar energy in Pakistan.
"We will welcome suggestions from energy experts to promote this sector," he said, warning that failure to support the solar sector at this stage could damage Pakistan's interests. He noted that a friendly policy for the solar industry could generate prosperity not only for businesses associated with renewable energy but for the country as a whole.
PSA President Adil Mahmood said solar energy was already contributing up to 40,000 megawatts to Pakistan's energy supply and argued that without this contribution the country would otherwise be experiencing five to seven hours of load-shedding every day.
He said the government was charging four paisa per unit, adding that it translated into a cost of around Rs1.5 million per MW per month, which he said needed to be removed.
Mahmood pointed out that the solar market had expanded rapidly when there was no tax on solar panels, but subsequent measures created hurdles in the way of the industry. He also mentioned that net metering had now been abolished, describing such developments as impediments to further promotion of solar energy.
He urged the government to abolish duties and sales tax on batteries and proposed the establishment of local lithium battery manufacturing plants, which could eventually produce batteries for export as well.

items.author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
items.content:
The government is likely to introduce additional gas tariff slabs to provide cheaper gas to consumers by bringing more people under the protected category net.
The Cabinet Committee on Energy (CCOE) has directed the Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division) to examine the proposal of introducing a more rational categorisation of protected consumers in the gas sector.
During discussions in a recent meeting of the CCOE, chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division) revealed that the evaluation carried out by the World Bank as well as advisory firm KPMG for the accumulation of circular debt in the oil and gas sectors over the last five years highlighted a substantial addition to the debt between 2019 and 2023 primarily on account of no increase in consumer gas prices and diversion of RLNG to domestic consumers.
On a query, the meeting was informed that according to an agreed definition with the IMF and World Bank, the circular debt meant "net financial burdens on Sui gas companies due to policy and regulatory decisions". Also, Sui gas companies use a circular debt reporting tool developed by the World Bank to report the debt stock digitally while the components of the circular debt include tariff differentials and power companies' receivables.
It was highlighted that due to lower bill collections by SSGC and SNGPL in proportion to their supplies, coupled with power-sector issues, the gas-sector circular debt had consistently increased, which adversely impacted the financial capacity of state-owned exploration & production companies to invest in their core business, which may turn those profitable entities into loss-making concerns and ultimately put a burden on the national exchequer.
A list of the key factors contributing to the circular debt was shared with the CCOE, which included delayed revision in consumer gas prices (2013-22), the gap between Ogra-determined revenue requirements of Sui gas companies, low recoveries owing to the power sector, diversion of RLNG to the domestic sector in winters (2018-23), inadequate budgetary allocation for subsidies under tariff commitments, pending GST refunds with the FBR, litigation on consumer gas price notifications, demand reduction from high-yielding captive power plants and CNG stations, and the RLNG tariff actualisation effective from February 2025.
The Petroleum Division shared a trajectory curve of the circular debt, showing a very sharp rise from June 2019 to June 2023 and a flatter trend from June 2023 to June 2026. The forum was also briefed on the urgent need to resolve gas bill recovery issues of SSGC in Balochistan, requiring high-level engagements.
The division requested for the settlement of power-sector receivables against supplies of domestic gas, RLNG and oil; settlement of RLNG actualisation tariff of the power sector amounting to Rs42 billion; payment of Rs83 billion by the FBR in GST refunds; and budgetary allocation of Rs160 billion for the elimination of cross-subsidies in the domestic sector to provide relief to the industry for economic growth.
The Petroleum Division also requested that the Finance Division may reach the closure of the ongoing discussions on the gas-sector Circular Debt Management Plan (CDMP) with the IMF, in response to which the Finance Division informed the meeting that the CDMP would be taken up with the fund during the loan programme review in September.
The CCOE considered a summary titled "Circular Debt in the Gas Sector" and gave directives that issues related to the power-sector receivables, tax refunds and the budgeting of subsidy be taken up for ultimate resolution in consultation with all stakeholders.

items.content:
State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) Governor Jameel Ahmad on Friday inaugurated the Pasban Remittance Reward Scheme, offering Rs16 billion in annual cash prizes to encourage overseas Pakistanis to send remittances through formal banking channels.
Launched under the auspices of the Pakistan Banks Association (PBA), the scheme is fully funded by the banking industry and will not impose any burden on the national exchequer.
Speaking at the launch ceremony, Ahmad said the initiative had been developed with the government and banking industry as a sustainable, market-oriented mechanism to attract workers' remittances through formal channels. He said remittances were vital for millions of Pakistani families, supporting household spending, education, healthcare, investment and economic opportunities.
The governor highlighted the improvement in Pakistan's external position, noting that the SBP's foreign exchange reserves had risen from below $3 billion in February 2023 to $21.4 billion. He said the recent buildup in reserves had primarily been supported by foreign exchange purchases from the market rather than external borrowing.
Workers' remittances reached a record $41.6 billion in FY26, compared with $21.7 billion in FY19, nearly doubling over the period, he added.
Under the Pasban scheme, a beneficiary receiving remittances equivalent to at least $100 each month for three consecutive months in a quarter will qualify for digital entries. Higher remittance amounts will generate additional entries proportionate to the amount received.

items.title: Returning to MoU
items.summary:
Mediatory efforts received a shot in the arm as the warring sides in the ongoing Middle East conflict surprisingly toned down their confrontational rhetoric. Much transpired on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly session, where officials from the US, Iran, Qatar and Pakistan collaborated to break the stalemate in talks. items.content:
Mediatory efforts received a shot in the arm as the warring sides in the ongoing Middle East conflict surprisingly toned down their confrontational rhetoric. Much transpired on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly session, where officials from the US, Iran, Qatar and Pakistan collaborated to break the stalemate in talks. Their primary focus was on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, normalising the global supply chain and bringing down oil prices.
The nod from Tehran, which is devising a plan with Oman to reopen the strategic water channel in the Persian Gulf within the next seven days, is a promising development. Likewise, Qatar reaching out to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and the consensus on brokering another ceasefire are momentous achievements. Pakistan pushed the envelope further by making both the US and Iran realise that going back to the Islamabad MoU is the way forward. This aspect has been squarely endorsed and appreciated by the UN secretary-general, too.
The need of the hour is to ensure that de-escalation takes place instantly. Reports that a format is being worked out for resuming parleys are encouraging; incidentally, these reports emerged after a huddle in the Oval Office between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. Pezeshkian demonstrated leadership when he told Fox News that his country is not interested in continuing the war and that the ball is in Washington's court. This needs to be read closely with reports that Tehran has hinted at reopening the Strait in exchange for the lifting of the US naval blockade and the unfreezing of its assets.
This impasse is already taking a toll on global economics. The suspension of shipping through the Red Sea's Bab El-Mandeb - as the Houthis have triggered another conflagration - is unnerving. Any broadening of the conflict across Yemen and its spillover into the wider region would be catastrophic. A one-point move can help address all eventualities: Iran and the US must return to the understanding reached in Islamabad. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian Foreign Minister, has convincingly floated that idea as the way forward.

items.content:
Pakistan Steel Mills (PSM) has been dead since June 2015, when the furnaces closed after gas was shut off due to non-payment of dues. Yet, 11 years later, the state remains in denial and refuses to give the mill a dignified funeral. In its life, the mill was the epitome of a white elephant - apart from a few years in the mid-2000s, the mill lost money every year of its five-decade operational history. But even in death, it continues to burn taxpayer money.
According to the Ministry of Industries, the closed mill haemorrhaged Rs79.3 billion over the past three fiscal years alone, with Rs24 billion lost in FY26. About 72% of the losses since FY24 were interest payments on legacy debt, which will continue to accumulate since the government is unwilling to pay to clear it, and buyers are not particularly interested in operating the mill. The finance ministry has also not helped the situation, as it has failed to follow its own internal advice to restructure PSM's debt through swaps and write-downs. Meanwhile, 'running' costs also painfully hit the exchequer, including salaries, utilities and pensions.
Part of the problem is that the governments in Islamabad and Karachi continue to live in a fool's paradise, believing that PSM can be revived into a profitable entity. The fact is that the cost of modernising and reactivating the mill while covering running and historical expenses makes this proposal a non-starter for most reputable investors. Even the current proposals, including one from Russia, are problematic due to Western sanctions. Public-private partnerships also risk sticking the government with the bill when they invariably fail. And even at its peak, PSM never produced a superior product - it relied on tariffs to make imported steel expensive and keep its own uncompetitive products profitable.
The best-case scenario at this point is thus not revival, but liquidation. Part-selling the real estate and scrapping the mill could probably cover most liabilities and still leave the government with a small profit. Maintaining the status quo, however, is just an insult to everyone.

items.content:
Sea levels are rising, and their consequences will be anything but gradual. A unanimous UN General Assembly declaration calling for stronger global action has brought renewed urgency to a threat that has long been treated as a distant consequence of climate change. For small island states, it raises the extraordinary prospect of territories disappearing beneath the ocean. For countries such as Pakistan, the danger may be less dramatic in appearance, but it is already creeping onto the coastline.
There is little room for complacency. Global sea level rose by almost six millimetres in 2024, the largest annual increase on record, while the pace of the rise has accelerated considerably over recent decades. What is measured globally in millimetres eventually translates into flooded settlements and eroding coastlines. Pakistan has particular reason to pay attention. Its coastline stretches more than 1,000 kilometres along Sindh and Balochistan and includes the densely populated metropolis of Karachi as well as the ecologically fragile Indus Delta. Low-lying areas along the Sindh coast are especially vulnerable to the combined effects of sea-level rise, coastal erosion, storm surges and saltwater intrusion. What is often discussed as a future climate threat is, for communities in the delta, already an unfolding reality.
Sea-level projections must become part of decisions being made today. Authorities must identify areas most vulnerable to inundation and erosion, and prevent further development from creating populations and assets that will become increasingly expensive, or impossible, to protect. Natural defences also deserve far greater attention. Mangrove forests along the Sindh coast and Indus Delta provide an important buffer against waves. Pakistan has made considerable efforts to expand mangrove cover, but plantation drives in isolation aren't enough.

items.author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
items.content:
Two controversies are rocking India today. Both about software. One is about the Indian government's decision to allow payment processing companies and banks to charge a 0.4 percent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions over INR 2000. And the second is about the centralisation of electoral rolls by the Election Commission of India through a software called ECInet.
The trigger of the second controversy was provided by The Indian Express journalist Ritika Chopra's brilliant expose. The Reporters' Collective has also done ace work on the matter. The gist of it is that the ECI is using software to lock out decentralised, local staff from the grid and making arbitrary changes to the electoral rolls. Goes without saying that the Muslim population has been disproportionately affected by the changes, which was also the crux of my September 12 piece, "Aap chronology samajhiye!" What interests me is what it all means. What if I told you that while minorities and Dalits are the ruling party's favourite whipping boys meant for amusement and votebank consolidation, they are not the targets? This emerging digital panopticon is meant to disenfranchise the real mark.
Ask yourself, how do you erase a majority? I will show you a half-century-long project to do just that, larger than the incumbent BJP government or the RSS.
A caveat for Pakistani readers: do not congratulate yourselves on being free from casteism. Prejudice changes nomenclature and hides in plain sight. When a member of the Indian elite says he does not believe in caste, he is not advocating for a casteless society or exogamy, but demanding you make peace with the status quo and not challenge their privilege. Caste prejudice is a daily reality in India. According to various human rights sources, Pratiloma (inter-caste) honour killings routinely exceed one thousand per annum.
The Vedas divide Hindu society into four varnas: Brahmins (priestly class), Kshatriyas (warriors and kings), Vaishyas (mercantile class) and Shudras (working class and artisans). The Vedas do not go out of their way to stigmatise the last category. That honour rests with another text called Manusmriti.
A fortnight ago I showed you how the ghost of RSS architect MS Golwalkar drives the ongoing SIR exercise and prejudiced citizenship laws today. The very same man hailed the author of Manusmriti as the "first and greatest lawgiver of the world," writing in his manifesto that the caste hierarchy is not a social flaw but a divine mandate: "Brahmin is the head, Kshatriya the hands, Vaishya the thighs and Shudra the feet... the Hindu People, is our God."
In his book Jyotipunj (2008), PM Modi canonises Golwalkar as his supreme ideological mentor, describing his life as "an unbroken yajna [ritual sacrifice]" for the nation. In Karmayog (2007), Modi rationalises the manual scavenging forced upon Dalit Valmikis as a divine duty rather than exploitation, writing it should continue as an "internal spiritual activity for centuries". A full-throated, fatalist endorsement of the varna system.
To grasp the scale of this hierarchy, consider the math established by Kanshi Ram, pioneer of India's lower-caste political awakening in the 1980s. He popularised the term Bahujan to define the oppressed castes as a collective 85 per cent of the country, identifying Shudras specifically as the single largest demographic majority at 52 per cent. Today, the Shudra population may exceed 60 per cent. Yet you hardly ever encounter the word Shudra in daily discourse. The reason is societal stigma and a deliberate state project of divide and rule. Power and resources remain controlled by the Brahmin-Bania alliance. Bania is a subset of the Vaishya varna. How do these upper castes control the overwhelming majority? By weaponising stigma, imposing sanitised secular labels, and endlessly splintering them.
The British referred to Shudras as the backward castes. Independent India rebranded them Other Backward Classes (OBCs). Then it linked the term to resources: certain Shudra communities were expelled for being affluent, while disadvantaged upper castes were slipped in. Modi's caste, Modh Ghanchi, belongs traditionally to the Vaishya varna, yet was included in the OBC category in 1994.
In 1990 the state finally implemented the Mandal Commission report, granting OBCs a 27 per cent reservation in public jobs and education. However, to prevent this demographic giant from ever consolidating, the Modi government weaponised the Rohini Commission in 2017 to sub-categorise the quota, fracturing collective Shudra identity by pitting thousands of sub-castes against one another for scraps.
That is not all. Through corrupt practices like paper leaks and the bureaucratic sleight of hand known as lateral entry, the Modi government leaves most OBC reserved seats unoccupied. Those already in the system are blocked by endless extensions granted to the upper-caste old guard.
To a marked community, visibility is a curse. To escape the Brahmin-Bania elite, the Shudra economy was historically cash-based and operated outside the formal banking system. Then came the Modi government with demonetisation and the siren song of the free JAM trinity: Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar biometric IDs, and Mobile connectivity.
Now that the informal bazaar is corralled inside the digital pen, the squeeze begins. The upcoming 0.4 per cent MDR on UPI transactions above INR 2000 is not a technical fee. It is a toll on the informal Shudra economy to be scaled up later. You trap them on a platform, extract their data, and charge them to access their own capital.
Amit Shah has the cunning of a municipal ward boss, but the strategic depth belongs to a technocratic vanguard in Bangalore. Collectives like iSPIRT engineered a digital panopticon disguised as public infrastructure.
The SIR exercise and ECInet may target Muslims and Dalits today to polarise the electorate, but the software is compiling a shadow ledger of the entire Shudra majority. By centralising voter rolls and gutting local oversight, the state ensures the 85 per cent can be partitioned, deleted, or managed at will.
After this come the supermajorities of 2029, engineered by cannibalising electoral rolls, delimitation boundaries and opposition parties. Then the secular constitution, along with all reservations, goes out the window and a Hindu Rashtra is proclaimed. Shudras should open the Manusmriti to see what this means for them. Under Manu, a Shudra raising a limb against a superior faced amputation, and coupling with a higher caste woman meant castration and execution.
If you are a Shudra reading this, you should know Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Dalits and Adivasis are merely in the way. You are the real target.

items.author: Imtiaz Gul
items.content:
During my recent four-week China assignment, I have been seeking insights into the evolving perception of Pakistan by the Chinese leadership. The traditional "time-tested, all-weather friendship" remains a cornerstone, yet Chinese companies appear to have lost the impetus to invest in the country.
My explorations in Shanghai and Beijing led me to an illuminating quote from Jiang Zaidong, the Chinese ambassador to Islamabad, shared on a local news network:
"Xinjiang's exemplary practice of social stability, economic prosperity, and harmonious coexistence underscores the profound significance of unity. Only through unity can we achieve victory. Regardless of the diverse ethnic groups and regions a country encompasses, collective efforts and shared aspirations can catalyse development momentum and foster a better life. We firmly believe that all political parties and sectors of Pakistani society will unite to promote national development and enhance the well-being of its people."
This quote, delivered by Jiang Zaidong, resonates deeply with the current political climate in Pakistan. While rooted in China's context, it carries a broader message to Pakistani ruling elites.
The Chinese ambassador elucidated the extensive efforts undertaken to foster unity among all ethnic groups across China since the 18th CPC National Congress, when President Xi Jinping embarked on a national mission of embracing all ethnicities.
In fact, the week commencing September 27th marks the inaugural Ethnic Unity and Progress Publicity Week, themed "Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, Forging Ahead on the Journey of Great Rejuvenation". The ambassador recalled that President Xi Jinping consciously pursued the policy of maintaining a balanced approach in addressing the diverse ethnic groups residing in China.
President Xi once likened the 56 ethnic groups of China to "56 flowers in a bouquet", emphasising the importance of party officials' focus on the well-being of all.
This poignant yet veiled message, I believe, was perhaps directed at Pakistani decision-makers and political elites. Without national unity, inclusivity and consensus, enduring progress is elusive.
Until recently, most Chinese officials, former ambassadors and academics refrained from raising critical questions regarding the trajectory of China-Pakistan relations over the past decade. However, the current situation has shifted.
The context is the lackluster progress of CPEC. Many Chinese believe that Pakistan treated CPEC as a blank cheque rather than an industrial catalyst. By prioritising short-term political gains over long-term economic strategy, Pakistan – according to former diplomats and officials – squandered an opportunity to embark on a path to industrialisation. They consistently highlight Islamabad's sovereign guarantees for Chinese Independent Power Producers (IPPs) and the nearly $1.6 billion in circular debt owed to them. Additionally, officials cite the chronic dollar shortages that have prevented Chinese companies from repatriating their profits, with approximately $2.3 billion in unpaid dues and blocked profits currently outstanding.
The prospects for rapid industrialisation are dimmed due to bureaucratic hurdles, the absence of clarity regarding the governing structure, the volatile security landscape, China's withdrawal from the flagship $8 billion Main Line 1 (ML-1) railway project, and the drastic reduction in CPEC-related investments for over a year. These factors are frequently cited by business executives and some officials.
Those familiar with Pakistan's internal dynamics candidly acknowledge that CPEC is facing challenges not only from non-traditional security threats (geopolitical factors) but also from internal governance bottlenecks.
"Pakistan's progress in aligning its actions with the primary objectives of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), which is to foster industrialization and self-reliance, remains inadequate," remarked a prominent think tanker. The expert emphasised the critical need for national unity and consensus to effectively implement policies and achieve equitable development.
Chinese area experts believe that Pakistan's economic growth, coupled with its industrialisation efforts and the establishment of production chains with potential value for China, can transform the nation into a formidable force. They assert that economic development driven by CPEC, coupled with Pakistan's military and diplomatic capabilities, can significantly enhance its regional standing.
Fortunately, Pakistan remains a valued political ally for China. While China seeks Pakistan to assume a more active leadership role in reshaping the Asian landscape, this is closely tied to Pakistan's economic situation and internal political challenges, another South Asia expert observed.
Pakistan is widely regarded as a formidable partner in addressing regional issues. Stronger and more friendly relations between Pakistan and the United States can help mitigate India's influence in Asia.
However, even the most effective diplomacy and advanced defence capabilities cannot fully compensate for economic resilience.
The challenge therefore lies in setting the house in order i.e. prioritising the well-being of Pakistan's citizens first rather than pursuing the quest for relevance abroad. Credibility will likely remain evasive as long as the intent on correcting the political economy is missing.
This Chinese message was even more visible when President Xi landed in Washington; the aircraft that flew him to the US was marked "Air China" – no special sign like US Air Force One!

items.author: Tashkeel Ahmed Farooqui
items.content:
The recent incident involving the grisly murder of a married woman and her three children in Karachi's Surjani Town neighbourhood must have shocked millions of people in the metropolis and across the country. Equally shocking was the subsequent 'encounter' killing of the accused while he was in police custody. According to media reports, police said the suspect was already in custody and was being taken to recover the alleged murder weapon when he snatched an officer's pistol, opened fire and injured the officer. Other policemen then returned fire and killed him.
The incident comes about two months after three suspects, arrested in connection with the robbery and murder of a doctor in the Clifton neighbourhood, were shot dead in crossfire after law-enforcement personnel took them to the city's outskirts to arrest their alleged accomplices.
In July, two policemen from the Awami Colony police station were arrested and charged with attempted murder for allegedly shooting and injuring two youths in what was described as a staged encounter near the Double Road Football Ground in Korangi.
In April, the Sindh High Court expressed serious concern over the killing of a suspect in a suspicious encounter. The court warned that allowing police to continue such actions would undermine the very purpose of the courts and erode public confidence in the judicial system.
Anyone who talks to Karachi's residents will hear widespread anguish over the deteriorating law and order situation, particularly the persistent problem of street crime and the rising incidence of mobile-phone snatching.
Yet extrajudicial killings cannot be presented as a solution to the city's law and order problems. The state cannot afford to replace due process with the barrel of a gun, regardless of the seriousness of the crime with which a suspect is charged. Every accused person has the right to a fair trial, and it is for the courts to determine guilt and award punishment on the basis of evidence.
The killing of suspects in custody, particularly when police describe their deaths as the result of encounters, raises serious questions about accountability and the credibility of investigations. It also deprives victims' families of the opportunity to see a case properly tried and a conviction secured through the judicial process. A dead suspect cannot stand trial, challenge the evidence against him or disclose the possible involvement of other accomplices.
The focus, therefore, should be on strengthening the entire criminal justice system rather than relying on encounters as a measure of police effectiveness. The police must conduct professional investigations, preserve evidence, obtain forensic support and prepare cases that can withstand scrutiny in court. Prosecutors, in turn, must be adequately resourced and closely involved in building cases, while courts must have the capacity to dispose of criminal cases expeditiously.
The ultimate measure of effective policing is not the number of suspects killed in encounters but the number of cases in which perpetrators are identified, arrested, prosecuted and convicted on the basis of solid evidence. A functioning criminal justice system must ensure that those responsible for heinous crimes are punished, but that punishment must follow a judicial process rather than an encounter.
Karachi's residents deserve both security and justice. Sacrificing one at the expense of the other is no solution. If the authorities are serious about restoring public confidence, they must ensure that every allegation of an extrajudicial killing is impartially investigated and that police officers found responsible for unlawful killings are held accountable. At the same time, greater investment is needed in investigation, prosecution, forensic capacity and witness protection so that suspected criminals can be brought before the courts and convictions secured on the basis of credible evidence.
Only then can the state demonstrate that it is capable of combating crime without compromising the rule of law.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
A new Chrome extension called Slop Mop is using Jev, a decision-making AI model, to identify and flag low-value writing on LinkedIn.
AI enthusiast, author, and business consultant Tom Frazier launched Slop Mop on Tuesday. The extension is free, requires no signup and is also available as open-source code on GitHub.
Unlike traditional AI detectors, Slop Mop does not try to determine whether a post was written by AI. Instead, it looks for patterns associated with poor-quality writing, regardless of whether a human or AI produced it.
How Slop Mop Identifies “Slop”
The extension uses nine indicators based on research from SEO firm Graphite Growth into writing patterns that appear more frequently in AI-generated content.
These include excessive hype, engagement bait, empty praise, overly polished lessons, flowery language, stiff wording, contrast-based definitions and posts designed to make users expand them while scrolling.
Slop Mop then uses additional questions to determine whether the content sounds like it was written by a specific person and whether it provides something useful to readers. Both factors can reduce the post’s slop score.
A separate question estimates whether an AI model likely drafted the content. However, that factor cannot trigger a flag by itself and can only reduce the score when the post otherwise appears to be human-written.
It Targets Bad Writing, Not Just AI Content
Frazier said the extension is designed to filter out low-value content rather than act as a conventional AI detector.
“Slop Mop flags poor human content equally to poor AI content,” Frazier told The Register, adding that AI-generated content can be good while human-written content can also be poor.
Posts that cross Slop Mop’s threshold can be flagged or hidden from a user’s LinkedIn feed. The posts are not deleted from LinkedIn and can still be reported through LinkedIn’s existing “Seems Like AI Slop” option.
The extension’s central question is whether a post is worth the reader’s attention.
Built as a Test for Jev
Frazier said his main reason for developing Slop Mop was to experiment with Jev, a probabilistic decision-making AI model from TypeSafe.
Unlike a chatbot, Jev is designed to make decisions for other software systems and is accessed through an API.
Frazier has open-sourced Slop Mop so developers can examine the project and experiment with Jev themselves.
Free Use Comes With a Daily Limit
Slop Mop currently operates through Frazier’s own Jev account and API key. To control costs, he has limited each installation to 250 analyzed LinkedIn posts per day.
Frazier said early usage has cost approximately $0.005 per user per day. He said he may reconsider the free service if the extension becomes widely popular.
For now, he is using the project to study Jev’s tuning parameters and build a dataset.
Frazier also said he could eventually expand Slop Mop to other platforms if enough users find it useful and the operating costs remain manageable.

items.author: Business Desk
items.content:
The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has established a National Faceless Centre (NFC) in Islamabad to shift tax audits and assessments to a centralized digital system.
The new setup is part of Pakistan’s New Tax Operating Model and is designed to reduce direct interaction between taxpayers and tax officials while limiting individual discretion in tax cases. The government had approved the model in principle in June.
Under the new mechanism, audit cases will be identified through a computerized, risk-based process instead of being selected by individual tax officers.
Once selected, cases will be automatically assigned to officers located anywhere in the country. The taxpayer will not be informed about the identity of the officer handling the case, while the officer will have no control over which cases are assigned to them.
The process will also separate the main stages of a tax case. One officer will conduct the audit, another will prepare the assessment, and a third will review the work before an order is issued.
This means a single officer will no longer control a taxpayer’s case from the audit stage through to the final decision.
Taxpayers will receive notices, submit responses, and attend hearings electronically through the FBR’s IRIS system. Physical verification or recovery, where legally required, will be handled separately by field teams.
The Finance Bill also provides a legal framework for faceless audits, assessments and appeals.
The post FBR Ends Direct Contact With Taxpayers appeared first on ProPakistani.

items.title: Jetour Launches T2 Facelift in China While Pakistanis Are Buying Older T2 Model
items.summary:
Jetour has launched the facelifted T2, sold as the Traveler 7 in China, with revised styling, an updated interior and new petrol and plug-in hybrid powertrains.
The update comes only weeks after the SUV was refreshed at the Chengdu Motor Show. It is also notable for Pakistan, where the T2 has only recently entered the market.
Jetour launched the T2 i-DM PHEV in July 2026, followed by the 2.0 XWD petrol variants in August. Local CKD assembly of the T2 i-DM also began earlier this month.
Exterior Design Gets a Cleaner Look

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Jetour has launched the facelifted T2, sold as the Traveler 7 in China, with revised styling, an updated interior and new petrol and plug-in hybrid powertrains.
The update comes only weeks after the SUV was refreshed at the Chengdu Motor Show. It is also notable for Pakistan, where the T2 has only recently entered the market.
Jetour launched the T2 i-DM PHEV in July 2026, followed by the 2.0 XWD petrol variants in August. Local CKD assembly of the T2 i-DM also began earlier this month.
Exterior Design Gets a Cleaner Look
The facelift retains the T2’s boxy proportions but reduces some of its previous rugged styling elements.
The front now features round headlights connected by a full-width light strip, replacing the previous square units. Jetour lettering has also been moved higher onto the bonnet, while the bumpers are now more integrated and body-colored.
At the rear, the SUV retains its vertical four-point taillights but receives a redesigned spoiler, smoother D-pillar treatment and a revised bumper. Several previously black exterior components, including the wheel-arch flares, are now finished in the body color.
New Petrol and Plug-In Hybrid Powertrains
The Chinese-market facelift continues to offer petrol and plug-in hybrid powertrains.
The entry-level petrol model uses a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine producing 184 PS and 290 Nm, paired with a seven-speed dual-clutch transmission and front-wheel drive.
Higher petrol variants receive a 2.0-liter turbocharged engine producing 250 hp and 390 Nm, along with all-wheel drive. The top version now uses an eight-speed automatic transmission instead of the previous gearbox setup.
The bigger technical change comes with the T2 i-DM PHEV. It retains a 1.5-liter turbocharged petrol engine producing 153 hp and 220 Nm, but its hybrid system now uses a single 307 PS electric motor and a one-speed dedicated hybrid transmission, replacing the previous three-speed DHT.
The PHEV is available with two LFP battery options:

Jetour claims up to 1,400 km of combined range under the CLTC cycle with the larger battery and a 70-liter fuel tank.
For comparison, the Pakistan-spec T2 i-DM currently uses an 18.4 kWh battery and has a claimed 90 km NEDC electric range.
Interior Gains More Technology
The facelift retains the 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster and 15.6-inch infotainment display, but the central screen now uses a more powerful Qualcomm Snapdragon 8255 processor, paired with 24GB RAM and 256GB storage.
The updated cabin also adds 10-way electrically adjustable seats, eight-point seat massage, a 23-speaker audio system, 256-color ambient lighting, a revised steering wheel, wireless phone charging and updated AI-based voice controls.
Driver-assistance technology has also been upgraded. Petrol models receive Chery’s Falcon 500 system, while the PHEV gets Huawei’s Qiankun ADS5 technology.
China Pricing
In China, the petrol versions of the facelifted T2 are priced between 149,900 yuan ($21,300) and 169,900 yuan ($24,100).
The PHEV versions are priced from 159,900 yuan ($22,700) to 179,900 yuan ($25,500).
Pakistan T2 Has Only Just Arrived
The facelift comes at an important time for Jetour in Pakistan because the current T2 has only recently been introduced locally.
The T2 i-DM PHEV launched at an ex-factory price of Rs. 12,795,000, while the 2.0 XWD costs Rs. 13,590,000 and the 2.0 XWD Dominator Kit is priced at Rs. 15,590,000.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
Honor is preparing a new Photography Master Kit for the upcoming Magic9 Pro Max, featuring two external telephoto converters designed to extend the phone’s optical zoom capabilities. The kit was shown in images shared by WHYLAB on Weibo ahead of the phone’s September 28 launch in China.
The kit includes the G200 and G500 telephoto attachments, with the larger G500 offering a claimed equivalent focal length of 500mm.
G500 Attachment Targets Long-Range Photography
The G500 is the larger of the two attachments and has been compared to a large camera lens. It is reportedly designed for situations such as concerts and bird photography.
The Magic9 Pro Max’s built-in periscope telephoto camera is said to offer an 85mm equivalent focal length. The G500 reportedly extends that reach by 5.88x, resulting in approximately 500mm.
Unlike digital zoom, the attachment uses additional optical elements to extend the camera’s reach. It clips around the phone’s camera module, making it a genuine optical telephoto converter rather than simply cropping the image.
However, its large size means it is not designed for everyday pocketable use. The G500 appears to be intended for situations where users specifically need a longer focal reach. It is also an official Honor accessory rather than a third-party product.
G200 Offers a More Portable Option
The second attachment, called the G200, is considerably smaller and offers an equivalent focal length of 200mm.
According to WHYLAB, Honor describes the attachment as being roughly thumb-sized. It measures 81mm and weighs 88 grams.
For comparison, last year’s Magic8 Pro 200mm attachment weighed 207 grams, making the new version more than half as light.
Other manufacturers are also exploring similar accessories. Vivo, for example, offers 200mm and 400mm attachments for its X300 Ultra.
Magic9 Pro Max Gets Two 200MP Cameras
The Honor Magic9 Pro Max itself is expected to feature two 200MP cameras as part of its imaging system.
The main camera reportedly uses a 1/1.28-inch sensor with an f/1.57 aperture, while the telephoto camera features a 1/1.4-inch sensor and an f/2.6 aperture.
Honor is also developing the imaging system in collaboration with ARRI, particularly for color processing.
The phone is expected to be powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset.
Pricing and Availability Remain Unknown
Honor has not yet revealed the price of the Magic9 Pro Max or the Photography Master Kit. The company has also confirmed that the camera kit will be sold separately as an optional accessory.
The stated 200mm and 500mm figures refer to the reach of the external attachments, rather than the native focal lengths of the phone’s built-in cameras.
The actual image quality produced by the G500 attachment also remains unverified until more testing becomes available. Honor is scheduled to officially unveil the Magic9 Pro Max in China on September 28.

items.author: Afaq Wajdan Malik
items.content:
BYD has released the first official images of its upcoming Yangwang flagship sedan, revealing a large luxury car with rear-hinged doors that have drawn comparisons with the Rolls-Royce Phantom.
However, the more significant development could be underneath the body. The sedan is being considered as a possible candidate for BYD’s first vehicle equipped with a solid-state battery.
Solid-State Battery Could Be the Bigger Story
BYD Executive Vice President Stella Li has previously said that a vehicle using the company’s solid-state battery technology will arrive in 2027, although she has not identified the model or confirmed when production will begin.
A luxury vehicle produced in relatively small numbers could provide a possible starting point for the technology while production remains expensive.
Most current EV batteries use a liquid electrolyte to transport lithium ions between electrodes. Fully solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid electrolyte.
The technology could potentially allow manufacturers to build smaller and lighter battery packs with higher energy density. It could also reduce some safety concerns associated with flammable liquid electrolytes.
However, solid-state batteries still face engineering challenges, including maintaining internal contact, durability and lithium growth that can damage cells.
BYD has not announced the sedan’s battery capacity, driving range or charging specifications.
Flash Charging Adds to the Speculation
One teaser image shows the Yangwang sedan alongside a BYD Flash Charging station. This has added to speculation about the vehicle’s battery technology, although the image does not confirm that the sedan will use a solid-state battery.
BYD already offers Flash Charging technology with its conventional Blade Battery 2.0, meaning the presence of the charging station alone does not establish a connection with solid-state batteries.
Solid-State Technology Is Moving Toward Production
Several automakers are developing or testing solid-state battery technology.
NIO already offers a 150kWh battery in some of its premium EVs, although battery supplier WeLion describes the pack as semi-solid-state because it still contains some liquid electrolyte. It therefore differs from a fully solid-state battery.
Mercedes-Benz has road-tested solid-state battery technology in an EQS, while BMW has tested all-solid-state cells in an i7. Toyota is also developing the technology and aims to introduce EVs using solid-state batteries in 2027–28.
BYD has separately said it plans to put its own solid-state battery technology into a vehicle in 2027, but has not identified the model.
What We Know About the Yangwang Sedan
The camouflaged sedan features a long and upright body, rear-hinged coach doors and a roof-mounted lidar sensor.
Yangwang has not yet revealed the interior or confirmed the vehicle’s final name, specifications, price or launch date.
The distinctive doors are likely to attract attention, but confirmation of a solid-state battery would make the sedan particularly significant for BYD’s next generation of EV technology.

items.author: Meha Agarwal
items.content:
In 1998, the newly incorporated Pine Labs was helping petrol pumps accept payments and manage loyalty programmes. Nearly three decades later, Pine Labs is a listed company that has expanded well beyond payments into online checkout, consumer financing, gift cards, card issuing and banking infrastructure
By Q1 FY27, the fintech was serving 11.5 Lakh+ merchants, alongside brands and financial institutions, across India, Southeast Asia and the Middle East. A string of acquisitions helped Pine Labs build out this expanding fintech stack.
While Qwikcilver added gift cards, Fave brought consumer rewards, Mosambee strengthened merchant acceptance, and Qfix and Shopflo expanded online payments and checkout. Similarly, Setu added fintech infrastructure, while Credit+ and Saluto brought issuing and enterprise rewards capabilities.
However, the breadth came at a cost. Despite raising nearly $1.6 Bn before making its public markets debut, Pine Labs struggled for years to turn expansion into consolidated profits. Payment hardware, employees, processing, cloud infrastructure and overseas operations all needed funding.
The next logical step was to get listed. But Pine Labs’ path to the public markets was anything but straightforward.
It first deferred a planned US IPO, reportedly targeting $500 Mn in 2022, amid a weak market. It eventually opted for an Indian listing, merging its Singapore holding company with its Indian entity in June 2025.
The payoff came in FY26, when Pine Labs reported its first full-year consolidated profit of ₹112.5 Cr, compared with a loss of ₹145.5 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue grew 19% to ₹2,710.6 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA jumped 57% to ₹559 Cr.
In its FY26 results, Pine Labs said indirect expenses, excluding ESOP costs, grew just 8% against 19% revenue growth. This operating leverage helped lift its adjusted EBITDA margin from around 16% to 21%, even as its contribution margin dipped from 76% to 75%.
Lower depreciation and amortisation, higher other income and a smaller exceptional charge also supported its bottom line. The reconciliation shows other income, excluding provision write-backs, rising from ₹44 Cr to ₹84 Cr, while exceptional charges fell from ₹37 Cr to ₹8 Cr.
Therefore, the profit improvement combined operating gains with benefits below the operating line.
Profitable segments like the Qwikcilver gift card and prepaid platform also contributed substantially to high-margin income.
But Q1 FY27 results show why Pine Labs’ turnaround story still warrants close scrutiny. Revenue rose 20% year on year (YoY) to ₹736.9 Cr and net profit more than quadrupled to ₹19.6 Cr, but adjusted EBITDA margin narrowed to 17.1% from 19.6%. The company attributed the pressure to business mix and additional investment.
Decoding Pine Labs’ Revenue Engines
Pine Labs still gets most of its revenue from its Digital Infrastructure and Transaction Platform (DITP), which comprises checkout infrastructure, affordability and value-added services, transaction processing and fintech infrastructure.
DITP generated ₹1,837 Cr in FY26, up 15% YoY, accounting for about 68% of operating revenue.
Meanwhile, Pine Labs is trying to increase revenue from its existing merchant network by selling more services — affordability/EMI, online payments, value-added services, etc. — rather than relying only on payment terminals. Mentioned in RHP as Issuing and Acquiring Platform, it contributed the remaining 32%, or ₹874 Cr in FY26.
But the competitive landscape is already crowded.
PhonePe has expanded beyond QR codes into soundboxes, card terminals and online payments. Paytm combines payment devices and processing with EMI and merchant lending, and ended FY26 with 1.5 Cr subscription merchants.
In September 2026, PhonePe announced plans to deploy more than 50 Lakh additional payment devices and hire over 20,000 frontline sales staff over the following year, with a substantial rural focus.
Online-first rivals are converging on the same opportunity. Razorpay commands payment acceptance, disbursals, lending and business banking, with an AI payments push extending its reach. Cashfree is building SME and cross-border offerings beyond its gateway.
Pine Labs’ competitive proposition is the combination: merchants can connect multiple acquiring banks, billing software and affordability offers through one platform. That integration gives them a reason to use more of its services, although its RHP cautioned that switching costs may not prevent them from moving transactions to rivals.
Earning More Beyond The Payment Device
As an offline merchant, Pine Labs’ business revolves around the digital checkout point (DCP), which connects cards, UPI, wallets and loyalty points with banks, payment networks and billing software, while handling acceptance and reconciliation.
Its RHP listed DCP subscriptions, hardware sales, installation and removal, automation services and maintenance as sources of in-store revenue. Average monthly revenue per DCP was ₹380.08 in FY25.
The network reached 20.3 Lakh DCPs in FY26 and 21.7 Lakh in Q1 FY27. Subscription income, however, does not rise simply because a checkout gets busier. Pine Labs needs either more paying deployments or higher revenue per deployment.
Transaction-linked affordability, value-added services and processing fees let it earn more from activity at those counters. Alongside this, Pine Labs is shifting more of the upfront device cost to merchants. Rau explained that getting merchants to buy terminals reduced its depreciation burden, although the device sales themselves earned lower margins.
Across the business, company-wide contribution grew 11% to INR 533 Cr in Q1 FY27, slower than revenue’s 20% growth. The shift in business mix and higher connectivity, distribution and operational costs weighed on margins.
Online payments take the model a step further.
Payment gateways, links and recurring collections generate transaction-value-linked fees without another device at the counter. The Plural launch in 2021 and Qfix acquisition in 2022 helped build this business.
Online payment revenue grew 56% in FY26, outpacing the group’s 19%, however its scale remains harder to judge, as the results did not disclose a separate revenue figure.
Selling More Through The Same Checkout
Beyond accepting payments, Pine Labs helps its customers sell. As Rau put it on the July 2026 call, “we help brands, banks, financial institutions, acquire new customers, convert those customers, engage with those customers.”
EMI is a key part of this proposition. For financed purchases, Pine Labs earns technology fees from merchants, brands and financial institutions, largely linked to transaction value. The lender provides the credit and takes on the repayment risk.
Affordability revenue grew close to 20% YoY in Q1 FY27, Rau said, despite electronics and mobile-phone price increases and supply disruptions. The share of DCPs generating Flow and affordability volumes reached 30%, up from 24% a year earlier, showing greater use of services across the existing network.
Demand shifts with the incentives banks and brands fund. On the Q4 FY26 earnings call, Rau described a large bank reducing offers on a leading smartphone brand as customers became willing to buy with fewer incentives. Banks were also backing newer categories, including electric vehicles.
“Our job is to come up with newer sectors, come up with newer touch points,” Rau said.
Non-electronics affordability volumes grew over 60% in FY26. Sustaining that expansion means finding purchases customers want to finance and banks and brands will support.
Moving Deeper Into Banking Infrastructure
Pine Labs’ relationship with financial institutions goes beyond merchant payments. Banks and fintechs also need infrastructure within their own applications. Pine Labs supplies APIs for customer verification, financial-data access, digital agreements and collections, allowing institutions to avoid building every connection themselves.
Its acquisition of Setu in 2022, reportedly for $70 Mn to $75 Mn, expanded its capabilities across payments, onboarding, digital signatures and financial-data analysis.
Pine Labs now wants to move further up the value chain by helping lenders make sense of the financial data flowing through these systems.
“The future of payments is not going to be only in terms of money movement, but also in terms of data movement,” Rau said on the July 2026 (Q1 FY27 earnings) call.
Six banks and NBFCs signed up for SignalIQ, which analyses financial data to support lending decisions. This creates another potential source of value beyond payments and data collection.
Pine Labs has not separately disclosed SignalIQ revenue or FinTech Infrastructure’s FY26 revenue contribution in the cited results.
Cards And Rewards Shift The Revenue Mix
While banking infrastructure deepens Pine Labs’ relationships with lenders, cards and rewards are changing the company’s revenue mix. The Issuing and Acquiring Platform’s revenue grew 30% YoY, from ₹671 Cr to ₹874 Cr in FY26, compared with 15% growth for DITP.
As a result, DITP’s share of group revenue fell from 72.1% in FY24 to 70.5% in FY25 and about 68% in FY26. Issuing and acquiring, meanwhile, increased its share from roughly 28% in FY24 to 32% in FY26.
The segment has two key pillars: Pine Labs Prepaid, which handles gift cards and rewards, and Credit+, which provides card-issuing and payment-processing technology to banks and fintechs.
For a retailer, Pine Labs Prepaid activates gift cards, maintains balances and processes redemptions. It also distributes cards to consumers and corporate buyers, including through Woohoo, for uses ranging from employee rewards to customer promotions and dealer incentives.
Pine Labs earns from both distribution and processing.
Credit+ embeds Pine Labs in a different part of the customer’s operations. It supplies systems for banks to manage credit, debit and forex card accounts and process transactions, as well as infrastructure for institutions supporting merchants that accept cards.
The Next Test Is Making Expansion Pay
Pine Labs has built multiple ways to monetise its merchant and financial-institution relationships. The next challenge is making that larger platform more efficient. AI is central to that effort, although the spending comes before the gains.
In FY26, Pine Labs invested around ₹24 Cr in AI-related initiatives: ₹20 Cr in capabilities, infrastructure and customer-facing automation, and ₹4 Cr in enterprise AI technologies and tools. The company says automation cut software testing cycles by more than 95% and improved developer productivity by 25%. It has not quantified the resulting impact on profits.
Servicing the existing network offers a more immediate opportunity. “Today, almost 50% of our terminals are self-healing,” CFO Sameer Kamath said on the Q1 FY27 call.
Automated diagnostics and recovery could reduce field-service visits and lower the cost of keeping merchants’ payment systems running. Pine Labs is also experimenting with payments initiated by AI assistants.
Its Q1 presentation said P3P, its agentic payments system, was live with Vijay Sales and Gullak, allowing payments within user-set rules. The company has not disclosed P3P revenue separately.
Competition is already emerging around AI-enabled payments.
Razorpay and NPCI unveiled a Claude-based payments pilot in February 2026, while PhonePe launched an AI integration tool in May to help merchants connect to its gateway. These serve different functions, but raise the same commercial question: will the tools win transactions or lower costs?
Expansion also needs people. Rau said Pine Labs added about 500 salespeople over six months, with full productivity typically taking 6 to 12 months. Those hires add costs before new merchant relationships deliver their full revenue potential.
That spending weighed on Q1 FY27. Data, cloud and technology costs rose 33% to ₹64 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA grew just 5% to ₹126 Cr, against 20% revenue growth.
Management reiterated FY27 revenue growth guidance of 21-23.5% and said it expects contribution margins to improve in the second half as processing and transaction-linked services increased.
From petrol pumps to banking systems, Pine Labs has built more ways to earn from a payment. Its first profitable year shows that breadth can support earnings. The next test is whether deeper customer relationships and lower servicing costs can sustain them as competition and expansion spending intensify.

Pakistan’s technology businesses must turn artificial intelligence adoption into measurable productivity gains and stronger export performance, this was observed by technology experts at the 22nd edition of P@SHA ICT Awards. The attendees emphasised the importance of connecting technological innovation with workforce readiness, global market access and reliable financial infrastructure to help businesses compete internationally.
Centred on the theme “Recognize. Celebrate. Elevate.”, the P@SHA ICT Awards assessed more than 1,380 entries across 10 main categories and 41 subcategories, showcasing the depth of Pakistan’s capabilities in AI, fintech, cybersecurity, digital government and enterprise solutions. The awards celebrated homegrown innovation and highlighted its potential to attract international customers and investment, strengthen technology exports and support sustained business growth.
Alongside this recognition, discussions explored how Pakistan can translate AI adoption into measurable impact, with a focus on workplace applications, workforce transformation and the development of the country’s AI ecosystem. Roundtable sessions examined adoption strategies, implementation barriers and return on investment, while emphasising stronger industry and academia collaboration, education and foundational AI literacy as essential to translating technological ambition into practical results.
For technology exporters, these themes underscored the need to translate AI capabilities into better service delivery, stronger workforce skills and measurable business outcomes. Turning those gains into international growth also depends on the ability to serve customers across markets, manage payments in multiple currencies and maintain predictable cash flows.
Payoneer supports this growth journey by helping businesses receive and manage international payments. Access to global financial networks gives technology companies greater flexibility to reinvest export earnings in talent, build AI capabilities and strengthen service delivery as they expand into new markets.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
If you’re shopping in the Rs. 65,000 – 75,000 bracket right now, you’ve got more choice than ever, and more conflicting marketing to sort through. Every brand has a phone aimed at exactly this budget, and on paper, most of them look similar: big battery, fast charging, solid durability, a 120Hz screen. The real differences lie in the details: how fast charging truly is, whether batteries last years instead of months, and whether durability is genuinely certified or just claimed.
Charging speed: the number on the box vs. the wait in real life
Fast charging claims span a wide range here. The Samsung Galaxy A17 tops out at 25W, the Redmi Note 15 at 33W, the Vivo Y31D at 44W, the Oppo A6 and the Infinix Hot 70 Pro at 45W, and the TECNO SPARK 50 Pro at 60W, the highest in the group. That gap becomes useful when you only have a few minutes before leaving home or work: on paper, the higher 60W charging ceiling gives the SPARK 50 Pro considerably more headroom for a quick top-up than the 25W–45W alternatives in this comparison.
Battery capacity: bigger isn’t always the full story
On raw capacity, the Vivo Y31D (7200mAh) and Oppo A6 (7000mAh) actually lead the pack, with the Infinix Hot 70 Pro, Redmi Note 15 and TECNO SPARK 50 Pro all around 6000mAh, and the Samsung Galaxy A17 notably smaller at 5000mAh. So, if all-day battery life is the only metric that matters, Vivo and Oppo have a real edge on paper.
Capacity alone doesn’t show long-term performance. TECNO rates the SPARK 50 Pro’s battery for more than 1,900 charge cycles while retaining over 80% capacity, which the company equates to roughly six years of typical use, useful for buyers who plan to keep a phone for several years rather than upgrade annually. This is backed by three charging modes (Super, Smart, Low-Temp) and AI Charging Protection against prolonged high-voltage charging.
Durability: The Part Most Phones in This Range Skip
Durability is one of the clearer areas of differentiation in this group, since several devices carry formal IP ratings and, in some cases, SGS certification. TECNO SPARK 50 Pro leads with IP68 to 6 metres (30 min), IP69 for 80°C water, Level 6 dust protection, and SGS Five-Star Drop certification (1.2m daily drops, 1.8m extreme drop, 41 falls). Vivo Y31D also carries IP68/IP69 and its own SGS Five-Star mark, but only to 1.5 metres (30 minutes).
The OPPO A6 features IP66/68/69 protection and can withstand submersion in up to 1.5 meters of water for 30 minutes. Infinix Hot 70 Pro reaches IP68 to 2 metres, while Redmi Note 15 (IP64) and Samsung Galaxy A17 (IP54) offer only splash resistance. That range matters for commuters caught in the rain, travellers, and anyone who uses their phone outdoors regularly.

Which One Should You Actually Buy?
There’s no single “best” phone here, it depends on what matters most to you. If a bigger raw battery number is your priority, Vivo Y31D or Oppo A6 edge ahead on paper. But for buyers who want the strongest overall package, fast, meaningful charging, a battery built to still perform years from now, and durability that’s independently tested rather than just claimed, the TECNO SPARK 50 Pro is the one that doesn’t ask you to trade one priority for another. It has the fastest charging in the group, and durability that’s independently tested rather than just claimed, at a competitive Rs. 74,999.

items.author: Ado Abubakar Musa, Jos
items.content:
Tension erupted in Kassa community, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area of Plateau State, on Friday morning after gunmen killed three vigilantes, including the youth leader of the community.
Women and youth in the community blocked the major Jos-Barikin Ladi Highway protesting against the attack.
The attackers reportedly stormed the community at about 1am on Friday and opened fire, killing the three vigilantes who were keeping watch on the community.
The development came four days after the state government imposed dusk-to-down curfew in three LGAs, including Barikin Ladi, Bokkos and Mangu to restore normalcy after reports of attacks and killings in the areas.
Ulama Forum demands probe, compensation over Niger, Mambilla killings
Ex-Rivers ADC gov’ship candidate, Ibraye, quits party
Speaking on the latest development, a resident of the community, John Dung, told our correspondent that the victims were members of a local vigilante group, who had been involved in efforts to safeguard residents from attacks.
He said the killing of the vigilantes sparked anger among residents, particularly women and youths, who took to the streets and blocked the major highway linking the community with Mangu.
The protesters reportedly called on soldiers stationed in the area to leave the community, expressing frustration over the repeated attacks despite the presence of security personnel.
One of the protesters, Mrs Esther Pam, lamented the killings, saying residents were tired of losing their loved ones to attacks.
“We are tired of people being killed and security operatives would just sit and do nothing. We urge them to go after the attackers,” she said.
Also confirming the incident, spokesman of the Berom Youth Moulders-Association (BYM), Rwang Tengwong, described the killings as sad and disturbing.
Tengwong said the victims were killed while protecting their community, adding that their deaths had further heightened fear among residents.
He said the vigilantes had been contributing to the security of the community by keeping watch and responding to threats, stressing that their killings were a serious setback to local efforts to protect residents.
The BYM spokesman called on security agencies to intensify efforts to track down the attackers and bring them to justice, urging authorities to take urgent steps to protect communities in Barkin Ladi and other parts of Plateau State.
The spokesperson of Operation Enduring Peace, Captain Polycarp Oteh, had yet to respond to inquiry from our correspondent on the incident, as of the time of filing this report.

Original | September 25, 2026 14:37 IST
Snapdeal parent AceVector’s ₹420 Cr IPO was subscribed 9% as of 14:12 IST on the first day of bidding, with investors bidding for 65.11 Lakh shares against 7.42 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data.
Retail investors led bidding, subscribing to 36% of their quota. They placed bids for 49.85 Lakh shares against 1.37 Cr shares reserved for them.
Non-institutional investors (NIIs) bid for 15.27 Lakh shares against their allocation of 2.06 Cr shares, subscribing to 7% of the portion.
Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) were yet to place bids against the 3.99 Cr shares earmarked for them.
The IPO will close on September 29 (Tuesday). AceVector has set a price band of ₹30-₹32 per share, valuing the company at up to ₹1,741.4 Cr ($181.7 Mn). Its shares are expected to list on the BSE and NSE on October 5.
The issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth ₹287 Cr and an OFS of up to 4.16 Cr shares, worth ₹133 Cr at the upper end of the price band.
Ahead of the public issue, AceVector raised ₹189 Cr from anchor investors yesterday. Helios Mutual Fund and Taurus Ethical Fund were the only domestic mutual funds to participate, together picking up 93.75 Lakh shares, or 15.87% of the anchor allocation.
AceVector plans to use ₹132 Cr of the net proceeds from the fresh issue for Snapdeal’s marketing and business promotion, and another ₹50 Cr for its technology infrastructure. The remaining proceeds will go towards acquisitions and general corporate purposes.
Founded in 2010 by Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal, Snapdeal once competed with Flipkart and Amazon before losing ground. Following the collapse of its proposed merger with Flipkart in 2017, it pivoted to a value-focused ecommerce model.
Besides Snapdeal, AceVector’s businesses include listed ecommerce enablement platform Unicommerce and consumer brands business Stellaro Brands. The group adopted the AceVector identity in 2022.
On the financial front, AceVector’s restated net loss narrowed nearly 64% to ₹45.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹126.3 Cr in FY25. Operating revenue rose 29.2% to ₹510.3 Cr from ₹395 Cr.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
The federal government on Friday increased the price of petrol by Rs2.02 per litre, while decreasing the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs3.59 per litre till September 28.
According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs391.30 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs408.53 per litre from September 26 to September 28.
The latest revision comes a day after the government decreased the price of petrol and HSD by 84 paisas and Rs2.63 per litre, respectively, for September 25.
Read: Govt decreases petrol by 84 paisas, HSD by Rs2.63 for Sept 25
On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.
Earlier this month, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.
Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.
Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.
On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.
Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.
Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.
Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.
Oil prices fell about 3% on Friday, on mounting hopes for a truce between the US and Iran, even as traders worried that increasing attacks against Saudi Arabia by Houthi fighters could disrupt supply from the Middle Eastern producer.
Brent futures fell $2.96, or 2.8%, at $103.64 a barrel by 12:12 pm EDT (1612 GMT). West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude fell $2.86, or 3.0%, ​to $91.75.
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a ​phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic ⁠blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.
In the Middle East, however, Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs are to discuss help for Saudi ​Arabia as it faces attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.
"Diplomatic hopes are essentially helping oil prices weather the latest military strikes in the Middle East, with ​crude trading moderately softer despite the attacks," said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.

Original | September 25, 2026, 13:15 IST
Digital lender Moneyview’s ₹1,092 Cr IPO was subscribed 3.55X by 13:15 IST on the second day of bidding. The public issue received bids for 82.65 Cr shares against 23.25 Cr shares on offer, according to BSE data.
Non-institutional investors (NIIs) led the demand, placing bids for 39.01 Cr shares against the 5.02 Cr shares reserved for them, translating into a subscription of 7.77X.
Within the category, the portion reserved for investors bidding between ₹2 Lakh and ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 10.08X. Meanwhile, the portion for bids exceeding ₹10 Lakh was subscribed 6.61X.
Retail investors subscribed to their quota 3.67X, placing bids for 43.02 Cr shares against the 11.72 Cr shares reserved for them.
The qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) portion received bids for 61.45 Lakh shares against the 6.51 Cr shares reserved for the category, translating into a subscription of 0.09X.
The issue ended the first day of bidding with a subscription of 1.44X.
Moneyview has fixed the IPO price band at ₹32-₹34 per share. At the upper end of the price band, the IPO values the company at around ₹5,985 Cr ($624 Mn).
The public issue comprises a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹750 Cr and an OFS of up to 10.05 Cr shares, amounting to around ₹341.7 Cr at the upper end of the price band.
The IPO will close on September 28 (Monday), while the company’s shares are scheduled to list on the stock exchanges on October 1 (Thursday).
Ahead of the IPO, Moneyview raised ₹327.5 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 9.63 Cr equity shares at ₹34 apiece. Seven domestic mutual funds subscribed to 6.96 Cr shares worth around ₹236.7 Cr. Other anchor investors included Goldman Sachs, Amundi Funds, 360 ONE, HDFC Life Insurance Company, and India Acorn Fund.
Cofounders and promoters Puneet Agarwal and Sanjay Aggarwal, along with investors such as Accel, Tiger Global Management, Ribbit Capital, and DI Investment, are selling shares through the OFS.
Moneyview intends to use ₹325 Cr of the fresh issue proceeds to support loan disbursals under default loss guarantee arrangements. Another ₹250 Cr will be infused into its NBFC subsidiary Whizdm Finance to augment its capital base, while the remaining proceeds will be used for general corporate purposes.
The lending tech company offers personal loans, payments, investments, and insurance through its digital platform.
On the financial front, Moneyview’s consolidated net profit jumped 2.6X to ₹173.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹67.2 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its operating revenue rose 50.2% to ₹1,041.1 Cr from ₹693 Cr during the period.
For FY26, Moneyview’s operating revenue grew to ₹3,351.2 Cr from ₹2,339.1 Cr in FY25. Its consolidated profit increased marginally to ₹242.7 Cr from ₹240.3 Cr due to exceptional losses of ₹206.7 Cr.
