items.content:
By Tony Afejuku
Let the Glitterer state straightaway that today’s subject is appearing for readers’ consumption by sheer luck. What this simply means is that the Glitterer had other things in his mind, of active choices to choose from, before a nudge from nowhere nudged him to pick, prettily, on our president directly now. Let the Glitterer be clearly clear. He legitimately had in his sumptuously active mind the following topics to dwell on: “Other stories and a story”; “New hunger in the land”; “The thing that is the thing to come”; “An insider glimpse of Olu of Warri’s fifth coronation anniversary”; “The funny humourist”; “Infantino”; “World Cup of woeful dreams”; and other ideas of almost perceptible and almost imperceptible ingredients. As a matter of fact, “Other stories and a story”, which was going to attend to the responses of some readers, active readers, of this column, was ready to be shared here from their intellectual and poetic insights. Its lucky day, and that of the other titles, will still enter the creatively journalistic soul of the Glitterer.
During a rare, favoured moment of this presidency, our leader elevated his presence to enter the Glitterer’s mind of dark humour and bile, catching the Glitterer utterly unready for the cynicism skulking there. This rare, lucky moment happened very recently when some Nigerian Catholic Bishops visited the president, our mighty leader, to tell him that the country is bleeding. Did our mighty leader accept the truth the Bishops, led by Cardinal John Onaiyekan, the Archbishop Emeritus of Abuja, told him? Of course, the President of Nigeria, the great man of gambit, did not agree with the Bishops. The bleeding country is already being throttled to the un-motorable road of a one-party state, which our lucky leader tried to deny outright against the grain of truth all about us. Without doubt, there is more than an adequate account/amount – if the Glitterer must employ this term – of hunger everywhere about us. Indeed, the failures, the current ingredients of failures, that is, of our serious leader’s administration, overwhelm us all. Let us attempt to list them: steadily rising inflation; frequent fuel price hikes; power failure; increasing poverty; declining education standards; increasing insecurity; economic downturn; debt increase; naira devaluation; and contrived democracy of a confirmed democrat drawing us backward.
In other words, the Glitterer is saying thus: The structural failures characterizing the current administration have created an overwhelming national crisis. This is evident in persistent inflation, escalating fuel costs, systemic power grid failures, and expanding poverty rates. These economic challenges are compounded by a decline in educational quality, heightened insecurity, mounting sovereign debt, and the continuous devaluation of the naira. Consequently, the administration’s governance model represents a regression in democratic substance.
The president and his presidencynologists will not agree with me, as the president himself did not agree with the Catholic Bishops who (through Cardinal John Onaiyekan) spoke for all of us Catholics and non-Catholics, Christians and non-Christians, and all of us Nigerians who keep on wondering about the luckless luck that has befallen Nigeria currently. But I don’t wish to be misunderstood. When President Tinubu’s gambit propelled him to the presidency in 2023, did we deduce that we would witness what we are experiencing now – as alluded to above? Of course not! This must be our collective answer.
Now when the Glitterer saw our leader of enormous power on television, and heard what he said, to wit, that all is fair in politics, he winced with pain. The powerful president’s statement, meaning any tactic is acceptable to win the 2027 presidential elections, really caused the Glitterer deep emotional pain and a sudden, nameless dread. And his mind spiralled into anxiety as he foresaw a dark, chaotic, and unclear future surrounding the upcoming 2027 presidential elections. In any case, will the elections happen? And if they happen, will they be the elections of the president versus his opponents, or will they be the elections of the president versus the rest of us?
This composer may not be losing faith in the presidential electorate and electoral process, although he believes that, after all is said and done, all Nigerian (and African) politicians in a post-colonial state such as ours are more or less the same. Our past presidents lived and survived/succeeded in office by wits. Is our powerfully powerful President Tinubu different from them? Or will his unlikely civilian successor be going to be different? Have our experiences over the years not told us that our presidents have exhibited tendencies to make one civilian president sound a bit like the other? Or is the current President of your country, my country, our country, going to step into his peculiar bog hole as the 2027 presidential elections approach?
Now the Glitterer wants to make a recommendation. There are occasions when he is like every writer. He begins a sentence, runs to the middle of it, and discovers that there is no way out short of retracing his steps and beginning again nicely and beautifully. We expect the presidencynologists to read this writing, and have a dialogue with the president on it. All of us will be lucky if they do so. It is morning yet on 2027 presidential elections day. The president of presidents still has ample time to kill the hunger in the land. Or did his gambit bring him to his present throne to bleed us to death? Who will remain in the land to rule over it after he has killed us all?
It is morning yet on 2027 presidential election day. His gambit still has time to wear a humane heart and face. He should heed the Glitterer. He cannot conquer and consume all of us – even if he can conquer and consume the presidential candidates who want our presidential throne. Mr Powerful President of presidents should rewrite his sentences. 
The post The president versus us appeared first on Vanguard News.

Nigeria has had not just super educators like Professors Wole Soyinka, Ebi Alagoa, Alvan Ikoku and Adamu Baikie, but also outstanding Education Ministers like Abudu Yusufu Eke and Babs Fafunwa.
The ongoing conflagration over the award of King’s College, KC, Lagos, to a group of its Old Boys again exposes the current leadership of the Education Ministry under Dr Tunji Maruf Alausa as retarded. Before analysing the KC issue, permit me to address this issue of incompetence in the Education Ministry.
I have made this point about the Ministry a number of times, including in its clumsy and profligate attempts to auction 33 hectares of the Federal Government College, Kano, school land.
In my May 2026 column titled ‘Minister Alausa: Little Learning Is Dangerous’, I pointed out that the Tinubu administration’s attempt to cut courses in the social sciences and arts because they allegedly do not lead to employment is illiterate and anti-intellectual. Also, in my July 6, 2026 column, ‘When Uneducated Minds Change the Education System’, I pointed out that, without consultations, the Ministry had, on September 3, 2025, ordered a major review of our national education curriculum. Then, just nine months later, the same Ministry, under the same Minister in the same Tinubu administration, announced that it was replacing the 6-3-3-4 education system with a linear 12-year one, exposing the administration’s lack of strategic and long-term thinking on education, which is the bedrock of development.
As I write, some of our universities are in turmoil, with a number of them on strike over non-payment of agreed allowances in public universities. But the administration, with Alausa as its arrowhead, is already sowing the seeds for the next round of crisis in the education sector.
The National Universities Commission, NUC Act (Cap. N81 and Section E3 of the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004), vests in the NUC the sole authority to lay minimum standards using the Benchmark Minimum Academic Standards, BMAS, under which all universities must operate.
It is also empowered to accredit academic awards in the country and evaluate programmes through peer-review panels, which inspect institutional facilities, curricula and staffing. Equally, the NUC is empowered to withhold or withdraw approval of academic programmes and exercise supremacy over professional degrees.
As far as I know, the NUC has not been found wanting, nor have the laws been reviewed. But the Tinubu administration, on Wednesday, September 9, 2026, decided to establish a parallel accreditation body, baptised the ‘Ministerial Committee’.
If there are no ulterior motives, the administration ought to have told the country in what way the NUC might be failing, consulted stakeholders like the Academic Staff Union of Universities, ASUU, and, if necessary, reviewed the relevant laws. But to set up a parallel body amounts to illegality.
Now, to the KC issue. The least expected of an Education Ministry is to educate and inform the public on any major issue it embarks on. But it is in this basic faculty that the Ministry is found wanting. Either because it has an inept and incapable leadership or a mischievous one imbued with a rogue mentality, it does not even engage in basic consultation with those its policies may affect.
For instance, it decided to hand over the management and administration of the 117-year-old KC to a group in the school’s Old Boys’ Association without consultations. This group of investors is empowered to impose fees, control teachers, make a profit on their so-called investment or, at least, break even. So, rather than being a social product, KC becomes a commodity that can be traded. Needless to say, the new investors, even if they pretend to grant some scholarships, would eventually price the school out of the reach of the poor, even the middle class. These Old Boys are likely to put a high price on an education and school that gave them free education.
In any case, if these men are so interested in education or making positive contributions, why can’t they establish their own school rather than seek to take over a school with a good pedigree?
The KC case raises another question. Can Old Boys administer medicine to an allegedly sick alma mater without adding poison? Given my experience with the Methodist Boys’ High School, Lagos Old Boys’ Association, MBHS OBA, the answer is yes! In the MBHS case, while the state government handed the school primarily to the mission, the Old Boys provided virtually every other facility, including teachers’ quarters, an assembly hall, a library, laboratories and water. Yet, we did not attempt to seize the school. We made, and are still making, all these contributions because the school provided us with the basic foundations that made us who we are today.
If there are no ulterior motives, why is the KC agreement shrouded in secrecy? Why were critical stakeholders, such as the students who will bear the brunt, their parents and guardians who will be forced to pay, the teachers whose careers as public servants may be jeopardised, and the unions and professional associations whose members will be affected, not consulted? Why were their inputs not sought? If the government claims it wants the best for the school and concession is the best option, why not make it open? Why must the school be handed to a set of people who may not have the professional competence to run it?
This move is nothing but racketeering. The prime land of the school is also an attraction. But I must admit that this prodigal trajectory did not start with the Tinubu administration. In 2006, the Obasanjo administration, with Dr Oby Ezekwesili as Education Minister, embarked on this same path. It wanted to hand over the Federal Government Colleges to private administrators and managers. There are, however, some remarkable differences between the two administrations. While Obasanjo, despite his military background, engaged in wide consultations, Tinubu, in spite of his pro-democracy credentials, did not engage in consultations. He simply decided to impose his will. Again, while Obasanjo backed away, Tinubu, as he did when he announced the immediate removal of the oil subsidy, simply handed the KC over. The pushback we are witnessing is not his re-reading of the situation, but the resistance he is facing from stakeholders.
Generally, education is not a commercial commodity to be bought and sold in the marketplace. Rather, it is a social vehicle to develop society. So, in educating our citizens, we are not doing them a favour; we are doing ourselves a favour. My advice is that the Tinubu administration should concentrate on mass education, especially of the 20 million out-of-school children. I come in peace.
The post Schools Concession: The Ministry of Education as a retarded child, by Owei Lakemfa appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
By Ivo Takor
The continuing rise in the price of petrol has moved beyond the realm of energy policy and economic statistics. It has become a serious question of human welfare, social justice and the ability of ordinary Nigerians to live with dignity.
Across the country, Nigerians are confronting a cost-of-living crisis in which the price of virtually every necessity is being pushed upwards by the rising cost of transportation and energy. Recent reports indicate that petrol is selling for about N1,430 per litre in major urban centres, with even higher prices reported in some less accessible locations.
For a worker earning the national minimum wage of N70,000 per month, the arithmetic is disturbing. Ten litres of petrol at N1,430 costs N14,300, more than one-fifth of an entire month’s minimum wage. The N70,000 minimum wage was established under the National Minimum Wage framework following the 2024 amendment.
Yet the worker must still eat, travel to work, pay rent, educate children, meet medical expenses, pay electricity bills and provide for other basic necessities.
This is why the petrol-price question cannot be examined solely from the standpoint of deregulation, market forces, international crude prices or exchange rates. Economic policy must ultimately be measured by its impact on human beings.
For millions of Nigerian workers, wages are increasingly becoming inadequate before they are even received.
Every increase in the price of petrol immediately affects transportation. Bus operators, taxi drivers, commercial motorcyclists, haulage companies and other transport providers understandably adjust their fares to reflect their increased operating costs. The worker therefore pays more simply to get to work and return home.
But the impact does not stop at the bus stop. Farmers pay more to move produce. Traders pay more to transport goods. Manufacturers and small businesses that depend on generators face higher energy costs. Distributors pay more to move products across the country. Eventually, these costs find their way into the prices paid by consumers.
Food, transportation, electricity, school expenses, healthcare and other household necessities consequently compete for a salary that has not increased at anything approaching the same rate.
This is effectively a reduction in real wages. A worker may still receive the same figure on a payslip, but that money buys progressively less.
The situation is even more troubling for Nigerians living below or close to the poverty line. A wealthy household may respond to a fuel-price increase by reducing discretionary expenditure. A poor household frequently has no discretionary expenditure to reduce.
The choices become painfully basic: food or transportation; medicine or school expenses; rent or electricity.
Low-income households spend a substantial part of their resources on necessities. When the prices of those necessities rise sharply, there is very little financial protection available.
Families may begin reducing the quantity or quality of food they consume. Medical treatment may be postponed. Children may be withdrawn from certain educational activities. Savings disappear. Borrowing increases. In that sense, rising petrol prices can become a poverty multiplier.
Particular attention must also be paid to pensioners and elderly Nigerians. Many elderly citizens depend on pensions, retirement savings or financial assistance from their children and extended families. Their capacity to increase their income in response to inflation is considerably limited.
At the same time, many require regular medication, hospital appointments and other healthcare services.
When transport fares rise, going to the hospital becomes more expensive. When distribution costs increase, medicines and essential commodities may become more costly. When the working members of a family are themselves financially distressed, their capacity to support elderly relatives also diminishes.
The welfare of elderly Nigerians therefore deserves specific consideration in any economic intervention designed to cushion the effects of rising energy prices.
Nigeria’s constitutional philosophy does not treat economic management as being completely detached from the welfare of citizens.
Chapter II of the Constitution sets out the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy. Among other objectives, Section 17 envisages policies directed towards adequate means of livelihood, just and humane conditions of work, protection of the health, safety and welfare of persons in employment, adequate medical facilities, protection of elderly persons against material neglect and public assistance in deserving cases. These principles provide an important framework through which public policy should be examined.
Government unquestionably has to confront difficult fiscal and economic realities. Sustainable public finances, energy security, domestic refining capacity and efficient markets are legitimate concerns.
But economic reform should also be accompanied by serious consideration of its distributional consequences.
A reform cannot be assessed only by what it saves the treasury. Its consequences for the market woman, factory worker, teacher, nurse, civil servant, pensioner, unemployed graduate and low-income household also matter.
Nigeria’s informal economy provides livelihoods for millions of citizens. The barber running a generator, the welder, the food vendor, the commercial driver, the tailor, the small retailer and the neighbourhood business owner all feel the impact of expensive energy.
Many cannot simply absorb repeated cost increases. They are left with three unpleasant choices: increase their prices, reduce their operations or close. Each option has consequences. Increasing prices transfers the burden to consumers. Reducing operations can reduce employment. Business closures destroy livelihoods altogether.
Fuel-price instability therefore has consequences not only for household welfare but also for employment and economic activity. The present conditions justify serious consideration of a coordinated package of measures rather than reliance on a single intervention.
One option under public discussion is a temporary wage award or cost-of-living support for workers whose purchasing power has been significantly weakened. The Nigeria Labour Congress has publicly proposed wage awards as one response to the current rise in petrol prices.
Policymakers could also examine targeted support for pensioners, persons with disabilities and the poorest households, ensuring that assistance is transparent, properly targeted and capable of being audited.
Transportation deserves particular attention. Expanded and reliable mass-transit systems can reduce the amount individual workers spend travelling to and from work. Support for high-capacity buses, rail transport and alternative-energy public transport could provide more durable relief than temporary cash payments alone.
There is also a case for continued examination of domestic refining, crude supply arrangements, competition within the downstream petroleum sector and national fuel-storage capacity.
Regulators should equally maintain effective market surveillance. Deregulation should not mean the absence of oversight. Nigerians are entitled to transparency concerning the factors determining pump prices and to protection against anti-competitive conduct or unjustifiable exploitation.
Beyond petrol, reliable electricity remains essential. As long as millions of households and businesses must generate their own electricity with petrol or diesel, changes in petroleum prices will continue to have an unusually large effect on the wider economy.
Government, organised labour, employers, civil society and other stakeholders have an important role in finding sustainable responses. Social dialogue should not begin only when frustration has reached the point of strikes and protests.
A functioning industrial-relations system should provide mechanisms through which economic evidence is shared, workers’ concerns are heard, government constraints are explained and practical compromises are negotiated.
The objective should not merely be industrial peace. It should be social justice accompanied by economic sustainability.
Nigeria needs economic reforms. It needs investment, infrastructure, domestic refining, fiscal stability and functioning markets. But Nigerians also need to survive long enough to enjoy the promised benefits of those reforms.
A worker who spends an increasing proportion of his salary merely travelling to work cannot indefinitely be told to endure. A pensioner choosing between medication and food cannot be treated as an unfortunate statistic.
A mother reducing her family’s meals because food prices have risen again is experiencing economic policy in its most immediate form.
A small business owner shutting down because energy costs have consumed the profit margin represents another job and source of livelihood potentially lost.
The current petrol-price surge therefore requires more than explanations about international markets. It requires careful examination of wages, transportation, pensions, social protection, domestic energy production, competition and electricity supply as interconnected parts of one national welfare challenge. Nigeria’s economic policies must ultimately serve Nigerians.
The enduring principle of decent work is that labour should provide a person with a reasonable opportunity to live in dignity. When full-time employment no longer provides sufficient protection against hunger, transportation hardship and inability to obtain basic healthcare, society has a legitimate reason to examine whether its economic and social protections remain adequate.
The challenge before the Federal Government is therefore to balance market realities with the constitutional aspiration of protecting the welfare of the people.
For workers, poor and elderly Nigerians, this is not an abstract debate about barrels of crude oil, exchange rates or market indices. It is about food on the table, transport to work, medicine in the cupboard and dignity in old age.
Those considerations deserve a central place in Nigeria’s economic response to the present fuel-price crisis.
•Takor, mni, is a human rights lawyer, trade unionist and pension advocate.

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
As the 2026/2027 school session begins across Nigeria, millions of parents face the familiar burdens of school fees, uniforms, books and transport. But for many, especially in conflict-prone communities, there is a more frightening question: will their children return home safely each day? The school, once regarded as a sanctuary of learning and hope, has increasingly become a target for terrorists and armed criminals whose abductions are traumatising families and threatening the future of education.
The latest situation in Borno State is particularly disturbing. In Askira-Uba Local Government Area, about 80 pupils abducted during attacks on schools in Mussa and Lassa in May and June 2026 remain in captivity, according to local education authorities. Only 56 of the area’s 113 primary schools are currently functioning, with 57 shut because of insecurity. Some of the abducted children have now spent more than 100 days in captivity.
The danger is not confined to the North-East. Schoolchildren in other parts of the country have also been targeted, demonstrating that criminal gangs are increasingly exploiting the vulnerability of educational institutions. This grim reality threatens to reverse whatever gains Nigeria has made in expanding access to education.
Governments must therefore make school security an urgent national priority. The Safe Schools Initiative cannot remain a collection of commendable policies, committees and announcements. It must translate into visible protection. The Federal Government has announced stronger collaboration among education authorities, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, the police, the armed forces and intelligence agencies. What is required now is effective implementation, monitoring and accountability.
Schools in vulnerable communities should have appropriate perimeter protection, controlled access, adequate lighting, emergency communication systems and clearly rehearsed evacuation procedures. More importantly, security agencies must maintain effective intelligence networks around schools and establish rapid-response arrangements with local communities. Existing school-safety intelligence and response mechanisms should be fully utilised rather than allowed to become another bureaucratic initiative.
The criminal economy behind school abductions must also be dismantled. Kidnappers, informants, financiers and other facilitators who enable these crimes must face the full weight of the law. Every successful abduction emboldens criminals, enriches their networks and erodes parents’ confidence in the school system.
Beyond the immediate security threat lies an even greater danger. Every school closed by insecurity creates room for illiteracy, child labour, exploitation, radicalisation and poverty to flourish. In communities already devastated by insurgency, prolonged school closures can produce a generation deprived of the opportunity to escape the cycle of violence and deprivation.
As classrooms reopen, therefore, governments must understand that protecting schools is an investment in Nigeria’s future. No child should have to choose between education and personal safety. The new academic year must mark a renewed national  determination to ensure that Nigerian schools remain places of learning, not hunting grounds for terrorists and kidnappers.
Education must prevail over terror.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
Ferran Torres continued the impressive start to his PsG career by scoring the opener as the French and European champions won 2-1 at bitter rivals Marseille in Ligue 1 on Sunday.
Spain World Cup final hero Torres came off the bench to replace Khvicha Kvaratskhelia just before the hour mark and headed in a Desire Doue cross to give PSG the lead in the 66th minute at the Velodrome.
That brought the game to life, with England midfielder Angel Gomes scoring an excellent equaliser for Marseille on 72 minutes only for PSG captain Marquinhos to win the game for the visitors three minutes later.
The Brazilian defender met a Nuno Mendes cross and had his initial effort saved by Marseille goalkeeper Jeffrey de Lange before bundling in the rebound.
United States star Timothy Weah, a former PSG player, was then sent off for a second booking as Marseille finished the game a man down.
Torres scored PSG’s winning goal in Brest last weekend and now has seven goals in six appearances in all competitions since joining the reigning European champions from Barcelona. He has only started three times.
“We knew that for us it was one of the most important matches of the season. We knew it wouldn’t be easy but we managed to get the victory,” Torres said at full-time, with PSG now up to sixth in the table, five points behind leaders Monaco after five fixtures.
“Now we can go away and play for our countries and disconnect from club football for a bit.”
Torres, whose extra-time goal gave Spain victory over Argentina in the World Cup final in the United States in July, is in the squad as La Roja play their first game since that tournament away to England in the UEFA Nations League next weekend.
Struggling Marseille have now suffered four straight Ligue 1 defeats, and five losses in a row in all competitions. They therefore find themselves in the relegation zone as club football takes a three-week break.
Monaco extended their unbeaten start to the campaign by beating Lens 2-1 on Friday, and the principality side are two points clear at the top of Ligue 1 from both Lyon and Paris FC.
Lyon hammered Rennes 4-0 on Saturday, while Paris FC won 2-1 against Strasbourg.
Lille missed the opportunity to move level on points again with Monaco as they lost 2-1 at Nice on Sunday.
Algerian international Mohamed Amoura got what proved to be the winner for Nice, with Japan’s Ayase Ueda scoring for Lille, his third goal in four games since signing from Feyenoord.
Former Aston Villa striker Cameron Archer scored in a third straight game for Auxerre as Will Still’s team defeated Brest 2-1.

items.content:
Niger State Governor, Umaru Bago, has called for an executive order from the Presidency or the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development to ban mining activities in locations identified as problematic across the state.
Bago made the call on Sunday during an interview on Channels Television’s Sunday Politics, following the deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners while in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC.
The governor said the state government required stronger intervention from the Federal Government because of limitations surrounding the enforcement of mining regulations.
Asked what his administration was doing about the presence of minors at mining sites, Bago said decisive action was needed to end the practice.
“I am in between the devil and the Red Sea because, as a governor, yes, it’s in my state. As a governor, I cannot just go and order the police or military to start shooting people or arresting people. As a governor, I can only make advocacy.
“But these people, because they have tasted the mining money, they cannot leave that side. We need decisive action. We need an executive order from the Presidency or from the Ministry of Mineral Resources to ban mining in certain locations where we have seen they are problematic. Once that is done, it can be enforced,” he said.
Bago said illegal mining had become a major challenge in Niger State, particularly with the increasing involvement of children in artisanal mining.
He expressed concern that the involvement of minors in mining was taking them away from school and exposing them to the dangers associated with mining activities.
The governor’s call came amid renewed scrutiny of mining activities in the state following the deaths of the 37 suspected illegal miners in NSCDC custody.

items.author: Usman A. Bello, Benin City
items.content:
An official of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) in Delta State reportedly drowned in the River Ethiope while pursuing a fleeing suspected drug offender in the state.
The incident reportedly happened in Obiaruku community, Ukwuani Local Government Area of Delta State, at the weekend.
It was gathered that NDLEA operatives in the area apprehended a suspected drug offender allegedly conveying illicit drugs and took him towards the River Ethiope Bridge, apparently to take him into custody.
Sources said the suspect suddenly escaped from the officers’ grip and, in a bid to evade arrest, jumped into the river.
Miners&#8217; Deaths: NSCDC parades suspended commandant, nabs more personnel
How 34-year-old man was found dead hours after leaving Jos residence
According to a source, in an effort to apprehend the fleeing suspect, the NDLEA officers reportedly entered the river in pursuit.
However, the operation turned tragic when one of the officers reportedly drowned in the process.
Another officer who also entered the river was said to have been rescued and rushed to a hospital for medical attention.
The suspect being pursued was also said to have escaped through the river during the incident.
Another source, who confirmed the incident, described it as a mystery, noting that the river was not deep enough to drown someone.
He said the corpse was later recovered and handed over to the NDLEA after traditional rites for people who drown in the River Ethiope were performed in Obiaruku.
He said certain rites, including the provision of a goat and other specified items, are required to be performed before the remains of a drowning victim can be released by the community.
When contacted, the Delta State Commander of the NDLEA, Halilu Hamidi, referred journalists to the agency’s spokesperson, Femi Babafemi, for response.
However, an NDLEA official confirmed the incident, saying investigation was ongoing to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident and determine the actual cause of the officer’s death.

The media officer said the troops also conducted cordon-and-search operations in communities across Bassa and Mangu Local Government Areas.

Oteh urged residents to support the military and other security agencies in tackling security challenges across the state.

items.content:
By Johnbosco Agbakwuru
ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu has celebrated the 66th birthday of his wife, First Lady Senator Oluremi Tinubu, describing her as his “truest friend and confidante” and declaring that, if life gave him another chance, he would choose the same path that led him to her.
Tinubu, in a birthday message on Sunday, addressed the First Lady as “Oluremi mi” and wrote: “Today, I celebrate the woman who has walked beside me with patience, grace and uncommon courage.”
The President invoked Yoruba wisdom and scripture, quoting the proverb, “Ìyàwó rere ni adé ọkọ rẹ̀” — “A good wife is her husband’s crown” — and adding that the Book of Proverbs, which she knows “far better than I do,” also speaks eloquently of the worth of a virtuous woman.
Tinubu credited his wife with sharing his burdens and understanding him in ways few others could.
“The burdens that were mine to bear often found their way onto your shoulders. The thoughts I could not put into words somehow found their way to you,” he wrote.
He recalled her composure during difficult periods, saying: “In difficult times, when the future was uncertain, you stayed calm beside me and prayed with me. Through all these years, you have remained the one who truly understands me.”
The President also praised her honesty, particularly her willingness to tell him difficult truths.
“I call you my truest friend and confidante because you speak the truth plainly, even on the days I would rather not hear it,” he said.
“After a demanding day, you wait until we are alone before telling me what I need to hear. I have always cherished you for that honesty.”
Tinubu highlighted the First Lady’s role in shaping their family and faith life, saying their children and grandchildren had grown under the influence of her prayers, values of faith and kindness.
“Our home bears the lasting imprint of your devotion. Our children and grandchildren have grown beneath the shelter of your prayers. They carry your values of faith and kindness wherever life takes them,” he said.
The President also praised her public service and compassion, saying Nigerians knew her for her kindness, generosity and steadfast faith.
“I have watched you touch lives quietly and consistently, offering hope and support to those in need,” he said.
Tinubu traced her humanitarian activities from their years in Lagos to her current national platform.
“From the New Era Foundation during our years in the saddle in Lagos to the Renewed Hope Initiative today, your care has reached many young boys and girls, widows, elderly citizens, and women farmers across the country,” he said.
He singled out her advocacy for people affected by tuberculosis and other diseases, describing her as “a compassionate advocate and a determined champion.”
Tinubu further said his wife’s compassion transcended ethnic, regional and religious boundaries.
“I know the prayers you offer for people whose names you may never know. I also know many whom you have helped without ever meeting them. For you, compassion has never recognised the boundaries of tribe, region or religion,” he said.
Reflecting on their years together, the President said their shared experiences had strengthened their relationship.
“A long journey teaches a man the true value of a good partner. We have travelled a long road together. I think of the difficult decisions we talked through for hours and the sacrifices no one else saw. Laughter and prayer carried us through many of them,” he said.
Tinubu ended the tribute with a declaration of enduring love and commitment.
“If life returned me to the beginning, I would choose the same road that led me to you. Through every mile, my heart has always remained at home with you.
“Happy 66th birthday, my darling Oluremi. I pray that God Almighty will grant you many more years in good health and joy. May the years ahead bring you the same comfort and happiness you have so freely given to me and many others.”
The post Tinubu to First Lady at 66: You’re my truest friend appeared first on Vanguard News.

items.author: Abubakar Sadiq Isah
items.content:
The Aku-Uka of Wukari in Taraba state, His Royal Majesty (HRM) Dr Ishaku Adda Ali, says the security crisis bedeviling the Kwararafa kingdom is something one cannot remain silent about.
Speaking during the 2026 Kwararafa People’s Assembly meeting in Abuja, over the weekend, he said the old Kwararafa Confederacy has been under bandits siege recently.
He said several communities in some parts of Benue, Kogi Taraba, Southern Kaduna, Nasarawa, Plateau and Niger have been devastated by bandits, herders-farmers violence, kidnapping, relentless campaign of displacement, which he said has emptied the entire communities and turned thousands of the people into refugees in their own country.
He said farmers could no longer go to their farms and traders could not also go to market due to the worsening security situation.
Ex-Kano pilgrims welfare board DG, Kofar Mata, dies at 70
2027: I’ll unseat Ahmad Lawan, says ADC candidate
“There are the children who can no longer go to school. There are elders whose ancestral homes have been reduced to ashes. We do not come here to accuse, but to say, we need help.”
“And we come here to say that the help must be real, it must be sustained, and it must reach the communities that are suffering, not stop at the level of communiques and conferences,” he said.
He, however, said he regretted how his Jukun kinsmen of the defunct Kwararafa confederacy have spent many years divided through political, religious and ethnic lines.
“If the Jukun, and the Idoma , Igala, Ebira, Alago, Nupe, Tarok, Angas, Eggon, Mighill, Ohafia, Bekwara, Yala, Gamai, Kare-Kare among others could build a common political house in the 15th century, what excuse do we have in the 21st century,” he asked.
Dr Ali, the Chief convener of the meeting, said he brought people together because for centuries, the defunct Kwararafa confederacy united the diverse peoples of the Niger – Benue confluence into a political and cultural formation that commanded the respect of its neighbours.
Also speaking, the Taraba State Governor, Agbu Kefas, said he was deeply honoured to stand before the gathering not only as governor of Taraba but as a proud son of Kwararafa kingdom and as Core- Convener of Kwararafa People’s Assembly 2026.
He said when the idea of the Kwararafa People’s Assembly meeting was brought before him, he could not hesitate to accept the responsibility of serving as the core -convener.
He said he accepted such responsibility personally as a son of Kwararafa who understands the importance of Kwararafa shared heritage and the duty, every kinsman of Kwararafa kingdom owes the future generations.
“For the avoidance of doubt, my role as a core-convener is not an official responsibility of the Taraba State government. This assembly is not Taraba state government programme and it is not intended to advance any personal, political, or sectional agenda,”he said.
He said his participation arose from his identity as a son of Kwararafa, saying he believes that the shared heritage could become a platform to peace, cooperation and national development.
According to him, the organizational support for the gathering came through the Kwararafa platform and the voluntary contributions of friends and supporters who believe in a purpose.
The governor, therefore, said the meeting serves as an opportunity for people with great history to come together to renew their shared vision and agree on how to contribute more effectively to the development of Nigeria.
He commended the Aku-Uka of Wukari who served as the Chief convener of the gathering, even as he clarified that the Kwararafa Heritage does not belong to Taraba state alone or ethnic group or one traditional institution, saying it belongs to all the people connected to the shared heritage.
In his goodwill message, the Ohimegye of Opanda -Umaisha kingdom, HRH Alhaji Usman Abdullahi, said the Ebira ethnic group of Nasarawa state were also descendants of Kwararafa empire.
He stressed on the need of every ethnic group under the Kwararafa kingdom to always share and identify themselves wherever they go or reside, adding that there should be a symbol of Kwararafa kingdom mounted in every traditional rulers palaces.
“Because having Kwararafa symbols in every palace will symbolise that anywhere you go, it will show that this is your brother,”he said.
The Ohimegye, therefore, appreciated the Aku -Uka of Wukari for convening the meeting, saying he hoped that after deliberation, there would be a communiqué for further future guidelines and conferences.
Our correspondent reports that among dignitaries at the event were the deputy governor of Kogi, Plateau and Nasarawa States as well as Ona of Abaji, the Andoma of Doma, Ohinoyi of Ebira land, Attah of Igala and several other traditional rulers.

items.title: U-20 Women’s World Cup: Semi-final fixtures confirmed
items.summary:
The semi-final line-up for the 2026 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup in Poland has been confirmed following the completion of the quarter-final fixtures.
Four teams — Italy, Spain, Colombia and North Korea — will compete for places in the final of the tournament.
Colombia secured the final semi-final spot on Sunday after edging Nigeria 1-0 in a closely contested quarter-final.
The South American side held on to its narrow advantage to end Nigeria’s campaign and book a place among the last four.
North Korea also advanced after defeating Canada 2-0 in their quarter-final encounter.
The two teams joined Spain and Italy, who had already secured their semi-final places following victories in Saturday’s quarter-final matches.
The semi-final action will begin on Wednesday, with Spain taking on Italy in the first encounter.
The second semi-final will see Colombia face North Korea, with both sides now two wins away from lifting the U-20 Women’s World Cup trophy.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
By Henry Umoru
ABUJA — Chairman of the Senate Committee on Interior, Senator Adams Oshiomhole, has called for a thorough, transparent and independent investigation into the deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, in Niger State.
Oshiomhole, who represents Edo North Senatorial District, said the investigation should establish the circumstances surrounding the deaths, including the conditions under which the detainees were held, the medical attention provided to them and those who survived, as well as the actual cause of death.
In a statement issued by his office on Sunday, the former Edo State governor said the fact that the deceased were arrested on allegations of illegal mining did not remove their right to humane treatment.
He said every person, regardless of the offence for which he or she was accused, deserved to be treated with dignity, respect and in accordance with the law.
Oshiomhole described the incident as tragic and urged relevant authorities to allow ongoing investigations to establish the precise circumstances surrounding the deaths.
He also called for an immediate assessment of detention and correctional facilities across the country to ensure that they meet acceptable standards of safety, sanitation, ventilation and human dignity.
The senator commiserated with the families, relatives and communities of the 37 deceased miners, praying for strength for them to bear the loss.
He also prayed for the speedy recovery of those who survived the incident and are receiving medical attention.
Oshiomhole commended Niger State Governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago; Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo; and the Commandant-General of the NSCDC, Professor Ahmed Abubakar Audi, for what he described as their prompt response to the crisis and steps taken to commence investigations.
He urged Nigerians to remain calm while the authorities establish the facts surrounding the incident.
The senator stressed that accountability, justice and respect for human dignity must remain central to the administration of the country’s detention and security system.

items.content:
The African Democratic Congress (ADC) candidate for Yobe North Senatorial District in the 2027 general election, Barrister Imamudeen Ahmed Talba, has vowed to unseat Senator Ahmad Lawan.
Talba stated this while speaking with journalists at the inauguration of the party’s Unified Campaign Council and commissioning of its new state secretariat in Damaturu.
He said he was persuaded to contest the seat by people from the district who, according to him, were demanding a change after years of representation by Lawan.
Talba said he was not initially interested in politics but accepted the call to contest after people in the district approached him.
NDLEA Officer Chasing Drug Suspect Drowns in Delta River
“If the people, if my people decide to invite me to contest, which I said no, and they insisted, that means they are ready for me to take over,” he said.
He said the people had expressed a desire for a new representative who would bring fresh ideas and address the challenges confronting the senatorial district.
“Let somebody new take over and let’s see what we can get, something new, so that we can achieve what we want to achieve,” he said.
Talba said Yobe North was faced with challenges including poverty, unemployment, poor infrastructure and inadequate educational opportunities.
He said the zone lacked industries and other sources of employment for youths who graduate from schools.
The ADC candidate said he would prioritise economic development, agriculture and infrastructure if elected.
He said efforts would be made to support farmers, revive economic activities and attract federal government intervention to the senatorial district.
Talba also called for the rehabilitation of the Nguru-Kano railway, saying it could boost the movement of agricultural produce and livestock and revive economic activities in the area.
He said the Northern Nigeria Meat Factory in Nguru should also be revived, adding that an agricultural development framework previously studied with Korean partners should be revisited.
“If we come on board, we are going to sit down and work on the economic development framework for the zone, and even for the state,” he said.
He said he would identify projects requiring federal intervention and pursue them, while also engaging the state government on matters within its responsibility.
On healthcare, Talba said he would prioritise the kidney-related health challenges affecting communities in the senatorial district.
He said research had been conducted into the causes of the disease but more action was needed to address the problem.
According to him, some residents from Gashua, Nguru and other communities travel long distances to access dialysis treatment.
He promised to push for the provision of diagnostic and dialysis facilities in Nguru, Gashua and other areas if elected.
“Having done the research, identifying the causes, why shouldn’t we work out and check the causes? If it’s water or something else, why shouldn’t we work on it?” he said.
Talba said his decision to contest was motivated by his desire to serve the people and not for personal gain.
“I was here to serve the people, not for myself. I didn’t come into politics for myself,” he said.
The state leader of the ADC, Alhaji Adamu Maina Waziri, said the party had inaugurated a 57-member Unified Campaign Council to coordinate its campaigns for the 2027 elections.
Waziri said the council would coordinate campaigns for the presidential, governorship, senatorial, House of Representatives and House of Assembly elections in Yobe State.

items.content:
By Udeme Akpan
The Vice President, Oil and Gas, Dangote Industries Limited, Mr. Edwin Devakumar, has assured prospective investors that the ongoing Initial Public Offering (IPO) of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery presents an opportunity to participate in one of Africa’s most strategic industrial enterprises, saying investors stand to enjoy significant value appreciation and attractive returns over the long term.
Mr. Devakumar said the refinery’s strong operational performance, growing market share, robust demand outlook and strategic position within Africa’s energy value chain make it an attractive investment proposition for institutional and retail investors.
According to him, the refinery has started making profits and was established to reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported refined petroleum products, strengthen national energy security, conserve foreign exchange, create employment opportunities and position the country as a major exporter of petroleum products to regional and global markets.
“The Dangote Refinery is one of the most significant industrial investments ever undertaken on the African continent. It addresses a critical gap in the energy sector while creating substantial economic value. Those investing in the refinery’s ongoing IPO are investing in a business with strong fundamentals, enormous growth potential and a proven capacity to generate sustainable returns,” Mr. Devakumar said.
According to him, “The objective is not merely to raise capital. It is to democratise ownership of a strategic national asset and allow millions of Nigerians and global investors to participate in the value being created by the refinery. We believe this is an opportunity for investors to become partners in Africa’s industrial transformation story.”
Mr. Devakumar said funds realised from the offering would support the company’s long-term growth initiatives, operational optimisation, expansion projects, working capital requirements and strategic investments across the petroleum value chain.
He emphasised that the refinery’s integrated business model, advanced technologies, large-scale production capacity, deep-water port infrastructure and extensive logistics network provide competitive advantages that are difficult to replicate elsewhere in Africa.
“The refinery is strategically positioned to serve domestic, regional and international markets. Demand for refined petroleum products across Africa continues to grow, and our scale, efficiency and location provide a unique advantage in capturing these opportunities. This translates directly into long-term value creation for shareholders,” he stated.
Mr. Devakumar explained that the refinery’s ability to process a wide range of crude oil grades, coupled with its production of petrol, diesel, aviation fuel, liquefied petroleum gas and petrochemical feedstocks, has created multiple revenue streams that, he said, strengthen the company’s earnings potential.
He further stated that the company remains committed to high standards of corporate governance, transparency, financial discipline, environmental stewardship and operational excellence, which he described as critical to sustaining investor confidence and shareholder value.
Once the IPO is concluded and the shares listed, he said the company’s commitment to accountability and transparency would become even stronger.
“Investors will benefit from regular financial disclosures, strict governance standards and a management team focused on driving sustainable growth and profitability,” he said.
Mr. Devakumar expressed confidence that the refinery’s future earnings potential, expanding export footprint and strategic role in Africa’s energy security would continue to attract investor interest.
“This IPO represents more than an investment opportunity; it is an invitation to participate in a historic enterprise that is redefining the African energy landscape. We are confident that investors who subscribe to the offer will be well-positioned to reap bountiful returns as the refinery continues its growth journey and delivers value to shareholders,” he concluded.

items.author: Akinbayo Wahab
items.content:
By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta
The Convener of The Alternative Movement and chieftain of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Otunba Segun Sowunmi, at the weekend commenced grassroots mobilisation in Ogun State in support of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s re-election bid in the 2027 presidential election.
Sowunmi, who spoke during a grassroots mobilisation programme in the Itoko area of Abeokuta South local government area of the State capital, said he was backing President Bola Tinubu because he believed the administration’s economic direction and policy choices were moving the country towards greater fiscal capacity.
According to him, Nigeria needs continuity in governance and sufficient time for governments to implement long-term policies, rather than changing direction every four years.
“We are here because I have chosen this day, in my capacity as a very strong grassroots leader here in Ogun State, especially as the promoter and convener of the Alternative Movement,” he said.
Sowunmi said he had consistently defended the economic policies of the Tinubu administration over the past years, arguing that a government needed adequate resources to execute its programmes.
“I have been screaming and shouting that the economic direction, the policy ideas, and the things that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu is doing are in the right direction for the country,” he said.
“You cannot run a nation on an agenda that says the country will not have money. Because if you don’t have money, what will you even be able to do?”
He claimed that increased revenues had created more resources at the federal, state and local government levels, and argued that the development process required policy stability.
Sowunmi said Nigeria should embrace what he described as the “principle of the pendulum”, under which political power alternates between the northern and southern parts of the country.
“I believe that, for us to be able to make this country a great nation and to hold it together, we must respect the principle of the pendulum,” he said.
“If it is the time of the Northern Protectorate, they should bring us a candidate we’ll take. If it is the time of the Southern Protectorate, they should give us a candidate we’ll take.”
He argued that democratic governance and policy implementation required continuity, citing countries such as Singapore and Malaysia as examples of nations that, in his view, achieved development through consensus and sustained policy direction.
“We cannot be changing leadership every four years. Democracy is very difficult, and the ability to implement policy requires a bit of time,” he said.
Sowunmi said the mobilisation would begin at the polling-unit level, with further engagements planned across the State.
He added that he planned to proceed with local government-level mobilisation before taking the campaign to the six local government areas in Ogun Central Senatorial District.
Sowunmi also said he would mobilise his political structure in Ijebu and other parts of the state in support of Tinubu.
“I will go and raise that structure and tell them that it has to be Bola Tinubu and nothing else,” he said.
‘Tinubu has an advantage in Southwest’
Sowunmi argued that political actors seeking the presidency outside what he considers the current political cycle should not underestimate Tinubu’s position.
“There is something called the principle of the planets. You will never see the moon and the stars come out when the sun is out,” he said.
“Anybody, especially from the Yoruba nation, who is calling himself anything when the sun is out is wasting his time.”
He further urged Yoruba voters to support Tinubu, arguing that the region should not be outperformed by other parts of the country in the number of votes cast for the President.
“I have come home to beg my people, Yoruba people, that you will not be ashamed,” he said.
“Because when the election is over and the people of the North-East, the North-West, and the North-Central produce more votes than you, then where will you put your face?”
Sowunmi also compared the 1999 and 2003 presidential elections, arguing that political fortunes could change significantly between election cycles.
“We are back to 2003. You did not give Obasanjo a significant number of votes in 1999, but by 2003, everything belonged to him,” he said.
Sowunmi said his support for Tinubu was also connected to his belief that Nigeria should avoid what he described as unnecessary political disruption.
“I am one of the people who worked very hard to ensure that we can have an arrangement of the pendulum. But right now, we can’t take unnecessary risks,” he said.
He also defended the principle of political rotation, recalling that former President Muhammadu Buhari, from the North, served two terms before Tinubu emerged as president in 2023.
“If power is in the North, Buhari did eight years. We did not disturb him,” he said.
“Now our son is there, breaking his back, breaking his head, working so hard, readjusting the country, doing all the things that need to be done.”
Sowunmi also criticised proposals that he believes would amount to a return to policies of the past, particularly regarding fuel subsidy.
“We have tried subsidy in this country. We started studying it from 1973, and between 1973 and date, we have seen the result. If it had worked, wouldn’t we have seen it?”
He also cited the rehabilitation of Nigeria’s refineries and the emergence of private-sector refining as part of his argument for continuing with the current direction of economic reforms.
“We have seen that nothing has worked,” he said. “They couldn’t even repair the refinery for so many years, and one private-sector person has run a refinery.”
Sowunmi urged Nigerians to look forward rather than return to policies he considers unsuccessful.
“No! We have left Egypt. Forward ever, backward never,” he said.

items.content:
Former Anambra State Governor and presidential candidate of the NDC, Peter Obi, has said he and his running mate, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, used a town hall meeting in Kaduna to engage directly with citizens on the challenges confronting Nigeria.
Obi disclosed this in a post on his Facebook page following the meeting, which he said was organised by the party as part of its series of engagements with citizens.
According to him, the Kaduna town hall followed a similar engagement recently held in Port Harcourt.
Obi said he attended the meeting with Kwankwaso and other party candidates after visiting the Sheikh Muhammad Sambo Memorial Islamic Institute in Rigachikun, Kaduna.
He said the engagement provided an opportunity for the political leaders to listen to citizens’ concerns, answer questions and receive contributions on critical national issues.
Obi said they reassured participants of their commitment to national unity, poverty reduction, investment in healthcare and education, as well as efforts to tackle insecurity.
He said the objective was to create conditions that would enable Nigerians displaced by insecurity to safely return to their homes, communities and farms.
The former governor also said the meeting addressed corruption and inefficiencies associated with the fuel subsidy regime, as well as the need to reduce the burden of fuel costs on Nigerians.
According to Obi, the country also needs an economy capable of enabling citizens to live decent and dignified lives.
He urged other political actors to engage directly with citizens and listen to their concerns.
“Let me use this opportunity once again to call on our opponents to also speak directly with the people and listen to their feedback,” Obi said.
He added: “The very essence of democracy is people-centred governance. Leaders and aspiring leaders must therefore leave their comfort zones and interface directly with the people they seek to serve.”
Obi thanked the party leadership and organisers of the town hall, while commending Kaduna residents for what he described as their commitment to supporting leadership that listens to their concerns.
He concluded with the campaign slogan: “A New Nigeria is POssible, and Nigeria will be OK.”

items.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi
JOS — Troops of Operation Enduring Peace have rescued two kidnapped victims, arrested 12 suspects and recovered weapons during separate operations in Plateau State.
Captain Polycarp Oteh, Media Information Officer for the operation, disclosed this in a statement on Sunday, saying the operations were conducted in different parts of the state.
He said troops of Sector 1, Sub-Sector 12, deployed at Lamingo, carried out an operation in the early hours of Saturday, September 19, following credible intelligence on the activities of suspected kidnappers operating around Rayfield and other parts of Jos North Local Government Area.
According to him, troops raided suspected criminal hideouts at Shere, Gwafan and Maza Hills, leading to the arrest of 11 suspects.
Oteh said intelligence obtained from two victims abducted from Gwafan Community on September 18 further assisted the operation.
“During preliminary investigation, the victims positively identified three of the arrested suspects as members of the syndicate allegedly responsible for their abduction,” he said.
In a related operation, troops of Sector 3 deployed in Bassa Local Government Area conducted a cordon-and-search operation at about 6pm on September 19 following credible intelligence.
The operation, Oteh said, led to the arrest of one suspect and recovery of a locally fabricated rifle.
He said troops were maintaining a presence in the area in an effort to apprehend other members of the suspected criminal syndicate.
Similarly, troops of Sector 8 deployed in Mangu Local Government Area conducted a confidence-building patrol along the Tul–Ntam–Angwan Mata–Deng-Deng axis.
During the patrol, troops apprehended a suspected criminal around the Water Board area after he allegedly attempted to conceal a weapon on sighting the soldiers.
A search of the suspect, Oteh said, led to the recovery of a locally fabricated automatic weapon, nine rounds of 7.62mm Special ammunition and a mobile phone.
The 12 suspects are in custody and undergoing further investigation, according to the military.
Oteh said the investigation was aimed at determining the activities of the suspected syndicate, identifying other members and facilitating follow-up operations against fleeing suspects.
The Commander, Operation Enduring Peace, Major General Maxwell Dangana, commended the troops for their professionalism, timely response and performance during the operations.
Dangana urged the troops to sustain the momentum of ongoing operations and deny criminal elements freedom of action within the Joint Operations Area.
He also appreciated the support and cooperation of residents and other stakeholders in Plateau State, stressing the importance of timely and credible information in combating criminal activities.
The commander assured residents of the operation’s continued commitment to protecting lives and property and strengthening peace and security across the state.

items.content:
The Chairman of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House, Otunba Abdulateef Owoyemi; his deputy and vice chairman, Otunba Dokun Ajidagba and Prof. Fassy Yusuf, and the Secretary, Pastor Jeremiah Salami, have dragged 12 other members of the family before the Ogun State High Court sitting in Ijebu-Ode over their purported removal from office.
The claimants in the suit are challenging allegations of financial inducement and manipulation in the selection process for the new Awujale of Ijebuland.
The four ruling house leaders, on behalf of themselves and the family, are asking the court to award N1 billion in damages against the 12 defendants for allegedly making unfounded allegations of financial inducement and other infractions against them.
They are also seeking a perpetual injunction restraining the defendants from parading themselves as the leaders or representatives of the royal house.

&#8216;A seat was secured but the President disappeared&#8217;, Atiku taunts Tinubu over UNGA absence
This was contained in a writ of summons marked HCJ/167/2026, dated September 16, 2026, and made available to journalists on Sunday.
Those sued include Pa Olusegun Olusoga, also known as “AK Black”; Ridwan Oduneye; Muyiwa Adeleye; Alhaji Taiwo Ajumo; Sikiru Adegunwa Oluwole; Hon. Kehinde Lawal; Lukman Logunleko Oludare; Prince Abdul Onalaja; Ashiru Mufutau; Prince (Barr.) Osiyemi Johnson; Prince Adeleke Adeyemi, also known as “Leke Adeyemi”; and Otunba Olukayode Otufale.
The claimants said that, following a resolution reached at a meeting of the ruling house on November 7, 2025, after an earlier meeting convened by the Ogun State Government at the Governor’s Office, Oke-Mosan, Abeokuta, on November 6, 2025, the three separate units of the ruling house, headed respectively by Owoyemi, Ajidagba and Yusuf, were formally merged into one ruling house.
They said the meeting unanimously adopted the leadership structure led by the trio.
According to the claimants, the leadership of the ruling house, led by Owoyemi, a former National President of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria, with the support of Ajidagba and Yusuf, had, on behalf of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House, been handling the nomination of the next Awujale from the family.
They said the leadership subsequently forwarded the list of nominated candidates to the Awujale Kingmakers, led by the Ogbeni Oja of Ijebuland, Chief Olorogun Dr. Sunny Kuku.
The claimants alleged that a breakaway unit of the family, including eight of the defendants, sometime in June, formed what they described as an illegal fact-finding committee to investigate allegations of unfounded and baseless financial inducement against the leadership of the ruling house.
They further stated that, at another meeting held on August 9, which they said was not ratified by the ruling house, the breakaway unit announced the submission of its fact-finding committee report and, based on the report, purportedly remove Owoyemi, Ajidagba and Yusuf as leaders of the family.
The defendants were also alleged to have written a letter dated August 11, 2026, to Governor Dapo Abiodun; the Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, Hon. Ganiyu Hamzat; the Chairman of Ijebu-Ode Local Government, Dare Alebiosu; the kingmakers; and others, notifying them of the purported removal of the ruling house leadership and urging them not to deal with the claimants on behalf of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House
The breakaway faction was also said to have, in a letter dated September 2, 2026, addressed to Governor Abiodun, the kingmakers, the Commissioner for Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, among others, announced the appointment of Otunba Olukayode Otufale as the “Single Unified Olori-Ebi” of the ruling house and directed that all future correspondence relating to the ruling house be channelled to him.
The claimants, however, averred that “the said representation is false in every material particular, that no ‘General Meeting’ capable of binding the entire Fusengbuwa Ruling House has been convened by lawful authority; and no valid resolution of the Ruling House, duly and lawfully constituted, has at any time removed the Claimants, or any of them, or appointed the 12th Defendant or any other person in their stead.”
They further averred that unless restrained by the court, the defendants would continue to hold themselves out to the state government, the kingmakers, the Ijebu-Ode Local Government and the general public as the family head and principal officers of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House.
They said this would cause irreparable prejudice to the claimants and the entire membership of the ruling house, as well as “serious detriment” to the pending and time-sensitive process for the selection of the next Awujale of Ijebuland, in which the ruling house has a substantial interest.
The four leaders therefore urged the court to grant, among others, the following reliefs “A declaration that the 1st Claimant is the duly recognized Olori-Ebi and Chairman, the 2nd Claimant the Deputy Chairman, the 3rd Claimant the Vice Chairman, and the 4th Claimant the General Secretary, of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House, Ijebu-Ode, pursuant to the Resolution of the Ruling House dated 7th November, 2025, and that they remain validly in their said respective offices.
“A declaration that neither the purported ‘Fact-Finding Committee’ constituted at the meetings of 7th and 25th June, 2026, nor the gathering(s) of 9th August, 2026 and 2nd September, 2026, nor any of the Defendants, was or is competent, under the native law and custom, tradition, or extant governing Resolution of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House, to remove, suspend, query, discipline, or purport to replace any of the Claimants from or in their respective offices.»
“A declaration that the purported removal of the Claimants, or any of them, from their respective offices as contained in and evidenced by the letter dated 11th August, 2026 titled ‘Notification of Removal from Office as Olori-Ebi and Chairman of Fusegbuwa Ruling House,’ and all resolutions, meetings and proceedings purportedly leading thereto is unconstitutional, unlawful, null, void and of no effect.»
“A declaration that the purported appointment of the 12th Defendant, Otunba Olukayode Otufale, or of any other person whomsoever, as ‘Single Unified Olori-Ebi’ or as holder of any principal office of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House as contained in and evidenced by the letter dated 2nd September, 2026 is unlawful, null, void and of no effect whatsoever.”»
They also asked the court for an order of perpetual injunction restraining the defendants, whether by themselves, their agents, servants, privies, associates, or any person howsoever described claiming through or under them, from parading, describing or holding out themselves, the 12th Defendant, or any other person, as the Olori-Ebi, Chairman, Deputy Chairman, Vice Chairman, Secretary or any principal officer of the Fusengbuwa Ruling House.
Among other reliefs, the claimants also asked the court to award N1 billion in general damages against the defendants for the injury allegedly occasioned to the reputation, standing and offices of the claimants collectively by the acts pleaded above.
The claimants stated that the damages sought were “without prejudice to, and exclusive of, any personal claim for damages by the 3rd Claimant in Suit No. HCJ/153/2026.”
The ruling house had dragged Governor Dapo Abiodun, the Awujale kingmakers and five others, including the Chairman of Ijebu-Ode Local Government, Dare Alebiosu, before the High Court sitting in Ijebu-Ode, seeking orders compelling the completion of the process for the selection of the next Awujale and Paramount Ruler of Ijebuland.
The suit, numbered HCJ/149/2026 and dated August 21, 2026, was filed by Otunba Owoyemi, chairman of the ruling house; Otunba Adedokun Ajidagba, deputy chairman; and Prof. Chief Fassy Yusuf, vice chairman of the royal house.
A vacation judge, Justice A. A. Omoniyi of Court 3, Ogun State High Court, sitting in Ijebu-Ode, had recently gave an interim ruling returning the suit filed by the ruling house against Gov Abiodun, the nine kingmakers and others to the administrative judge for reassignment.
Justice Omoniyi said he would be embarking on his annual vacation within the next one week and might not return to duty until January 2027.
He said he was aware of the urgency of the suit, numbered HCJ/149/2026 and filed on August 21, 2026, but was constrained by time, having only one week left before embarking on his annual vacation.
Omoniyi subsequently adjourned the next hearing date to this Wednesday, September 23, 2026
The Awujale stool became vacant in July 2025 following the death of Oba Sikiru Adetona at the age of 91, after 65 years on the throne.
The government halted the selection process in January 2026, citing petitions from security agencies and stakeholders, following an earlier suspension over procedural concerns in December 2025.
A total of 95 aspirants — 94 princes and one princess — had emerged from the ruling house nomination process held in Ijebu-Ode in December before the government halted the selection process.

items.content:
The inauguration of the September SNIDs (Sub-National Immunization Days) for polio vaccination, took place today at the Rotary Club of Karachi Community Centre in Gulistan-e-Jauhar.
The National Chair PolioPlus Committee Aziz Memon who is also a Past Trustee of The Rotary Foundation, together with EOC (Emergency Operations Centre) Focal Person, Dr. Ahmad Ali Shaikh, Shahzad Sabir, District Governor, Rotary District 3271, DGE Fahad Sikandar inaugurated the September SNIDs. Also attending the event was Humayun Qureshi, President Rotary Club of Karachi and several Rotarians.
The upcoming SNIDs scheduled from Sept 21 to 27, 2026 will target 31 million children in 115 polio high-risk districts across the country in areas of Balochistan, Gilgit-Baltistan, Islamabad, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, and Sindh. These SNIDs will cover all children under the age of five years.
Three large scale nationwide campaigns have already been implemented since the beginning of the year covering 45 million children, where some targeted high-risk areas were administered OPV (Oral Polio Vaccine) with fIPV (fractional Injectable Polio Vaccine) to strengthen immunity in weak and malnourished children, who are quick to fall prey to the Polio virus.
Speaking on the occasion, Aziz Memon stated; “Polio eradication is a collective responsibility. Parents and caregivers play a crucial role by ensuring their children receive all the recommended doses, including routine immunizations. Rotarians facilitate polio frontline workers during campaigns, and play a significant role in monitoring NIDs/SNIDs in their districts, engaging with local community leaders, to promote polio vaccination and counter misinformation and myths.”
Pakistan and Afghanistan remain the only 2 countries in the world where polio has not been eradicated. It is encouraging though that polio cases in Pakistan have significantly reduced over the years.

items.title: Rising remittances, falling exports
items.summary:
Pakistan is receiving more dollars from overseas Pakistanis while earning less at home, slowing momentum from its own productive economy. This is the paradox confronting policymakers: remittances are rising strongly, but exports are struggling to maintain their pace, trade deficit is widening, foreign direct investment remains weak and domestic investment is insufficient to create jobs for a rapidly growing young population.
