items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
Sindh has taken its first province-wide measure of the gender divide - and the numbers paint a picture of progress alongside some stubborn gaps, with millions of girls still out of school and women remaining heavily underrepresented in the police and judiciary.
The province's first-ever gender equality report, released by the provincial government on Friday, records gains in maternal health, women's employment and political participation, but flags persistent disparities in literacy, school enrolment, economic opportunities, digital access and representation in decision-making.
Unveiling the report, Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah directed all provincial departments to undertake targeted reforms based on its findings, strengthen gender-sensitive governance and improve women's and girls' access to education, healthcare, employment and public representation. The report was presented at the Chief Minister House by CM's Special Assistant on Human Rights Rajveer Singh Sodho.
Describing the report as a new policy tool for the province, CM Shah said its findings would help the government identify areas where progress had been made and those requiring urgent intervention, while guiding evidence-based planning, resource allocation and institutional reforms.
"Gender equality is not only a matter of social justice but also a fundamental requirement for sustainable development," CM Shah said, adding that the findings would help strengthen policies and programmes aimed at empowering women and girls.
According to the report, Sindh's population reached 55.69 million in 2023, growing at an annual rate of 2.57%. There were 108.76 men for every 100 women.
The health sector recorded progress, with the provincial health budget rising from Rs214.5 billion in 2023-24 to Rs267.54 billion in 2024-25 and estimated to reach Rs318.22 billion in 2025-26.
The maternal mortality ratio fell from 314 to 224 deaths per 100,000 live births, while the neonatal mortality rate stood at 24 deaths per 1,000 live births, the report said.
Education, however, remained a major challenge. The literacy rate stood at 68% for men and 47% for women, while female literacy in rural areas was only 27.52%. More than 4.08 million girls aged between five and 16 remain out of school, according to the report.
Women's representation in the justice and law-enforcement sectors also remained low. Women account for only 4.34% of the police force, 18.3% of prosecutors and 13.7% of judges.
The report recorded 3,085 reported cases of gender-based violence in 2024, underscoring the need for stronger protection mechanisms and improved access to justice.
The report also highlighted gains in political participation. The number of registered female voters has crossed 12 million, while the number of women contesting elections increased from 23 in 2018 to 53 in 2024.
Women's labour-force participation rose from 43.8% to 46.2%, while the number of employed women increased from 2.48 million to 3.32 million.
Despite the gains, the report identified barriers to women's full economic participation, including limited access to digital connectivity, financial inclusion, skills development, entrepreneurship and decent employment.

items.title: 8 charged to court over disappearance of toddler in Bayelsa Church

items.content:
Bayelsa State Police Command has charged eight suspects to Court over the sudden disappearance of Amarachi Blessing Ogbonna, a one-year, ten-month-old female child, from a church premises in the State on June 21, 2026.
Amarachi had gone missing during a church service after the mother dropped her at the children section of the church, but after the service, the children’s teachers could not explain the whereabouts of the child.
Police spokesman in Bayelsa State, DSP Musa Mohammed, said in a statement on Friday that eight suspects have been charged to court, awaiting arraignment, as investigation continues to recover the missing child.
He said, “The Bayelsa State Police Command is aware of the narrative making the rounds on social media platforms alleging inactivity by the Police following the sudden disappearance of Amarachi Blessing Ogbonna, a one-year, ten-month-old female child, from a church premises in Bayelsa State on 21st June, 2026.
School Proprietor arrested for allegedly defiling 9-year-old pupil
Ammunition Shortage Limiting Our Response to Attacks, Sokoto Guards Lament
“The Command wishes to state, for the avoidance of doubt, that the narrative does not reflect the true nature of the event. Upon receipt of the report, the operatives of the Violent Crime Response Unit (VCRU), acting on the directive of the Commissioner of Police, swiftly took over the investigation from Ekeki Division and commenced intensive investigative efforts.
“In the course of the investigation, suspects connected to the disappearance were identified and arrested. Based on the facts and evidence so far established, eight suspects have been charged to court and are awaiting arraignment before the High Court of Bayelsa State, Yenagoa Judicial Division, in Charge No. BYHC/YHC/CR./81/2026. Other persons whose involvement was not established were released on bail.
The Command further clarified that the delay in the arraignment of the suspects was not due to police inaction, but arose from the vacation of the courts.
The statement added that the courts resumed proceedings this week, and the matter is expected to proceed accordingly.
The statement added, “While the suspects await arraignment, the Police investigation remains active, with sustained efforts directed towards the safe recovery of Amarachi Blessing Ogbonna and her eventual reunion with her family.
“The Command is pursuing all credible leads and will continue to take every lawful step necessary to unravel the circumstances surrounding her disappearance.
“The Bayelsa State Police Command therefore urges members of the public to exercise caution in relying on unverified narratives circulating on social media, particularly on sensitive cases involving children, as such narratives can create unnecessary public apprehension and obscure the facts of an ongoing investigation.”

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
Pocket FM is betting heavily on AI to improve its content economics and lift its EBITDA margin to 15%-20% from around 5% currently, cofounder Prateek Dixit told Inc42.
Dixit did not disclose a timeline for achieving the margin target. However, he said AI already powers about 90% of Pocket FM’s production, while its post-production process is entirely AI-driven. Overall, AI is involved in 80%-90% of the startup’s creative processes.
The audio series platform is using AI to reduce production costs, accelerate content creation, and scale its IP across languages, geographies, and entertainment formats.
The margin expansion target comes shortly after Pocket FM claimed to have crossed $500 Mn in annual recurring revenue (ARR).
Founded in 2018 by Dixit, Rohan Nayak, and Nishanth KS, Pocket FM offers audio content across multiple languages and genres. Backed by Lightspeed, StepStone Group, Tencent, and Times Internet, the startup has raised $196 Mn to date. It was last valued at $750 Mn during its $103 Mn Series D funding round in 2024.
The startup claims its entertainment ecosystem comprises more than 7.7 Lakh titles, 5.5 Lakh creators, and 5.5 Bn hours of playtime and engagement data. It also has more than 1.4 Mn hours of text and voice content.
Inside Pocket FM’s AI Content Engine
As part of its broader AI push, Pocket FM has launched Sherpa, a fiction-writing platform designed to help creators build long-form stories spanning anywhere from 10 to 1,000 episodes.
The platform is currently free for all writers, and Pocket FM does not expect it to become a revenue generator in the near term.
“Closed-source frontier models can write one or two episodes reasonably well, but they struggle with long-form planning across 100 or 200 episodes and with creating strong IP. That was the thought process behind launching Sherpa,” Dixit said.
Unlike a single generative AI model, Sherpa uses multiple specialised agents across ideation, research, story planning, prose generation, feedback, and narrative memory. The platform is intended to maintain consistency across characters, relationships, conflicts, and storylines extending over hundreds of episodes.
Dixit said Sherpa’s planning and prose models use Pocket FM’s proprietary data, while its assistant layer can draw on frontier models such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
“We have around 2.5 Mn hours of content on the platform, which is massive and gives us proprietary engagement data. We have used this data to train a model for writing great prose,” Dixit said.
Taking Pocket FM’s IP Beyond Audio
The startup is now looking to expand into new geographies while taking its existing IP into additional entertainment formats, Dixit said.
It plans to enter Japan and South Korea over the next six to eight months. It is also exploring markets such as the Netherlands, Belgium, Turkey, and the Scandinavian countries.
Beyond audio, Pocket FM is evaluating interactive storytelling and gaming opportunities, although Dixit said no specific launches have been finalised.
Pocket Saga is currently the startup’s key video bet. Through the platform, Pocket FM is adapting its existing IP into long-form, AI-generated anime content.
Dixit said Pocket Saga titles could run for 50 to 100 hours, comprising two-to-three-minute episodes, with individual shows potentially spanning 1,000 to 2,000 episodes.
The strategy follows Pocket FM’s decision to shut down Pocket TV, its short-form video drama product. Dixit said Pocket TV suffered from weak user retention and operated in a segment where AI had increasingly commoditised short-form video production.
The cofounder declined to comment on Pocket FM’s IPO and fundraising plans. Recent media reports suggest that Pocket FM is looking to raise $100 Mn to $120 Mn at a valuation of about $2 Bn. However, Inc42 could not independently verify this.

items.title: Public servants told not to feed sensitive data into AI
items.summary:
Government employees have been barred from uploading classified documents and other sensitive information to public artificial intelligence (AI) tools under the National Cyber Security Handbook 2026-27 issued by the National Cyber Emergency Response Team.
The handbook, issued under the Pakistan Information Security Framework 2026, lays down a set of rules governing the use of AI in government affairs.
Officials will be required to use only AI tools and platforms approved by their respective departments, while government emails, software source code and citizens' personal information have also been prohibited from being shared on public AI platforms.
According to the National CERT, providing sensitive information to AI platforms carries the risk of data leaks and unauthorised use.
The handbook directs government employees not to upload classified documents to public AI tools. They have also been instructed not to share government email content or software source code on such platforms.

items.content:
Government employees have been barred from uploading classified documents and other sensitive information to public artificial intelligence (AI) tools under the National Cyber Security Handbook 2026-27 issued by the National Cyber Emergency Response Team.
The handbook, issued under the Pakistan Information Security Framework 2026, lays down a set of rules governing the use of AI in government affairs.
Officials will be required to use only AI tools and platforms approved by their respective departments, while government emails, software source code and citizens' personal information have also been prohibited from being shared on public AI platforms.
According to the National CERT, providing sensitive information to AI platforms carries the risk of data leaks and unauthorised use.
The handbook directs government employees not to upload classified documents to public AI tools. They have also been instructed not to share government email content or software source code on such platforms.
Citizens' personal information is also not to be uploaded to public artificial intelligence tools.
Government officials will be allowed to use only those AI tools and platforms that have been approved by their departments.
The handbook further instructs employees to remove names and other sensitive information from AI prompts and files before submitting them to such tools.
Any accidental disclosure of confidential information must be reported immediately to the relevant IT or cybersecurity team, according to the National CERT.

items.author: Shahbaz Rana
items.content:
Ambassador Alexandra Berg von Linde has said that Sweden is looking forward to renegotiating the Bilateral Investment Treaty and a Pakistani official said that both sides would hold the first round in November to rewrite the 45-year-old pact due to Islamabad's concerns over international arbitration.
The Swedish ambassador emphasised the need for continued efforts to honour Pakistan's international commitments under the duty-free access scheme of Europe, known as the Generalised System of Preferences Plus (GSP+). She was speaking during the launching ceremony of the Sweden-Pakistan Business Guide 2026-28.
"Sweden is very much looking forward to restarting negotiations over updating the Bilateral Investment Treaty," remarked Linde.
Her remarks came after Pakistan sent a notice to terminate the 1981 treaty as part of its strategy to renegotiate all the existing investment treaties. Islamabad was keen to review the investment treaties to avoid huge fiscal exposures due to international arbitration.
The government has appointed an investment ombudsman for dispute resolution and has also approved a template for the treaty, which it wants to apply with all partner countries.
A government official said that the first round of talks between Pakistan and Sweden was scheduled for November 17-18 in Islamabad. The government has also been negotiating its investment treaty with Hungary, hoping for an early agreement with these two nations.
The Swedish ambassador also spoke about the GSP Plus scheme. "Continued efforts need to be made to advance international commitments under the GSP Plus," she said.
She was the second European ambassador in the past less than three weeks having echoed such comments, which were earlier made by the Netherlands ambassador.
EU Ambassador Raimundas Karoblis also said on Friday in Lahore that Pakistan would have to show progress on implementation and formulation of various laws and conventions necessary for availing itself of the next GSP Plus status.
Karoblis urged exporters to take immediate measures for implementation of the requisite conventions and to engage with the government with reference to concerns of the European Commission, especially those relating to human and labour rights, governance and environmental issues, to facilitate the path for future extension of the GSP Plus for the next 10 years.
Federal Commerce Secretary Jawad Paul said that the government had successfully completed its fifth review under the EU's GSP Plus status. He stated this while speaking as chief guest at the launch of the Sweden-Pakistan Business Guide 2026-2028.
He added that preparations were already underway for formal re-application. Paul expressed confidence that compliance with international obligations would enable Pakistan to transition smoothly into the new EU regulatory framework.
According to the GSP+ monitoring report that the EU released recently, the club of 27 nations asked Pakistan that "to ensure further GSP+ eligibility and compliance with international commitments", it had to reverse negative developments that took place from 2023 to 2025.
"Grave concerns remain as significant systemic challenges persisted in the implementation of human rights conventions, with a deterioration of the situation relating in particular to enforced disappearances, minority rights, freedom of media and freedom of expression and peaceful assembly," stated the report.
The monitoring report stated that impunity for human rights violations continued to be a major concern. The EU said that Pakistan needed to take robust steps to reverse negative trends in relation to enforced disappearances and violations of freedom of expression. "In this regard, laws on blasphemy, cybercrime (such as PECA), defamation, counterterrorism and sedition should be amended or repealed."
The European Commission has already approved new GSP regulations, from January 1, 2027 until the end of 2036. This completes the review process and transitions from the 2012 Regulation to the new GSP Regulation.
According to the European Commission, the new GSP will provide reduced or zero tariffs on imports from 65 developing countries for the next decade, supporting poverty reduction and sustainable development. Moreover, the updated GSP strengthens accountability by linking trade benefits more closely to human and labour rights, climate and environment, and good governance. It also introduces improved monitoring, greater transparency, and reinforces and updates the links between trade preferences and compliance with international standards.
It does so by increasing the number of relevant international conventions beneficiaries must adhere to, and by introducing an urgent withdrawal procedure, which allows for the suspension of preferences in case of serious and systemic violations of the principles underpinning such conventions.
Finally, the new GSP includes an automatic safeguard on rice imports, protecting EU producers while preserving the development objectives of the scheme. In practice, this means that if imports from a beneficiary rise sharply above the average of their past imports over 10 years, the EU will suspend preferential rates for the rest of the year and introduce a tariff rate quota (TRQ) for the following year to prevent market disruption.

items.author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
items.content:
The Punjab government has asked the federal government to give representation to all provinces in the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) along with federal representatives in a bid to deal more effectively with administrative matters in the hydrocarbon sector.
The centre has sent a summary to the Council of Common Interests (CCI), seeking to exclude the role of provinces in day-to-day administrative affairs of the oil and gas sector.
The summary has been circulated to the ministries of finance, planning, development and special initiatives, law & justice, Cabinet Division and Attorney General (Pakistan) along with provinces of Sindh, Punjab, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan for views and comments.
However, the provinces have objected to the proposal of bypassing the CCI while tackling every-day oil and gas-related administrative matters.
The government of Punjab has partially supported the proposal and has stated that regulatory bodies should function independently in accordance with the prevailing laws, rules, regulations and policies.
Furthermore, it said, there should be representation from all provincial governments and the federal administration in those regulatory bodies. If any provincial government has grievances about any regulatory or administrative decision, it may refer it to the CCI.
The government of Sindh has objected to the proposal (iii) of the summary and stated that Article 172(3) envisaged vesting of oil and gas, lying within the province/territorial waters adjacent thereto, jointly and equally between the federal government and provinces. It confers equal title on provinces with the right to dispose of oil and gas with the federal government by becoming a co-licensor.
Therefore, the proposal may be amended that all administrative matters about the management of entities operating in the oil and gas sector are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the federal government and the respective provincial government and need not to be submitted to the CCI.
The government of Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa was of the view that the power of parliament could not be denied but in the present context, the parliament could not legislate contrary to the true letter and spirit of Article 172(3) of the Constitution.
"There can be no cavil that Article 172(3) of the Constitution envisages the vesting of oil and gas resources within provinces or the territorial waters adjacent thereto, jointly and equally in the federation and concerning province(s)," it said. "As such, the provinces have an equal say as the federal government in deciding the fate of these resources. The federal government in the exercise of its executive powers is to act as a fiduciary under Article 172(3) for provincial rights and not as an absolute owner."
The government of Balochistan conveyed that policy matters and amendments needed to be formulated with approval of the CCI and regulatory decisions should be taken by the regulator concerned in accordance with the rules and guidelines imparted at the CCI level.
"Furthermore, excluding the CCI from the administrative matters is not tenable since the cumulative provisions of Article 154, 156 and 172(3), read with Entry 2 of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution, provide for enhanced supervisory role of the CCI in the operational framework for mineral oil and natural gas," it said.
"In terms of Articles 154 and 172(3) by the apex court, it falls within the domain of the CCI to deliberate upon and render appropriate policy guidelines on the scope and modalities of executive authority of the CCI/provinces in the operational and management framework for mineral oil and natural gas."

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
Federal Minister for Finance Muhammad Aurangzeb addressed the "Fireside Chat: Pakistan: External Shocks Remain Manageable" at the JP Morgan Emerging and Frontier Markets Opportunities Conference in London, outlining Pakistan's progress in restoring macroeconomic stability and its priorities to move towards investment, capital formation, exports and private sector-led growth.
The conference saw strong interest in Pakistan from leading global institutional investors and top money managers, with 55 global investment funds engaging with the Pakistani delegation through a number of one-on-one meetings and a full investor session. Discussions focused on Pakistan's future economic direction, investment opportunities and the sustainability of its ongoing economic transformation. Amin Khowaja, CEO and Country Head JP Morgan Pakistan, was also present during the meetings.
Setting out the government's economic direction, the finance minister outlined six key priorities: bringing permanence to macroeconomic stability and strengthening fiscal and external shock-absorbing capacity; moving from stabilisation to sustainable and responsible growth driven by productivity, investment and exports; staying the course on structural reforms; moving from aid to trade and investment; expanding access to finance for people and communities; and positioning Pakistan for the new economy, including digitalisation, blockchain and Web 3.0.
Aurangzeb said that over the last three years, Pakistan's overriding task had been to restore macroeconomic stability and rebuild credibility. He noted that significant progress had been made in fiscal consolidation, external-sector stability, inflation, debt management and international market access.
GDP growth recovered to 3.7% in FY26, while fiscal deficit declined to 2.6% of GDP, a multi-year low.

items.author: Usman Hanif
items.content:
Pakistan's digital payments ecosystem is moving beyond the early adoption phase, with instant payment infrastructure increasingly being integrated into everyday financial transactions, according to banking and payment industry officials.
According to the State Bank of Pakistan's Payment Systems Quarterly Review, 3.7 billion retail transactions were recorded during January-March 2026. Digital channels accounted for 3.4 billion transactions, or approximately 92% of the total, with the digital transaction value reaching Rs68.3 trillion.
"The digital payments ecosystem is entering a phase where the focus needs to shift from access to adoption," said Muhammad Hamayun Sajjad, CEO Mashreq Pakistan, the country's first newly launched digital bank to offer the full suite of Raast services. It has just introduced Raast Person-to-Merchant (P2M) payments, allowing merchants to receive instant payments through QR codes and customers to pay through digital banking channels.
Raast processed approximately 742 million transactions worth Rs23.27 trillion during the quarter. Person-to-person (P2P) payments accounted for 664 million transactions valuing at Rs18.88 trillion compared with 603 million transactions worth Rs15.69 trillion in the preceding quarter.
Total Raast transactions increased from 295.7 million in the second quarter of fiscal year 2024-25 to 371.2 million in the third quarter and 412.1 million in the fourth quarter. The volume rose to 543.9 million in the first quarter of FY2025-26, 645.7 million in the second quarter and 742 million in the third quarter.
By March 2026, Pakistan had 95.8 million branchless banking mobile app users, 28.9 million banking mobile app users and 7.3 million electronic money institution wallet app users, highlighting the expanding base of consumers with access to digital financial services.
Raast Payments Pakistan CEO Ahson Bin Saeed said the next phase of the national payment infrastructure would involve strengthening the system, broadening participation and ensuring that institutions could build reliable and accessible payment experiences on top of it.
He said the launch of Raast P2M was another step towards translating the national payment infrastructure into everyday use for merchants and consumers.
However, industry stakeholders have pointed to commercial and behavioural challenges that could affect the pace of adoption.
"The adoption of Raast in Pakistan is progressing at a relatively fast pace; however, a significant part of this momentum appears to be driven by regulatory encouragement and the strong push from the regulator, rather than entirely by organic market demand," said iPath CEO Abdus Samad Khan.
He said the absence of a direct consumer-fee model created commercial challenges for banks, fintechs and payment service providers. Unlike the previous inter-bank funds transfer model, Raast P2P and P2M payments are required to remain free for consumers.
While this benefits users, service providers must recover the costs of technology, infrastructure, compliance, customer support and transaction processing through other revenue streams.
Khan also identified limited consumer awareness and merchant behaviour as challenges. Many consumers remain unfamiliar with how Raast works, where it can be used and how it differs from other digital payment channels.
In some cases, merchants reportedly encourage customers to pay in cash or use established wallets such as easypaisa and JazzCash instead of formal Raast merchant payment channels, limiting the growth and visibility of the P2M ecosystem.
Merchant payments are emerging as the next major frontier for digital payments. According to the State Bank, more than 2.6 million merchants had been onboarded or registered their aliases for Raast P2M by the end of March 2026.
The challenge, however, is to convert merchant registration into regular usage. Smaller businesses face issues related to onboarding, reconciliation, settlement, digital literacy and perceptions regarding taxation and transaction records.
State Bank's Director of Digital Innovation & Settlements Department Muhammad Imad Uddin said the central bank remained focused on developing the regulatory and technological foundations for a more connected and inclusive payments landscape. The real measure of progress, he added, was how effectively the infrastructure was adopted across the ecosystem.
The government allocated Rs3.5 billion to support Raast P2M QR transactions between September 2025 and June 2026.

items.author: editorial
items.content:
A dozen kidnapping cases registered in Islamabad in a single day should alarm the capital's police authorities. The incidents involve a newborn taken from PIMS Hospital, a teenage boy allegedly abducted from his home, several young women who disappeared, and two drivers who went missing along with vehicles. Whether every case ultimately proves to be an abduction is for investigators to establish. What cannot be ignored is the sheer number of families who turned to the police on the same day.
The question is why so many people can disappear in a city that has invested heavily in surveillance and policing. Islamabad has a dense network of cameras and a police force that regularly highlights improvements in its crime-fighting capabilities. Yet technology is of little value if it does not translate into rapid intervention. In cases involving children, every hour matters. There are several possible explanations for the apparent rise in such reports. Some disappearances may involve family disputes, voluntary departures, elopement or other circumstances that are initially reported as kidnapping. Others may involve genuine abductions, criminal exploitation or attempts to obtain ransom. The police must establish these distinctions through proper investigation rather than allowing all missing-person cases to be treated alike. But neither should an abduction be prematurely reduced to a domestic matter simply because the circumstances are unclear.
Islamabad Police needs to tell citizens what is happening. A single day's cases may eventually prove to be unrelated. But when so many families report disappearances at once, the burden is on the authorities to establish whether there is a wider pattern. Residents of the capital should not have to wonder whether their police force is discovering crimes after they happen or preventing them before they do. Security is ultimately measured by how quickly the state responds when someone disappears.

items.author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
items.content:
A lingering fear of my childhood, after I was exposed to Planet of the Apes at an early age, was the erosion of known reality beyond recognition. You see, at the end of the novel the protagonist escapes the ape planet only to find out that Earth has also been taken over by apes. The original movie showed that it was all happening on Earth all along. The 2001 Tim Burton version restored the original ending.
I don't know whether it was the novel or the movie which was responsible, but I soon started having nightmares. I am away for some reason, but when I return home or to school, something has changed. Sometimes it was the language, sometimes parents or friends, and sometimes the entire cultural context. And I cannot begin to tell the torments these nightmares did to me.
Many decades later, as a middle-aged man, I contend with a different question. What do you do when, one by one, all your nightmares start coming to life? A writing career is beautiful, but it is not clearly your passport to action. It cultivates a different sort of person. Where you think your strongly worded call to attention can dislodge some of the best-laid plans. And in my early writing career, I had some luck in doing just that. But now the erosion of reality has reached a new scale, and I don't find writing entirely equipped to bring about that kind of change.
Before you complain about the abstract nature of the discussion, let me assure you that I will come to solid examples soon enough. Until then, bear with me.
We knew that below the veneer of socio-political and economic calm, there existed a deeper, more complicated, at times troubling, reality. But even so, the structural integrity of reality was intact, and we thought that if we tried hard enough, the complications of the underlying reality could be resolved. Darkness is the absence of light; to get rid of it, all you need to do is light a candle. That kind of stuff. The faith in the fundamental goodness of humans was still a given. But the past decade has witnessed the rapid disappearance of this veneer.
Take India, for example. We always knew that the country had communal, casteist, governance-related and poverty-related issues. But to students of political history like me, India was still a shining proof that democracy could work despite so many handicaps. It all changed in 2014 when the Modi government took over and started transforming the country into an ideological project. As it sought to dismantle each institution and safeguard, one by one, democracy was reduced to a label. And populist governments look for quick-fix, feel-good solutions. So, India's weaknesses were not weaknesses but a proud part of its legacy to be celebrated and rubbed in your face. Any objective criticism of this was a hostile conspiracy, not a critique. India's diplomatic muscle had grown during the Manmohan Singh government's time. Now it would be used to bolster one man's image and his less-informed worldview, both at home and abroad.
Then came the European situation. The continent that gave us the Enlightenment principles first grappled with the post-9/11 Islamophobia and then gave in to a frightening resurgence of the borderline fascistic far right.
And then the US. If, like me, you have grown up on a healthy diet of Hollywood and American culture, you must be aware that behind occasional brashness and self-involvement beats a beautiful and kind heart which wants to fix things and help others. But the post-9/11 bitterness has distilled into a culture of self-harm, which is quite atrocious. Just look at what the media did to itself even before Donald Trump first came to power. Highlighting a weakness is a journalist's job. But being on the prowl to catalogue everything offensive and to scandalise various national moments isn't.
And our beloved Muslim world. First the Taliban. Then Al-Qaeda and 9/11. The Arab Spring and the resulting civil wars. And whatever the current situation is. October 7, the Gaza war. Israel's expanding forever war. Then the Iran war, which should have concluded after the signing of the MoU between the US and Iran?
Tell me, how does it feel to know that a Houthi-launched drone was downed attempting to enter Makkah's airspace? Muslims on both sides and the holiest city of Islam? Do you need any further proof of how many nightmares have come to life?
The erosion of peace after the MoU is the most fascinating, if frightening, case study. Iran was about to get everything on a platter. Its sanctions-impoverished population could get all the wealth they could imagine. But then, out of nowhere, its hardliner establishment chose war over victory.
An incorrigible optimist, I am tired of hoping that this war will end soon. There are elements on every side who do not want this war to end. But we seldom think about the silent elements. For instance, everyone talks about America, Israel, Iran and the Gulf countries. But nobody takes note of the pain India, under Modi, suffered seeing Pakistan playing its role in the peace process. Then India's Ajit Doval meets the Iranian NSA, and Iran's position suddenly hardens. Attacks on Israel and Abraham Accords signatories stop, and Saudi Arabia starts getting attacked. Saudi Arabia, which refused to play any part in the war, played a very important role in the peace process and even dislodged the Israeli influence from Somalia and Yemen, and is now suddenly being attacked by Houthis.
The ongoing Iran war and last year's Israeli war on Iran both revealed how badly compromised and infiltrated the Iranian deep state is. Could such elements be playing into the hands of foreign interests?
What is Saudi Arabia's fault? That instead of joining the Abraham Accords or becoming another base of Adani's operations, it signed a defence agreement with India's arch-enemy Pakistan, and then the Makkah Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Turkiye? Is the main purpose to start a war between Iran and Pakistan so that Pakistan has to handle three hostile borders at once? Is it why the terror elements in Balochistan are getting a boost from New Delhi?
Truth is, a lot of these tragedies befall us because of men like Ajit Doval, who would burn the entire world down in the name of patriotism and then also burn down their own country to please their political masters. You must suffer the next level of cognitive dissonance to not notice what kind of pain you are bringing to this world, what horrible world you are building, and how it is only negatively affecting your own country. They can congratulate themselves on being competent, but competence only increases the moral burden. You were given these gifts in life, and this is what you did with them?
"For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" – Mark 8:36

items.author: Imtiaz Gul
items.content:
When foreign ministers Wang Yi and Seyed Abbas Araghchi met in Beijing on September 17, both agreed that safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz required a reinforced, multilateral security architecture in West Asia.
Yi offered China's support for de-escalating tensions in the region, while Araghchi consented that the transformation in the security landscape required security cooperation among regional countries to preclude interference by foreign forces. Both countries agreed that the present tensions are rooted in the US and Israeli military attacks against Iran early this year.
During the meeting, Yi also said that relations between Tehran and Beijing are significant due to their strategic partnership, and that Beijing is keen on strengthening and developing these ties.
Yi's messaging was consistent as ever; peace and tranquility in the Middle East and West Asia, as well as peaceful conflict resolution based on respect for sovereignty of individual nations.
Only a few days earlier, during the recent 18th BRICS summit in India, similar messages resonated across the conference hall. President Xi Jinping anchored his speech in multilateral cooperation, the urgency for upholding the international rule of law, respect for sovereign equality, and perusal of the peaceful settlement of disputes. And China, Xi declared, is ready to act as an anchor, a stabilising force for achieving these ideals. He reiterated the need for expanding the Global South, instituting AI collaboration and joining hands for global-governance reform.
Curiously, however, Xi avoided mention of counter-terrorism and security issues and presumably - as a tactical move - allowed the Indians to slip the explicit condemnation of the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam attack into the New Delhi Declaration. The inclusion of this text represents a notable diplomatic success. It gave the Indians a "feel-good" diplomatic achievement, with no last minute altercation since the Chinese leadership did not want to inject any negativity on the occasion of Xi's visit after seven long years.
From the Indian perspective, inclusion of issues such as cross-border movement of terrorists, terror financing, safe havens, accountability for perpetrators and supporters, rejection of double standards and zero tolerance into BRICS was a diplomatic achievement.
For Beijing, this was a small concession in view of the big challenges that China as a BRICS lead country is trying to deal with – very much reflective of the Confucian spirit of accommodation and peaceful conflict resolution.
Quietly but consistently, the leadership pursues planning for the future while staying clear of international conflicts, securing internal stabilisation through people-centric policies and at the same time pursuing nation's long-term economic interests abroad.
Conversations with scholars and officials as well as the major contours of Beijing's policies are quite enlightening and guide you to an unmistakable conclusion; contemporary Chinese statecraft, security doctrine and social policy continue to draw heavily on Confucian and Mencian ideas of legitimate authority.
Mencius was an ancient Chinese philosopher and one of the most important figures in Confucianism. He is traditionally regarded as the "Second Sage" second only to Confucius himself.
Mencius taught that coercion can compel outward compliance but never wins genuine allegiance; only virtue and moral example secure lasting loyalty.
This distinction underpins the classic contrast between the brittle "hegemonic way" (badao), which relies on coercion, and the sustainable "kingly way" (wangdao), in which others follow voluntarily because they recognise the ruler's benevolence and competence.
"A confident state first puts its own house in order, strengthening domestic stability and social cohesion so that foreign policy need not manufacture external enemies for internal legitimacy."
When this Mencius quote resonated through the Beijing conference hall on September 16, it must have reminded several Asian participants of the situation in their own countries, where rulers tend to rely on 'foreign enemies' to address domestic legitimacy issues.
This was a remarkable speech by Chan Chun Sing, Singapore's Defence Minister, when speaking of the present day "security dilemma" – a combination of wisdom, sagacity and cautious public policy.
"How do we strengthen our own security without weakening the security of others, or without aggravating the insecurity of others," asked Sing in what appeared to be an indirect jibe at the USA's strident policies concerning Veneuzuela and Iran.
Without directly accusing the US of triggering the current security crisis in the Gulf following its attacks on Iran since early this year, the Singapore defence minister implicitly dubbed phrases such as "freedom of navigation" (through Hormuz) or "sanctions" (on Iran) as unnecessary stunts. In other words, it is like sailing warships near the other's coast just to show off, or adding new punishments for no clear reason. It's like taking money out of that account. Building up that trust again is slow and hard. But you can drain the whole account in a single moment - one bad decision and all the trust is gone.
Sing's was a brilliant summation of the current paradox accompanying the Trump administration's Middle East policy – total exceptionalism vis-a-vis Israel, and absolute strident, self-serving attitude towards Iran. This also resonated the present day Chinese approach in international relations: the more responsible major powers are, the less concerned small countries will be.
Equally compelling message in Sing's speech was that "leadership confident at home doesn't need foreign enemies to hold itself together, and can therefore act in its 'enlightened long-term interest' abroad."

items.title: The challenge of parenting in our age!
items.summary:

items.author: M Zeb Khan
items.content:
A child begins life completely dependent on parents, yet the ultimate purpose of upbringing is to produce an adult capable of thinking, deciding and living without constantly requiring parental direction. Much of our difficulty with parenting in Pakistan comes from forgetting this paradox. Parents naturally want the best for their children, but "the best" can mean very different things. Sometimes it means producing a replica of ourselves. Sometimes it means producing an idealised version of the child we wish we had been. Sometimes it means preparing children intelligently for the realities of their own age. And sometimes, unfortunately, parenting amounts to little more than providing food, education and shelter while leaving emotional and intellectual development largely unattended.
The first temptation is self-projection. Many Pakistani parents imagine their children as extensions of themselves. A doctor wants another doctor, a businessman expects someone to continue the business, and parents who struggled for social mobility often decide very early what prestigious career their children must pursue. There is nothing wrong with transmitting experience or values. The problem begins when guidance becomes replication. A child is biologically connected to the parent but psychologically belongs to a different generation. Temperament, interests and circumstances may all be different. When parents insist that children reproduce their choices, inheritance can quietly become imprisonment.
A second tendency is perfectionism. Children must attend the best school, secure the highest grades, enter medicine, engineering, civil service or some fashionable profession, and speak impeccable English. Social comparison strengthens the pressure. Another child's examination results, university admission or professional achievement quickly becomes a benchmark against which one's own child is measured. Children may gradually conclude that their value depends upon performance. Failure becomes frightening not merely because something has gone wrong, but because parental approval itself appears endangered.
At the opposite end lies parental disengagement. Some parents confuse freedom with absence. They provide material necessities but know remarkably little about what their children think, fear, watch, believe or experience. In an era when smartphones, algorithms, influencers and peer networks compete constantly for children's attention, parental withdrawal does not create a neutral space. It simply allows other forces to become the educators. The more sensible alternative is realistic parenting - raising children for the world they are entering rather than the world their parents remember.
This distinction has become especially important in Pakistan. Parents who grew up believing that a university degree automatically produced a secure career are raising children in an economy where qualifications alone increasingly guarantee very little. AI is transforming professions. Employment patterns are changing. Information is abundant while judgement is scarce. Communication, adaptability, emotional intelligence, creativity and the capacity to learn continuously may matter as much as traditional academic credentials.
Realistic parenting therefore requires a change of question. Instead of asking, "How can my child become what I want?", parents might ask, "What capacities will this child need to flourish twenty years from now?"
Yet realism should not mean surrendering children completely to contemporary culture. Children should understand technology without becoming enslaved by it; become ambitious without measuring human worth entirely through money; develop confidence without arrogance; compete without losing empathy; and learn independence without abandoning responsibility toward family and society.
The most constructive model may therefore be developmental parenting. Such parents neither manufacture replicas of themselves nor attempt to engineer perfect children. They provide values without dictating every conclusion, boundaries without suffocation, freedom without abandonment and guidance without permanent control. Their authority changes as the child grows. Parenting that refuses to evolve eventually becomes control.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Nigerian startup Dynalimb Technologies is making mobility care more accessible across Africa through 3D innovation, combining medical expertise with technology to improve how people with limb loss and mobility challenges live their lives.
The Dynalimb team collectively has more than 25 years of experience in prosthetics and orthotics, but for co-founder and COO Blessing Aniefiok, a trained prosthetist and orthotist, the startup’s roots are deeply personal.
“My aunt experienced limb loss related to diabetes, and seeing her journey made me understand that limb loss is not simply about losing a body part. It affects someone’s ability to work, care for their family, participate in society and live independently,” she told Disrupt Africa.
That experience, combined with what Aniefiok and the rest of the team were seeing in clinical practice, motivated them to think differently about how prosthetic and orthotic care could be delivered.
“Our team saw first-hand how difficult access to prosthetic and orthotic care could be. During our exposure to clinical settings, we encountered patients who have to wait for weeks or months to receive prosthetic or orthotic devices,” she said.
The Dynalimb team began exploring 3D technology to address some of these challenges.
“At the time, there was very little local reference material or established infrastructure for using 3D technologies in prosthetics or orthotics in Nigeria, so much of our early work involved learning, experimenting and developing the processes ourselves,” said Aniefiok.
Since then, however, they have made some serious leaps, and what began as a clinical solution has evolved into Dynalimb – a technology-enabled mobility company working across three connected areas.
First, it develops 3D-printed prosthetics and orthotics, which reduce the time, cost, and complexity associated with conventional manufacturing methods.
“For example, a traditional basic prosthetic device in Nigeria can cost upwards of ₦1.6 million (US$1,200) and take approximately 4–6 weeks to produce. Our average prosthetic device costs around ₦800,000 (US$600) and can be delivered in about seven days, depending on the device and clinical requirements,” Aniefiok said.
The startup has also developed a platform, DynaX, which aims to provide the digital infrastructure for prosthetic, orthotic and rehabilitation care. DynaX brings together tools for digital measurement and scanning, patient management, virtual clinical collaboration, therapy support and other elements of the patient journey.
“One of the key areas we are addressing is the reliance on manual processes such as plaster or POP casting, paper records and fragmented communication between patients and healthcare professionals,” Aniefiok said.
“Our long-term vision is for DynaX to become infrastructure that connects the different stages of mobility care from assessment and measurement through device design, manufacturing, rehabilitation and follow-up.”
Finally, given the team’s belief that technology alone is not enough, Dynalimb also maintains a strong clinical component.
“Our team consists of trained prosthetists and orthotists who work directly with patients and healthcare institutions,” said Aniefiok.
This combination of clinical expertise, digital technology, and 3D manufacturing is central to the startup’s model.
“Ultimately, we are not simply trying to manufacture cheaper prosthetic devices. We want to make the entire mobility-care journey more accessible, efficient and dignified,” Aniefiok said.
The potential impact here is significant. Over 30 million people across Africa need prosthetic, orthotic and rehabilitation services, yet access remains limited because of cost, long production times, shortages of trained professionals, centralised services and inefficient clinical processes. The problem is particularly significant in Nigeria and other African markets where specialist services are concentrated in a relatively small number of locations.
Uptake has been encouraging and has grown significantly as awareness of what Dynalimb is doing has increased.
“We have now served over 1,000 patients. Our customers include individuals seeking prosthetic and orthotic care as well as healthcare institutions. We have also seen increasing interest from hospitals that want to improve how they deliver prosthetic, orthotic and rehabilitation services,” Aniefiok said.
Dynalimb has been primarily founder-led and grant-supported in its early stages, with VC funding in the early-stage health-tech space hard to come by.
“Healthcare hardware and manufacturing businesses require capital. We have had to balance investing in equipment, technology, people and product development while generating revenue and keeping our services affordable for patients,” Aniefiok said.
As a result, Dynalimb has participated in several startup and innovation programmes to access capital. One of those was the Standard Chartered Foundation’s Women in Tech Accelerator. The programme, implemented locally by the Enterprise Development Centre (EDC) with support from Village Capital, is a multi-region initiative which supports impact-creating, tech-enabled, women-led startups in building thriving businesses across Africa, the Middle East, and Pakistan.
While the funding is helpful to boost Dynalimb’s manufacturing capabilities, Aniefiok said the benefits from the programme are felt more widely.
“For an early-stage company, one of the biggest benefits of a programme like this is having access to mentorship, networks, visibility and a community of other founders. The programme helped us strengthen different aspects of the business and gave us the opportunity to step back from day-to-day operations and think more strategically about growth,” Aniefiok said.
“It also provided credibility. When you are building something relatively new in a specialised sector such as prosthetics and 3D healthcare technology, external validation matters. Being selected for a programme backed by the Standard Chartered Foundation helped demonstrate that what we were building was addressing a real problem worth solving.”
Dynalimb’s primary market is Nigeria, which Aniefiok said offers a strong environment in which to develop and validate its clinical, manufacturing and digital systems before expanding across Africa.
“We are already engaging with healthcare institutions and partners in Nigeria, and our current focus includes strengthening our presence across key cities and building institutional partnerships,” she said.
“Our short-term expansion strategy is to deepen our Nigerian operations, including growing our hospital partnerships and establishing stronger operational capacity across locations such as Lagos, Abuja, Port-Harcourt and Kano.”
Beyond Nigeria, the startup’s broader vision is to expand into other African markets where the same challenges exist.
“We are particularly interested in markets such as Ghana, Kenya and Rwanda, where there are significant needs around access to prosthetic and orthotic services and where partnerships with local healthcare providers can help us enter the market responsibly,” Aniefiok said.
“We don’t intend to simply export products. Our approach is to build local partnerships and adapt our technology and service model to each market. The long-term vision is to build a scalable African mobility-care infrastructure that allows more people to access quality prosthetic, orthotic and rehabilitation services regardless of where they live.”

items.title: Trump bans CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House
items.summary:
US President Donald Trump said ‌on Friday he is banning three ⁠major ​news outlets - CNN, MSNOW and Politico - from the White House ​in his latest move to crack ‌down on the independent press.
Trump wrote ​that he is banning the outlets for allegedly "reporting FAKE NEWS" in a move that is likely to be challenged as conflicting with the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech ⁠and a free press.
"Media Outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES ‌when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America," Trump wrote on social media. "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow."
https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117293599348325006
CNN, MSNOW (now MSNBC), Politico and the National Press ⁠Club did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNN's team ⁠remains at the White House ​working as if ‌it were a normal Friday

CNN, MSNOW (now MSNBC), Politico and the National Press ⁠Club did not immediately respond to requests for comment. CNN's team ⁠remains at the White House ​working as if ‌it were a normal Friday afternoon, CNN reporter Brian Stelter said on air.
Trump has a long history of bickering with members of the press corps and has stepped up his complaints during his second term in office. And he has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programs he dislikes or which have joked about or criticized him or his administration, calling on the Federal Communications Commission to strip disfavored ⁠broadcast stations of their licenses.
Read: Trump Media's quarterly loss widens to $238 million from $20 million a year earlier
In 2019, the White House credential of Brian Karem, a Playboy magazine correspondent, was suspended after ⁠he traded insults with Sebastian Gorka, then an aide to the president, in the White House Rose Garden. A judge later ordered the White House to reinstate Karem's credential.
Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has openly badgered reporters, particularly from US television networks. Last year, he also banned the Associated Press from the usual pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news agency did not adopt Trump's preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico, which Trump ⁠has instructed executive branch employees to refer to as the Gulf ​of America.
US Representative Frank Pallone, the lead Democrat on the House of Representatives Energy and Commerce Committee, called Trump's action censorship.
"If Trump thinks banning media outlets from the White House will make his presidency seem less like a failure, he's delusional," Pallone said.

items.author: Abdulyassar Abdulhamid
items.content:
The Federal Government has assured Nigerians that a thorough, transparent and impartial investigation will be conducted into the deaths of persons arrested during enforcement operations against suspected illegal mining activities in Niger State.
Minister of Information and National Orientation, Mohammed Idris, gave the assurance in a statement on Friday, expressing deep sorrow over the tragic incident in the Wushishi/Lukoto axis of the state.
The development follows the suspension of the Niger State Commandant of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, by the Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, who also ordered a full investigation into the circumstances surrounding the deaths.
Idris said the Federal Government had taken immediate steps to establish the facts, stressing that the protection of the lives, dignity and fundamental rights of every Nigerian remained a solemn responsibility of the government.
Plateau begins crackdown on houses without toilets
Education is not a scam, Senator tells Nigerian students
“The swift action taken by the Honourable Minister of Interior underscores the seriousness with which the Federal Government views this matter. The investigation will be allowed to establish exactly what happened, and the Government assures Nigerians that appropriate action will be taken based on its findings,” Idris said.
The minister extended the condolences of the Federal Government to the Governor of Niger State, Mohammed Umaru Bago, the government and people of the state, traditional leaders and residents of Wushishi, as well as the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.
He stressed that while the government remained committed to combating illegal mining and other unlawful activities threatening national security, economic resources and the environment, enforcement operations must be conducted within the law and with respect for human life and dignity.
Idris further assured Nigerians that anyone found culpable would not be shielded, while cautioning against prejudging the outcome of the investigation.
“There will be no attempt to shield anyone found culpable. At the same time, we mustn”t prejudge the outcome of the investigation. The Government’s responsibility is to ensure that the facts are established and that justice is served.”
He appealed for calm in Wushishi and across Niger State, urging residents and all concerned parties to allow the investigation to proceed without interference.
The minister assured the families of the deceased and the people of Niger State that the Federal Government shared in their grief and remained committed to establishing the circumstances surrounding the tragedy.
He prayed for the repose of the souls of the deceased and for Almighty Allah to grant their families, the Wushishi community and the government and people of Niger State the strength to bear the loss.

items.author: Palak Sharma
items.content:
When Swiggy entered India’s online food delivery market back in 2014, it was the first one to solve the problem of getting a meal from a restaurant to a customer’s doorstep. Zomato joined the race a year later in 2015.
But over the years, Swiggy has taken a path that has made its business increasingly different from simply being a food-delivery marketplace. It started with food delivery in 2014 and gradually expanded into groceries, dining, supply chain and a string of smaller experiments.
The company’s food delivery business generated an operating revenue of ₹2,208 Cr in the June quarter of FY27 with an operating profit of ₹299 Cr in the quarter under review. However, overall, Swiggy recorded a loss of ₹791 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Quick commerce was the biggest drag, with Instamart reporting an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹778 Cr, despite generating ₹7,907 Cr in GOV.
This is where Swiggy’s business model gets interesting.
Beyond the delivery and platform fees that form a similar revenue base for Zomato, Swiggy has built a core business that is increasingly generating profits, while continuing to invest in newer businesses that could widen its addressable market.
The difference, however, is that Swiggy’s food delivery business still continues to bring in most of the revenue while Zomato is now a part of Eternal and contributes only 15% of the total top line.
The margins brought in by the food delivery business are being invested to fuel Swiggy’s quick commerce bet and “platform innovations”, which is a space to test new formats, price points and operating models.
The Q1 FY27 earnings call makes that approach even clearer. Swiggy said it evaluates opportunities across pricing, formats and even separate apps, while trying to preserve the economics of its core platform.
With food delivery and other established businesses providing an existing consumer base, technology stack and fulfillment network, the company can test new initiatives without building every capability from scratch.
But before looking at what these newer bets could become, it is worth understanding the business that continues to anchor Swiggy’s P&L.
Swiggy’s Food Delivery & Supply Chain: The Core That Pays
The foodtech has two very different established businesses at the heart of its P&L: food delivery, and supply chain & distribution (SC&D).
Let’s decode the most popular segment first.
At the most basic level, Swiggy earns from the restaurant, the consumer and the wider platform. Its food delivery revenue comprises pre-agreed commissions from restaurant partners, advertising revenue from restaurants, platform fees charged to users, and subscription revenue when it comes to food delivery.
There is also a revenue that comes from offering business enablement solutions to the restaurant partners.
Furthermore, Swiggy does not recognise user delivery charges passed on to delivery partners as part of its revenue. These charges are included in its separately defined gross revenue, net of applicable discounts.
However, it takes “service charge” as revenue collected from users/delivery partners for use of technology platforms, which is also not disclosed.
So, on a ₹500 food order, the customer’s payment is split across the food value going to the restaurant, delivery-related amounts going to the delivery partner, discounts and fees, while Swiggy’s recognised revenue comes from the monetisation streams it retains.
Operationally, Swiggy’s food delivery GOV grew 17.4% YoY to ₹9,490 Cr and monthly transacting users rose 17.8% YoY to 19.2 Mn in Q1 FY27, ultimately resulting in operating revenue of ₹2,208 Cr.
The next question is how much of that monetisation survives after serving the orders. Swiggy answers this via contribution margin.
Swiggy calculates food delivery contribution margin (CM) after deducting delivery and other charges, platform-funded discounts and other variable costs from adjusted revenue. In Q1 FY27, this margin stood at 7.6% of GOV. On the other hand, adjusted EBITDA is further calculated after deducting the operating cost, which stood at a 3.1% margin on GOV for the June quarter.
The quarter, however, saw a sequential dip in food delivery’s CM and adjusted EBITDA margin. This is where Swiggy’s cost to achieve EBITDA profitability for food delivery is hidden.
The management said that the sequential dip in food delivery margins was partly due to higher investment in delivery-partner availability and the annual wage hike. Meanwhile, the blame was also given to seasonality.
At the same time, the company said improved take rates and operating leverage helped drive the 70-basis-point YoY improvement in adjusted EBITDA margin.
This creates an interesting balancing act for Swiggy. More delivery partners available at the right time can improve the customer experience and support order growth.
But keeping that capacity available also adds to costs. The business therefore has to grow order density fast enough for the additional orders to absorb those fulfilment costs. Interestingly, Swiggy’s average transacting restaurant partners also declined QoQ to 2.6 Lakh from 2.8 Lakh earlier.
Food delivery, however, is not Swiggy’s largest revenue-generating segment. Its supply chain & distribution business reported ₹3,195 Cr in revenue in Q1 FY27, making it the biggest contributor to the company’s revenue from operations for the quarter.
SC&D works very differently from food delivery. It is an inventory-led B2B business through which Swiggy purchases products and distributes them to merchant partners. This makes the business much more revenue-heavy, but also brings a corresponding cost of purchasing the products that it distributes.
However, revenue alone does not tell the full story of Swiggy’s business mix — which we will see ahead.
While these established businesses form the foundation of Swiggy’s P&L, the company’s biggest consumer growth bet is operating on a very different set of economics: Instamart.
Instamart: The Growth Engine That Is Still Burning
Instamart burning cash is hardly new for Swiggy. What has changed is the trajectory of that burn.
In Q1 FY27, the quick commerce business reported GOV of ₹7,907 Cr, up 40% YoY and operating revenue of ₹1,232 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA loss stood at ₹778 Cr (adjusted EBITDA margin at 9.8% of the GOV), declining by ₹80 Cr sequentially, even as the business continued to expand.
The picture changes when we talk about Instamart’s contribution margin, which improved to -0.2% of GOV, from -1.8% in the previous quarter. The difference between these two numbers is important to understanding where Instamart stands today.
Swiggy said contribution margin had turned positive on a monthly basis in May, although the full-quarter margin remained at -0.2%. This means Instamart has almost reached order-level contribution break-even. Besides this, revenue per order rose to ₹108 from ₹97.
More than 45% of its stores were contribution margin positive in Q1 FY27, with five of its seven largest cities also reaching positive contribution margins. Still, we cannot say that Instamart is closer to EBITDA profitability based on the CM improvement alone.
The gap in CM and adjusted EBITDA profitability reflects the broader cost base of running and scaling the network. Instamart now operates 1,171 active dark stores with 1,089 orders per store per day in Q1 FY27.
Yet Swiggy says the overall network is operating at only around 40% utilisation, with significant headroom remaining. At the same time, management expects to add around 75 stores in Q2 because of volume growth in high-growth neighbourhoods.
The company is betting on transacting user base increase as well as frequency increase for Instamart’s growth, Swiggy’s chief financial officer Rahul Bothra said during Q1 earnings’ call.
And that growth will not only depend on how many people use Instamart, but also on what they buy, and how large their baskets become.
Swiggy’s Experimental Sandbox: Where Are The Bets
Beyond Food Delivery, Instamart and its other established businesses, Swiggy has a separate platform innovations segment that acts as a sandbox for testing new consumer propositions and business models.
The company describes it as a set of incubators aimed at creating more frequent and meaningful touchpoints with users.
“Platform innovation by its nature is something that we are not committing ourselves fully to. As we have said, once the product hits both product market fit (PMF) as well as what we call business market fit (BMF), that is when it will get its growth capital, and it will have its own economics from there on,” Bothra further said during the earnings’ call.
The portfolio under this head has changed quickly, with some experiments being launched, tested and discontinued. Toing, for instance, was launched as a separate offering targeting price-conscious consumers such as students and early-jobbers, using a different marketplace model for low-AOV meals.
In the latest disclosures, Swiggy’s CEO Sriharsha Majety said that Toing is different from conventional food delivery across delivery fees, proposition, cuisine, last mile, economics and the value proposition for consumers.
The commission model around this product is also different as restaurants’ fee is supposed to be low so that they can offer food at a lower price. Besides, Crew is another offering that Swiggy currently classifies under its platform innovations segment.
Initially, the product allowed users to find, shop and get delivered anything “from golf course to caddy bookings to reliable and clean cabs, sourcing exclusive hotel rates to even a Hawaiian shirt”. Earlier this month, the product pivoted to a “dedicated personal travel concierge offering”.
Apart from these, Swiggy also runs its sports subsidiary called Swiggy Sports and extensions of the food delivery services including Bolt, 99 Store, Late Night Eats, Food On Train, Eatright, and DeskEats.
The portfolio also comes with the possibility of exits. Snacc, Swiggy’s standalone food-delivery experiment, was shut in the previous quarter, and Bothra said some operating costs related to the closure were recognised in Q1 FY27.
For now, this means the segment remains an investment pool for Swiggy, with the company absorbing the cost of testing whether these propositions can scale. Platform innovations reported ₹51 Cr in operating revenue against a segment loss of around ₹131 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Swiggy does not disclose the individual revenue or cost contribution of Toing, Crew or its other experiments, making it difficult to attribute the segment’s loss to any one product.
At the same time, Bothra added that a larger portion of the investment in platform innovations during the quarter went towards Toing, particularly marketing-led customer acquisition.
This is where Swiggy’s Food Delivery profitability becomes important to the broader business model. The company has a mature business generating operating profit, while platform innovations continue to absorb investment as Swiggy tests new propositions.
The strategy, therefore, is not simply to maximise revenue from every experiment today, but to use the existing platform and its economics to find businesses that can eventually stand on their own.
The Price Of Swiggy’s Scale
Swiggy’s expanding portfolio also comes with a sizable cost base.
In Q1 FY27, the company reported ₹7,813 Cr in total expenses, against ₹6,812 Cr in revenue from operations.
The biggest expense was purchases of stock-in-trade at ₹2,978 Cr. This is largely linked to Swiggy’s supply chain & distribution business, where the company purchases products that are subsequently sold to its merchant partners.
The SC&D segment generated ₹3,195 Cr in revenue in Q1 FY27, making it one of the largest businesses on Swiggy’s books by revenue, even though the segment remained around break-even at the operating level.
In comparison, food delivery generated a lower revenue pool than SC&D, but contributed ₹299 Cr in segment profit, while the much larger SC&D business operated with far thinner economics.
The second-largest major cost was delivery and related charges at ₹1,750 Cr. This includes costs associated with the delivery network and therefore cuts across the businesses that rely on Swiggy’s fulfilment infrastructure.
It is also where the scale of Swiggy’s operations becomes visible: the company is not only paying to acquire customers and build businesses, but also to keep the delivery network available to serve them.
Advertising and sales promotion accounted for another ₹1,160 Cr during the quarter. This bucket is particularly relevant for a company still investing in new categories and consumer propositions. However, Swiggy does not provide a consolidated expense split that allows this amount to be attributed to a particular segment or product.
Employee benefits added ₹662 Cr, while depreciation and amortisation stood at ₹298 Cr and finance costs at ₹53 Cr. The remaining ₹915 Cr was classified under other expenses.
Taken together, these costs show that Swiggy’s profitability challenge is broader than the losses from Instamart and platform innovations alone. The company is operating a large fulfillment, technology and employee base across multiple businesses, while continuing to invest in growth.
That also explains why the profitability of individual businesses does not immediately translate into consolidated profits. Food Delivery generated a ₹299 Cr segment profit in Q1 FY27, but the wider portfolio continued to carry the costs of scaling quick commerce, running SC&D and incubating new businesses.
The next question, therefore, is not just how much Swiggy spends, but where the company is willing to keep spending despite the losses.

items.author: Bambang Dwi Atmoko
items.content:
Sepuluh tahun setelah pertama kali diperkenalkan, LG InstaView mencatat penjualan kumulatif lebih dari 5,3 juta unit secara global. Angka tersebut menjadi bagian dari perjalanan kulkas premium LG yang memperkenalkan panel kaca pada pintu sebagai cara baru untuk melihat isi kulkas tanpa harus membukanya.
LG memperkenalkan InstaView pada 2016. Sepanjang satu dekade pemasaran global, perusahaan menyebut rata-rata penjualannya setara dengan sekitar satu unit setiap menit di seluruh dunia.
Pencapaian tersebut kini dirayakan LG Electronics Indonesia melalui sejumlah program untuk pengguna InstaView di Tanah Air. Di antaranya adalah melalui program berbagi pengalaman bagi pengguna lama dan layanan pembersihan gratis. Program berlangsung secara nasional pada 18–25 September 2026, bertepatan dengan perayaan satu dekade kehadiran InstaView secara global.
“Program ini kami siapkan sebagai apresiasi besar bagi konsumen kami di Indonesia. Seturut dengan pencapaian besar pemasaran kulkas LG InstaView di dunia sepanjang satu dekade sejak kemunculan perdananya,” ujar Ha Sang-chul, President of LG Electronics Indonesia.
LG InstaView Berawal dari Panel Kaca yang Bisa Transparan
Salah satu ciri yang membedakan LG InstaView adalah panel kaca pada salah satu bagian pintunya. Dengan mengetuk panel tersebut dua kali, bagian kaca dapat berubah menjadi transparan sehingga pengguna bisa melihat isi kulkas tanpa membuka pintu.
Konsepnya sederhana: pengguna dapat mengecek isi kulkas terlebih dahulu sebelum memutuskan membuka pintu. LG memosisikan fitur ini bukan sekadar sebagai elemen desain. Dengan tidak perlu membuka pintu setiap kali ingin melihat isi kulkas, frekuensi buka-tutup pintu dapat dikurangi. LG menyebut hal tersebut sebagai salah satu aspek yang mendukung penggunaan energi yang lebih optimal.
Namun, dalam konteks pencapaian satu dekade, yang menarik bukan hanya teknologinya. LG melihat nilai InstaView di mata pengguna ikut berkembang seiring waktu. Menurut Jungsoo An, Product Director Kitchen Home Appliance Solution LG Electronics Indonesia, pada awal kehadirannya konsumen lebih banyak mengapresiasi aspek fungsional, seperti kemudahan melihat isi kulkas dan mengurangi kehilangan udara dingin ketika pintu dibuka.
Kini, menurut LG, semakin banyak pengguna yang juga melihat InstaView sebagai bagian dari pengalaman dapur modern yang lebih praktis dan rapi. Perubahan persepsi tersebut juga berkaitan dengan desain. Rumbi Lahari Simanjuntak, Head of Product Marketing Kitchen Home Appliance Solution LG Electronics Indonesia, mengatakan sejumlah ulasan terbaru turut memberikan perhatian pada desain premium InstaView dan kesesuaiannya dengan ruang tinggal modern.
Selama satu dekade, LG juga menyebut InstaView telah mendapatkan sejumlah pengakuan internasional di bidang desain dan inovasi. Di antaranya Red Dot Design Award, iF Design Award, IDEA, dan CES Innovation Award.
LG Ajak Pengguna Indonesia Ceritakan Pengalaman Memakai InstaView
Untuk merayakan pencapaian tersebut di Indonesia, LG menghadirkan LG InstaView Digital Challenge. Program ini ditujukan bagi pengguna yang telah memakai kulkas LG InstaView selama minimal lima tahun. Peserta diminta membagikan foto bersama produk yang dimiliki sekaligus cerita mengenai pengalaman penggunaan yang paling berkesan melalui pesan langsung ke akun Instagram @lgindonesia.
LG akan memilih dua cerita untuk mendapatkan masing-masing satu unit kulkas LG InstaView terbaru. Bagi LG, program ini sekaligus menjadi cara untuk mengetahui bagaimana pengalaman pengguna berubah setelah memakai produk tersebut selama beberapa tahun.
Persyaratan minimal lima tahun juga menarik karena membuat program ini tidak hanya berfokus pada pemilik produk baru. Cerita yang dicari justru berasal dari pengguna yang telah melewati periode penggunaan cukup panjang.
Selain mengajak pengguna berbagi cerita, LG Electronics Indonesia menghadirkan LG Bright Care Service selama periode perayaan satu dekade InstaView. Program ini berupa layanan kunjungan ke rumah untuk melakukan pembersihan menyeluruh pada kulkas LG InstaView. LG menyebut layanan tersebut memiliki nilai manfaat hingga Rp350.000 dan diberikan secara cuma-cuma selama program berlangsung.
