By Adegboyega Adeleye
Saudi Pro League club Al-Taawoun have been ordered to play their next two home league matches behind closed doors and fined 100,000 Saudi Riyals (£20,000) over offensive chants directed at Al-Hilal midfielder Ruben Neves involving his late friend and former team-mate Diogo Jota.
Al-Taawoun supporters repeatedly chanted “Jota” at Neves during their side’s 6-0 defeat by Al-Hilal on Saturday, prompting widespread condemnation from the Saudi football authorities, both clubs and Cristiano Ronaldo.
Jota, a former Liverpool and Portugal forward, died alongside his brother Andre Silva in a car crash in Spain in July 2025, aged 28.
Neves was a close friend and former team-mate of Jota at Wolverhampton Wanderers and with Portugal. He was also a pallbearer at Jota’s funeral and wears Portugal’s No. 21 shirt in his memory.
Neves responded to the supporters during the match before telling reporters afterwards: “I just hope they don’t go to pray later after what they did.”
Ronaldo, who played alongside both Jota and Neves for Portugal and currently plays for Saudi club Al-Nassr, called for the fans responsible to receive lifetime bans.
“The league must take action and punish this kind of fan behaviour,” Ronaldo said on social media.
“This is no longer football, and there have to be limits. People who behave like this should never be allowed to enter a stadium again.”
The incident occurred during Al-Taawoun’s 6-0 defeat to Al-Hilal, with Neves playing 75 minutes before being substituted.
Al-Hilal subsequently filed a formal complaint with the Saudi Arabian Football Federation (SAFF), calling for action against the supporters involved.
“The company expressed its absolute rejection of such actions targeting players or their families, or intended to cause personal offence,” Al-Hilal said in a statement.
Al-Taawoun also condemned the behaviour and said it did not represent the club or its supporters.
“Such conduct is completely unacceptable and does not represent Al-Taawoun, its supporters or the values for which its terraces are known,” the club said.
Al-Taawoun added that it would take the necessary measures in coordination with the relevant authorities to prevent a recurrence and hold those responsible accountable.
The Saudi Arabian Football Federation and Saudi Pro League also condemned the chants, saying the conduct was inconsistent with the values of Saudi football and the principles of sportsmanship.
They said exploiting personal tragedies for abuse or provocation was unacceptable and had no place in Saudi football.
The authorities said relevant committees had identified the conduct in question and were investigating the incident, with action to follow under the applicable regulations.
Jota scored 65 goals in 182 appearances for Liverpool after joining the club from Wolves in 2020. He also scored 14 goals in 49 appearances for Portugal.
Neves has continued to honour his late friend since his death, including through his Portugal shirt number (21) and a tattoo on his leg showing the pair embracing.

items.content:
By Kingsley Omonobi
The Inspector-General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu, has proposed the establishment of an Orange Economy Security and Intellectual Property Coordination Desk within an appropriate existing structure of the Nigeria Police Force (NPF) to strengthen the protection of Nigeria’s rapidly expanding creative economy.
Disu made the proposal on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, while delivering a lecture to participants of Senior Executive Course 48, 2026, at the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies (NIPSS), Kuru, Plateau State
The lecture, titled “The Orange Economy and Entrepreneurship for Sustainable Development in Nigeria: The Role of the Nigeria Police Force,” examined the nexus between security, entrepreneurship and the growth of the country’s creative industries.
IGP Disu identified film, music, fashion, publishing, advertising, digital content, gaming, tourism, heritage and the arts as sectors increasingly driven by entrepreneurship, technology and intellectual property.
He stressed that their contribution to employment, investment and national development could be enhanced through effective security and intellectual property protection.
Disu said the proposed coordination desk would facilitate specialised policing, inter-agency collaboration, dedicated reporting mechanisms and stronger engagement between the police and stakeholders in the creative sector.
He also advocated an intelligence-led and partnership-based approach to tackling organised piracy, counterfeiting, cyber-enabled fraud and other crimes affecting creative enterprises.
The IGP emphasized the importance of financial investigations, where applicable, to trace proceeds linked to criminal networks operating through payment accounts, digital wallets, advertising revenues, logistics networks and online distribution platforms.
Ghe IGP called for stronger collaboration between the NPF, the Nigerian Copyright Commission and other relevant institutions towards ensuring intellectual property protection
He further identified the protection of film locations, concerts, festivals, tourism sites and cultural assets, improved cybercrime response, preservation of digital evidence and sustained engagement with creative communities as areas requiring greater police attention
He also highlighted the preventive role of legitimate economic opportunities, noting that credible pathways from talent to lawful income and employment could help reduce young people’s vulnerability to criminal activity.
According to Disu, “Piracy, fraud, extortion and other forms of criminality not only undermine businesses but also discourage investment and weaken innovation across the creative economy.
He stressed that policing the sector must balance public safety with the rights and protections necessary for creativity and enterprise to flourish, adding that professional, accountable and rights-respecting policing remains critical to building confidence among creators, entrepreneurs and investors.
Disu reaffirmed the commitment of the Nigeria Police Force to working with government agencies, industry stakeholders, creative professionals and communities to strengthen intellectual property protection, secure creative enterprises and create an enabling environment for innovation, investment and legitimate economic activity.

items.content:
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Kano State has named Alhaji Muhammad Sani Abacha, son of Nigeria’s late Head of State, General Sani Abacha, as its governorship candidate for next year’s election.
The party said the decision followed the withdrawal of the earlier nominee, Muhammad Bello Dalha.
At an expanded state executive committee meeting in Kano on Wednesday, the state party Chairman Dr. Bello Gambo Bichi, said an affirmation was conducted in line with the party’s constitution and electoral laws.
He said, “Last time we did a primary election in which Muhammad Bello Dalha was declared winner. But following consultations among stakeholders in Kano and Abuja, the candidate decided to withdraw.
Supreme Court affirms Gombe as SDP chairman
FG mourns Olu Jacobs, says his legacy will never fade
“The law says that as a result of withdrawal, a replacement primary must be held. That is what brought us here today. We have affirmed Muhammad Sani Abacha as the gubernatorial candidate of our great party in Kano State,” Bichi explained.
The affirmation was followed by a replacement primary election where Abacha was formally declared winner by the panel chairman, Dr. Abba Abdullahi.
Abdullahi confirmed that the exercise was conducted in line with the party’s guidelines and electoral regulations, and that Abacha had satisfied all requirements for nomination.
As part of reconciliation efforts, the party also resolved its internal factional disputes by conceding the deputy governorship slot to the Kabiru Tanimu Turaki group.
As a result, the former factional Chairman of the party and ex‑commissioner for land and agriculture, Alhaji Yusuf Ado Kibiya, was named as the new deputy governorship candidate.
“After wide consultation and reconciliation, we agreed to give the deputy governorship slot to the Turaki faction here in Kano. With this, there is no more faction in Kano PDP. We have reconciled,” Bichi said, adding that representatives of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) witnessed the process.
The PDP chairman also disclosed that some National Assembly and State Assembly candidates were also replaced as part of the reconciliation process to accommodate the faction.
He insisted that the party was now united and “waxing stronger” ahead of the polls.
Daily Trust reported that Abacha has been the party’s candidate in consecutive elections.
In 2023 governorship election, he came a distant third, trailing the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the election won by the then New Nigeria People’s Party (NNPP).

The nature and severity of João Pedro’s injury were not disclosed.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
By James Ogunnaike
The Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU), has faulted the Federal and state governments over the continued non-payment of three-and-a-half months’ salaries withheld from university lecturers and the uneven implementation of the December 2025 agreement with the union.
ASUU President, Prof. Christopher Piwuna, disclosed this while speaking on Frontline, a current affairs programme on Eagle 102.5 FM, Ilese-Ijebu.
Pawn said the union had expected the agreement reached with the Federal Government in December 2025 to usher in greater stability in the university system, improve lecturers’ welfare and address longstanding challenges confronting public universities.
He, however, expressed disappointment that several provisions of the agreement had either not been implemented or were being implemented inconsistently by the Federal and state governments.
“It’s really painful to have a conversation on issues like this. Our expectation, when we signed an agreement in December 2025, was that we are going at this time to talk about the progress that we have made, the stability in the system and concern ourselves with issues that affect Nigerians,” he said.
The ASUU president said the agreement covered improved salaries, funding for public universities and research support, among other provisions, but maintained that implementation had fallen short of the union’s expectations.
Piwuna also raised concerns over the continued withholding of part of the salaries owed lecturers from the previous administration, saying three-and-a-half months out of the seven-and-a-half months withheld were still outstanding.
According to him, the Federal Government had paid four months of the withheld salaries, leaving a balance of three-and-a-half months.
He said the outstanding salaries remained a major source of concern for affected lecturers, adding that the union expected the government to resolve the matter.
Beyond the withheld salaries, Piwuna said some universities were still facing difficulties implementing the new salary structure, while lecturers in some institutions remained uncertain about the payment of their full entitlements.
“As we stand now, funding is not properly being done according to what was agreed to. Individual universities have to embark on strike before salaries are being paid. Some universities are cut off from the new salary structure,” he said.
The ASUU president said the implementation challenge was not restricted to the Federal Government, noting that state governments also had obligations towards universities under their control.
He said while some state governments had commenced implementation of the December agreement, others had yet to fully comply, resulting in disparities in the conditions of service across public universities.
Piwuna cited Abia State Governor, Alex Otti, as one of the governors who had commenced implementation of the agreement.
“Only Governor Alex Otti of the South-Eastern part has implemented it,” he said.
He urged other governments to fulfil their commitments, stressing that ASUU had continued to engage relevant government officials through meetings and correspondence rather than immediately resorting to industrial action.
“We have engaged them; the Minister of Education at federal level, we engaged Senator Larry Tejuosho, the chairman of the implementation committee monitoring the Federal Government agreement. We have reminded them to do the needful,” Piwuna said.
On funding for education, the ASUU president said inadequate financing remained one of the major challenges confronting Nigeria’s public university system, particularly in the areas of research, infrastructure and human capital development.
He called for sustained investment in education, arguing that adequate funding was essential if Nigerian universities were to produce research and innovation capable of competing in the global knowledge economy.
Piwuna said governments should work towards dedicating up to 26 per cent of their annual budgets to education, describing such spending as an investment in national development rather than an expenditure that should continually be reduced because of competing demands.
“Every government should at least aim to supply or to fund their budget or dedicate their budget up to 26 per cent to education, and Nigeria is not an exception,” he said.
He, however, disclosed that ASUU had compromised during negotiations with the Federal Government by agreeing to a 15 per cent education budget benchmark, while recognising the financial difficulties involved in achieving the higher target immediately.
“So while negotiating with the government, we told the government to reduce the budget to 15 per cent and they agreed. Although it may be difficult, it can be done incrementally,” he said.
Piwuna said the agreement reached in December 2025 contained specific provisions for funding public universities, improving lecturers’ salaries and establishing mechanisms to strengthen research.
“The agreement, when we signed it, had provision for funding for public universities. It had provisions for improved salary, and it had provision for research council, amongst others,” he said.
He stressed that stronger investment in research was necessary for Nigerian universities to contribute meaningfully to national development and generate knowledge capable of competing beyond the country.
According to him, underfunding the education sector has implications not only for universities but also for research, innovation, human-capital development and the wider economy.
“We all know the value of education and we expect our leaders to carry out policies and actions that will promote education,” he said.
Piwuna said ASUU remained committed to dialogue with the Federal and state governments but urged the authorities to address the outstanding issues surrounding lecturers’ salaries, the implementation of the December 2025 agreement and funding for public universities.

items.author: Daily Trust
items.content:
Governor Uba Sani has redeemed his ₦30 million pledge to young innovators, by providing direct financial support to advance promising projects in technology, scientific research and innovation.
The grant was announced during the 2026 International Youth Day Conference in Kaduna on September 4, but the cheques were presented to the beneficiaries at the Ministry of Youth Development on Wednesday.
Beneficiaries include a team of computer engineering students from Ahmadu Bello University (ABU), Zaria, which developed a smart walking aid for visually impaired persons, as well as Al-Amin Mohammed Idris and Shamsudeen Jibril, winners of the National Board for Technology Incubation (NBTI) NEXTGEN Challenge.
Also supported was Fauziyya Muhammad Auwal of Kaduna State University (KASU), founder of the space technology initiative ASTHERA. Auwal is the first female astronaut candidate with Titan Space Industries and Nigeria’s first female analogue astronaut selected for the 2026 LunAres Research Station mission in Poland.
Eight microchip designers who were selected for specialised training under the Kaduna State Human Capital Development Initiative also received financial support.
Presenting the cheques on behalf of the Governor, the Commissioner for Youth Development, Barrister Gloria Ibrahim, said the intervention demonstrates the administration’s commitment to moving youth empowerment from promises to practical support.
“His Excellency, Governor Uba Sani decided to provide financial support to these young people to help them take their innovations further,’’ the Commissioner added.
Barrister Ibrahim said that the ‘’Ministry was established specifically to support our young people, and we expect you to use these resources to build your future, expand your work and bring greater recognition to Kaduna State.”
She explained that although time constraints prevented some of the invited innovators from making presentations during the International Youth Day Conference, the Governor however directed that they should also benefit from the intervention.
Speaking at the presentation, the Commissioner for Information and Culture, Malam Ahmed Maiyaki, said the ₦30 million intervention reflects the administration’s emphasis on sustained investment in young people, education and innovation.
“This ₦30 million is an investment in your ideas, research and future,” Maiyaki said, adding that “Governor Uba Sani is investing in the next generation, and we expect you to translate this support into deeper research, stronger innovations and practical solutions that can compete anywhere in the world.”
Maiyaki said the intervention forms part of a broader approach to youth and human-capital development, citing state support that has helped expose local innovators to international opportunities and facilitated partnerships in areas including renewable energy and rural electrification.
He also pointed to the administration’s investment in educational infrastructure, including an eight-kilometre road project at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, and its inclusion of young people in governance, with more than 40 per cent of political appointees under the age of 40.
Maiyaki urged the beneficiaries to regard the grants as seed support for greater accomplishments rather than an endpoint.
“What matters ultimately is not the amount presented today, but what you build with it. Kaduna has talented young people capable of developing solutions to real problems. Government’s responsibility is to create the environment, open doors and provide the support that enables good ideas to move from laboratories and workshops into solutions that improve lives.”

items.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye
FIFA has confirmed that a review of the abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) investment proposal will be presented to the FIFA Council, following criticism over the lack of answers surrounding the controversial plan.
According to Reuters, the confirmation came after Danish Football Association president Jesper Moller criticised FIFA for failing to answer what he described as “critical questions” about the shelved proposal at a Legal Committee meeting.
“FIFA Standing Committees advise and assist the FIFA Council in their respective fields in line with FIFA’s Statutes and Governance Regulations,” FIFA told Reuters in a statement.
“As previously communicated, a review of the withdrawn FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal will be presented to the FIFA Council.”
The FIFA Council has 37 members, including president Gianni Infantino, eight vice-presidents and 28 members elected by FIFA’s member associations.
The FFE proposal, launched by Infantino, sought to sell commercial stakes in FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup, to outside investors.
The plan triggered widespread opposition, with UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and CONCACAF among the football bodies calling for changes to FIFA’s leadership structure.
The proposal was subsequently withdrawn following the backlash, while the fallout has continued to put pressure on Infantino ahead of the FIFA presidential election in March 2027.
Several European football associations have since withdrawn their support for Infantino’s re-election bid, while Greek FA president Makis Gagatsis and former Germany national team director Oliver Bierhoff joined UEFA’s call for a leadership change on Tuesday.
However, Reuters reported that people familiar with the discussions said Infantino retains sufficient backing to secure another term, prompting opponents to consider strategies focused on limiting his powers rather than defeating him at the ballot.
The FIFA presidential election is scheduled for March 18, 2027, in Rabat, with Infantino seeking a fourth term.
Moller had previously criticised FIFA after the FFE proposal was not placed on the agenda of the Legal Committee meeting, saying the governing body had declined to provide answers to questions surrounding the project.

The Christian Association of Nigeria (CAN), Benue State Chapter, has dismissed reports circulating on social media and other platforms alleging that Governor Hyacinth Alia was planning to demolish the association’s secretariat in the state.
The Acting Chairman of CAN in the state, Rev. Jonathan Ugbede, described the report as false and malicious, insisting that the governor had never contemplated demolishing the secretariat.
Ugbede, who spoke while reacting to the speculation, said the allegation was completely detached from reality and urged members of the Christian community in the state to disregard it.
He expressed satisfaction with the governor’s prompt response to the allegation, noting that Alia had already debunked the report.
According to him, the governor’s response was consistent with his administration’s relationship with the Church and other religious institutions in the state.

Reacting, Ugbede appreciated Alia for his prompt clarification and appealed to politicians not to drag the Church into partisan politics.
“I am happy that the governor has come out promptly to debunk the allegation. The publication is malicious, false, baseless and completely detached from the truth.
“The political class should not drag the Church into the murky arena of politics. The Church belongs to everybody and should remain an institution that promotes peace, unity and the wellbeing of the people,” he said.

The acting chairman urged Christians across Benue State not to panic over the report but to disregard the publication and its sponsors.
He said the report was allegedly fabricated to create disunity and strain the relationship between the Church and the governor.

By Edwin Phillip, Lafia
Members of the Judiciary Staff Union of Nigeria (JUSUN), Nasarawa State branch, on Wednesday staged a peaceful protest at the premises of the State High Court headquarters on Shadam Road, Lafia, in compliance with the indefinite strike declared by the union.
Our correspondent reports that the union members carried placards with various inscriptions demanding, among other things, the implementation of salary increases and financial autonomy for the judiciary.
Some of the placards read: “Let’s have our financial autonomy, time is now,” “Let’s have our right” and “Give us 40 percent increase in salary.”
The main entrance of the court premises was, however, manned by a combined team of security personnel to prevent any breakdown of law and order.
Addressing the protesters, the state Chairman of JUSUN, Comrade Mas’ud Ubangari, urged members to remain united, focused and law-abiding as they pressed for the implementation of their demands.
Ubangari said the enforcement of the industrial action would be sustained peacefully until the state government and the Judicial Service Commission addressed the union’s demands.
However, the Covering Director of Information and Protocol, Nasarawa State High Court of Justice, Mrs Esther Agube Ogidis, said the state Chief Judge had already put measures in place to address the demands of the judiciary staff.
She questioned the decision to embark on the industrial action despite an order of the National Industrial Court restraining the union from proceeding with the strike.
Similarly, the Director of Civil Litigation, Nasarawa State Ministry of Justice, Alhassan Sabo, described the industrial action as illegal.
Sabo appealed to the JUSUN leadership to respect the interim injunction issued by the National Industrial Court restraining the union from commencing or declaring the strike pending the hearing and determination of the matter.
The judiciary workers are demanding the implementation of a 58.1 per cent salary increase, financial autonomy for the judiciary and a 40 per cent peculiar allowance, among other demands.

items.title: US Federal Reserve Increases Interest Rate First Time Since 2023
items.summary:
The US Federal Reserve has raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75-4 percent, its first rate increase since July 2023.
The decision came after the Federal Open Market Committee’s September 15-16 meeting which realized that inflation was still above the Fed’s 2 percent target and economic conditions were pretty bad.
The increase was approved unanimously by the voting members of the committee.
The Fed’s latest projections also point to the possibility of another 25-basis-point increase before the end of 2026, although future decisions will depend on incoming economic data.
The latest move reverses the rate cuts seen in 2025, when the Fed lowered borrowing costs as inflation eased.
Higher US interest rates can increase global borrowing costs and put pressure on emerging-market currencies and capital flows. The Iran war in particular has strained key factors supporting the US economy.

items.content:
…says campaign should be issue-based, not personal attacks
By Ike Uchechukwu, Calabar
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate in Cross River State, Sir Arthur Jarvis Archibong, has challenged anyone with evidence of criminal wrongdoing against him to make it public.
Archibong, who spoke with journalists in Calabar on Wednesday, was reacting to a recent advertorial which he alleged was linked to the state government and intended to damage his reputation ahead of the 2027 governorship election.
He said his campaign would remain focused on issues and development rather than personal attacks.
“I dare anyone with criminal records against me to make same public or forever remain silent.
“I am an honest, clean, and hardworking citizen of Cross River State in particular and Nigeria at large.
“I have no criminal records on any matter, anywhere in Nigeria,” he said.
Archibong alleged that the advertorial was an attempt to undermine his political standing across the state’s three senatorial districts.
He also criticised the state government’s performance, alleging shortcomings in infrastructure and human development.
The PDP candidate further alleged that the advertorial contained accusations against the administration relating to cultism and syncretism.
He also alleged that there was a plan to deploy cult groups to cause violence before, during and after the 2027 elections.
“We are aware that this government is planning unprecedented violence through cultism before, during, and after elections, but we are not afraid because God is our shield and buckler,” he said.
Insisting that his campaign remained anchored on issues rather than personal attacks, Archibong accused the government and its supporters of engaging in what he described as personality-driven politics.
He added that any response from his camp would be in reaction to what he considered provocations from the administration.
Reacting to the allegations, the All Progressives Congress (APC) dismissed Archibong’s claim of a planned deployment of cult groups for electoral violence as baseless.
The party’s state Publicity Secretary, Emmanuel Inyang, said Cross River residents had remained supportive of the APC because of what he described as the administration’s achievements in the state over the past three years.
Inyang described Archibong’s allegations as the position of a party that was not prepared to face the electorate, and urged the PDP to prepare for the 2027 election.
He said the PDP should get ready to face what he described as defeat at the polls.

items.content:
Two-thirds approval required as Sixth Alteration Bill moves to 36 legislatures
By Henry Umoru, Abuja
The National Assembly has transmitted the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, to the Houses of Assembly of the 36 states for consideration and approval.
With the transmission, the National Assembly asked the state legislatures to consider the bill in accordance with their respective legislative procedures and communicate their resolutions to the National Assembly after completing their deliberations.
The Clerk to the National Assembly, Kamoru Ogunlana, disclosed this on Tuesday in a statement.
The transmission marks the commencement of the next phase of the constitutional alteration process and was carried out pursuant to Section 9 of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, and a directive from the leadership of the National Assembly.
The National Assembly also emphasised that the state legislatures remain constitutionally independent in considering the proposed amendments.
Section 9 of the Constitution requires a bill seeking to alter its provisions to be approved by resolutions of not less than two-thirds of the Houses of Assembly of the 36 states before the National Assembly can proceed with the alteration.
However, the Constitution does not prescribe a specific deadline for state Houses of Assembly to communicate their resolutions.
Ogunlana said the National Assembly nevertheless expects the state legislatures to complete their consideration and communicate their decisions within 30 days of receiving the bill.
He stressed that the 30-day period is an administrative timeframe and does not constitute a constitutional deadline.
“It is noted that the Constitution does not prescribe a specific period within which the State Houses of Assembly are required to communicate their resolutions on a constitutional alteration Bill.
“Nevertheless, in the interest of an orderly, coordinated and timely conclusion of the constitutional alteration process, the State Houses of Assembly are expected to consider the Bill and communicate their respective resolutions to the National Assembly within 30 days of receipt.
“For clarity, the 30-day period is an expected administrative timeframe and does not constitute a constitutional deadline,” he said.
Ogunlana said the National Assembly recognised the constitutional responsibility vested in the state Houses of Assembly and would respect their independence throughout the process.
“The National Assembly recognises the constitutional responsibility vested in the State Houses of Assembly and respects their independence in the consideration of the Bill,” he said.
He explained that the transmission was intended to facilitate the orderly discharge of the state legislatures’ constitutional responsibilities and not to dictate the outcome of their consideration.
He also assured that the National Assembly would adhere strictly to constitutional requirements and due process as the exercise progresses.
“The National Assembly remains committed to ensuring that the constitutional alteration process is conducted in strict compliance with the Constitution and in accordance with the principles of due process, institutional cooperation and respect for the legislative responsibilities of all tiers of the legislature,” Ogunlana said.
The 36 Houses of Assembly are now expected to commence their respective legislative consideration of the Sixth Alteration Bill.
After receiving their resolutions, the National Assembly will determine the next steps required under the Constitution.
Ogunlana said: “Upon receipt of the resolutions of the State Houses of Assembly, the National Assembly will proceed with the necessary steps in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.”
The transmission of the bill to the 36 state legislatures brings the constitutional amendment process to a critical stage, with the required state-level approval now forming the next major step before further action by the National Assembly.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
The Emir of Kano, Muhammadu Sanusi II, has expressed regret over delaying the entry of telecommunications companies (telcos) into Nigeria’s financial services sector while he was governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN).
Sanusi, who spoke on Wednesday at the launch of the 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria (A2F) survey by Enhancing Financial Innovation & Access (EFInA), said telcos already had the infrastructure and reach that could have accelerated financial inclusion, particularly in underserved communities.
“One of my regrets as CBN governor was delaying telcos’ entry into financial services,” he said.
The former CBN governor, however, said financial inclusion should not be measured simply by the number of people with bank accounts or the ability to transfer money.
“Opening an account and moving money is not the same thing as earning money or moving people out of poverty,” he said.
Sanusi said financial services should be linked to the real economy, particularly agriculture, manufacturing and other productive sectors.
He cited the example of groundnut farmers in Kano, saying a company producing ready-to-use therapeutic food for malnourished children had to import peanuts from Argentina because local farmers were unable to produce the commodity to the required quality.
According to him, the solution was not simply to place farmers on digital financial platforms but to train them, improve their productivity and connect them with buyers.
He said financial inclusion should create a link between farmers, markets and manufacturers.
Sanusi also urged the CBN to prioritise price stability, warning that inflation posed a major threat to savings and wealth creation.
“There is no enemy to savings, no enemy to wealth that is bigger than inflation,” he said.
The traditional ruler also advocated the use of transaction data generated by fintech companies and payment service providers to develop savings, pension and insurance products for Nigerians who may not have conventional banking relationships.
He said platforms with extensive transaction data and reach in rural communities could channel small amounts from transactions into savings, pensions or insurance where appropriate systems were available.
Sanusi suggested that even N100 could be deducted from a transaction and directed towards savings or insurance.
He also said insurance products could be designed to protect market traders against risks such as fire outbreaks and farmers against crop failures.

items.author: Ado Abubakar Musa, Jos
items.content:
The Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, on Wednesday visited Plateau State following recent killings in parts of the state, assuring residents that the Nigeria Police Force would strengthen security operations and bring perpetrators to justice.
Disu, who paid a condolence visit to the Plateau State Government, said the Police remained committed to providing a secure environment, stressing that sustainable peace and development required continuous collaboration among security agencies, government and communities.
Speaking during the visit, Disu said the purpose was to discuss the killings in Mangu and other parts of the state.
“I am on the Plateau to discuss issues bothering on the killings in Mangu and other parts of the state. We are not happy with the situation and I can assure you we have made some arrests.
“Having gone round and engaged with stakeholders to have lasting solutions to the problem, I can assure you people have hope and confidence in the police and we will continue working together in synergy and collaboration for a secure environment.
“We are intensifying community engagement and intelligence gathering to identify threats early, protect vulnerable communities and bring perpetrators to justice.
“Building trust between security personnel and communities is important, and I urge residents to provide credible and timely information to enable security agencies prevent attacks and apprehend criminals.”
Receiving the IGP, Governor Caleb Mutfwang, represented by his Deputy, Ngo Josephine Chundung Piyo, commended the Police leadership for its response to the security situation and the decision to visit the state to assess developments firsthand.
“We commend the Police leadership for responding promptly to the security situation and visiting the state to assess developments firsthand.
“The visit is a demonstration of the IGP’s commitment to protecting lives and property, and the state government places a high premium on sustained collaboration with the Police and other security agencies in maintaining peace and security.
“The state government has made tremendous efforts in strengthening security, and we appreciate the IGP for deploying a new Commissioner of Police to Plateau State and strengthening the Police Command’s capacity to work with the state government, sister security agencies, traditional institutions and communities.”
According to her, effective security required more than the deployment of personnel, noting that robust intelligence gathering, community engagement and timely response to emerging threats were also essential.
The Deputy Governor appealed to the IGP to activate and deploy officers to the Mobile Police Barracks in Gashish, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area.
She said, “The facility has remained moribund since its establishment.
“Putting the facility to full operational use would strengthen police presence and improve response capabilities in communities within the axis.”
She also urged residents to remain vigilant and avoid actions that could worsen tensions in affected communities.
“Residents should avoid reprisals that could further escalate tensions in affected communities,” she said.

items.title: The A’uwẽ-Xavante people's denunciation of megaprojects in Brazil
items.summary:

items.author: Guest Contributor
items.content:
‘There can be no legitimate development when its realization depends on the destruction of what sustain a people’s existence’
Originally published on Global Voices
An Indigenous person carries a flag for the campaign ‘Let the A’uwẽ-Xavante Keep Dreaming’ in front of the UN building in Geneva, Switzerland. Photo by Cultural Survival, used with permission.
This article, written by Djalma Ramalho (Aranã Caboclo), was originally published on the Cultural Survival website on August 17, 2026. It is republished here in an edited version with permission. Learn more about their campaign here.
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.
Under a heavy sky, on the shores of Lake Léman in Geneva, Switzerland, red words cut across the landscape. In front of the Jet d’Eau of Bains des Pâquis, Geneva’s emblematic fountain, two messages appeared: “Let the A’uwẽ-Xavante Keep Dreaming” and “Stop the megaprojects fragmenting Ró, the A’uwẽ-Xavante territory.”
The intervention marked the international launch of a campaign led by A’uwẽ-Xavante leaders, communities, and organizations, during the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (EMRIP) in July 2026. They are an Indigenous group from Brazil’s Centre-West region, with a population of around 25,300. According to the 2022 Census, Brazil has 1,694,836 people who identified as Indigenous, from 391 ethnicities.
While government representatives debated international policies and standards inside the United Nations, the Indigenous delegation occupied public space to convey a message: There can be no legitimate development when its realization depends on the destruction of the material, spiritual, and political conditions that sustain a people’s existence.
Dreaming is not a metaphor
For the A’uwẽ-Xavante people, dreaming is a concrete dimension of social, spiritual, and political life. In her research on dream performance among the A’uwẽ-Xavante, anthropologist Laura Graham demonstrates that dreams establish relationships among the living, ancestors, and immortal beings. Songs received during sleep are shared with the community and may become collective performances that bring together narrative, music, dance, memory, and cultural continuity.
In one episode documented by Graham, an elder recounts receiving songs from ancestral creators intended for the living, so that by singing them collectively, the A’uwẽ could continue to exist as A’uwẽ. The dreamer, therefore, does not appear as the individual owner of a creation, but rather as a mediator of knowledge that belongs to, and circulates among, the people as a whole, and becomes part of the community’s living heritage.
In recent years, according to the leaders who developed the campaign, dreams have also begun to convey warnings related to growing pressures on their territories. The expansion of railways, highways, hydroelectric projects, monocultures, and other large-scale developments is, therefore, understood not merely as a physical transformation of the landscape, but as a threat to the relationships that make it possible to receive, transmit, and enact this knowledge.
To defend the right to dream, then, is to defend the territorial conditions that make dreaming possible.
Ró: Cerrado, world, territory, and life
The word Ró also has no full equivalent in the conventional translation of “territory.” Geographer Maria Lucia Cereda Gomide explains that Ró can simultaneously mean “Cerrado, world, our land, everything.” It refers to a territorial and cosmological complex that extends from the village space to the Cerrado [biome in Central Brazil], encompassing its waters, animals, plants, and the spirits that inhabit this world. Ró is a living network of relationships. It encompasses hunting, gathering, and fishing grounds; ancient villages; burial grounds; rivers and pathways; medicinal plants; ceremonial sites, and ancestral presences that sustain collective life.
A technical note by the Brazilian Anthropological Association, published in 2025, emphasizes that A’uwẽ-Xavante territoriality depends on practices such as journeys through the Cerrado, the gathering of roots, fruits, and fibers, fishing, hunting, and circuits of reciprocity that connect families, clans, age groups, and different Indigenous lands. Territorial fragmentation, therefore, compromises not only access to natural resources but also the ability to perform ceremonies, transmit knowledge, and maintain the social and cosmological relationships through which the A’uwẽ constitute themselves as a people. It would also cut across relationships that cannot be contained within the administrative boundaries drawn by the state.
So, the message projected in Geneva – “Let the A’uwẽ-Xavante Keep Dreaming” – is a demand for the protection of the integrity of Ró and for the continuity of their existence itself. A’uwẽ-Xavante leader Hiparidi Top’tiro states in the campaign’s document: “Any project that affects one of our territories is a problem for the entire A’uwẽ-Xavante People.”
Territories, lives, and dreams cut by tracks
The campaign’s central demand is protection of the rights of the A’uwẽ-Xavante people in the face of the construction of the Center-West Integration Railway (FICO), also known as EF-354. Presented by the Brazilian government as a strategic project to reduce logistics costs and expand freight rail transport, it is part of a broader corridor designed primarily to move soybeans, corn, and other commodities produced in the region. By advancing the project without ensuring adequate free, prior, and informed consultation, the Brazilian state has failed to protect the rights of Indigenous peoples.
The FICO Railway is a federal project of approximately 1,641 kilometers (1,020 miles) under the responsibility of Infra S.A. Its first section, covering approximately 363 kilometers (226 miles), between Mara Rosa, in the state of Goiás, and Água Boa, Mato Grosso state, is currently being built by the mining company Vale as compensation for the early renewal of another concession. Studies and administrative processes related to the route have identified Xavante territories within its area of influence, raising serious concerns about territorial, environmental, social, and cultural impacts.
In May 2026, Infra S.A. itself reported that approximately 80 kilometers (50 miles) of the final portion of the section currently under construction depended on the completion of the Basic Environmental Plan – Indigenous Component (PBA-CI) and on negotiations with Xavante communities. This makes clear that the relationship between the railway and Indigenous territories is not merely indirect, but a central issue affecting the project’s implementation.
The technical note issued by the Brazilian Anthropological Association states that the railway affects areas of traditional occupation, claimed lands that aren’t yet demarcated, gathering areas, former villages, burial grounds, waterways, and sacred sites. The document recommends suspending construction and the installation license until adequate consultation has taken place, and altering the route so that the railway does not cross A’uwẽ-Xavante territoriality.
The campaign’s advocacy brief, Let the A’uwẽ-Xavante Keep Dreaming, launched in Geneva, argues that FICO cannot be assessed merely as an isolated railway line. It is part of a broader architecture of highways, railways, waterways, and export corridors that is likely to intensify commodity flows, non-Indigenous occupation, and economic pressure on already fragmented territories.
Consultation under dispute
In February 2026, the Coordination of Indigenous Organizations of the Brazilian Amazon (COIAB) denounced irregularities in the consultation process related to FICO. According to the organization, meetings scheduled for some Indigenous lands were held at very short intervals, leaving communities insufficient time to conduct internal discussions in accordance with their own decision-making processes. They also documented reports of pressure on Indigenous leaders, the absence of independent technical assistance, and communication difficulties among communities distributed across territories that have historically been fragmented. The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office (MPF) opened an administrative proceeding to monitor the consultation process.
Both the International Labour Organization (ILO) and the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples establish that states must consult and cooperate in good faith with Indigenous Peoples before approving projects affecting their lands, territories, or resources, to obtain their Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC).
Consultation does not simply mean informing a community that a project will proceed but also respecting their decision-making timelines, freedom from coercion, and ability to withhold consent from measures that could compromise their future.
To Europe: Coloniality also travels by rail and electric car
The intervention in Geneva carried a particular symbolic weight. The city is home to the United Nations Office and to numerous institutions connected to the international human rights system. Indigenous representatives are often given only a few minutes to present territorial conflicts shaped by decades of violations.
The campaign also challenges the contradictions of the so-called green transition. Railways, logistics corridors, mining operations, and large-scale infrastructure projects are frequently presented as necessary instruments for building a low-carbon economy. Yet when they advance without the effective participation of affected people, they can reproduce long-standing colonial mechanisms: territorial appropriation, the concentration of economic benefits, and the transfer of environmental and social costs onto Indigenous peoples and traditional communities.
The projection in front of the Jet d’Eau confronted this paradox. Europe, historically implicated in the colonization of Indigenous territories, remains connected to these regions through networks of finance, consumption, mining, agribusiness, and export infrastructure. Changing the energy source without transforming these relationships is not enough. A transition that continues to treat Indigenous territories as sacrifice zones may be technologically new, but it remains politically colonial.
For the A’uwẽ-Xavante, a fragmented territory does not simply mean a reduction in physical space. It means the interruption of pathways, songs, ceremonies, memories, and ancestral relationships. No megaproject can claim to represent the future if its existence depends on destroying the dreams of those who have always cared for the land.
Written by Guest Contributor

items.title: Pakistan Attracts 80% More Foreign Investment in August 2026
items.summary:
Pakistan’s net foreign direct investment (FDI) rose by 80 percent year-on-year (YoY) to $316 million in August 2026, according to State Bank of Pakistan data compiled by Topline Securities.
Net FDI in August also shows a 77 percent month-on-month (MoM) increase compared to $179 million in July 2026. This took 2MFY27 net FDI to $495 million, up 24 percent YoY.
On August 7, Pakistan also entered a strategic defense pact with the Saudis, which helped reinforce remittance channels and increase investments.
The power and financial business sectors recorded the highest foreign investment inflows during August.
On a country-wise basis, China, Canada and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) remained the largest net contributors to Pakistan’s FDI during the month.

items.author: Anadolu Agency
items.content:
The Taliban wants formal diplomatic relations with the US but said Washington must first address the legacy of its two-decade war in Afghanistan, Taliban spokesman Abdul Qahar Balkhi told CBS News in an interview.
Five years after the Taliban returned to power following the US withdrawal, Balkhi portrayed the end of the foreign military presence as the administration's main achievement, while acknowledging persistent unemployment, economic difficulties and public dissatisfaction.
“The greatest achievement obviously Afghanistan has had is the end of occupation,” said Balkhi, arguing that the country had since seen improvements in security, trade, investment and infrastructure.
Read: Mushahid Hussain says 9/11 promoted 'Greater Israel' agenda, caused US decline
He claimed Afghan exports rose from $750 million in 2020 to nearly $2 billion, while the number of factories increased from 1,500 to 6,000. He also said the government had been able to pay civil servants and attract billions of dollars in investment.
Balkhi acknowledged, however, that “there are areas where we haven't met the expectation of the general population,” citing widespread unemployment and other challenges.
The interview on Tuesday also highlighted Afghanistan's continued diplomatic isolation. Russia is the only country to have formally recognized the Taliban government.
Balkhi argued that Afghanistan was already engaging diplomatically with several countries and questioned the practical meaning of formal recognition.
On relations with Washington, he said Kabul wanted diplomatic ties with “every single country of the world, including the United States,” and would welcome the reopening of the US Embassy and American investment in sectors such as minerals and gas.
He also rejected calls by US President Donald Trump for Afghanistan to return billions of dollars worth of American-funded military equipment left behind after the 2021 withdrawal. CBS reported that roughly $7 billion in US military hardware remained in Afghanistan.
“That’s the assets of the state of Afghanistan,” said Balkhi, rejecting any deal linking the equipment to the release of Afghan funds frozen abroad.
Asked about the argument that American taxpayers paid for the equipment, Balkhi responded, “The Americans did a lot of things. Americans killed a lot of people, destroyed the majority of the country. Should they not be paying for that first?”
Balkhi demanded the release of Afghan central bank assets frozen by Washington, saying the funds belonged to the Afghan state rather than the Taliban government.
Also Read: Pakistan open to talks with Afghanistan
On the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, Balkhi said the Taliban condemned attacks on civilians and reiterated its commitment under the Doha agreement that Afghan territory would not be used to attack the US or any other country.
The interview also focused on restrictions on women and girls. Regarding the suspension of public schooling for girls from seventh grade onward, Balkhi said alternative forms of education remained available and rejected reports of girls attending clandestine classes despite the restrictions.
“There is no such thing as secret schools,” he said, describing the arrangements as homeschooling or madrasa, or Islamic, education.
Looking back at the war that followed the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001, Balkhi said Afghanistan had learned that conflicts should be resolved through diplomacy.
“War is not the solution, and occupying Afghanistan certainly isn't to your benefit,” he said, urging greater cooperation for Afghanistan's reconstruction and development.

items.title: Fact check: Viral video does not show Saudi imam arrested for criticising Saudi government and US
items.author: Fact Check By iVerify
items.content:
Several users, the majority of whom appear to be Saudi Arabia-based accounts based on their profiles and previous posts, have been sharing a video on X since September 13, 2026, allegedly showing the arrest of a mosque imam in Saudi Arabia for criticising the Saudi government over the United States’ policy in the region. However, the video is old and was originally published on March 3, 2018. 
The ongoing US-Iran war in the Middle East began on February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran. The conflict has since expanded across the region, with Iran launching attacks against US and Israeli interests and several US allies in the Middle East.
In early September, the conflict also intensified between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi military and energy infrastructure, while Saudi Arabia has carried out retaliatory strikes in Yemen. The escalation has further widened the regional conflict and disrupted vital energy and shipping routes.
How it started
On September 13,  a Saudi Arabia-based user shared a video on X, claiming that it showed the arrest of a mosque imam in Saudi Arabia. The Arabic caption accompanying the video translates to: “Arrest of the mosque imam in Saudi Arabia for his condemnation and criticism regarding America’s policy in the region. They didn’t even wait for him to finish the sermon.”
The post gained 1 million views.
Another Saudi Arabia-based user shared the same video on September 14, with the same caption. 
The post also gained 1 million views.
On September 15, another user shared the same clip with the same caption. The post gained 126,800 views.
Several other users also shared the video in a similar context, as seen here, here,  here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, and here, collectively gaining 23,240 views.
Methodology
A fact-check was initiated to determine the veracity of the claim due to its virality.
A reverse image search of the video yielded a Facebook post published on March 3, 2018, containing the same footage.
The Arabic caption accompanying the video claimed that during a Friday sermon at a mosque in Saudi Arabia, the preacher criticised the Al Saud family and its attempts to normalise relations with Israel before security personnel forcibly removed him from the pulpit.
The post also included a response attributed to Saudi authorities, which stated that an elderly man had climbed the pulpit before the official preacher and insisted on delivering the sermon.
 According to the statement, security officials intervened and removed him from the pulpit, while a spokesperson for the Ministry of Islamic Affairs said the man was mentally ill.
Another Facebook post from the same date made a similar claim in its Arabic caption, which reads: “The preacher of the Friday sermon spoke about Jewish people and corruption, due to which he was arrested.”
The video resurfaced on Facebook on December 25, 2021, with a post claiming that the imam had “called the current government a religious failure and the current ruler an agent of the US and Israel,” after which security forces allegedly removed him from the pulpit and hanged him.
The post further claimed that the incident took place in the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah and portrayed the alleged execution as punishment for “speaking the truth.”
In a similar context, the claim was also shared in October 2024, on X by two India-based users with a history of sharing multiple false claims in their past posts.
A keyword search was conducted to determine whether international or prominent Middle Eastern media outlets had reported on the incident.  No relevant reports were found from international outlets. 
However, Saudi Arabia-based Arabic media outlets, including Shehab News, Okaz, Al-Riyadh and Khabarni and a Turkish news agency, Anadolu Agency reported on this particular incident in 2018.
Shehab News published an article on March 2, 2018, titled: “Video: Sheikh forcibly removed from the pulpit during Friday sermon in Saudi Arabia”.
The report stated that an elderly man was forcibly removed from the pulpit at Al-Jabriya Mosque in Yanbu after refusing to leave.
 It cited a source from Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Islamic Affairs, which described the man as “mentally ill,” while noting that social media users had shared different accounts about the reason for his removal. 
On March 3, 2018. Okaz published an article titled “Medina Police: Yanbu preacher is mentally ill and was handed over to his family” on March 3, 2018.
 The report said the video had been circulating on X and showed an elderly man being removed from the pulpit by a security officer and worshippers at a mosque in Yanbu. 
The article had an official comment from the Medina Police spokesperson; it said the man was in his seventies, had a medical record for psychological disorders, and was handed over to his family for continued treatment and care.
Al-Riyadh also posted the official statement of the Medina police on the incident on March 3, 2018.
 In the statement, the police spokesperson Major Hussein Al-Qahtani said that the person seen ascending the pulpit and “uttering incoherent phrases” in the video is a citizen in his seventies who “suffers from psychological disorders and has a medical record in a specialized hospital”.  
None of the reports reviewed identified the man as the mosque’s imam. Instead, they described him as an elderly man and ‘mentally ill’ who attempted to deliver the Friday sermon before the official preacher.
Fact-check status: false
The claim that the viral video shows an imam being arrested for criticising the Saudi government and the US is misleading.
The video is from 2018 and unrelated to the claim.

items.title: PM Shehbaz Installs Help Desks At Petrol Pumps
items.summary:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered help desks at petrol pumps to assist people with registration for the government’s fuel subsidy scheme.
The decision was made during a meeting in Islamabad on September 16 to review progress on the PM Special Relief Scheme, which provides fuel subsidies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles up to 800cc.
The help desks will include government officials, volunteers and petrol pump staff. They will guide eligible people through registration and other required steps.
Officials told the Prime Minister that the scheme has now been launched across Pakistan, including Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, after starting as a pilot in Islamabad.
Registration requires only four details: CNIC number, vehicle number plate, province of registration and vehicle registration date.
The government said the number of successful registrations is gradually increasing and provincial governments are supporting the nationwide rollout.

items.author: Arooj Fatima
items.content:
London Mayor Sadiq Khan has formally joined the House of Lords after being granted the title of Lord Khan of Tooting.
Khan took the oath in the upper chamber of the British Parliament as a Labour life peer, marking another major milestone in his political career. Official parliamentary records show that he was created Baron Khan of Tooting for life through Letters Patent dated August 20.
The peerage takes its name from Tooting, the London area where Khan was born and which he represented in Parliament for 11 years before becoming mayor. Members of his family attended the ceremony along with about a dozen Labour MPs from London, including Dawn Butler, Tulip Siddiq, and Rupa Huq.
Khan was introduced to the House of Lords by former Labour leader Lord Kinnock and human rights lawyer Baroness Kennedy of The Shaws. He took the traditional oath, signed the official roll and an undertaking to follow the House of Lords Code of Conduct.
He was sworn in alongside another new Labour peer, Lord Roberto Neri, director of UK Music. Neri was accompanied by Lord Kennedy of Southwark and Baroness Kennedy of Cradley Heath.
After taking their oaths, the two new peers were welcomed in the chamber before shaking hands with Lord Speaker Lord Forsyth of Drumlean. Khan later met Leader of the House of Lords Baroness Smith of Basildon, her deputy Lord Collins of Highbury, and former EastEnders actor Lord Cashman as he left the chamber.
The peerages of Khan and Neri were announced during the final week of Sir Keir Starmer’s time in Downing Street.
Before entering Parliament, Khan worked as a solicitor specializing in human rights law. He was elected as MP for Tooting in 2005 and represented the constituency until 2016. During Gordon Brown’s government, he held several positions and eventually served as Minister of State for Transport.
Khan was first elected Mayor of London in 2016 and went on to win three consecutive terms, becoming the first person to achieve the feat. His time in office has also made him the longest-serving Mayor of London since the position was created in 2000.
As mayor, Khan has led London through major challenges, including the COVID-19 pandemic, terrorist attacks, and environmental issues. He is London’s first Muslim mayor.
Khan was also awarded a knighthood for political and public service. King Charles formally knighted him during a ceremony at Buckingham Palace in June 2025.

items.content:
Analyst figures showed cellular IoT modules remained resilient in the face of memory component shortages which are hammering the smartphone sector, with shipments of the specialised units up 15% year-on-year in H1.
IoT Analytics estimates module shipments were aided by an acceleration during Q2, though its numbers also indicate the technology involved is a key element and may explain why the market has so-far resisted the broader component problem.
The research specialist believes shipments of LTE Cat 1 bis modules dominated the sector in H1, stating “5G deployment has been relatively gradual” and focused more around “higher-value applications”.
It is reasonable to conclude the lean towards established LTE equipment may have alleviated some of the component woes affecting broader device markets and IoT Analytics acknowledged expectations of increased prices for memory and other apparatus may have led some companies to bring orders forward.
Senior principal analyst Satyajit Sinha said it is unclear if the performance of the IoT module market “reflects underlying demand and how much is being pulled forward by longer lead times and rising component costs”.
Although cautious, Sinha noted the steady demand for LTE Cat 1 bis modules and fresh projects could contribute to continued shipment strength in the back-half of the year. The flip-side to this would be in making predictions for 2027 harder.
Other insights in IoT Analytics’ H1 numbers are RedCap and eRedCap modules remained nascent. The company stated the units are “only beginning to move from roadmap into volume” as devices become available and demand is spurred by rising standalone 5G coverage.
“NB-IoT continues to slip” from a peak in Q1 2024.
The company noted China remained the largest market for IoT module shipments, but stated those in India registered the swiftest growth.

items.author: Usman Hanif
items.content:
KARACHI
Pakistan recorded a current account deficit of $543 million in the first two months of FY27, the State Bank of Pakistan's latest figures show. It was 36% narrower than the $853 million gap in the same period of last year, supported by robust remittance inflows.
August alone recorded a $98 million shortfall, down from $445 million in July (revised up from an earlier $328 million) and from $324 million in August 2025. On paper, it is a sharp improvement. Underneath, the arithmetic is familiar.
Goods and services exports in August rose only about 5% year-on-year to $3.33 billion. Imports rose faster, by about 8%, to $6.64 billion. Workers' remittances of $3.66 billion, up nearly 17% from $3.14 billion a year earlier, closed most of the hole. July-August remittances were about $7.3 billion, up 14.7%. The current account looks better when the diaspora sends more money.
August goods exports were at $2.51 billion, up only 3.8% year-on-year, against imports of $5.68 billion, up 7.4%. The monthly goods deficit widened 10.4% to $3.17 billion. For July-August, the goods deficit rose 18.1% to $7.12 billion, with exports up 7% and imports higher by 13%.
SBP's free-on-board (fob) goods series was even flatter in August, about $2.46 billion against $2.49 billion a year earlier, while the goods and services deficit for July-August FY27 widened to $6.75 billion from $5.96 billion. After successive textile packages and export-led growth claims, the factory basket is barely moving. Machinery, transport and metals imports are rising with activity.
August services exports were $872 million against $677 million a year earlier, up 29%. July-August services exports reached $1.81 billion versus $1.41 billion. Exports of telecommunications, computer and information services were $394 million in August, up 17% year-on-year but down 6% month-on-month. Other business services rose 36% while transport gained 28%.
Pakistan is drifting towards a services-and-remittances external account while merchandise trade stays anemic. That changes who earns the foreign exchange: more urban, skilled, digital, and leaves industrial employment and the old textile complex less central to the balance of payments than the official industrial policy still assumes.
The country recorded travel exports of $110 million in August against $43 million a year earlier, up 156%. July-August travel receipts were $222 million versus $90 million. The FY26 travel exports had already jumped by more than half.
IT exports surge
Pakistan's IT exports rose 17% year-on-year to $394 million in August 2026, according to Topline Securities. The monthly figure was down 6% from July's $417 million, a dip Topline attributed mainly to fewer working days rather than a break in demand.
The August print keeps the sector on a double-digit annual path that has now stretched across a full year of monthly readings. Receipts were $337 million in August 2025 and have since held a higher band, peaking at $437 million in December 2025 before settling in the mid-to-high $300 million through early 2026 and recovering above $410 million from March through July.
Two-month (July-August) receipts of IT exports for FY27 reached $811 million. On a trailing-12-month basis, exports stood at $4.7 billion, up 21% from $3.9 billion a year earlier. That TTM level is consistent with the record $4.6 billion booked for full-year FY26, when the sector grew about 21% and met the lower end of the government's then-target range.
Net IT exports – exports minus related imports – were $336 million in August, up 10% year-on-year. The high net export is why the industry matters for the external account: software, freelancing and IT-enabled services add foreign exchange with a far smaller import bill than goods.
The policy bar is higher than the current growth. Under the Uraan Pakistan plan, the government has set an FY29 target of $10 billion for IT exports. "Under Uraan Pakistan, the government has set an FY29 target of $10 billion in IT exports; this implies a CAGR of 28.4% till FY29," noted Topline Securities.
The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 28.4% is well above the roughly 17-21% pace of last year. Reaching that target will require more than volume in routine outsourcing. It will need larger enterprise contracts, higher-value work in areas such as AI, cybersecurity and product development, deeper market access, and a larger pool of export-ready firms.
The year-on-year gains in August show the IT sector is still scaling. However, the month-on-month dip and the gap to the 28%-plus CAGR show that the next leap is not automatic.
Foreign investment jumps
The net foreign direct investment (FDI) reached $316 million in August, up 80% year-on-year and 77% month-on-month, taking 2MFY27 net FDI to $495 million, up 24%. Power and financial business led; China, Canada and the UAE were the named sources. Total foreign investment in August was $358 million against $133 million a year earlier. Portfolio investment recorded an outflow.

Federal Minister for IT and Telecom Shaza Fatima Khawaja delivered a virtual address, "Pakistan's digital transformation and opportunities for partnership with Japan", at the Pakistan Business Seminar, organised by the Japan External Trade Organisation (Jetro) in collaboration with the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB) in Tokyo.
The seminar brought together senior government officials, business leaders, technology executives and industry leaders from both countries, exploring opportunities to further strengthen collaboration in technology sectors.
Abdul Hameed, Ambassador of Pakistan to Japan, Shuichi Akamatsu, Ambassador of Japan to Pakistan, Faisal Jeddy, CEO PSEB, Akiko Okumura, Executive Vice President Jetro, and Naritoshi Takayama, Deputy Director-General, Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry of Japan also attended the event.
Highlighting Pakistan-Japan longstanding friendship, Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja emphasised that the next chapter of partnership would be defined by digital and technological collaboration. Outlining Pakistan's digital transformation agenda, the minister highlighted the country's expanding digital infrastructure, including more than 161 million broadband subscribers, a 17,200-kilometre fibre optic backbone, and the release of over 750 MHz of spectrum during the year to support next-generation connectivity and 5G.
Emphasising the complementary strengths of the two countries, Shaza Fatima said Japan brings world-class precision, technology and engineering expertise, while Pakistan offers a young population, scale and a rapidly expanding pool of digital talent.
With 68% of Pakistan's population under the age of 30 and more than 75,000 IT graduates and software engineers entering the workforce annually, she underscored the country's strong potential as a technology and innovation partner for Japanese industry. The minister called for greater Japanese investment in Pakistan's technology sector, including the establishment of R&D and development centres.

items.author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
items.content:
The Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) and the Petroleum Division have pointed out exploitation of the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) pricing formula and policy framework that have caused market distortion and significant price anomalies.
Sources said that the issue was taken up in a high-level meeting of the National Price Monitoring Committee (NPMC). During the sitting, Ogra presented a detailed briefing on the existing LPG pricing mechanism, highlighting that the prevailing discrepancy between notified and actual market prices primarily stemmed from the exclusion of import parity in the current pricing formula. The meeting was informed that necessary policy revision by the Petroleum Division and Ogra had remained pending since 2023. Director General (LPG), Petroleum Division, said that the original policy framework was tailoured for domestic producers but was subsequently applied to importers, thereby distorting market pricing and creating significant price anomalies. The notified Ogra rate was found much below the rates charged in different cities, especially Gwadar (Rs330/kg) and Turbat (Rs350/kg) – both districts have borders with Iran.
The committee was also briefed by the chief (nutrition), Ministry of Planning, Development & Special Incentives on the results of quality testing conducted by the Pakistan Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (PCSIR) for edible oil, ghee and milk. Its findings highlighted serious quality concerns across the tested samples. Specifically, the analysis of edible oil and ghee revealed elevated levels of trans-fatty acids, peroxide value and free fatty acids, alongside non-compliance with requirements of Vitamin A fortification.
Similarly, the testing of milk samples indicated widespread non-compliance with prescribed quality standards, particularly showing lower protein and fat contents. The chair expressed serious concern over the degraded quality of essential food items, particularly in rural areas, and the severe health risks posed by such substandard commodities to the public.
To address the quality gaps, the chief (nutrition) suggested the formulation of a comprehensive national-level testing framework for essential food commodities, consisting of relevant stakeholders. It was further recommended that guidelines be established for mandatory quarterly testing of essential edibles, with the progress and findings regularly shared with the forum. Dr Mubarak Ali, Consultant (Food & Agriculture), also endorsed the proposal and further suggested that strict compliance measures may be taken.
Chief economist proposed that the Ministry of National Food Security and Research may convene a meeting with representatives of oil and ghee manufacturers, packaged milk producers, Ministry of Science and Technology and provincial governments to deliberate on the testing outcomes. He further suggested that the PCSIR may conduct random testing to validate the consistency of the results on a quarterly basis. After deliberations, the NPMC decided that the Ministry of National Food Security would hold a meeting with representatives of ghee, edible oil and milk producers/ associations to discuss the findings of PCSIR report and take corrective measures within 15 days.
It was also decided that the food ministry, in consultation with the Ministry of Commerce, Ministry of Industries and Production, Ministry of Science and Technology, provincial and regional food authorities, ICT administration and other stakeholders, would develop a comprehensive national framework for the regular quality assessment of edible oil, ghee, milk and other food-related commodities.
It agreed that the minister for petroleum, in consultation with Ogra, would address the prevailing discrepancy between the notified and actual market prices of LPG. Additionally, the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulation and Coordination shall look into the poor quality and high prices of drugs available in markets and submit a report to the NPMC.
The chief nutrition office was told to submit the findings and recommendations of the PCSIR report regarding the quality testing of ghee, oil and milk to the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC) for information and necessary directives.
